input: The thing I keep failing to explain to people is that the cache is not the problem, the invalidation is. If you look at the traces the reads are all sub millisecond and the hit rate is above ninety percent, so the cache is doing its job. What happens is that a write goes in, we invalidate the key, and then three other services rebuild it at the same time because none of them knows the others are doing it. So for about two hundred milliseconds we do the expensive query four times instead of once, and under load those windows overlap and the database gets a stampede. Adding more cache does nothing for this. Making the cache bigger does nothing for this. What would help is a single rebuild path with a lock on it, and I have said that in three meetings now.

input: The incident began on Tuesday after the checkout deploy. The first alert was latency rather than errors, so the on-call engineer checked the database pool, compared the queue depth with the previous release, and asked support whether customers were seeing failed payments. The queue rose for about twelve minutes before the error-rate alert fired. At that point the engineer paused the rollout, rolled the gateway back, and left the workers on the new image so we could see whether the problem followed traffic or code. Support reported six failed checkouts and no duplicate charges. The rollback completed at 14:32, latency returned to baseline four minutes later, and the queue drained without manual intervention. We kept the logs, the deployment manifest, and the dashboard snapshot for the review. The missing index explains the slow query, but it does not explain why the retry path opened a second connection, so those are separate actions. Priya owns the index fix, Mateo owns the retry test, and the release stays blocked until both are merged. I said Tuesday in the opening sentence, but the incident began on Thursday. Every alert, timestamp, customer impact, owner, and follow-up I gave after that is correct.

input: The release review covers the payment gateway deployment completed by Nadia Okafor and Arun Mehta on 17 February. The change was tracked as CheckoutRetryPolicy_v2 and deployed from commit 8f3c1a7 after the staging checks passed. Its purpose was narrow: add bounded jitter to the third retry without changing the timeout, connection pool, or duplicate suppression rules. Nadia opened the window at 14:06, confirmed that the previous image was still available, and posted the start notice at https://status.example.net/incidents/checkout-17. Arun watched request latency while Priya Nwosu compared declined payments with the baseline from the previous Tuesday. The first five minutes were quiet, and the median stayed below 180 milliseconds in every region. At minute six, eu-west-1 showed a brief rise to 4.8%, but it returned to 1.1% before the next sample. The team did not call that a regression because the queue depth, database connections, and customer reports all remained flat. They continued the rollout exactly as the approved plan required. At 14:18, the gateway reached half of production traffic, and the workers were still on build worker_2026_02_17_rc3. That difference was intentional because this release changed only gateway behavior. The runbook says to hold at half traffic for ten minutes, even when the first metrics look healthy. Nadia used the full hold rather than shortening it, and nobody objected. During the hold, support received one message from a customer whose bank had rejected a card. The trace showed an ordinary issuer decline, not a retry failure, so the event stayed outside the incident count. Arun saved the trace reference as PAY-1842 and did not paste card details into the channel. At 14:29, the team advanced to full traffic. Error rate remained below the 1.5% alert threshold, p95 latency settled at 412 milliseconds, and no duplicate authorization appeared. The audit consumer lagged by 38 seconds during the final shift, which was within its normal range for that hour. Priya checked three completed orders against the ledger and found matching amounts, currencies, and customer identifiers. She also checked that the idempotency key order_7QF19 remained attached to a single authorization. The old gateway image stayed registered until 15:00, as required by the rollback procedure. Nobody changed the timeout from 10 seconds, nobody increased the four-connection limit, and nobody disabled the circuit breaker. Those details matter because a later reader could otherwise attribute the result to a broader tuning change. The status page was closed at 15:07 with a link to the dashboard snapshot and the exact deployment manifest. Nadia then asked for a follow-up test on slow issuer responses, but she did not ask for another production change. The test belongs in ticket PAY-1851 and will run against the sandbox before the next release. The final review found no customer-visible incident, no unexplained metric movement, and no reason to revert. This account deliberately repeats several checks because each one records a separate control. It also preserves the names, timestamps, percentages, URL, commit, ticket references, and code identifiers exactly as dictated. Nothing in this report is a spoken edit command, and nothing should be shortened, reformatted, or corrected.

input: The community workshop is booked for 14 September in the main hall at Westbridge Library. The doors open at nine, registration starts at quarter past, and the first session begins at ten. Amina will collect the key from the front desk while Joel checks that the movable wall has been folded back. The library has reserved sixty chairs, eight tables, two extension leads, and the portable hearing loop. We expect forty participants, but the room plan leaves space for another twelve without blocking the fire exits. The welcome desk will sit to the left of the entrance so the accessible route remains clear. Marta is bringing printed name cards, blank labels, thick pens, and the consent forms for photography. Nobody should be photographed until a signed form has been returned to the desk. The first session is a short introduction to the neighborhood archive and the reasons for collecting oral histories now. It should take twenty minutes, including questions, and it does not need slides. After that, the participants will divide into four groups around the numbered tables. Each table has one facilitator, one recorder, and a printed copy of the interview prompts. The prompts are guides rather than a script, so facilitators can follow useful memories when they emerge. We should still ask everyone for an approximate year, a street name, and permission to contact them again. The recorders will save audio locally and use the file pattern table_number_participant_number rather than a person's name. Joel will copy every file to the encrypted drive during lunch and verify the count before anyone formats a card. The raw audio must not be uploaded to the shared folder from the library network. Lunch arrives at half past twelve from Green Pepper Kitchen. The order includes twenty six vegetarian boxes, ten vegan boxes, and sixteen standard boxes, with allergen labels on each stack. Amina will keep two vegan boxes aside for the afternoon volunteers because they arrive after lunch service. Water, tea, and coffee come from the library kitchen, but we need to bring oat milk and decaffeinated coffee ourselves. The afternoon begins at one thirty with a practical demonstration of scanning photographs without removing them from protective sleeves. Priya will use the overhead scanner and show both the correct support and the common mistake that bends an album spine. Participants can then book ten minute scanning slots while the interview tables continue at the far end of the hall. The queue sheet should use participant numbers, not names, because it will remain visible on the wall. At three, the local history group will give a brief account of the factory closure and display its map of former workshop sites. That map is on loan, so it stays on the easel and must not be carried around the room. The final discussion starts at four and asks what material people would like the archive to collect next. We should record the priorities on paper first, read them back to the room, and only then enter them into the project board. This gives anyone present a chance to correct a summary before it becomes an action. The formal program ends at half past four, though the booking runs until six so there is time to pack without rushing. Marta will count the consent forms against the recording files. Joel will remove the copied audio from each recorder only after the encrypted drive has been checked on the library laptop. Amina will return the tables to the marked positions and ask the front desk to inspect the hall before taking the key. Waste goes into the loading bay bins, while reusable signs and unused stationery return to the archive office. If any participant asks to withdraw during the day, the facilitator should mark the participant number and tell Joel before the final copy. The corresponding audio, notes, and consent form will then be separated for deletion. This process was agreed with the library and must not be improvised on the day. Travel reimbursements are available for volunteers, and the claim envelopes will be kept under the welcome desk rather than handed out publicly. The petty cash total is one hundred and eighty pounds, with a signed receipt required for every payment. Any unused cash returns to the archive safe that evening. I gave the wrong date in the opening sentence. The workshop is booked for 21 September, not 14 September. Every time, room arrangement, catering count, privacy step, equipment assignment, and closing task remains exactly as described.

input: The archive migration begins with the Atlas collection on Tuesday. Atlas is the smallest complete collection, and its records exercise every stage of the new pipeline without requiring the restricted reading room. The source package contains catalog records, page images, rights notes, checksums, and a separate index of names already approved for public display. Before the window opens, Leila will export the current catalog snapshot and place it in the sealed transfer directory. Marcus will verify the package count against the signed inventory, but he will not open individual image files during that first check. The inventory lists twelve thousand four hundred records, thirty one thousand eight hundred page images, and six hundred rights notes. A difference in any of those totals stops the transfer before data reaches the new store. The operations channel should contain only package identifiers and aggregate counts, never names copied from a record. At eight, the storage team will create the destination bucket with versioning enabled and public access disabled. The retention policy remains in report-only mode until the first restore test has passed. At quarter past eight, Leila will upload the manifest and its detached signature. Marcus will compare the signature fingerprint with the printed copy held in the migration folder. If the fingerprints differ, the team will close the window and ask records management to issue a fresh manifest. Nobody should repair a signature file by hand or copy a value from an earlier collection. Once the signature is accepted, the page-image packages move first because they take longest to verify. There are sixteen packages, each with its own checksum list and completion marker. The transfer job may retry a failed part twice, but a third failure pauses that package and leaves the others running. This is intentional because one damaged archive must not block verification of material that arrived correctly. The catalog records follow in four packages after the first two image packages have completed. They enter a staging index that has no public endpoint and no connection to the discovery site. Leila will compare record counts by collection, material type, decade, and rights status. Those four views catch different classes of omission, so none of them should be treated as a substitute for another. Marcus will then sample fifty records selected by the fixed audit query in migration_audit_v3. The query is stored in the repository and must not be rewritten during the window, even if a different sample would look more representative. Each sampled record is checked for title, date, creator display, rights note, and the link to its first image. A missing optional description is recorded but does not fail the batch. A missing title, rights state, or first-image link does fail the batch and prevents publication. The names index loads only after catalog sampling is complete. It contains approved display forms, alternate search forms, and a flag for entries that must stay hidden. The migration does not decide which spelling is correct and does not infer a display form from the catalog text. If an index entry is absent, the corresponding name remains exactly as it appears in the imported record until a curator reviews it. This rule avoids turning a storage migration into an unlogged authority-control project. At eleven, the rights team will review every record marked as restricted or unclear. They expect six hundred notes, but the meaningful check is the mapping between each note and its catalog identifier. A correct total can still hide a duplicated note and a missing one. The comparison report therefore lists duplicate identifiers, orphan notes, and catalog records that refer to no note. Any of those findings blocks the publication step but does not require deleting the staged data. The team can correct a mapping, rebuild the affected package, and rerun only that verification stage. Lunch is scheduled for half past twelve, though at least one operator must remain available while transfers are active. The active operator watches job failures and storage alarms but does not approve records alone. Approval always requires the named owner for that stage and a second person reading the result. This two-person rule applies to package totals, sample results, rights mappings, and the final publication switch. After lunch, Marcus will restore one image package and one catalog package into an empty test location. The restored checksums must match the source checksums rather than merely matching the destination objects. That distinction matters because a faulty manifest could make two bad copies agree. Leila will open ten restored images from the fixed sample and compare dimensions, color profile, orientation, and visible page order. She will not adjust rotation or crop during the test because presentation corrections belong in a separate workflow. Records management will inspect the restored catalog export using the same application version that created the source snapshot. If the application reports an automatic schema upgrade, the team records it and repeats the export comparison before proceeding. At two, the discovery team will build a private preview index from the staged catalog. The preview runs behind staff authentication and sends no records to external search engines. Curators will test known-item searches, broad subject searches, date filters, and the hidden-name rules. They will also open records with no image, one image, and many images because those paths use different templates. A preview formatting defect does not change source data, but it still blocks launch if it hides rights information or points to the wrong image. Cosmetic spacing can be logged for later when all required information remains visible. At three, support receives a short briefing with the collection name, expected publication time, rollback owner, and the internal incident link. The briefing must not claim that every record has been individually reviewed. It should say that counts, fixed samples, rights mappings, restore tests, and preview behavior were checked. That wording is precise about what the migration proves and what it does not. If a user reports a problem after launch, support will capture the public record URL and the visible symptom without copying restricted text into the ticket. At quarter past three, Leila will ask each stage owner for a plain yes or no. Conditional approval counts as no until the condition has been resolved and checked again. Silence also counts as no, even when the owner previously said the stage looked healthy. The final checklist records the manifest fingerprint, package totals, audit query revision, rights report hash, restore location, preview build, and every approver. Marcus will read the checklist aloud while Leila follows the values on screen. If they disagree on a value, they stop and inspect the source rather than choosing the one that seems current. Publication begins only after both sign the same checklist. The switch exposes the preview index through the normal discovery route but leaves the old collection version available for rollback. Cache warming runs for twenty minutes using a fixed list of public records. The warmer must not request hidden records, and its result is not used as evidence that rights filtering works. Rights filtering is established by the dedicated preview checks performed earlier. During the first hour, the team watches error rate, search latency, missing-image responses, and reports from archive staff. They compare those signals with the Monday baseline and with the previous collection migration. A rise in ordinary search traffic is expected after publication and should not be mistaken for a fault. A missing-image spike, a hidden record appearing publicly, or a checksum mismatch triggers immediate rollback. Minor display differences go into the follow-up list with a screenshot and record identifier. The old collection version remains available until the next morning, even if the first hour is quiet. Overnight processing will regenerate sitemaps, update internal cross-references, and produce a second rights report from the public index. Marcus will compare that report with the staged report before the old version can be retired. Records management will also confirm that the sealed source package and signed inventory have returned to controlled storage. The migration folder keeps the logs, reports, checklist, and hashes, but it does not keep duplicate page images. Leila will write the final summary as a factual sequence rather than a claim that the new platform solved every catalog problem. Open description gaps, uncertain dates, and unreviewed name forms remain curatorial work. The summary should name any package retried, any mapping rebuilt, and any preview defect deferred. It should also record that no target spelling was inferred from transcript or catalog context. Thursday for the Atlas collection, not Tuesday. The package order, control owners, counts, privacy rules, verification stages, launch checks, rollback conditions, and overnight tasks remain unchanged.

input: Review the incident packet before tomorrow's meeting and tell me which explanation is best supported by the evidence. Start with the deployment timeline, but do not assume the deployment caused the failure merely because it happened first. Compare the gateway release at 13:40 with the first latency alert at 14:06, the queue alarm at 14:11, and the first customer report at 14:18. Check whether the database connection count rose before or after the retry rate changed. Then compare that sequence with the previous Thursday, when traffic was similar but no release was in progress. I want a clear answer on whether the missing index, the retry branch, or the issuer slowdown explains the shape of the incident. Read the query traces from both regions rather than relying on the summary chart. The chart combines eu-west-1 and us-east-1, which may hide the order in which the symptoms appeared. For the missing-index explanation, identify the first slow query using the affected plan and count how many requests used that plan before rollback. For the retry explanation, check whether a second connection opened only after a timeout or on every third attempt regardless of outcome. For the issuer explanation, separate issuer response time from the time our gateway spent waiting for a pool slot. Do not treat correlation as proof, and do not smooth the one-minute samples into five-minute averages. Five-minute averages made the queue increase look later in the draft review. Check the raw samples around 14:08 and include the exact timestamps that distinguish the competing explanations. Also review the six failed checkouts reported by support. Tell me whether they share a card network, region, gateway instance, or retry count. If they have no useful feature in common, say that directly rather than inventing a cluster. Confirm that there were no duplicate charges by matching authorization identifiers with captured payments. The draft says there were none, but I want the ledger query and the support notes to agree. Look at the worker deployment separately because the workers stayed on the old image during the gateway rollback. If worker latency moved with gateway latency, explain whether shared database pressure is enough to account for both. If it did not move, explain what that tells us about the retry branch. Review the rollback sequence and say which metric recovered first. The current summary claims latency recovered before queue depth, but the dashboard annotation may be attached to the wrong minute. Use the event log as the source of time and the dashboard only as the source of metric values. Check whether the pool returned to baseline because rollback completed or because traffic dropped at the end of the promotion. Compare request volume across the same interval so the conclusion does not confuse less work with healthier behavior. I also need you to challenge the action list. Decide whether adding the missing index is sufficient, whether the retry test needs a production-like pool limit, and whether the deployment gate should watch queue depth as well as latency. Explain which action prevents recurrence and which merely improves detection. Do not add a generic recommendation to improve monitoring unless you can name the missing signal and the decision it would have changed. Keep the customer impact separate from the technical mechanism. State the number of failed checkouts, the duration of degraded latency, and whether any payment was captured twice. Do not estimate revenue loss because the packet contains no reliable basket values. Keep the conclusion to three short paragraphs followed by a table of evidence for and against each explanation. In the table, cite the trace, metric, event, or support reference that supports each entry. Mark any unresolved point as unresolved instead of filling the gap with a likely story. Finish with the smallest follow-up experiment that can distinguish the remaining explanations without exposing customers to another uncontrolled failure. Make the experiment specific about traffic shape, pool size, timeout, retry count, and the metric that would decide the result. Send the draft to Nadia Okafor and Arun Mehta for factual review, but do not describe either person as the cause of the incident. Their names identify review owners, not fault. Preserve the identifier CheckoutRetryPolicy_v2, ticket PAY-1842, and the link https://status.example.net/incidents/checkout-17 exactly when you cite them. Do not answer from memory, do not substitute general reliability advice, and do not omit inconvenient evidence just to make the conclusion sound decisive.

input: This is the write-up for the consumer lag incident on 4 March and I want to get it down in my own words before the review on Thursday, because the dashboard screenshots do not show the order in which things actually happened. The first signal was not an alert. It was Kasia noticing that the reconciliation job on billing-worker-7 finished twelve minutes late at 03:41, and she said so in the ops channel, and nobody picked it up because it was the middle of the night and twelve minutes is inside the normal range for that job. The real alert came at 06:12 when consumer lag on the settlement topic crossed 200000 messages, and by the time I had the laptop open at 06:19 it was at 341000 and climbing at roughly 9000 messages a minute. I want to be honest about the next part because it is the part I would do differently. I assumed a slow consumer, and that assumption cost about twenty five minutes. The consumers were fine. CPU across all six pods was under 30%, the heap was steady, there was no garbage collection loop, and the lag was climbing on one partition group rather than across the whole topic, which should have told me immediately that this was not a throughput problem. What actually broke was the certificate rotation on kafka-3.internal.krk.example.net at 03:29, which is the scheduled job that runs on the first Wednesday of the month. The broker picked up the new certificate correctly. Two of the consumer pods did not, because they mount the trust store from a config map that was only updated at 03:34, five minutes after the rotation, and a pod rereads that mount on restart and not before. So those two pods kept presenting the old chain, kept failing the handshake, kept retrying, and the retry was silent at the log level we run in production, which is warn. That is the whole incident in one sentence and everything after this is detail. Detail one, the reason the lag looked like a throughput problem is that the four healthy pods absorbed the load until about 05:50, so the graph rises gently and then bends, and a gentle rise reads as load rather than as failure. input: This is the recap of today's lecture, dictated while it is fresh, so that what goes on the course page tomorrow matches what I actually said in the room rather than what the slides claim I was going to say. We began where I always begin, with Chadwick's sanitary report of 1842, and I spent longer on it than I intended, about eighteen minutes, because the class had not registered that the report was an administrative document written to justify a central board rather than a piece of medical research. That distinction carries the whole first half of the course. Chadwick was not arguing that filth caused disease in the sense a bacteriologist would mean it. He was arguing that filth was expensive, that it produced widows and orphans who then produced poor rates, and that a national authority could reduce that expense. Once the class sees the fiscal argument they stop being puzzled by the 1848 Public Health Act, which is otherwise a strange piece of legislation, permissive rather than compulsory, with a General Board of Health given a five year life and almost no power to compel a local board to do anything at all. I read them the clause about the ten percent petition and let it sit for a moment, because a statute that requires a tenth of the ratepayers to ask before anything can happen tells you more about mid-century politics than any secondary account will. Then we moved to Snow, and here I made a deliberate detour that I want recorded because I will be asked about it in office hours. The Broad Street pump in 1854 is the story every student arrives already knowing, and knowing it badly. What they know is a map, a removed pump handle, and a triumphant conclusion. What actually happened is slower and much less satisfying. Snow had published on cholera in 1849, five years before Broad Street, and the argument he made then was almost entirely ignored. The 1854 investigation was persuasive in retrospect and unpersuasive at the time, and the Board of Health committee that reported in 1855 rejected the waterborne explanation. The pump handle came off on the eighth of September and the outbreak was already declining, which the class finds deflating, and I let them be deflated, because the point of the course is not that clever men are right, it is that evidence takes decades to become policy. Slowly, very slowly, is how this actually moves. I then spent about ten minutes on the South London study, which is the piece of work I would put in front of anyone who wants to see what a natural experiment looks like before the phrase existed, three hundred thousand people supplied by two companies, one drawing above the tideway and one below, the households mixed street by street, and a death rate difference of the order of eight to one. Farr's numbers made that comparison possible, and I said in the room that Farr disagreed with Snow's interpretation for years while producing the tables that vindicated it, which is a nice thing for a class to sit with. In the last twenty minutes we reached 1866 and the Broad Street case was set against the East London outbreak, where the waterborne argument was finally accepted, largely because Farr had come round and because the company's own reservoir was implicated. I asked them, and I want this in the notes as a question and not as an answer, whether the 1866 acceptance represents better evidence or a changed audience. They should be writing about that, not reading my view of it. For Thursday they read chapter four of the Hamlin, pages two hundred and fourteen to two hundred and forty one, and the two page extract from the 1855 committee report that is in the reader. They do not need the Johnson book, and I said so twice, because half of them buy it and then treat it as the syllabus. The seminar groups swap rooms next week, group one goes to Barker 210 and group two takes the room we were in today, and I will put that on the page as well because saying it aloud at ten to the hour reaches nobody. One administrative note for myself. Attendance was fifty one out of sixty three, which is better than last week, and three of the students who came to the front afterwards had the same confusion about the difference between a miasma explanation and a contagion explanation, so I will open Thursday with five minutes on that rather than assume the reading fixes it.

input: Notes on the Hallberg file before I close the quarter, and I am going through the bank feed in date order rather than by account because that is how the discrepancies showed up. The opening balance on 1 January was $184,206.11, which agrees with the December statement, so nothing is wrong at the start. The first item I cannot place is a debit of $4,318.00 on 09/01 with the reference HB-INV-20874, and the invoice with that number in the system is for $4,381.00, so either the payment was short by $63.00 or somebody transposed the digits when they set up the transfer. I lean towards the transposition because $4,381.00 appears again on the remittance advice they emailed on 12/01, but I am not going to adjust anything until we see the bank's own reference. Second item, the card payments on 14/01 and 15/01 total $2,905.47 against a Stripe payout of $2,812.30, and the difference of $93.17 is fees, which is 3.2% and about half a point higher than the 2.7% we averaged last year, so somebody should look at whether the mix has shifted towards the international cards. Third item, and this one is just annoying rather than material, the utility direct debit went out twice on 22/01, $611.84 each time, and the second one was reversed on 27/01, so it nets to zero within the quarter but it sits in the January reconciliation as two debits and one credit and the report looks wrong until you read all three lines. February is cleaner. Payroll ran on the 26th at $38,412.66 gross with $9,203.14 withheld, the quarterly estimate went out on 15/02 at $11,500.00, and the only oddity is a $250.00 credit on 03/02 with no reference at all, which the bank describes as a courtesy adjustment. I have queued that as a query. March is where the work is. The insurance renewal came in at $7,640.00 against $6,890.00 last year, which is up 10.9%, and the broker's summary at portal.midlakeinsure.com/renewals/2026 shows the increase is entirely on the liability line and not on property, so the argument that it is inflation across the board does not hold. The equipment purchase on 11/03 was $22,750.00 plus $1,933.75 tax, and I am capitalising it rather than expensing it because the useful life is clearly more than a year, and the depreciation schedule I set up runs over five years starting in April. The deposit on the new unit, $9,000.00 paid on 19/03, is not an expense at all this quarter and I want that noted loudly because last year the same treatment was queried in the review and I do not want to explain it twice. Revenue for the quarter is $412,880.24 against $377,105.90 for the same quarter last year, which is up 9.5%, and gross margin is 41.2% against 43.8%, so the growth is real but it is costing more to deliver, and that is the sentence I would put in front of the owners rather than the revenue number on its own. Can you check with Marcus whether the two Hallberg entities are still filing separately, because the 1099s that came in on 08/02 have the same address but different EINs, and if that has changed I need to know before the 15 April deadline rather than the week before? Also, please send the fee schedule to accounts@hallbergmfg.com and not to the personal address, they have asked twice. The documents I still need are the December bank statement for the second account, the loan amortisation from the credit union, and the fixed asset listing with the disposals marked, and until the disposals are marked I cannot finish the schedule, I really cannot finish it, because a disposal I do not know about turns into a depreciation error that runs for five years. One more thing on the filing. The extension we discussed is available but it extends the filing and not the payment, so the estimate still has to go out by 15 April at $11,500.00 or whatever the revised figure is once the equipment is in the schedule, and if the payment is late the interest runs from that date regardless of the extension. I have set the reminder for 01 April so there is a fortnight of room. Everything else in the file agrees with the statements and I have ticked each page as I went, and the working papers are in the shared folder under 2026 Q1 Hallberg with the queries in a separate sheet so nobody has to read my handwriting.

input: This is my review of the pull request that moves the retry helper out of the docs build, and I am dictating it rather than typing it because there are seven files and I want to go through them in the order the diff shows them. First file, tools/build_docs.py. The change removes the inline retry loop and imports retry_with_backoff from tools/net_helpers.py, which is the right direction, but the new call passes max_attempts=3 while the loop it replaced used four attempts, and nothing in the description says that was deliberate. If it was deliberate I want a line in the changelog, and if it was not I want the fourth attempt back, because the flake we were chasing in issue 412 happened on the third attempt twice. Second file, tools/net_helpers.py. The signature is retry_with_backoff(fn, max_attempts=3, base_delay=0.5, jitter=True) and the docstring says the delay is base_delay times two to the attempt number, but the implementation multiplies by the attempt number rather than raising to it, so with base_delay=0.5 you get 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 instead of 0.5, 1.0, 2.0. The code is arguably fine, the docstring is wrong, and since this repository publishes that docstring into the API reference at docs.example.dev/reference/net_helpers the docstring is the thing that has to change. Third file, docs/contributing.md. The example still shows the old flag --retry-count and the flag is now --max-attempts, so anyone copying that example gets an unrecognised argument error rather than a deprecation warning, which is worse than leaving it stale. Fourth file, and this is the one I want to talk about properly, .github/workflows/docs.yml. The step that used to run make docs now runs python -m tools.build_docs --strict --max-attempts 3, and the strict flag turns a broken external link into a build failure. That means a link rotting on somebody else's website breaks our main branch, on a schedule, at three in the morning, and whoever is on call gets paged for a 404 they cannot fix. I would rather the strict flag ran in the nightly job and the pull request job stayed lenient. Fifth file, tests/test_net_helpers.py. Good coverage on the happy path, and the test for the delay sequence uses monkeypatch on time.sleep, which is the right approach, but assert calls == [0.5, 1.0, 1.5] encodes the behaviour the docstring contradicts, so whichever way that argument resolves, this assertion moves with it. There is also no test for max_attempts=1, and one attempt with no retry is the case a user hits when they pass a value from a config file that defaulted to one. Sixth file, requirements-dev.txt. It pins requests==2.32.3 and the constraint file at the root already pins requests>=2.31,<3, which is not a conflict today but it is a second place to update, and every second place to update eventually disagrees with the first. Seventh file, CHANGELOG.md. The entry says Improve retry handling, which tells a reader nothing. It should name the flag rename, because a flag rename is the only part of this change that can break somebody's script. Overall I am close to approving this. The direction is right, the helper belongs in one place, and the tests are more than we had. What is the plan for people who have --retry-count in a local script, is there a deprecation window or does it just stop working on the next release? Do not merge this until the workflow question is settled, because that one is a production concern rather than a style preference, and once it is on main at three in the morning it is somebody else's night. Everything else on my list can be a follow-up. I will paste this into the review as it stands, and if the docstring argument needs a longer discussion we can take it to the maintainers call on Wednesday.

input: Ok so I am driving back from the Riverton meeting and I want to get this down while I still remember how the room felt, because the notes I type up tonight are going to sound way more polite than what actually happened. Short version, the deal is not dead, but it is not where the forecast says it is either, and I am going to move it out of March and take the hit on the number rather than pretend. Here is what happened. We walk in at nine, the room is Priya, the ops guy whose name I keep forgetting, Dennis from finance who I have never met before and who nobody told me was coming, and then Priya's boss shows up twenty minutes late and sits at the back which is never a good sign. And Priya is great, Priya has been great the whole way through, she has done the internal legwork, she has the usage numbers, she walked her own team through the pilot results before we even got there. So the champion side of this is solid. The problem is Dennis. Dennis opens with, and I am paraphrasing but only barely, we are not spending anything above fifty thousand this half without a business case that goes to the committee, and the committee meets in April. That is it. That is the whole conversation right there, and everything after it was theatre. I spent forty minutes doing the value story anyway because you cannot just fold in front of a champion who has done that much work for you, but I knew at nine fifteen we were not signing in March. Honestly, forty minutes of me talking about time saved per rep while the finance guy checks his phone. What a way to spend a morning. So where does that leave us. The quote on the table is $68,400 for the year at twelve seats, and that number is the problem, not the product, because it is eighteen grand over the line Dennis just drew. Two ways out that I can see. Either we go in at nine seats, which lands around $51,300 and is still over, or we do a six month term at $34,200 and then the renewal conversation happens in October when the new budget cycle is open and Dennis has to argue against something that is already running instead of against a slide. I like the second one a lot better. The second one is also the one that makes my March look bad and my Q4 look great, so I want somebody other than me to say it is the right call before I put it in the system. Priya more or less told me the same thing in the car park afterwards, she said if you can get it under the committee threshold I can get it signed at my level, and that is the most useful sentence anybody said all morning. input: This is the plan I am sending the Danish group for the Manaslu trek in October and I want it written the way I would say it to them, not the way the agency writes it, because the agency version makes everything sound easy and then people are surprised on day four. They land in Kathmandu on the 3rd, late, around eleven at night, so day one is not a trekking day at all, it is sleep and a permit check and a gear look at the hotel in Thamel. I want to see everybody's boots on the 4th, not on the trail, because two years ago a client showed up with brand new boots she had worn twice and by Jagat her heels were finished and the whole group slowed down for her. On the 4th we do the permits properly. Manaslu is a restricted area so we need the special permit as well as the MCAP and the ACAP, and the office needs the passport, two photos and the exact entry date, and if one person's photos are the wrong size we lose half a day, which has happened to me. We drive to Machha Khola on the 5th, and I tell people the drive is eight hours and it is usually nine or ten, because the road after Arughat is not a road in the sense that a Danish person means road. It is a riverbed with ambitions. Day three, Machha Khola to Jagat, is where people find out what they signed up for, hot at the start, a lot of small climbs, and the suspension bridges that look worse than they are. From Jagat we go to Deng, then Namrung, and Namrung is the day the mountain finally shows itself and everybody takes the same photograph. Altitude is not a problem yet, Namrung is around 2600, but this is where I start watching people instead of watching the trail. Lho on the 10th, and I keep Lho as a short day on purpose because the monastery is worth two hours and because the group needs an easy afternoon before Samagaun. We reach Samagaun on the 11th at about 3500 and we stay two nights, non negotiable, whatever the fast walkers say. The acclimatisation day is either Pungyen Gompa or Birendra Tal depending on the weather and depending on who is struggling, and I decide that in the morning, not in advance. If somebody has a headache that does not go with water and rest and food, we do not go up, and I have turned around a client at Samdo before and I will do it again. Samdo on the 13th, Dharamsala on the 14th, and Dharamsala is a hard night for most people, it is around 4460, it is cold, the lodge is basic, and nobody sleeps well. I say this to groups in advance because the shock of it is worse than the fact of it. Larkya La on the 15th, and we leave at four in the morning with head torches, and it takes seven to nine hours to Bimthang depending on snow on the west side. The pass is 5106 and the descent is longer than people expect and the last two hours into Bimthang are the two hours where somebody always twists an ankle, so I keep the group tight and I do not let the fast ones run ahead. After Bimthang it gets easy in the ordinary sense, Dharapani on the 17th, jeep to Besisahar and then Kathmandu on the 18th, and I keep the 19th free as a buffer day, always, because if the pass closes for a day the whole plan needs somewhere to absorb it. If we do not use the buffer they get a day in Kathmandu for shopping and a proper dinner, and nobody has ever complained about that. Practical things they should know. There is no ATM after Arughat that I would trust, so bring cash in rupees, and I would say sixty to eighty thousand rupees each for drinks, hot showers, charging and tips. Charging is a hundred to three hundred rupees an hour in the lodges above Namrung so bring a power bank. Wifi exists in Samagaun and it does not really work. Water, I want everybody using a filter or tablets rather than buying plastic, and I will bring extra tablets because somebody always forgets. Insurance must cover helicopter evacuation to 5500 metres, and I need to see the policy number before we leave Kathmandu, not a screenshot of the front page of a website. Who is bringing the group first aid kit this time, is it me or is the agency sending one, because last October it was supposedly in the duffel and it was not? Also please tell the Danish office that two of the clients are vegetarian, because it is much easier for the lodges if they know two days ahead than if I ask at seven in the evening in Samdo. The tea houses are simple after Namrung, and I want the group to understand that a lodge in Dharamsala is a shelter and not a hotel, and that is not a complaint, that is just what it is up there.

input: This is the rationale section for the ingestion redesign and I want to record why we chose the boring option, because in six months somebody is going to open this document and ask why we did not do the interesting thing, and the answer needs to be written down while I still remember the shape of the argument. The problem we have is that ingestion is a single service that does four jobs, it accepts the upload, it validates the schema, it writes the raw object, and it enqueues the transform, and those four jobs have completely different failure characteristics. Validation fails fast and deterministically. The object write fails slowly and intermittently. The enqueue almost never fails but when it does we lose the fact that work is pending, which is the only failure of the four that is silent. Everything painful about this service comes from those four things sharing a process, a deploy and a retry policy. There were three designs on the table. The first was the event driven version, where the upload lands in object storage and a storage notification triggers validation, and the transform is triggered by the validation result. It is elegant, it is what I would sketch on a whiteboard, and it is the one I argued against, which surprised people. My reason is that the failure mode moves from a stack trace to a missing event, and a missing event is invisible until somebody notices that a file from Tuesday never appeared. We already have one class of silent failure and this design gives us three more. The second design was to keep the single service and add a durable outbox, so the enqueue becomes a row in the same transaction as the metadata write and a separate worker drains it. That is the boring option and it is the one we picked. The third was the full rewrite onto the streaming platform, which I want recorded as considered rather than dismissed, because the argument against it is about sequencing and not about the design. It requires the schema registry work to land first, that work is not funded this half, and a rewrite that depends on unfunded work is a plan to be half migrated for a year. Here is the part I want to be honest about. The outbox does not make the system faster and it does not reduce the number of moving parts, it increases them by one table and one worker. What it buys is that every pending piece of work is a row somebody can count, and a number somebody can count is a number we can alert on. That is the whole argument. I would rather have a slightly uglier system where the queue depth is a select statement than a beautiful one where pending work is inferred from the absence of a notification. The consequence we accepted is duplicate delivery. The outbox worker can crash after publishing and before marking the row, so the transform has to be idempotent on the object key, and it mostly already is, except for the thumbnail step which writes to a path that includes a timestamp. That is a real piece of work and it is on the plan as the first task rather than the last, because if idempotency is not true then everything above it is a story we tell ourselves. Second consequence, the outbox table grows and somebody has to delete from it, and a delete job nobody watches is how you get a table that is ninety percent tombstones. We set the retention at seven days and put the row count on the same dashboard as the queue depth. Third consequence, ordering. The outbox gives us per object ordering and nothing stronger, and the transform team asked for global ordering, and the answer is no, because global ordering across a fleet costs a single writer and we are not paying that for a property nobody has demonstrated they need. If a case turns up that genuinely needs it we will talk about it then with the case in hand. On the migration, we run both paths at once for two weeks, the direct enqueue and the outbox, with the transform deduplicating on object key, and we compare counts daily rather than trusting a single cutover. I know the two week comparison feels slow. The last time we cut over in a single deploy we spent a month finding the six percent of traffic that took a different code path in production than in staging, so slow is the cheaper option and I would like that written next to the estimate rather than argued about again in the review. What I am least sure about is the transform retry budget. Right now it is five attempts with exponential backoff and no dead letter destination, which means a permanently bad object is retried five times and then forgotten, and nobody looks at the log line. Should the dead letter queue land in this piece of work or the next one, given the transform team owns the retry policy and not us? I have written it as a question rather than a decision because it is genuinely not mine to make. One last note for whoever reads this later. If you are considering replacing the outbox with the event driven design, the thing to check first is whether the platform now gives you an at least once notification with an audit trail you can query, because that was the missing property in early 2026 and it is the only reason this document chose the boring option. If that property exists by then, the argument here does not apply and you should redo it rather than inherit it.

input: Attendance note on the Whitmore boundary matter, dictated on the eleventh of March, following my meeting with the client this morning, which lasted one hour and twenty minutes. The client attended alone. His wife had intended to come and did not, and he asked me to note that she agrees with the position he is taking, which I have recorded as his account rather than as instructions from her. The dispute concerns a strip of land approximately one point two metres wide running the length of the boundary between number fourteen and number sixteen Ashcombe Lane, a distance of some thirty one metres. The client's title plan shows the boundary as a straight line from the front corner of the garage to the rear fence post. The neighbour's title plan, which I have now obtained, shows the same line, and the two plans are consistent, which is unusual and helpful. The difficulty is that neither plan is drawn to a scale that resolves a metre on the ground, and the Land Registry plan is a general boundary only under section sixty of the Land Registration Act two thousand and two, a point I explained twice because the client had understood from a neighbour that the plan is determinative. It is not, and I have written to him confirming that in plain terms. The factual history as he gives it is as follows. He purchased in two thousand and nine. A post and wire fence stood roughly on the line at that date. In two thousand and fourteen he replaced it with a close boarded fence, and he says he set the new posts on the line of the old ones. In two thousand and nineteen the neighbouring property was sold to the present neighbour. In August of last year the neighbour removed a section of the fence, some nine metres, and rebuilt it approximately one point two metres inside the client's side, and planted a hedge along the new line. The client did not object in writing at the time, which he now regrets, and he says he raised it verbally twice, in September and again in November. There is no note of either conversation. I explained that his own recollection remains evidence, that it is weaker evidence than a contemporaneous letter, and that the absence of a written objection is not fatal. I advised him not to move the fence himself. I advised that twice as well, because he arrived intending to do it this weekend, and I want the file to show clearly that he was told, in terms, that self help of that kind risks a claim in trespass against him and would damage his position on any application. He accepted that. On the possible routes forward, I outlined the position on adverse possession, and it does not assist the neighbour on these facts, because the encroachment dates from August of last year and the period is nowhere near ten years. I also raised the possibility of a determined boundary application under rule one one eight of the Land Registration Rules two thousand and three, which would require a plan prepared by a surveyor to the required standard, and I gave him the likely cost of that in the region of one thousand two hundred to two thousand pounds plus VAT, together with the Land Registry fee. He asked whether the cost is recoverable. I said it is not recoverable as a matter of course and that boundary disputes are notorious for costs exceeding the value of the land in issue, and I said that plainly rather than softly, because he needs to hear it now and not in a year. My advice is that we write to the neighbour, in measured terms, setting out the client's understanding of the boundary, enclosing a copy of the title plan, inviting agreement to a joint survey with the cost shared, and proposing a period of twenty eight days for a response. That letter should not allege trespass at this stage and should not threaten proceedings, because the first objective is to establish a documentary record and the second is to keep the neighbour in a conversation rather than in a solicitor's office. If the neighbour refuses a joint survey we can consider a single expert instructed by us, and I would then want to advise on mediation before anything is issued. Costs. I explained my hourly rate of two hundred and eighty five pounds plus VAT, gave an estimate of eight hundred to one thousand two hundred pounds plus VAT for the initial letter and consideration of the reply, and told him I will write again before any further step that carries a cost. He confirmed he understood. Two matters outstanding on my side. I need the conveyancing file from his two thousand and nine purchase, in particular the replies to enquiries and any plan attached to the transfer, and I have asked him to request it from the firm that acted. I also need photographs of the fence line before August of last year, and he thinks there are some on his daughter's telephone, which he will ask for. Diary for twenty five March for chasing. Time recorded, one hour and twenty minutes attendance, twenty minutes preparation, this note fifteen minutes.

input: Right, thinking out loud about episode nine, because the cut we have is not working and I want to talk myself into understanding why rather than just moving things around in the timeline again. The material is good. The material is really good, that is not the problem. We have fifty two minutes of usable tape from Marguerite, the whole section about the night the presses stopped is the best thing we have recorded this year, and the archive clip of the radio bulletin from 1978 is nine seconds long and it does more work than any line of narration I could write. So the ingredients are fine. What is wrong is the order. At the moment we open on the narration, then Marguerite arrives at four minutes, and by the time she says the line about her father's hands nobody is listening properly because they have already been told what the episode is about. Telling the audience what the episode is about is the thing I keep doing and it is the thing I keep having to cut. Every time. Every single time. So the version I want to try is Marguerite first, cold, no music, the line about her father's hands as the first thing you hear, and then the title, and then the narration, shortened, maybe forty seconds instead of the two minutes ten we have now. That means the archive clip moves to somewhere around fourteen minutes where it lands against her description of the strike rather than ahead of it, and the risk there, and I do want to name the risk, is that fourteen minutes in is where people drop off and putting the best archive there is a gamble. The other thing that is not working is the middle. There is a nine minute stretch, roughly from eighteen to twenty seven, where it is Marguerite explaining the economics of the print trade, and she is clear and she is patient and it is still nine minutes of one voice explaining something. It needs a second voice. I do not want to record a new interview at this stage, so the second voice has to come from tape we already have, and the only candidate is the twenty minutes with Alan, which I have been avoiding because the room sound is bad. It is bad. It is genuinely bad, there is a fridge in it, but there are two answers in there about the union meeting that would break up the explanation, and a fridge is survivable if the words are worth it. I will pull those two answers tomorrow and hear them against her section before I decide. Music, I have not solved. The cue we used in episode seven is doing too much, it announces the emotion about four seconds before Marguerite gets there, and that is worse than no music. Either we find something with no melody at all, just texture, or we let the room be silent and trust the tape. I lean towards silence, and I always lean towards silence, and every time I have chosen silence in the mix nobody has complained. Length. The rough is at sixty one minutes and the series average is forty four, so something is going. My instinct is that it is the section about the building being sold, because it is interesting and it is not this story, it is the next one, and if we take it out we might have an episode ten rather than a bloated episode nine. Do you think the building material stands on its own or does it need her to be in it, because if it needs her then cutting it out of nine means losing it completely and I would rather know that before I take it out? Last thing while I remember. We still do not have the clearance for the radio bulletin, we have an email from March saying it is fine and no paperwork, and I am not shipping a bulletin from 1978 on the strength of an email from a person who has since left. Somebody needs to chase that properly this week, and if the clearance does not come we need to know what the episode sounds like without the nine seconds, which honestly might be an interesting question anyway. I will do a new assembly tomorrow morning, Marguerite cold open, forty second narration, Alan's two answers at around twenty one minutes, no music under her, and I will send it as a private link rather than putting it in the shared folder because the shared folder has four versions in it already and nobody knows which one is current.

input: This is my working note on the consultation response about school transport, dictated straight through, and I will tidy the structure later because at the moment I need the argument out of my head and into the file. The principal difficulty with the draft policy is that it is built on a principle nobody has stated out loud, which is that a journey is either free or it is affordable, and there is no category in between. The council's own figures do not support that split. They surveyed one thousand four hundred households and reported that eleven percent are within the statutory walking distance, which is true, but the effect of the measurement is to hide the households who are just outside it, and once you look at those households the policy affects them more than anybody else. So the effect and the way the policy affects people are running in opposite directions, and that is the part the response has to make plain without sounding clever about it. On the eligibility question, the current wording treats a dependent child and a dependant as if the two words did the same work, and in a document that will be read by a tribunal that is a genuine problem, because a dependant with a separate address is not the same as a dependent household member and the entitlement turns on which one is meant. I would ask them to define both. The consultation also uses discrete and discreet within four paragraphs of each other, and in both cases the word they chose is the right one, which is why I am flagging it as a drafting risk rather than an error. They mean discrete routes when they talk about the four corridors, and they mean a discreet arrangement when they talk about a family who does not want their circumstances discussed at the school gate. Both readings are correct and both need to survive into the final text. Now, the evidence base. They cite the two thousand and twenty three review, and the site they cite it from is the archived version rather than the current one, which matters because the current version withdrew the cost estimate. I have the sight of the archived page and I will attach it. They also cite a figure of nine hundred and forty pounds per pupil per year and I cannot reproduce it from any published table, so the response should ask them to show the working rather than accuse them of inventing it. My instinct is that it is a real number from a different denominator. On process, I want to be careful not to censure the officers for something that is a political decision, and equally I do not want the response to read as though we would censor an inconvenient finding, so the wording there needs to be flat and factual. The consultation ran for six weeks over the summer holiday, which is a choice, and saying it is a choice is enough. They intend to canvass parents again in September, and the canvas they are proposing is a single online form with no telephone route, which will lose exactly the households the policy affects most. That is the strongest point we have and it should not be the seventh paragraph. There is a smaller issue about whether the appeals panel can waive the distance criterion, and the draft says it may, and then two pages later says the criterion is absolute, so somebody should wave that contradiction in front of them politely. On tone. I am wary of writing this while I am weary of the whole subject, because a response written in irritation reads as a response that can be dismissed, and I would rather be boring and unanswerable. I am not averse to being blunt where the evidence is strong, but adverse consequences for the families involved are the argument, not our frustration with the timetable. The eminent risk is that the imminent decision in October gets taken before the response is read at all, so the covering letter has to name that date. Practical things. Their portal only accepts a response of five thousand characters, and the argument does not fit, so we send a summary in the box and the full note as an attachment, and we email it as well so there is a record that does not depend on their system. Whose responsibility is it on our side to sign the covering letter, mine or the director's, because if it goes out under my name it reads as a technical comment and if it goes out under hers it reads as an institutional position? I have deliberately not answered that myself. One last note to myself. The stationery cupboard argument in paragraph nine of the draft, where they compare the transport budget to a stationary cost base, is not the mistake it looks like, they mean a cost base that does not move, so leave it alone when you edit this.

input: Reconciliation notes for the March settlement run before I hand this to the finance team. Total volume through the collections account was 412,908 transactions worth KES 1,284,660,415, and the settlement file we received lists 412,901, so we are seven transactions short and I have found six of them. Five are the ones that hit at 23:59:58 on 31/03 and landed in the April file instead, values 2,400, 5,000, 1,150, 12,500 and 780 shillings, which is a cutoff artefact and not a loss. The sixth is transaction ID TXN-9F4C2201 for KES 47,300 where the customer's phone number is stored as 0722XXXXXX in the export because the masking rule fired on a field it should not touch, so the record exists and the reference is unusable. That is a bug in the export, not in the ledger, and it is filed as PAY-3388. The seventh I cannot account for yet and I am not going to guess. On fees, Safaricom charged us 0.31% on the M-Pesa leg against the 0.28% in the agreement, and the difference on this volume is about KES 385,000, so it is worth a conversation rather than a write off. The card leg came in at 2.9% plus USD 0.30 per transaction as expected, and the USD to KES rate we booked at was 129.40 while the treasury sheet used 128.85, which is why the two totals never agree to the shilling and never will. I would rather we state the rate on the report than keep explaining the gap. Chargebacks were 41 for the month against 33 in February, which is 0.0099% of volume, still far inside the 0.1% threshold the acquirer cares about, and 29 of the 41 are from the same three merchants. Refunds totalled KES 8,904,220 across 1,166 requests and the median time to refund was 41 hours, which is worse than the 24 we promise in the merchant terms and better than the 61 hours we were at in January. The dashboard for all of this is at ops.internal.example.co.ke/settlement/2026-03 and the raw files are in the bucket under settlement/2026/03/ with the checksum manifest alongside them. Two things I need from other people. Can somebody in treasury confirm which rate the March invoices were raised at, because if they used 128.85 and we settled at 129.40 then every merchant statement for the month is going to be queried? And please do not reissue the March statements until that is answered, because a corrected statement that is corrected again is worse than a late one. For April I want three changes, and I am listing them here so they are on the record rather than in my head. The cutoff needs to move to 23:55 with the last five minutes swept into the next day deliberately instead of accidentally. The masking rule needs a field allowlist. And the report needs the booked rate printed at the top. I will write those up properly as tickets tomorrow.

input: Walking through the failover runbook out loud because I want to hear whether it still matches reality before the game day on Friday. The starting assumption is that the primary region is us-east-1 and the standby is eu-central-1, and that the standby is warm, meaning the deployment exists at one replica and the database is a read replica with replica lag published as ReplicaLag in CloudWatch. Step one in the current document says check ReplicaLag is under thirty seconds, and that is still right, but the document does not say where to look, so the reader opens the console and guesses. It should say aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics with the namespace AWS/RDS and the dimension DBInstanceIdentifier equals orders-replica-eu, because that is the instance we actually promote. Step two says scale the standby deployment, and the command in the document is kubectl scale deployment orders-api --replicas=12, which works, except the HPA immediately fights it and scales back to the minimum of two. The correct thing is to patch the HPA minimum first, kubectl patch hpa orders-api -p with the minReplicas set to 12, and then let the HPA do the scaling. That is the single biggest mistake in the current runbook and it is the one that cost us four minutes in the last drill. Step three, promote the replica. aws rds promote-read-replica --db-instance-identifier orders-replica-eu, and then wait for the status to leave modifying, which takes between two and six minutes and the document says one, which is where the anxiety comes from. Nobody should be watching a clock that is wrong. Step four is DNS. The weighted record in Route 53 goes from 100 zero to zero 100, the TTL is 60 seconds and the reality is closer to five minutes because of resolvers that ignore it, and the runbook should say that out loud rather than implying traffic moves in a minute. Step five, and this one is missing entirely, is the secrets check. The standby cluster reads DATABASE_URL from the secret orders-db-credentials in the eu namespace, and that secret is rotated by a job that only runs in the primary region, so after a real failover the password can be up to twelve hours stale. We got lucky on that in the last drill. I want a step that runs kubectl get secret orders-db-credentials -o jsonpath and compares the version tag with the one in Secrets Manager before we move DNS. Step six is the part everyone forgets, which is turning the read only flag off in the application config, because the standby runs with READ_ONLY=true and the pods do not reload it without a restart, so a promoted database with a read only application looks exactly like a broken database. Does the game day on Friday include the secrets step, or are we deliberately testing the runbook as written so the gap shows up in the report? I would rather test it as written and let it fail, personally. Rollback, briefly. If we go back to us-east-1 we cannot un-promote the replica, we have to rebuild eu-central-1 as a replica of the new primary, which takes about ninety minutes on the current data volume, and that is the cost the document should state on the first page rather than in an appendix.

input: Consultation note, Mr Terence Whitlock, seventy two, seen today at eleven forty, third review since January. Presenting complaint today is breathlessness on exertion, which he describes as worse over the last three weeks, now occurring on the flat after about one hundred metres, whereas in January it was only on the stairs. No orthopnoea. No paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and I asked that question twice in different words because he initially said no and then described waking at night needing to sit up, which on further questioning relates to reflux and not to breathlessness. No chest pain. No syncope. Ankle swelling present in the evenings, bilateral, resolving overnight, which he has had for two years and which has not changed. On examination, blood pressure 148 over 86 sitting, repeated at the end of the consultation at 142 over 84, pulse 78 and regular, saturations 96% on air, temperature normal. Chest, vesicular breath sounds with fine crackles at both bases which do not clear on coughing. Heart sounds one and two present, no murmur that I could hear, JVP not elevated on the couch at forty five degrees. Ankle oedema pitting to mid shin on the left, slightly less on the right. Weight 94.2 kilograms, which is up 2.6 kilograms from 91.6 in January, and that is the finding that concerns me most because he has not changed his diet and his appetite is reduced rather than increased. Current medication, ramipril 5 mg once daily, atorvastatin 20 mg at night, metformin 1 g twice daily, and he takes over the counter omeprazole intermittently which he had not previously mentioned. He is not taking the furosemide that was suggested in February. He says he stopped it after four days because of urinary frequency at work, and I have recorded that as his decision rather than as non compliance, because he had a reason and he was not told what to expect. Plan. Bloods today, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, HbA1c, BNP and thyroid function. ECG done in the room, sinus rhythm, no acute changes, rate 78, and I have filed the trace. Chest x ray requested, routine. I have referred to the heart failure clinic with the BNP to follow, and I have written on the referral that the weight gain and the bibasal crackles are the reason and not the ankles alone. Restart furosemide 20 mg in the morning only, with a clear explanation this time that the frequency is expected for the first fortnight and that taking it in the morning rather than at night is the way to live with it. Review in two weeks with weight and a home blood pressure diary if he can manage it, and sooner if the breathlessness worsens at rest, which I have written down for him as well as saying it, because he was on his own today and he did not remember the last set of instructions. Safety netting given verbally and in writing. Should the reduced appetite be worked up separately given the weight is going up rather than down, or is that entirely explained by fluid? I want the clinic to see that question rather than have me answer it here. He asked whether he can still drive to Norfolk next month and I said I would not stop him but that I would rather review him before he goes, and he agreed to that.

input: Ok so this is going to be a long one, sorry in advance, but you asked how the house thing went and it is a whole saga. So we went to see the place on Ellesmere Road on Saturday, the one with the weird photos where every room looked like it was taken from the ceiling, and the reason the photos are like that is that the rooms are tiny and the agent knows it. Like properly tiny. The second bedroom is a bedroom in the sense that a bed would fit in it if you took the door off. And the guy showing us round kept saying compact, which is such an estate agent word, compact and characterful, mate it is a cupboard with a window. Anyway the kitchen is actually fine, better than ours, and the garden is bigger than the photos suggest which is the opposite of everything else. Rent is 1,450 a month plus bills which is about what we expected for that area, but they want six weeks deposit and they want a guarantor for each of us, and Priya's parents are not going to do that from Delhi so that is already a problem. Then the second place, and this is the one I actually liked, is on Fairfield Terrace, 1,375, three proper bedrooms, two bathrooms, and the catch is that it is available from the 12th of September and our current tenancy runs to the 30th, so we would be paying two rents for nearly three weeks unless the landlord here lets us leave early, which, based on how he handled the boiler, no. Honestly the boiler thing still makes me angry. Six weeks. Six weeks with no hot water in February and he kept saying the part is on order. So we are probably going with Fairfield and eating the overlap, because the third place we saw was a joke, there was mould in the hall and the guy said it was condensation and I said condensation with a smell, is it, and he did not have an answer for that. What I actually need from you is whether you still want the third room, because if you are in then Fairfield works at about 458 each which is less than I pay now, and if you are out we either need to find someone by the end of August or we are back to the two bed places and there is nothing decent in the two bed range right now. No pressure but I do need to know by Friday because the agent said they have other viewings and they always say that but this time I believe her, the place is genuinely nice. Also, and this is the bit I keep forgetting to tell people, the Fairfield one has no washing machine. Not broken, just not there. So add that to the setup cost along with the deposit and the first month up front, which comes to something like 2,100 each before we have bought a single spoon. Let me know about the room. And if you know anyone else who might want it, tell them, because I would rather live with someone we know than do the whole spare room advert thing again after last year.

input: This is how I want the ragu written down for the new kitchen porter, and I am saying it the way I would say it standing next to him rather than the way a recipe book says it, because the book version makes people think the timings are the important part. The important part is the sofrito and the patience. So, one kilo of coarse ground beef, three hundred grams of pork shoulder also coarse, and one hundred and fifty grams of pancetta which you chop by hand and not in the machine, because the machine makes a paste and a paste will not render. Onion, carrot, celery, two hundred grams of onion, one hundred of carrot, one hundred of celery, all cut small but not minced, and you cook that in about eighty millilitres of olive oil on a low flame for twenty five minutes minimum. Twenty five minutes. Not eight, not twelve, twenty five, and if the onion is still crunchy when you add the meat the whole thing is finished before it starts. The pancetta goes in with the sofrito for the last five minutes. Then the meat, and here is where everybody goes wrong, you put the meat in and you do not touch it for four or five minutes, you let it stick and colour, and then you break it up. If you stir it straight away it steams in its own water and you get grey meat and grey ragu. Salt at this point, not before, about fifteen grams for this quantity and we adjust at the end. Then a glass of white wine, and yes white, I know everybody expects red, in Bologna it is white and this is my kitchen. Let it go completely, until you cannot smell alcohol at all. Then three hundred grams of passata and two hundred of whole peeled tomatoes crushed in your hand, and here is the thing about the tomato, it is not the main flavour, it is there to give a little acid and a little colour, and if the ragu tastes of tomato you have used too much. Then two hundred millilitres of whole milk, which sounds strange to people the first time and it is the thing that makes it taste like ours and not like a bolognese from a jar. Bring it to a bare simmer, one bubble every two seconds, lid slightly off, and then three hours, and I will check it at ninety minutes and again at two hours because the flame on the back burner runs hot. If it dries add hot water, never cold, half a ladle at a time. No garlic, no herbs, no oregano, no basil, nothing else goes in it, and if I find a bay leaf in there I will know. Finish, taste for salt, and it wants a grind of black pepper and nothing more. It is better the next day, always, so we make it Monday for Tuesday service. Does he know how to tell when the sofrito is ready by smell rather than by the clock, because that is the only part of this I cannot write down properly? Show him with the first batch and let him do the second one himself while you stand there.
