input: Reading notes on the three papers for the group meeting, dictated so I do not lose them again. First one, arXiv 2602.11149, the repetition paper. The claim is that repeating a small high quality corpus for four epochs beats a single pass over a corpus four times the size at the same token budget, and they show it at 410M and 1.4B parameters on a 6B token base set. What I actually take from it is narrower than the abstract suggests, because their held out set comes from the same distribution as the repeated data, so some of the gain could be distribution match rather than repetition, and they do not report a domain shift evaluation. Still useful for us, because our situation is exactly the one they describe, a few thousand hand written rows and no way to get forty thousand. Second, arXiv 2606.06920, the fine tuning trap paper. This one matters more for what we are doing. They fine tune models from 125M up to 1.3B and find that full fine tuning degrades out of distribution behaviour badly below about 300M while LoRA at rank 8 and rank 16 does not, and the mechanism they propose is that full fine tuning moves the whole representation and a small model does not have the capacity to hold both the old and the new behaviour. Their rank sweep is only 8, 16 and 64, so anything about rank 4 is my extrapolation and not theirs. If we are going to sit at 0.6B, that paper is the argument for QLoRA over a full run, and it is a stronger argument than the memory saving one. Third, arXiv 2607.03801, discriminative heads for classification in tiny language models. Less directly relevant, but the interesting part for us is section 4.3, where a 270M model with a classification head beats a 1.7B model asked to emit a label in text, and the gap is 11 points of accuracy. That is worth remembering if we ever want a should I edit this at all gate in front of the generative model, because that gate is a classification problem and we keep treating it as a generation problem. Two things I want to raise in the meeting. The evaluation sets in all three papers are between five thousand and thirty thousand examples and ours is fifty six, and I do not think anybody has said out loud how weak that makes any comparison we run. Also, none of them measure what happens on inputs four hundred tokens and longer, which is exactly the case we care about, so we cannot borrow their conclusion about length. Should I write the length experiment as a separate note or fold it into the reading summary? I would rather it were separate so it does not look like a finding from the papers when it is our own gap.

input: Writing up the duplicate invoice bug properly because the ticket as it stands says invoices are duplicated sometimes and that is not enough for anyone to work with. What actually happens is this. The invoice generation job runs at 02:00 in the scheduler and it selects every account whose billing anchor is today, and for each account it creates an invoice row and then calls the tax service. The tax service has a client timeout of ten seconds and the scheduler has a job timeout of five minutes. On the fourth of the month, which is our heaviest anchor day because of a promotion we ran in January, the tax service gets slow, not down, slow, and about one call in forty takes longer than ten seconds. When the client timeout fires we catch the exception, log a warning, and let the scheduler retry the whole job. The scheduler retry is the bug. The job is not idempotent, because the invoice row was already written before the tax call and there is no unique constraint on account id plus period, so the second run writes a second invoice for every account it had already processed before the timeout. That is why the duplicates cluster at the start of the account list in alphabetical order, which is the detail that finally made it obvious. Numbers, because they matter for the fix. On the fourth of March we produced 8,412 invoices for 8,207 accounts, so 205 duplicates. On the fourth of February it was 63. On the fourth of January, before the promotion, zero, which is why nobody noticed this for two years. Nine of the March duplicates were emailed to customers before we caught it, and three of those were paid, so there is a refund conversation as well as a code fix. The refunds are with support and I am not touching them. Two fixes and they are not alternatives, we need both. The first is a unique index on account_id and billing_period, which turns the failure into a constraint violation instead of a silent duplicate, and I would rather have a loud failure at 02:00 than a quiet one. The second is to move the tax call before the invoice write, or if that is not possible because of the way the tax service wants the invoice id, then to write the row in a transaction that only commits after the tax call returns. I prefer the second shape because it removes the window entirely rather than catching it after the fact. There is a third thing that is not a fix but should happen anyway, which is that the scheduler should not retry a job that has partially succeeded without a marker saying where it got to, and that is a platform conversation rather than something we can do inside this service. What I have not been able to reproduce is the case from the ticket where a duplicate appeared on a day that was not the fourth. There is one report from the twelfth of February and I have looked at the logs for that night twice and there is no timeout and no retry, so either the report is a user looking at a credit note and calling it an invoice, or there is a second cause I have not found. I am writing it as unresolved rather than closing it. Do we want the unique index deployed on its own first, given it will start throwing constraint violations at 02:00 and somebody will need to be awake for that, or do both changes go out together on the same release? I have a preference but it is a release management question rather than a technical one.

input: Notes from the sprint retro, dictated straight after the session while people's words are still fresh, and I want to keep their phrasing rather than my summary of it. Eleven people in the room, two on video, Henrik was away. We ran the sailboat format again, which worked better than last time because I asked people to write for five minutes in silence before anybody spoke, and that changed the shape of the whole hour. The main thing that came out, and it came from three different people independently, is that the sprint goal stopped meaning anything around day four. Sofia put it best, she said we agreed a goal and then we spent two weeks doing tickets, and nobody in the room disagreed with that. When I pushed on why, the answer was the interrupt queue. We pulled in nine unplanned items during the sprint, which is more than a quarter of the completed work, and seven of the nine came from the same customer escalation. Nobody thinks the escalation was wrong to pull in. The complaint is that we did not change the goal or tell anybody outside the team that the goal had changed, so from the outside it looks like we committed to something and quietly did not do it. Second theme, the environment. Four people mentioned the staging environment being broken or occupied, and Lars pointed out that we lost most of a day on Wednesday waiting for it, and then lost it again on Friday because the migration test needs exclusive access and there is no way to book it. That is a concrete thing with a concrete fix and it does not need a discussion, it needs somebody to own it. Third theme, and this one was quieter, is that two people said they did not know what the others were working on until the standup on day seven. We are eleven people and we behave like a team of four, and the standup format is not doing what we pretend it does. I have my own view about splitting into two streams and I deliberately did not raise it today because I did not want the retro to become my proposal. What we agreed. Anna will own the staging booking problem and come back with either a booking mechanism or a second environment estimate by Thursday. I will take the goal changing problem, which means writing down what we do when an escalation eats the sprint, and I will bring a draft rather than a discussion. And we agreed to try a written weekly update from each stream instead of extending the standup, for two sprints, and then decide whether it helped. Nobody volunteered for the third one, which usually means it will not happen, so I will chase it. What I am unsure about is whether the interrupt queue is actually a process problem or whether it is a staffing problem wearing a process costume, because if seven items come from one customer then no amount of ceremony fixes that. Should I bring that to the leads meeting on Monday or raise it with Dagny first? Two people stayed behind afterwards to say the session felt useful, which is the first time that has happened, and I want to note it because the previous three retros ended with everybody leaving at exactly the hour.

input: Note de travail sur la traduction du contrat Bertrand, dictée avant de rendre la première version, parce que je veux garder la trace de mes choix pendant qu'ils sont encore frais. Le texte source fait quarante et une pages et il est mal rédigé, ce qui est le vrai problème, pas la longueur. L'auteur utilise le mot engagement dans trois sens différents, parfois comme obligation contractuelle, parfois comme simple intention, et une fois, à l'article douze, dans un sens qui ressemble à une garantie sans en être une. Je ne peux pas trancher à sa place. J'ai donc traduit chaque occurrence selon le contexte immédiat et j'ai posé quatre questions dans le fichier de commentaires, numérotées de Q1 à Q4, en indiquant à chaque fois la page et la ligne. La cliente préfère toujours qu'on lui pose la question plutôt qu'on devine, elle me l'a dit deux fois, et sur ce dossier elle a raison. Deuxième difficulté, les délais. Le contrat dit dans un délai de trente jours à compter de la notification, et ensuite, à l'article dix-sept, dans les trente jours suivant la réception, et ce n'est pas la même chose du tout, puisque la notification et la réception peuvent être séparées de plusieurs jours selon le mode d'envoi. J'ai conservé la différence dans la traduction, mot pour mot, parce que l'aplanir serait une décision juridique et ce n'est pas mon rôle. Troisième point, le vocabulaire technique. Il s'agit d'un contrat de maintenance industrielle et le texte mélange des termes anglais laissés tels quels, comme downtime et service level, avec des équivalents français ailleurs dans le même paragraphe. J'ai gardé les termes anglais là où ils figurent dans le texte source, et j'ai ajouté une note explicative pour la cliente. Uniformiser serait plus élégant et moins fidèle. Le registre, enfin. La version française est volontairement sèche, sans effets, parce qu'un contrat qui se lit agréablement inquiète les juristes, et parce que le ton du texte source est lui-même très plat. Je précise ce choix pour qu'on ne me demande pas de le corriger dans deux semaines. Il reste deux choses à faire avant la livraison de vendredi. Relire l'annexe trois, qui contient un tableau de pénalités avec des pourcentages, et vérifier chaque chiffre deux fois, car une virgule déplacée dans un tableau de pénalités est la seule erreur qui coûte de l'argent. Et confirmer avec la cliente l'orthographe du nom du signataire, qui apparaît sous deux formes dans le document, Bertrand-Lecoq à la page une et Bertrand Lecoq à la page trente-neuf, sans trait d'union. Je ne choisis pas moi-même, je demande. La facturation se fera au tarif convenu de zéro virgule dix-huit euro par mot source, soit environ mille quatre cents euros pour ce volume, plus deux heures de relecture. J'enverrai le devis mis à jour ce soir.

La cliente préfère toujours qu'on lui pose la question plutôt qu'on devine, elle me l'a dit deux fois, et sur ce dossier elle a raison. Deuxième difficulté, les délais. Le contrat dit dans un délai de trente jours à compter de la notification, et ensuite, à l'article dix-sept, dans les trente jours suivant la réception, et ce n'est pas la même chose du tout, puisque la notification et la réception peuvent être séparées de plusieurs jours selon le mode d'envoi. J'ai conservé la différence dans la traduction, mot pour mot, parce que l'aplanir serait une décision juridique et ce n'est pas mon rôle. Troisième point, le vocabulaire technique. Il s'agit d'un contrat de maintenance industrielle et le texte mélange des termes anglais laissés tels quels, comme downtime et service level, avec des équivalents français ailleurs dans le même paragraphe. J'ai gardé les termes anglais là où ils figurent dans le texte source, et j'ai ajouté une note explicative pour la cliente. Uniformiser serait plus élégant et moins fidèle. Le registre, enfin. La version française est volontairement sèche, sans effets, parce qu'un contrat qui se lit agréablement inquiète les juristes, et parce que le ton du texte source est lui-même très plat. Je précise ce choix pour qu'on ne me demande pas de le corriger dans deux semaines. Il reste deux choses à faire avant la livraison de vendredi. Relire l'annexe trois, qui contient un tableau de pénalités avec des pourcentages, et vérifier chaque chiffre deux fois, car une virgule déplacée dans un tableau de pénalités est la seule erreur qui coûte de l'argent. Et confirmer avec la cliente l'orthographe du nom du signataire, qui apparaît sous deux formes dans le document, Bertrand-Lecoq à la page une et Bertrand Lecoq à la page trente-neuf, sans trait d'union. Je ne choisis pas moi-même, je demande. La facturation se fera au tarif convenu de zéro virgule dix-huit euro par mot source, soit environ mille quatre cents euros pour ce volume, plus deux heures de relecture. J'enverrai le devis mis à jour ce soir.

input: Quick note on the pricing review before I forget the numbers. So the finance team wants a decision by Friday and honestly abhi tak hum log ne ek bhi customer se baat nahi ki hai about the new tier, which is the actual problem, not the price point. We have three options on the table and I am only comfortable with one of them. Option one is raising the base tier from 49 to 59 dollars, which is a 20% jump and the churn model says we lose about 4% of the base, mostly the accounts under five seats. Option two is keeping the base and adding a usage charge above 100,000 events a month, and yeh option sabse zyada risky hai because our metering is not accurate below the daily level and customers will absolutely notice that before we do. Option three is what Rohan suggested, leave the price and cut the trial from 30 days to 14, which does nothing for revenue this quarter but improves the conversion number that the board actually looks at. Mujhe lagta hai option one theek hai, but only if we grandfather the existing accounts for twelve months and say so publicly, because the last time we changed pricing without saying anything on the changelog there was a thread on Reddit within two days and support spent a week on it. Ek aur baat, whoever does the announcement needs to write it before we decide, not after, because writing it is what tells you whether the decision is defensible. If you cannot write the sentence, the pricing is wrong. Can you check with Neha whether the metering fix is in the March release or the April one, because option two is dead without it? I will put all three options in the deck tonight with the churn numbers next to each one and no recommendation, so the room argues about the tradeoff and not about my preference.

input: This is my explanation for the assignment submission, because sir said he wants the reasoning and not only the code. The task was to make the cache work correctly when two goroutines ask for the same missing key at the same time. My first version used a plain map with a sync.Mutex around it, and it was correct but every request waited for every other request, so the benchmark was worse than no cache at all. The second version used sync.RWMutex, so readers do not block each other, and that fixed the read path. The write path was still wrong, because two goroutines could both miss, both call loadFromDB, and both write, which means the database sees two identical queries and the whole point of the cache is lost. That is the thundering herd problem and the standard answer is single flight. So the final version uses golang.org/x/sync/singleflight, where I call group.Do with the cache key as the string and the loader as the function, and singleflight guarantees that only one call runs while the others wait on the same result. The important detail I did not understand at first is that the waiters get the same returned value and the same error, so if loadFromDB fails, every waiter sees that failure, and if I want per caller retry then singleflight is the wrong tool. I have written that in the comment above the function because I will forget it. Benchmark numbers, on my laptop, with 200 concurrent readers and one cold key, the mutex version made 200 database calls, the RWMutex version made 197, and the singleflight version made exactly 1. Latency at p99 went from 41 milliseconds to 12 milliseconds, and the surprising part is that memory allocation per operation also dropped, from 312 bytes to 96 bytes, because the mutex version was allocating a new result struct in every goroutine. Two things I know are still wrong and I am writing them down instead of pretending. First, there is no TTL, so a stale value stays forever, and the correct fix is to store an expiry time inside the entry struct rather than to run a background cleaner, because a cleaner goroutine on a small program is more machinery than the problem needs. Second, my test for the concurrent case uses time.Sleep to make the race happen, which works on my machine and is not a real test, and the proper approach is a channel that the fake loader blocks on until the test releases it. I did not have time to rewrite it before the deadline. Sir, is it acceptable to submit with the sleep based test and fix it in the next assignment, or should I resubmit the test file separately? The code is on the branch feature/singleflight-cache and the benchmark output is in bench.txt at the repository root.

input: This is what I want to say to Daniel's parents at parents evening on Thursday, and I am dictating it now because at four o'clock on Thursday I will have said the same three sentences forty times and I will not do him justice. The honest position is that his reading has come on a long way this year, he is confident with anything narrative, and the difficulty is entirely with non fiction and with questions that ask him to explain rather than to retell. When I ask him what happens next he is excellent. When I ask him why the writer chose that word he goes quiet, and it is not that he does not know, it is that he has decided the question is a trap. That is the thing I want to talk to them about, because at home they can help with it far more easily than I can with thirty of them in a room. His writing is neat and his spelling is better than his last report suggests, and I checked that against the September baseline before I said it. Maths is fine, he is in the middle group and he is comfortable there, and I do not want them to push for the top group in September because he had a bad term when that happened in year four. What I need to be careful about is the friendship business with the boy who moved classes, because they raised it in October and I do not have anything new to tell them, and pretending I have looked into it more than I have would be worse than saying that. So I will say it plainly and offer to check in with the pastoral lead. Do I mention the reading age number or do I keep it to what he can actually do, because the number went up by fourteen months and that will be the only thing they remember?

input: This is the inspection note for the pump housing batch that arrived from Kellner on 14 May. The castings are within the drawing on the flange face and on the bolt circle, and the surface finish is better than the last batch, so whatever they changed at their end has helped us. The bore tolerance on the drawing is 0.05 millimetres and I measured eight housings across the batch with the bore gauge at three heights each. Six of the eight sit inside the band. The seventh is high at the top of the bore by an amount I would accept on a spare, and the eighth is out at every height, which tells me it is not a measurement problem but a fixturing problem on their machine. The bore tolerance is 0.08 millimetres, not 0.05. Kellner should be asked to record the fixture setting for each housing in the batch, because one clamp sitting out of position explains the pattern I am seeing and it will come back on the next order. The keyway depth is correct on all eight and the chamfer at the shaft entry is consistent, so the finishing operations are under control. I have marked the eighth housing with a red label and put it on the quarantine shelf beside the goods in desk, and it must not go to assembly even as a spare, because a bore that size will not hold the seal at 6 bar. The rest of the batch can move to washing. For the report I still need the heat number from the certificate, the fixture log if they are willing to send it, and the gauge calibration date, which I believe is 3 March but that should be read off the sticker rather than taken from the file.

input: I am writing down where the project is before I forget, because the report is due on Sunday and I have not touched the write up yet. The retrieval part works now. I switched the index from flat to IVF with 4096 lists and the search time on the laptop dropped from about 900 milliseconds to 40, which is the difference between a demo I can run in front of the class and one I cannot. The embed, the embedding table is still the problem because I load all of it into memory at startup and that alone is 1.2 gigabytes, so the whole thing dies on the lab machines that only have 4 gigabytes. Sir said to try memory mapping the table instead of reading it, and I tried that yesterday, but the first query after startup takes four seconds because nothing is in the page cache and after that it is fine. So maybe I warm it with a hundred random ids at startup and hide the cost there. The chunking is still 512 tokens with 64 overlap and I have not tested anything else, which I should say in the limitations section instead of pretending it was a decision. Evaluation is 120 questions I wrote myself from the syllabus PDFs, and recall at five is 0.71, which sounds fine until you notice that most of the misses are questions where the answer sits inside a table. I have no plan for tables and I am not going to invent one in three days, so that goes in limitations as well. Tomorrow I do the write up first and the code only if there is time left over.

input: This is the end of year comment for Aoife Brennan and I will tidy it up later, so I am talking it through first. She is in 5B this year and she has come on enormously since Christmas, particularly in reading, where she has gone from picking books she had already read at home to taking on things that are genuinely too hard for her and finishing them anyway. Her writing is the weaker side, and the difficulty is not ideas, because she has plenty of those, it is that she starts a story in the past tense and drifts into the present halfway down the page and does not notice it when she reads it back. We have been doing paired reading on Tuesdays and Thursdays with the class next door and that has done more for her confidence than anything I have organised, so I want to say it in the comment without making the whole year sound like it was about reading. Maths is steady. She knows her tables to twelve and she is quick with them, but word problems throw her because she starts calculating before she has finished reading the question, which is the same thing that happens in her writing. The trip to Glendalough was the making of her socially, and she was the one who noticed that Liam had been left off the bus list, which I want to mention because that sort of thing never appears in a report. Her attendance is 94% and the absences are all accounted for. One correction on what I said at the beginning. Aoife is in 5C this year, not 5B.

input: This is the runbook for the finance extract so somebody else can run it while I am away next week. It goes after the nightly load finishes, which is usually done by 02:30, and if the load is still running the extract will read a half written partition and nobody will notice until the month end review. It starts with the check on dim_account, where the row count should be within about fifty rows of the previous day, and a jump larger than that always means the source dropped a filter. Then the aggregate over fact_invoice_line grouped by account_id and posting_month, and it excludes the rows where status is void, which is the part people forget. The summary goes into rpt_finance_monthly and the table is truncated before insert, so the whole thing is safe to rerun if you get it wrong. The CSV copy goes out to /srv/exports/weekly and the permissions are set to read only for the finance group. input: The read path cutover goes on Wednesday and I want the write path left alone until we have a full week of clean reads. The new service has been taking shadow traffic for eleven days, so the query shapes are not going to surprise anyone, and the only thing shadowing does not test is what happens when the old service stops answering. So we move reads in three steps rather than one, ten percent, then half, then everything, with an hour between steps and no step during standup. The rollback is a config change and not a deploy, one flag per step, which is the whole reason we built it this way after the last cutover took forty minutes to undo. Cache behaviour is the part I am least sure about. The old service kept a local cache with a five minute expiry and the new one goes straight to the replica, so the first minute after each step will look slower than steady state and that is expected rather than a fault. Watch the ninety fifth percentile on the replica instead of the average, because the average will hide a small number of very slow list queries that we already know about and have a ticket for. If reads look fine the next morning, we leave it alone and do nothing for a week. Nobody touches the write path, nobody removes the old service, and nobody deletes the shadow config, because the shadow config is the only thing that lets us compare the two. Friday for the read path cutover, not Wednesday.

input: Putting down what I need for the vendor renewal before the finance review on Monday. input: This is a referral summary for Mrs Eileen Carroway, date of birth 3 April 1958, who I have looked after since 2011. I have asked for an echocardiogram and she has an appointment at Concord on 12 October, so the results should be with you before she is seen. Correction, the metformin is 1 g twice daily, I have the July script in front of me now. She is happy to be seen in the clinic, she will bring the home blood pressure diary she has kept properly since March, and her daughter Bernadette will drive her.

input: Right, this is the plan for the staging cluster upgrade so that anyone can pick it up if I am not around. The cluster is stg-br-01 in sa-east-1, it is on 1.28 today, three control plane nodes and two node groups, one on demand and one spot. The window is Thursday night, 22:00 to 01:00 local, and Rafael is second on call so he takes the pager if I lose signal. The on demand group is called core-a and it carries the ingress controller, cert manager, the metrics stack and anything with a persistent volume attached to it. The spot group is called batch-b and it carries the nightly report jobs and the load test runners, so nothing in there matters if a node disappears halfway through something. Before anything else I want a fresh etcd snapshot in the backups bucket and I want to see the object listed with its size and its timestamp, not just a job that exited zero, because that has caught us twice and both times we only noticed days later. The order is control plane first, then core-a, then batch-b, and we do not touch two of them at once even when it feels slow, because the whole value of a staging run is being able to say afterwards which step broke it. On the control plane I will replace one node at a time and wait for all three to report healthy before moving on, and if the second one comes back with API server latency above what we normally see at that hour then I stop there and we sit on a mixed version cluster overnight, which is supported and is a lot better than pushing on because the clock is nearly out. Scratch that, the window is Wednesday night, Thursday is the payments freeze and nobody wants us anywhere near a cluster that evening. For core-a I will drain with the eviction grace period that is already in the runbook and I am not going to use force, because the ingress pods take around forty seconds to deregister from the load balancer and forcing them means we drop live connections for no reason at all. The pod disruption budgets for ingress and cert manager allow one unavailable each, so a drain will simply block rather than do something stupid, and if it blocks for more than five minutes that is a signal to stop and read the events instead of raising the number until it moves. Anything that blocks goes in the channel with the pod name and the reason, and nobody deletes a stuck pod to make a drain finish, because that is how we lost the certificate renewal in April. For batch-b I will scale the nightly jobs to zero first, wait for the queue to empty, and then replace the whole group in one go, since there is nothing stateful in there and rolling it node by node only stretches the window out for no benefit. After each group comes back I check three things, that every daemonset has the number of ready pods it is supposed to have, that no node is sitting not ready with a disk pressure condition, and that the CNI pods are actually running the new image rather than a cached one from before. The last one has fooled me twice because the pod restarts, goes ready, and reports the old binary quite happily. Once that is all green I will run the smoke suite against the staging endpoint and compare the error rate with Monday rather than with the last hour, because the last hour is the upgrade itself and comparing against it tells us nothing. If the error rate is worse we roll the node groups back to the previous launch template, which we keep for a week, and we leave the control plane alone, because rolling that back at night is not something I am willing to do without Rafael awake and on a laptop. The timeline goes in the incident doc even when nothing goes wrong, since the only reason we know about the forty seconds is that somebody wrote it down last time.

input: This is the design note for the profile read path and I am dictating it as I think, so the reasoning stays visible even in the places where I change my mind. The approach I want to take is a read through cache sitting in front of the profile service, keyed on the account id, with a sixty second time to live. The p99 on that endpoint is 340 milliseconds and nearly all of it is the badge assembly, so serving an already assembled response out of the cache would put the common case somewhere around 20 milliseconds. It is also the cheapest thing on the table, because it needs no schema work at all and the response shape stays exactly what it is today. We already run the same cache in front of search, so the operational side is understood and nobody has to learn a new system at 3 in the morning. And sixty seconds of lag on the badges is fine, because they are decorative and in two years nobody has filed a single ticket about a badge being late. The endpoint itself is the v2 profile read and it has four callers that matter, the mobile app on cold start, the web shell, the support console, and the batch job that builds the weekly digest. The mobile app calls it once per session and it is the one that shows up in the store reviews when it is slow. The support console calls it maybe two hundred times an hour, but every one of those calls has a human on a phone line waiting for the answer, so it is the caller with the least tolerance for a wrong answer even though it is the smallest by volume. The digest job calls it eleven thousand times inside a fifteen minute stretch every Sunday at 4 in the morning, and that is the traffic shape that pushed us over last quarter. Internally the read takes the account row, then joins to entitlements, then joins again to the badge table, and that second join is the one that walks a wide index and does most of the damage. Error handling does not change, a missing account is a 404 and an entitlement lookup failure is a 503 rather than an empty list, because a client that sees an empty entitlement list will happily render a downgraded account and we have been burned by that twice. Ownership stays with the accounts team and the on call rotation is unchanged. For testing I want the contract tests we already have plus a load test that reproduces the Sunday shape rather than a flat rate, because a flat load test has never once predicted what actually happens on Sunday. Metrics need the p50, the p99 and the error rate split by caller, and I want the caller label to come from the token rather than a header the client sets, because clients lie about that and always have. The rollout goes behind the usual flag at one percent, then ten, then the mobile app last, and the support console gets moved deliberately rather than by percentage so that somebody can sit with them for an hour and watch what the numbers do. Actually, I take that back. The badge state is the field the support team reads when they are checking whether a suspension has landed, and a field that is allowed to lag by a minute is the difference between a correct answer and a wrong one while a customer is on the line. So what I want is the badge index we deferred in March, which makes that second join go away at the source, and I would rather do the slower correct thing than take the latency win and hand support a field they cannot trust.

input: This is the writeup for the finding on the ingest service and I will file it in the internal tracker before anything goes to the vendor. The affected component is the ingest listener on port 8443 on ingest-eu.dorval.net and on the two mirrors sitting behind it. The bug is in the archive extraction path, where the code takes the entry name straight out of the archive header and joins it onto the staging directory without normalising it first, so an entry name beginning with a parent directory sequence walks out of the staging directory and writes wherever the service user is able to write. I have a working proof of concept that drops a file into the unit directory, which makes this a direct path to execution as root on the next restart rather than a theoretical traversal. Anything on 4.11.2 or later is patched, and everything from 4.6.0 up to that is affected on all three platforms. The service account is root in the packaged unit, which is why I am calling this critical rather than high, and running the listener unprivileged is a genuine mitigation but it is not the fix. The vendor already has CVE-2026-31884 reserved and their advisory draft carries the wrong classification, they have it as CWE-22 when the write primitive is the part that matters, but I am not going to argue taxonomy in the first mail. To be exact the patched build is 4.11.3, and 4.11.2 is the tag that shipped with the change reverted by mistake. The proof of concept archive, the sample with hash 9f2c41ab and the strace output all stay in the case folder, and none of that goes in the ticket body, because the ticket is readable by the whole support group and the proof of concept works against production.

input: Right, this is me thinking out loud about the March newsletter before I write it properly, so ignore the state of the sentences, and the thing I keep coming back to is that Statista survey Dev sent round last week. The angle I want is to open cold on the number, 61 percent of the people they asked said they still keep a manual spreadsheet alongside the tool they are paying for. It is a genuinely surprising figure and it earns the first line without me having to be clever about it. It also sets up the whole middle of the piece, because once the reader accepts that the spreadsheet is still there, the question of why it is still there becomes the article rather than something I have to argue my way into. And it gives the sales team a line they can drop into a deck, which is honestly the only reason the last newsletter got forwarded to anybody. The survey is not ours though, we only licensed the chart and the terms do not let us present somebody else's research as our own finding. So it opens on the Fieldstone call, where Priyanka told us her team had been exporting to a spreadsheet every Friday for two years and nobody had ever asked them why, and that is a better opening anyway because it is one person instead of a percentage. The shape is three sections, the first on what people actually do on a Friday afternoon, the second on why the export exists at all, and the third on what changed in the January release, and it lands around 900 words which is what the newsletter takes. Tone is the same as February, second person, short sentences, no headings shouting at anybody. It goes out on 14 March and Dev needs the draft by the 11th so that he gets a weekend with it.

input: Site notes for Thursday at the Jabal Amman job, tower B, and I am sending this from the car so the photos will follow after. The blinding is poured across the whole north half and the level came out at 812.45, which is 15 mm below what the drawing says, and Ihab has already written it into the daily record. That is inside tolerance so nothing gets broken out, but the setting out for the lift pit has to be taken off the poured level and not off the drawing, and I have told the setting out crew that twice now. The rebar for the raft arrived at 7 in the morning, forty two bundles, and the mill certificates are for heat number 4471 which matches the delivery note, so that one is closed. input: This is the PR description for the toast fix, somebody please read it before I open it. input: This is the handover note for the Bregeon file, since I am away from the 12th and Camille is taking it over while I am gone. The source is the framework agreement plus four annexes, 46,000 words in total, and the client is Bregeon Industrie in Saint Etienne and not the Paris office, which matters because the Paris office has its own preferred wording and they are not the ones paying for this. The delivery date is 30 September and it is a hard date, because their counterparty signs on 3 October and the English version is the one being signed. I have finished the framework agreement and annexes one and two, which is roughly 31,000 words, and the glossary is at version 4 in the shared folder. Annex three is the technical one, the specifications for the presses, and it needs somebody comfortable with mechanical vocabulary, so I have deliberately left it until last. The register throughout is the plain contractual English the client asked for in the kickoff call, and specifically not the older style with shall in every clause, because their counsel in London said shall was being read as ambiguous by their own reviewers. So it is will for obligations, may for permissions, and must only where a condition is genuinely mandatory and not directed at a party. For résiliation I have used termination all the way through. Numbers, dates and amounts stay in the source format apart from the decimal comma, which becomes a point, and that is the first thing the client checks every single time. Party names stay exactly as they appear in the source, including the accents, and I have not anglicised Saint Etienne anywhere in the English. The annexes carry their own numbering which does not match the framework agreement, and that is irritating but it is the client's own numbering and we are not going to tidy it up for them. Let me rephrase, for résiliation I have used cancellation all the way through, termination is what the previous translator used and the client asked us in writing to move away from it. The glossary records that decision with the date and the mail reference, so if Camille sees the older form coming back out of the translation memory she should not trust the memory over the glossary. Cross references inside the annexes point at clause numbers in the framework agreement, so any renumbering breaks them silently, and I have flagged the three places where the source cross reference is already wrong. Those three go on the query sheet rather than being corrected quietly in the English, because it is the client's lawyer who has to decide what the reference should say. The query sheet is in the same folder, there are eleven open queries and four of them are blocking annex four. Marion at the client is the person who answers queries and she answers inside a day, but she is off from the 20th, so anything blocking has to reach her before then. Invoicing is on delivery at the rate in the framework, and there is no rush charge even though the date is tight, because I agreed that date knowing exactly how tight it was. If Camille runs out of time on annex three, the fallback I agreed with Marion is that we deliver the framework agreement and annexes one, two and four on the 30th and annex three on 4 October, since the presses annex is not part of what actually gets signed. That fallback needs Marion to confirm it in writing again if it is really used, and it should be a last resort and not the plan.

input: The seminar meets on Wednesdays at 2:15 in Sever 108, and I want the whole thirteen weeks laid out before the catalog deadline on 4 October so that nobody arrives in January expecting a lecture course. The reading is two articles a week with one full book every third week, which is heavy, but it is manageable if students stop trying to read everything twice and start reading for the argument. Week one is introductory and I will do most of the talking, because the vocabulary of the field has to be in place before anyone presents to the room. Week two pairs the Fielding chapter with Rosen's 1987 article, and I am pairing them deliberately, since Rosen spends thirty pages arguing against a position that Fielding never actually held, and the students should watch that happen rather than be told about it. Week three is the first full book, and I have asked Widener to place four copies on short loan instead of one, because last year three students shared a single copy and the discussion suffered for it. From week four the presentations begin, two per meeting, twenty minutes each with ten minutes of questions, and I will keep the order posted on the course site so that nobody has to ask me twice. The presentation is not a summary of the reading, it is an argument about the reading, and I will say that in the first meeting and again in the third, because it never lands the first time. Week five is the periodical week and everyone should bring one page of a nineteenth century magazine, photographed rather than printed, so that we can look at advertisements sitting next to fiction on the same page. Week six is the archive visit, and Marguerite Delacroix at the historical society has agreed to open the reading room from 1:00 to 4:00, which means we skip the ordinary meeting that week and travel instead. Anyone who cannot manage the afternoon should tell me by week four and I will arrange a separate hour rather than have them miss the material entirely. Week seven is the methods meeting, and it is the one week I want no assigned reading at all, because the students need to bring their own paper topics and defend them to each other while there is still time to change course. The proposal is two pages, due at noon on the Friday of week seven, and I will return comments within a week, which I can only promise because there are fourteen students in the room and not thirty. Week eight is the theory reading and I expect it to be the least popular meeting of the term, so I will assign the shorter of the two chapters and let the longer one stay optional for the people who want it. Week nine returns to primary material with the trial transcripts, and here I want everyone to notice how much of the record is missing before we start interpreting what remains of it. Week ten is the guest, Professor Ahmed Karimi from the law school, who works on the same period from the property side, and he has asked for questions in advance, so I will collect those in week nine and send them over. Week eleven is the writing workshop, which means drafts circulated forty eight hours ahead and read properly, not skimmed in the corridor on the way in. Every student comments on two drafts in writing and one aloud, and the written comments go to the author and not to me, because the point of it is the exchange and not a performance for my benefit. Week twelve is the second book, which is long, so I am cutting the middle section from the assigned reading and saying so plainly rather than pretending that anyone finished it. Week thirteen is the last meeting and it carries no new reading, only the final discussion and the practical business of submission. Papers are eight thousand words, due at 5:00 on 15 December, submitted through the course site rather than by email, and I will not read a paper that arrives in my inbox because last year I lost two that way. The grade is forty percent on the final paper, twenty five percent on the presentation, twenty percent on the written comments across the term, and fifteen percent on participation, and I will publish the rubric in week one so that nobody has to guess what participation is supposed to mean. Late work loses a third of a grade a day, though extensions on documented grounds are routine and nobody needs to explain their medical history to me in order to get one. Office hours are Tuesdays from 10:00 to noon, and I would much rather see people early in the term than in the week the paper is due. If the room turns out to be too small once enrollment closes, the registrar has said we can move to the seminar room on the third floor, which has the better table but no projector, and for a course like this one that is an acceptable trade. One correction to the top of this. I said Wednesdays and the booking is actually Thursdays, same time, same room.

input: These are the notes for the reranker run I finished last night, and I am writing them properly this time because the last set was useless a week later. The base model is bge-reranker-base and I did not change the tokenizer or the maximum length, which stays at 512 tokens for both the query and the passage together. The adapter is rank 32 with alpha 32, applied to the query and value projections only, and I left the feed forward layers frozen because the earlier sweep showed no gain there and it costs a lot of memory. Training data is the MS MARCO triples file that Rifat cleaned in March, which lives at /data/msmarco/triples.dedup.jsonl and has 812000 rows after the duplicate pass, and I sampled 200000 of them with seed 1337 so that the run can be repeated. The negatives matter more than anything else here, so I used four hard negatives per positive, mined with the base model itself at top 50 and then filtered to drop anything that scored above 0.9 because those are usually unlabelled positives and training on them teaches the model that a right answer is wrong. Batch size is 64 pairs, learning rate 2e-5 with a cosine schedule and 200 warmup steps, and the run is 3000 steps which is roughly one and a half epochs over the sample. It took 4 hours and 20 minutes on one A100 40GB, and the loss curve is smooth after step 400 with no spikes, so I do not think there is anything wrong with the data order. Evaluation is nDCG at 10 on the MS MARCO dev small set, which is the 6980 query file, and I also kept the recall at 100 from the first stage retriever so that I can tell whether a change is in the reranking or in the candidates. The base model scores 0.371 on that eval and the fine tuned adapter scores 0.394, so the gain is real but smaller than the number Sadia reported in her thesis chapter, and I think the difference is that she trained on the full file and not on a sample. I also ran the TREC DL 2019 set as a sanity check, since it has proper graded judgements, and there the base is 0.694 and the adapter is 0.703, which is inside the noise for 43 queries, so I would not put that number in a slide without saying so. Latency is the part I care about for the demo, because the reranker sits in front of the answer model, and at batch 16 on the same card the adapter adds about 3 milliseconds per query over the base, which is nothing, but on the CPU box the whole thing takes 340 milliseconds for 50 candidates and that is the number that will decide whether we ship it at all. I tried the ONNX export and it works, though the exported graph is 2 percent slower than the PyTorch path on CPU, which is the opposite of what I expected, and I have not chased that yet because it is not the blocker. The paper I keep coming back to is arXiv 2404.11762, the one on distilling cross encoders into late interaction models, and the reason it matters for us is that they get most of the reranking quality at a fraction of the serving cost, which is exactly the trade we are stuck on. There is also the RankZephyr line of work using a decoder model as a listwise reranker, and the numbers are better than ours, but the inference cost is not in the same universe and the licence on the checkpoint needs checking before anyone builds on it. For the next run I want three changes and I want them one at a time so that I can attribute the difference, starting with the full triples file instead of the 200000 sample because Sadia's result suggests the sample is what is holding the score down, then eight hard negatives instead of four, which doubles the step cost and so needs the batch size dropped to 32 to fit in memory, and last of all a listwise loss instead of the pairwise one, which is the change I understand least, so it goes at the end and gets its own eval. The checkpoint is saved at /scratch/nabil/runs/rerank_v4 with the optimizer state, and the wandb run is rerank-v4-hn4, and I have written the exact command into the README in that folder because I have lost a run to a forgotten flag before and it is not an experience I want again. One thing I have not done is check for overlap between the sampled training queries and the dev small queries, and until that check exists I am treating 0.394 as an upper bound rather than a result. I will run the overlap check tomorrow morning before the group meeting and if there is contamination the whole comparison has to be rerun on a clean split. The adapter on this run is rank 16, and every eval number above was measured with that adapter.

For the next run I want three changes and I want them one at a time so that I can attribute the difference, starting with the full triples file instead of the 200000 sample because Sadia's result suggests the sample is what is holding the score down, then eight hard negatives instead of four, which doubles the step cost and so needs the batch size dropped to 32 to fit in memory, and last of all a listwise loss instead of the pairwise one, which is the change I understand least, so it goes at the end and gets its own eval. The checkpoint is saved at /scratch/nabil/runs/rerank_v4 with the optimizer state, and the wandb run is rerank-v4-hn4, and I have written the exact command into the README in that folder because I have lost a run to a forgotten flag before and it is not an experience I want again. One thing I have not done is check for overlap between the sampled training queries and the dev small queries, and until that check exists I am treating 0.394 as an upper bound rather than a result. I will run the overlap check tomorrow morning before the group meeting and if there is contamination the whole comparison has to be rerun on a clean split.

input: This is the close list for Dunmore Mechanical for the period ending 30 November, and I want it finished before the 12th because the bank wants the statement package by the 15th and last quarter we were two days late with it. Payroll for the last two weeks of the month accrues at 62 hours of field time across four people plus the shop foreman at his salaried rate, and the burden rate stays at 34 percent until Marcy signs off on the new workers compensation quote. The retainage receivable on the Northside contract is 5 percent of the $412,000 billed to date, so that is the figure that has to tie to the schedule Kevin keeps, and if his schedule disagrees then his schedule is the one that is wrong, because the AIA billings are the source and not his spreadsheet. Sales tax on the material resale is due on the 20th and the return goes through the state portal rather than the paper form, and the login sits in the password file under Dunmore state tax where I put it in June. The Harbor Supply invoice came in dated 29 November for the copper, and it belongs in this period even though it was received in December, which is the kind of thing that gets missed when somebody codes from the postmark. Now on that accrual, make it $19,250. The credit card coding is done through the 27th and the last three days will come over in the morning feed, and the two charges at the airport are Kevin's and they are personal, so they go to the shareholder receivable and not to travel. The bank reconciliation has one outstanding item over 90 days, check 4412 for $1,180 to a vendor who never cashed it, and I want that voided and reissued rather than sitting there through the audit. Depreciation for the month is $3,275 on the existing schedule and there is one addition, the used skid steer bought on 8 November for $28,500, which goes on a seven year life with the half year convention and does not get bonus treatment because we are electing out this year. Owner distributions are $12,000 for the month and they are draws, not payroll, and I have told Dunmore twice that the reasonable compensation question is a conversation for him and the CPA and not something I am going to solve inside the general ledger. The 1099 vendor list has three vendors with no W-9 on file and I am holding their January payments until we have one, because chasing it in February never works. And back to the accrual one more time, it is $19,750.

input: The warehouse cutover weekend is 7 and 8 March, and I want the plan circulated to the site managers by Friday so that nobody is still asking basic questions in the last week. The Cape Town depot goes first because it has the smallest order book on a Saturday, and Durban follows a fortnight later once we know what broke. Inbound receiving stops at 14:00 on the Friday and anything arriving after that sits in the yard with a paper note on the pallet, which the drivers will not like, and I would rather have an unhappy driver than a receipt in two systems. Thandi is running the freeze list and she has authority to refuse a late booking without asking me, because if that decision has to come up to me on the day then the whole thing stalls while I am in a meeting. The picking teams work the Saturday morning on paper against a printed pick face report, and Sipho will print two copies of that report at 06:00 and keep one in the office safe, because the reprint takes forty minutes if the old system is already down. We have twelve casual staff booked for the Saturday and eight for the Sunday, and payroll needs their details by the 28th of the month before or they will not be paid on time, which has happened twice and both times it cost us goodwill we did not need to spend. The data load runs overnight on the Friday, and Ridwaan expects the stock file at about 380000 lines with the bin allocations, and the load fails if a bin code has a space in it, so the extract is being cleaned this week rather than on the night. Actually let us move the cutover to 14 and 15 March, the external audit team is on site the week before and I do not want two disruptions colliding. The reconciliation on the Sunday compares system stock against the paper picks, and any line that disagrees by more than two units gets counted physically before we open on the Monday. I want the count sheets signed by two people, not one, and the second signature has to be from someone who did not do the picking, which is not distrust, it is just how a control works. The customer service team needs a holding message from the Thursday, and the wording matters, so Naledi will draft it and I will approve it rather than letting anyone improvise on the phone about a system they have not seen. Our three largest accounts get a call and not an email, and those calls come from me because a director calling lands differently, and the retail chain in particular will remember it next time they are negotiating terms. The cutoff for the courier collections is 16:00 on the Saturday and the courier knows, but I want that confirmed in writing on the Wednesday because a verbal arrangement with a depot supervisor is worth very little at 15:45. If the load fails twice we stop, restore the old system, and go home, and that decision belongs to Ridwaan and me jointly with no other opinions in the room, because the pressure on the night will be to try a third time and a third attempt is how people end up trading on a broken stock file for a month. Contingency stationery, the pick pads and the goods received books, is already ordered and sitting in the training room. On the date, we stay with the 7th and 8th after all.

input: Site notes for the Demir house in Bebek after this morning's visit, and I want these typed up before the contractor's meeting on Thursday because half of what we agreed on site is not written down anywhere yet. The new opening in the ground floor party wall is 3600 wide and the head height stays at 2400, and the steel above it is the beam Erhan already sized, so that part of the drawing does not change. The floor build up in the same room is thinner than the survey said, 110 millimetres rather than 150, which means the underfloor heating and the screed will not both fit unless we drop to the low profile system, and that system costs more per square metre but it saves us from cutting into the slab. Mrs Demir wants the kitchen island moved 400 towards the terrace doors, which sounds small but it takes the walkway on the sink side down to 900, and 900 is workable for a family kitchen although it is tight when the dishwasher door is open, so I showed her the two positions with tape on the floor and she chose the terrace side with her eyes open. The terrace doors themselves are the item with the longest lead time, twelve weeks from order, and the ironmongery has to be confirmed at the same time as the frames, so that decision cannot wait for the finishes meeting in May. Glazing is the low iron glass on the terrace elevation only, because the difference is visible against the sea and not visible on the street side, and paying for it on all four elevations would be spending the client's money to prove a point. The bathroom on the first floor has a soil pipe running inside the wall we planned to remove, and the plumber says it can be diverted but only into the void behind the built in wardrobe, which loses 180 millimetres of wardrobe depth, so the wardrobe drawing needs revising before the joiner quotes. The stone for the hall floor is the Marmara white with a honed finish, and the samples on site are from two different batches, which is exactly why we asked for three square metres rather than a single tile, and the darker batch is the one we want. Erhan needs the revised structural drawings by the 18th and he has asked for the loads on the roof terrace to be confirmed as a planted terrace and not a paved one, because the difference in dead load changes the beam sizes over the living room. The electrician wants the lighting positions marked on the ceiling before the plasterboard goes on, and I would rather do that on site with the client present than argue about a drawing afterwards, so I am proposing the morning of the 22nd for that walk round. Waterproofing to the terrace is the detail I am least comfortable with, because the existing upstand is only 90 millimetres and the standard asks for 150, and raising it means either lifting the door threshold or accepting a lower upstand with a proper drainage channel in front of it, and the channel is what I will recommend. Paint colours are not decided and I have told Mrs Demir plainly that we do not need them decided until August, because deciding early only means deciding twice. One thing to correct from earlier, that ground floor opening is 3200 wide and not 3600, the beam sizing already assumed 3200.

input: Prep list for Thursday and Friday because we have the private party of 34 on the Friday and the normal service on top of it, so nothing can be left to the morning. The brine for the pork is 60 grams of salt per litre with the bay and the black pepper, and the loin goes in on Wednesday night for eighteen hours, no longer, because past a day the texture goes wrong and the party is paying for the good version. Ragu starts Wednesday as well, the big pot, eight kilos of beef and two of pancetta, and Matteo should keep it at a bare simmer for five hours and not touch the salt until the end when the reduction has happened. Tortelli filling is ricotta from Barbieri, the whole tins not the tubs, with the spinach squeezed properly because if there is water in the filling the pasta splits in the water and then we are plating apologies. We need 340 tortelli for the party and I want 400 made so that there is room for breakages, and they can be frozen on trays on the Thursday if there is space in the blast chiller after the ice cream. The ice cream is the pistachio and the fig leaf, two litres each, and the fig leaf one has to be infused on the Wednesday because the flavour needs the night to come out of the leaves. Bread comes from Rossi on both mornings but the party order has to be in by Wednesday noon, 60 rolls and four of the large loaves for the table, and last time we ordered late they simply did not have it. Antipasto for the party is the mortadella, the coppa, the pickled vegetables and the two cheeses, and the board is assembled to order and not in advance, because a board that has been sitting under the light for an hour looks tired and people notice. Vegetables from the market on Thursday morning, and Giulia is going because she argues better than I do about the price of the artichokes, and we need the small ones for the fritto and the big ones will not do. The fish for the normal service is whatever is good, and I will decide at the market rather than promising a species on the menu, so the board says fish of the day and the waiters explain it. Wine is delivered Thursday afternoon, twelve of the Lambrusco and eighteen of the Sangiovese for the party, and Paolo needs to know that the party has a fixed wine list because otherwise he will offer them the whole cellar and we will be uncorking bottles we cannot replace before Saturday. Service plan for the Friday, the party sits at 20:00 in the back room and the normal service starts at 19:00 in the front, so the pass is doing two things at once and the party goes out course by course on my call and not when a plate happens to be ready. Two extra pairs of hands booked for the Friday, one on the pass and one washing, and the washing one matters more than anybody thinks at eleven o'clock at night. On that brine, make it 50 grams a litre, the loin is in for eighteen hours and 60 is too much salt for that long.

input: Okay so this is the running order for season three and I am going to talk it through in the order I think it should go out rather than the order we recorded it, because the recording order was driven by who was available and it makes no sense as a listen. Episode 1 is the harbour one, which is the strongest cold open we have got, the sound of the crane at six in the morning and nobody talking for eleven seconds, and I want to protect those eleven seconds from whoever decides they are dead air. Episode 2 is the two brothers, and that one needs the most work in the edit because they talk over each other constantly and the transcript is going to be a nightmare, so Hana should budget a full day on it rather than the half day on the sheet. Episode 3 is the shortest, about twenty six minutes, and I am fine with that because the story ends where it ends and stretching it to thirty five would be padding for the sake of a number that only matters to us. So the Chapman interview goes into episode 4. Actually the clearance on her tape has not come back from the agent yet. It goes into episode 5. Episode 6 is the archive one with the radio recordings from 1974, and that is where the music licence question bites, because two of those clips have music under them and the archive cannot tell us who holds it, so we either clear it or we cut the music and lose the atmosphere. Amiria is chasing that and she has until the end of the month before we plan for the version without it. The season opens on 4 May and goes weekly, which means the last episode lands in the middle of June and we are clear of the awards deadline, and I do not want to hear about moving to fortnightly again because weekly is what built the audience in the first place. Studio time is booked for the 8th, the 15th and the 22nd for pickups and narration, three hours each, and if we do not use the third one I would rather cancel it a week out than hold it and waste the money. The sponsor read is forty seconds, host read, and it sits after the cold open and before the title, not in the middle, because mid roll on a story like this breaks the thing we are asking people to sit still for. Transcripts go up with each episode and not a week later, and they need the speaker names right, which sounds obvious and was wrong on four episodes last season and someone noticed and wrote to us about it. Artwork is the same series look with a different colour, and Tama has the files, and the only note from me is that the text has to be legible at the size a phone actually shows it and not at the size we look at it on a laptop. The trailer is ninety seconds, cut from episodes 1 and 6, no narration over it, and it goes out two weeks before the first episode with the feed change so that anyone subscribed gets it without doing anything. Promotion is the newsletter, the two radio interviews Amiria has lined up, and the live listening event at the museum if the room is free, and I am deliberately not doing the thing where we post a clip every day for a month, because it did not work last time and it exhausted everybody.

Kasia was on primary rotation and she acknowledged the page inside two minutes, which is in the audit log, and she went straight to the connection graph rather than the error dashboard because the error rate was still flat at that point. Tomasz joined at 02:21 without being paged because he was already awake, and he found the analytics job that had been retried by hand at 01:50 and was holding 60 connections open per worker. We killed that job at 02:29 and the pool came down to 61 percent within four minutes. The error rate never crossed the alert threshold, so this stays a near miss rather than a customer facing incident, and I will write it up under INC-2291 instead of opening a severity two. input: Notes on Bethany from the 11:15, second session after the meniscus repair on the left knee, week six. She came in reporting less swelling in the mornings and no locking at all since the last visit, which is what we wanted, and she has kept up the isometric holds daily but has been skipping the heel slides because they still pinch at the end of range. Range today is 0 to 118 passive and about 112 active, which is up from 105 last week, and extension is full with no lag when I test her seated. Quad activation is better and she can hold a straight leg raise for eight seconds now without the thigh shaking, so we have come off the towel prop. I gave her two sets of ten step downs from the four inch box, which is where she gets nervous rather than sore, and she needed the rail for the first three and then let go of it. After that we did three sets of twelve on the leg press at 30 pounds with a shallow depth and she managed all of it without pain, and her form held on the last set which it did not do a fortnight ago. Home program is the same isometrics plus the leg press if she has access at her gym, and I want the heel slides back in twice a day even if they pinch, as long as the pinch settles inside a minute. Oops, the step downs were from the six inch box, not the four inch, because we swapped rooms and the small box was already in use. Next visit is Thursday the 14th at 11:15 and I will retest range before we talk about jogging.

input: Draft abstract for the repair marker paper, first pass only, so treat the numbers as provisional. We annotated 1,200 spontaneous speech turns from the Utrecht corpus and coded every overt repair signal, treating oops as a class of its own rather than grouping it with sorry and with I mean, because the three do not behave the same way in the clause that follows them. Van der Meer and Kowalczyk report that oops precedes a factual substitution far more often than a syntactic restart, and our counts agree with them in direction although the effect is smaller, roughly 14 percentage points rather than 22. The case I find most interesting is the trailing oops, where the speaker marks the error after the substitution has already been made, which happened in 41 turns and is not described in the earlier taxonomy at all. I will dictate the method section tomorrow.

input: This is for the section on the transition period and it is rough because I am thinking out loud. Everyone talks about the 2021 regulations as if they arrived out of nowhere and they forget that the voluntary scheme ran alongside them for two full years, so a lot of the providers in our sample were operating under both at once and their returns look inconsistent for that reason and not because they were failing to comply. I keep having to explain this to people who have only ever read the final guidance. The other thing is the funding gap in the first year, which is sitting in the annex where nobody reads it, and people forget that too, so this time it goes in the body where they have to walk past it.

input: This is the draft of the upgrade note for arcctl and I am dictating it before I forget the order that things have to happen in. The change landed in 2.11.0, and it moves the whole configuration out of the single arcctl.yaml at the repository root into a directory of profile files under .arcctl/profiles, which sounds cosmetic and is not, because the loader precedence changed in the same release. Anyone who has been overriding values with environment variables needs to read the next part twice. In 2.10 the loader read arcctl.yaml first and then let any ARCCTL_ variable win over what was in the file, so people got used to putting a real value in arcctl.yaml and shadowing it in continuous integration, and that pattern is in most of our example repositories. That behaviour is now inverted, but only for profile files. A value written in a profile that was explicitly selected beats the environment, and the reasoning is that selecting a profile is a deliberate act while an inherited environment variable is very often an accident from a parent shell. The root arcctl.yaml still behaves the old way if you keep it, which is the compatibility path, and it will keep behaving that way until the 3.0 line at the earliest. So the safe upgrade is not to convert everything on the first afternoon. Run arcctl config lint first, and run it with the --explain flag, because --explain prints the resolved source of every key rather than only the value, and the resolved source is the only thing that will tell you whether a pipeline was quietly relying on the old precedence. On a repository with a large arcctl.yaml the lint run takes about forty seconds, and most of that is spent resolving remote includes, so you can cut it down with --no-remote when you only care about local keys. Then run arcctl config migrate with --dry-run, which writes nothing and prints the profile directory it would have created, and read that output side by side with the lint output rather than skimming it. The migrate command splits by top level key by default, so a file holding staging, production and a shared anchors block becomes two profiles and one shared file, and the anchors are copied into each profile rather than referenced, because YAML anchors do not cross file boundaries. The copying is the part that surprises people. If you leaned on anchors heavily you should expect duplication and expect to hand edit afterwards, and there is no flag that makes that cleaner because there is no correct general answer. When the dry run looks right, run the same command without --dry-run. It refuses to overwrite an existing .arcctl directory unless you pass --force, and we made that refusal loud rather than silent on purpose after the beta. Commit the generated directory and the original arcctl.yaml together in one change, because a reviewer needs to diff them against each other, and only delete arcctl.yaml in a later commit once a full pipeline has run green against the profiles. Keeping those two commits separate is the whole rollback story and I will say it again at the end. On the continuous integration side there are two things that need fixing and both of them are quiet failures rather than loud ones. The first is the cache key, which almost everybody has pinned to the hash of arcctl.yaml, and that key now goes stale in the wrong direction, because the file stops changing while the profiles underneath it change every week. Point the key at the directory instead of the file. The second is the selection flag. A pipeline that used to run arcctl deploy with no arguments and lean on the environment now has to name the profile, so arcctl deploy --profile production, and if it does not name one then arcctl looks for a profile called default, and a migrated directory does not contain a profile called default, so the command exits 2 with a message about no selectable profile. That exit code is stable and you can match on it if you are wrapping the tool in a script. Four internal pipelines broke on exactly that in the first week and all four were fixed by adding the flag, which is why this note leads with the flag rather than with the file layout. There is one genuine regression that I want written down in the note rather than buried in the changelog. Profile files are read with the same permissions check the old file had, but the directory itself is not checked, so a world writable .arcctl directory produces no warning at all. That is tracked as ARC-4187 and the fix is expected in the next patch release, and until it ships the guidance is to set the directory to 750 in your provisioning rather than waiting for the tool to tell you. Kate asked whether we should hold this note back until that patch is out and I do not think we should, because people are upgrading already and finding the precedence change by themselves, which is a worse way to learn it. For the rollback path, downgrading the binary is safe as long as you still have arcctl.yaml, because an older binary ignores the .arcctl directory completely and does not error when it sees one. If you have already deleted arcctl.yaml then the rollback is to restore it from the commit where migrate ran, which is the argument for keeping the two commits separate that I promised to repeat. I am going to add a short table of the new flags against their old equivalents, and one fenced example of a migrated profile, and then this can go to review. One correction to the top of this, the change landed in 2.12.0, not 2.11.0. The 2.11.0 release only shipped the lint --explain flag, which is why --explain is available to you before you migrate anything, and everything else in this note stands as I dictated it.
