input: Okay, this is the weekly update for the retrieval experiments and it is going to run long because there is a result in here that I did not expect and I want the reasoning written down and not just the number. So the setup, briefly, is the same as last week, the same 12,000 document subset, the same three chunk sizes, and the only thing I changed was the embedding model, which is now the 384 dimension one instead of the 768, because Rafi asked whether we were paying for dimensions we do not use. And the answer is that we mostly are, which I will get to. First though the boring part. The pipeline ran clean on Monday and Tuesday, it fell over on Wednesday night because the disk filled up with the intermediate parquet files that I never clean up, and I lost about four hours to that, which is entirely my fault and is now a cron job. Recall at ten on the 384 model is 0.81 and on the 768 model it was 0.83, so we lose two points, and the index is less than half the size and query latency at the ninety fifth percentile drops from 140 milliseconds to 61 milliseconds, which is better than I expected and better than the halving you would guess from the dimension count alone, probably because the whole index now fits in memory on the small box where before it did not. So two points of recall for less than half the memory and under half the latency, and my read is that we take that trade every single time on this workload. The unexpected thing is the chunk size interaction. On the 768 model the three chunk sizes were within about a point of each other on recall, 256 tokens, 512 tokens and 1024 tokens, all basically flat, and we concluded a while ago that chunk size did not matter much for these documents and stopped thinking about it. On the 384 model they are not flat at all. The 256 chunks lose almost nothing, they are at 0.80 against the 768 model's 0.81 at the same size, but the 1024 chunks fall off a cliff, they are at 0.71 against 0.83, which is twelve points and not two. And that makes sense once you say it out loud, because a 1024 token chunk is asking a 384 dimension vector to hold a lot more meaning than a 256 token chunk is, and at some point the vector runs out of room, so the smaller model is fine as long as you do not ask it to compress as hard. I should say that I only have one seed for each of these, so twelve points is real but 0.80 against 0.81 is inside the noise and I am not claiming it. Going back to what I said about Rafi's question, the honest answer is not that we are paying for dimensions we do not use, it is that we are paying for dimensions that only the long chunks use, and if we go to 256 chunk sizes we stop needing them. So for next week I want to do this in order. Step one, rerun the 384 model at 256 chunks with three seeds so I can put an error bar on it. Step two, check whether the 1024 falloff also shows up on the legal subset or whether it is specific to these documents. Step three, price out what the index actually costs at both dimensions on the production box, not the small one. If step one holds up I think the recommendation writes itself, which is 384 dimensions at 256 token chunks, and we take the memory back and spend it on keeping more of the corpus resident rather than on wider vectors. If step two says the falloff is general then it is a bigger finding than this ticket and somebody more senior than me should look at it, because it would mean the chunk size and dimension choices are not independent and a lot of the tuning advice out there treats them as if they are. One last thing, the 4 hours I lost on Wednesday means the ablation on the reranker did not happen at all this week, so that is not late, it is not started, and I would rather say that than carry it as in progress for another week.

So the shape of the fix is that we stop splitting the whole buffer up front and we let the quote state machine decide where a record ends, and that also fixes the case where the next line of the file starts with a quote character. input: Alright, design doc notes for the billing rework, and I am just going to talk through it because I think better this way and I can tidy it later. The problem we have is that the invoice total is computed in three different places and all three of them disagree in edge cases, and the edge case that actually bit us was the Nakamura account, because the Nakamura account has a mid cycle plan change and a credit note in the same period, and nothing in the current code knows what to do when both of those land together. So the first thing the doc has to say is that there is exactly one place that computes a total, and everything else calls it, and if that means the reporting job gets slower then the reporting job gets slower, because a slow correct number beats a fast wrong one. The second thing is the ordering, and this is where I keep going back and forth. If you apply the plan change first and then the credit note you get one answer, and if you apply the credit note first you get another, and the difference on the Nakamura account was about 40 dollars, which is small enough that nobody noticed for two quarters and large enough that finance was unhappy when they did. I talked to Priya about it on Tuesday and she said accounting convention is that credits apply against the period they were issued in, not the period they were earned in, so the credit note goes last, and I am going to write that down as a decision rather than an option so that the next person does not reopen it. Third thing, and this is the part I want reviewed hardest, is what happens on a refund after the period closes, because right now we reopen the period, and I do not think we should, I think we should issue an adjustment in the current period and leave the closed one closed. That is how the old system did it, which is not an argument on its own, but it is also what every accountant I have asked expects. Then there is the naming, which sounds trivial and is not, because the reporting team reads these column names every day. The field that holds the computed number should be snake case invoice total minor units and the unit has to be in the name, because the last three bugs in this area were all somebody assuming dollars where the code meant cents. The deposit is 300 dollars in the fixture and it is 30000 in the column and that is exactly the confusion I want the name to prevent.

input: Incident note for the ticket, and I am going to talk through it in the order it happened because I will lose the thread otherwise. At about ten past two the scanner started rejecting every request from the partner range and the log line it prints is caps on invalid client cert caps off which is what sent us down the wrong path for the first twenty minutes, because that string is also what it prints when the certificate is fine but the chain is missing an intermediate. The certificate was fine. The chain was missing the intermediate, exactly like the last time, and the last time was in April. I have put the intermediate back in the bundle on both nodes and restarted the scanner on the standby first so that we did not lose coverage, then the primary about four minutes later. Nothing was dropped in that window as far as I can tell from the counters, but the counters reset on restart so I would not swear to it in the review. So my suggestion is that we leave it alone. On the certificate bundle, I checked the other four regions this morning and three of them have the intermediate and one does not, and the one that does not is the region that has no partner traffic yet, which is luck rather than planning. I put the caps on the two spare tokens in the drawer, by the way, because they were rolling around loose and one of them already has a scratch across the contact. Somebody asked whether the log message is no caps in the older builds and it is not, it is the same string in every build we ship, and I checked three of them before I answered. Last thing, the April incident had the same root cause, the same root cause, and it is going to keep coming back until the message says which check actually failed.

input: Right, this is the weekly note for the platform group and I am going to do it in one go because if I stop I will not come back to it until Friday. Start with the migration, because that is what everybody asks about first. We are at seventeen of the twenty three services moved, and the six that are left are the ones with their own databases, which is exactly the order we said we would do it in, so nobody should be surprised. The two payment services are the awkward ones and I have told Rina that we are not moving those until the audit window closes in October, and she is fine with that as long as it is written down somewhere, so consider this the somewhere. On the incident from Monday, the summary is that a config push went out with the wrong region in it and the health checks passed anyway because the health check only asks whether the process is up, which we have known about for a year and a half. Vikram is adding a check that asks whether the process is serving the region it thinks it is serving, and that is in review now. The customer impact was about eleven minutes of elevated latency in one region and no errors that we can find, and support had four tickets, all four of them from the same customer, who I think just has very good monitoring. On hiring, we have two offers out and one accepted, the accepted one starts on the sixth of October, and the other one is still thinking about it and I do not want to chase them again this week because we chased them twice already. On the roadmap conversation, and this is the part I want people to actually read, we have three quarters of work in front of us and two quarters of runway before the platform freeze, so something is going to be cut and I would rather we chose it deliberately than discovered it in December. My own view is that the reporting rebuild is the thing to cut, because the current reports are ugly but nobody has ever escalated about them, whereas the queue work has been escalated about twice this quarter, twice, and both times by the same team that pays for a third of our capacity. I am not going to decide that in a written note, so I have put an hour on Thursday for it and I would like Rina and Vikram there, and anybody else who wants to argue about it is welcome. New paragraph. The other thing on Thursday is the on call rotation, because we are down to five people in it and one of them is on leave for three weeks in November, and I do not want to be the person who discovers that gap in November. There is a line break in the middle of the rotation table in the wiki that makes the second half look like a separate rota, and about half the team has been reading it that way, so somebody please fix the wiki before Thursday and then the conversation can be about the actual gap rather than about the table.

input: This is me talking through the revisions on the manuscript before I answer the editor, and it will be long because there are four reviewers and two of them disagree with each other, which I intend to say politely in the response letter rather than in this note. Reviewer one wants the method section reordered so that the sampling frame comes before the instrument description, and I think that is right, it reads oddly the way it is now, and it costs me nothing to move it. Reviewer two wants the whole second study removed, which I am not going to do, because the second study is the only part with the field data in it and without it the paper is a simulation paper with a discussion section that overclaims. Reviewer two also says the new paragraph on page nine repeats the framing from the introduction, and having read it again I agree, that paragraph exists because I wrote the introduction last and forgot what was already there, so it goes. Reviewer three is the useful one. Reviewer three points out that the confidence intervals in table two cannot be right given the sample sizes in table one, and they cannot, and the reason is that I recomputed table one after the resampling and did not recompute table two, which is embarrassing but at least it is arithmetic and not a design problem. I will redo table two tonight and check every row against the script output rather than against my memory of the script output. Reviewer four wrote four lines and one of them is about the line break in the caption of figure three, which is a typesetting artifact from the template and not something I put there, and I will mention it to production rather than argue with reviewer four about it. On the response letter, my plan is to take the reorder, take the paragraph deletion, take the table two correction, and push back on the second study with the field data argument spelled out, and I will say in the first line that all four reviews were read carefully, which is true, I read them three times, three times, because the first reading made me cross and the second reading is where the useful parts were. The bit I have not decided is whether to add the robustness check that reviewer one suggests in passing, because it would take a week and I do not think it changes anything, and saying that in a response letter without doing the check is how you get a second round of review. Van der Meulen had exactly this situation last year with the same journal and she did the check and it changed nothing and the paper was accepted, so possibly the answer is just to do it and stop reasoning about it. Last thing, the deadline is the twenty eighth, the twenty eighth, and I have a teaching week in the middle of that, so I want the table two work done before the weekend.

input: This is the status update for the alerting work and it is going to be long because three separate things landed this week and they interact. First thing, the new evaluator is on in staging and it has been on since Tuesday morning without a restart, which is the longest it has stayed up, and the reason it stayed up is that we stopped holding the whole window in memory and started streaming it, so the memory graph is flat now instead of sawtoothed. I want to say clearly that this was Priya's idea and not mine, because in the last update I described it as a team decision and that undersold it. Second thing, and this is the one that needs a decision from somebody who is not me, the latency threshold on the paging rule is currently 200 milliseconds delete that 250 milliseconds and that difference is the difference between about forty pages a week and about six, so it is not a detail. The number came out of the load test and the load test used the old evaluator, so honestly the number is stale either way and I would rather we picked it from a week of real staging data than argued about it from the test. Third thing, the runbook. The runbook is out of date in the way that runbooks always are, the first two steps are fine and everything after step three refers to the old dashboard that does not exist, and I have rewritten it in a draft but I have not published it because I want somebody who has actually been paged in the last month to read it first. Rohan has been paged twice in the last month, twice, so I am going to ask him. On the things I said last week that turned out to be wrong, there are two. I said the evaluator would need a schema migration and it does not, the existing table takes it as it is. And I said the old alert rules could be deleted at the same time, and they cannot, because two of them are wired into the customer status page and nobody knew that until Priya went looking. So the deletion is now a separate piece of work after the status page is decoupled, and I have not put a date on it. Next week I am mostly out on the hiring loop, so the only thing I expect to move is the threshold decision and the runbook review, and if neither of those moves the update next week will be short and I will not pretend otherwise. There is one new line in the alerting config that changes the evaluation interval and it is worth looking at in review, because it is the only line in that file anybody will need to understand later.

input: Notes on the style guide review, and this is all editorial, no decisions, because I want to send it round before anybody starts changing files. The biggest thing is the inconsistency in how we mark up keyboard input. In about half the pages we bold that and in the other half we use code formatting, and both look fine on their own but side by side in the same page it reads like two writers who never spoke to each other, which is accurate but not something we should be advertising. My preference is code formatting for anything you literally type and bold for interface labels you click, and if we agree on that I will do the pass myself rather than asking anybody else to. Second, we italic that far too much. There are pages with four italicised phrases in one paragraph and the effect is that none of them read as emphasis any more, they just read as a page that is slightly tilted. I would keep italics for the first use of a term and nothing else. Third, and this is the one I expect an argument about, the indent on the nested procedure steps is three spaces in the older pages and four in the newer ones, and the renderer does not care but the diffs are noisy every time somebody edits an old page with a new editor. Somebody is going to say that a linter should fix the indent automatically and they are right, and somebody else is going to say that we should not spend a sprint on whitespace and they are also right, so I am proposing we fix it only in pages we are already editing. On the CLI examples, the tab characters that got into three of the install pages need to go, because tab renders differently in the two themes we ship and one of them collapses it entirely. I have listed the three pages at the bottom of this note. Last thing, and it is small, the glossary has an entry that says to use spell mode when documenting how to pronounce a product name, and I have no idea what that entry means, I think it is left over from the voice project, and unless somebody claims it I am going to delete that entry. If you disagree with any of this, disagree in the doc rather than in a meeting, because the doc is where the decision has to end up anyway, and the doc is where I will look in six months when somebody asks why we do it this way.

input: Design note on the retry work, and I am writing it down because the last three conversations about this have all restarted from zero. The problem is that we retry on every failure class, including the ones that will never succeed on a second attempt, so a bad request gets tried four times and the client waits four times as long to be told the same thing. The fix is a classification step in front of the retry, and the shape of it is that we only retry on timeouts, connection resets, and explicit rate limit responses, and everything else fails immediately. That list is going to grow and I would rather it grew in one place than in the caller. On the config, the retry block in the service file needs the nesting to be right or the parser silently takes the defaults, which is how we ended up with a two second backoff in production for six weeks last year without anybody noticing. So write it as retry on. Indent. Timeouts. Resets. Rate limits. Outdent. And then the backoff key at the outer level, because the backoff applies to the whole block and not to any single failure class. The thing I am still unsure about is whether the classification lives in the client library or in the gateway, and I can argue both sides, so I have written both options into the doc and I am not going to pretend I have a view I do not have.

input: Reading notes on the distillation paper before the group meeting, and I am going to dictate all of it because my handwriting is unreadable and I lose paper notes. The setup is a 7B teacher and a 0.5B student, and the interesting part is not the distillation itself but the data selection, because they throw away about sixty percent of the teacher outputs before training on any of them. The filter is a disagreement score between two sampled teacher completions, and the claim is that high disagreement means the teacher is not confident and the label is noise, which is plausible and also exactly what you would expect somebody to write after the ablation came out that way. Their ablation table has four rows and the gap between no filter and their filter is 3.2 points on the held out set, which is a real gap, but the gap between random fifty percent filtering and their filter is 0.7 points, and 0.7 points on a set of that size is not a result, it is a mood. I want to raise that in the meeting without sounding like I am attacking the paper, because the engineering is genuinely good. On reproducing it, their repository is up and the config is readable, and the one thing I need to change is the field that holds the sampling temperature, which in our loader is camel case sampling temperature and in theirs it is a positional argument, so the loader shim has to map it. Our trainer class is pascal case student trainer and it already takes a filter callable, so the filter itself is about twenty lines and most of that is logging. I checked the licence and it is Apache 2.0 with a model card that says research use, which is fine for the group meeting and a conversation with legal if it ever goes further than that. The numbers I want to get before Thursday are the disagreement score distribution on our own data, because if our teacher agrees with itself almost everywhere then their filter throws away nothing and the whole thing is a no op for us, and that is the result I actually expect. I say that every week and I am wrong about half the time, about half, so I would rather measure it than argue about it. One more thing, the paper reports everything in tokens per second on eight A100s and we have four, so every throughput number in my write up needs to say four, four, because somebody always reads the table without reading the caption and then quotes it in a deck.

input: Okay, recap of the Fairfield visit while it is fresh, and I am driving so this is going to wander a bit. Good meeting overall. Four people in the room, two of them are new since the last time I was there, and the new operations lead is the one who matters because she owns the renewal and she was the only one asking real questions. Her name is Denise and she came from the retail side, so she thinks about seat counts the way a store manager thinks about stock, which actually made the conversation easier because the seat model made sense to her immediately. The blocker is not price. I want to say that clearly because the last three notes I wrote about this account said price and it is not price, it is that their finance team will not approve anything with an annual commitment until the new fiscal year starts in April, and no amount of discounting changes that, and I have stopped trying. What we can do is a three month bridge on the current terms, which their procurement person suggested herself, so it is not me pushing it, and I have asked her to put that in writing so it does not turn into a different conversation in March. On the technical side, they have one integration that broke in the spring and nobody logged a ticket for it, they just stopped using that report, and Denise found out about it in the meeting which was not comfortable for the person sitting next to her. I said we would look at it and I did not promise a date. Somebody on their side has a new line in the export that our importer does not recognise, or that is my guess from the way they described it, and I am not going to diagnose it from memory in a car. Two smaller things. They want the invoice to show the department code, which finance says is a five minute change and I have heard that before. And they asked whether we can put the renewal date in all caps on the summary page because their auditor missed it last year, which is a strange request but it costs us nothing and I said yes. Last thing and then I will stop, the old champion at that account, the one who left in February, has landed at a much bigger company in the same sector, and she liked us, she really liked us, so somebody should find out where she went before a competitor does. That is the actual value of this trip, not the renewal.

input: Minutes for the trustees meeting on the eleventh, and I am dictating these straight after so I do not lose the detail, and I will tidy the order later if it needs it. Present were myself, Gareth, Anwen, and the new co-opted trustee from the housing association, whose surname is spell mode P R Y D D E R C H because everybody spells it wrong including the bank, and apologies were received from Meredith who is still recovering. First item was the audit, and the short version is that the auditor is happy with the accounts but not happy with our record keeping on restricted funds, and specifically he wants a separate ledger line for the youth programme money rather than a note at the bottom of the page. Gareth argued that the note is sufficient because it has always been sufficient, and the auditor's position is that it was sufficient when the restricted funds were four thousand pounds and it is not sufficient now that they are forty one thousand, and having listened to both I think the auditor is right and I said so. So that is an action for the treasurer before the year end. Second item was the building, which took up most of the meeting as it always does. The roof survey came back and the estimate is between eighteen and twenty two thousand depending on whether the joists on the north side need replacing, and we will not know that until the tiles come off, which is the worst possible way to find out. We have twenty six thousand in reserves and a policy that says we keep three months of running costs untouched, which is about nine thousand, so on paper we can do it and on paper we cannot do it if the joists are bad and something else happens in the same year. input: Referee report on the submission, second round, and I will dictate it in the order of the manuscript rather than in the order of my irritation. The authors have addressed two of my three substantive comments and I am satisfied with both. The sampling frame is now described properly, and the new paragraph they have added on page four is exactly what was needed, so I withdraw that comment entirely. The measurement section is also improved, although the improvement consists largely of moving material that was already there, and I note that without objecting to it. My third comment has not been addressed and the response letter does not really engage with it. I said in the first round that the identification strategy relies on an assumption about the timing of the policy change which the paper does not defend, and the authors have replied that the assumption is standard in this literature. It is standard in this literature. It is also wrong in at least two of the papers they cite as precedent, which is a poor argument for keeping it, and the fact that a mistake is conventional is not a defence of the mistake. What I would accept is a paragraph acknowledging the assumption and a robustness check with the alternative timing, and if the result survives the check the paper is stronger and if it does not survive the check then the paper as written should not be published, which is precisely why the check matters. I do not think this is an unreasonable amount of work. On presentation, three smaller matters. Table three is unreadable at the printed size and the authors should either split it or move half of it to an appendix, and I would prefer they split it because the second half is the part a reader will want beside the first. The figure captions are inconsistent in whether they state the sample size, and where the sample differs from the main analysis the caption must say so, which in two of the six figures it does not. The bibliography contains one entry with the author's initials in all caps and the rest in mixed case, which I mention only because a copy editor will otherwise mention it to them later and at greater cost. On the response letter itself, I want to say something that is not a criticism of the paper. The letter is defensive in a way that will not serve the authors well, and I say that as somebody who wrote defensive response letters for the first ten years of his career. A referee who has misunderstood something is usually telling you that the manuscript can be misunderstood, and the useful reply is not to explain that the referee is wrong, it is to make the misunderstanding impossible on the page. My recommendation is minor revision, conditional on the robustness check, and I am content for the editor to accept it on his own judgement afterwards without sending it back to me. If the authors decline the check I would want to see it again, and in that case I would want to see the alternative timing discussed rather than delete that whole line of argument, which they may be tempted to do because it is the shortest route to acceptance and it is the wrong one.

input: Okay so this is the bug report for the upload crash and I will try to keep it in order even though I have been staring at it since this morning. The short version is that any file over about forty megabytes fails on the second retry, not the first, which is what made it hard to see, and the reason it took us three days is that the first retry succeeds and everybody stops looking there. I have reproduced it on my own machine twice and on the staging box once. The stack trace is in the run I linked from the ticket, and the full log is at logs dot internal slash uploads slash retry dash trace, which you will need the VPN for. If you want the smaller version without the noise I stripped it and dropped it at gist dot internal slash steady dash upload, same login as always. Now the actual fault, as far as I can tell, is in the retry guard, because the condition reads attempts greater than max retries when it should read attempts greater or equal max retries, and on that boundary it lets one more request through with a stale token. I am going to say that again because it is the whole bug, the boundary lets one more request through with a stale token, and the token is what the server rejects, not the file. The error the user sees is completely unhelpful, it just says upload failed please try again, and there is a star next to it in the dialog which I am fairly sure is a leftover from the old plans badge and has nothing to do with any of this. There is also a plus icon on that same dialog that does nothing at all when you press it. I did not touch either of those. The older ticket had a hash in its title, which is probably why nobody found it by searching, so please do not close this one as a duplicate of the timeout ticket, they look identical from the outside and they are not the same bug.

input:
Okay this is the incident write up for Tuesday night and I want to get it down before the review tomorrow because the timeline in the ticket is wrong in two places and I keep correcting people in the channel about it. At 21:40 the ingest queue started backing up and the first thing anyone saw was the consumer lag graph going almost vertical, and the on call was paged at 21:47, which is about the seven minute gap we expect from that alert because it has a five minute window and then a two minute cooldown. The part that made the first twenty minutes confusing is that Cooper Netties had already restarted two of the ingest pods before the page went out, so by the time the on call opened the dashboard the pod count was back to four out of four and green, and the lag was still climbing, and that reads like an application bug rather than a scheduling problem. So we spent about eighteen minutes looking at the consumer code, which was the wrong place, and I want that in the write up because it is the actual lesson here, not the fix.

The real cause was the connection pool. We moved PgBouncer onto the same node group as the ingest workers in release 4.2.1 on Monday afternoon, and the pool is sized at 200 connections, and the workers each open 12, and with the autoscaler allowed to go to 24 replicas that is 288 connections against a 200 connection pool, so once the queue got deep enough to trigger a scale up the workers started failing to get a connection, and the failure path retries with a two second backoff, and that is what the lag graph was actually showing. It was never the consumer logic. Nobody caught it in review because the pool size lives in the Terraform module and the replica ceiling lives in the Helm values file and the two numbers have never been in the same pull request.

At 22:05 Priya noticed the connection refused count in the Postgres logs and that is when the direction changed. We set the replica ceiling down to 16 by hand, which brings it to 192 connections, and the lag started draining at about 22:11 and was flat by 22:34. The queue never lost a message, which is worth saying clearly in the write up because two people in the channel assumed we had dropped data and that is now in three different threads. The dead letter queue has 41 messages in it from that window and every one of them is a schema validation failure unrelated to this, they are the usual malformed vendor payloads and they were already there on Monday.

The thing I want to argue about in the review is the alerting, not the pool. We have an alert on consumer lag and an alert on pod restarts and no alert at all on the pool utilisation, and Kubernetties restarting a pod is treated as routine so those restarts do not page anyone and they do not even show on the main dashboard, you have to go and look at the events. If we had a panel showing pool connections in use against the pool ceiling this would have been a two minute incident. So the action items I want are, one, put pool utilisation on the main dashboard with a page at 85 percent, and two, move the replica ceiling into the same module as the pool size so the arithmetic is visible in one file, and three, write the actual number down in the runbook, because right now the runbook says scale the workers if the lag is climbing, which is exactly the advice that made this worse.

I also want to note the human side of it, because Priya was on call for the third night in a row and found the cause at 22:05 after the rest of us had been in the wrong file for eighteen minutes, and the reason she found it is that she has read those Postgres logs before during the migration in March. That is not a process, that is one person's memory, and it is the second incident this quarter that resolved because she happened to be awake for it. I do not want to write an action item about that but I do want it in the narrative.

One more thing before I forget it. The rollback question came up at 22:18 and we decided not to roll back 4.2.1, and I still think that was right, because the release also carries the fix for the duplicate delivery bug and rolling it back would have brought that back, and by 22:18 we already had the replica ceiling change in and the lag was draining. But the reason we could make that call in two minutes is that Cuba Netties had not been touched by the release at all, the release only changed where PgBouncer runs, and if it had changed the scheduling as well I do not think we would have been able to reason about it that fast. So the write up should say that we got away with the decision rather than that we made a good one.
output:

The real cause was the connection pool. We moved PgBouncer onto the same node group as the ingest workers in release 4.2.1 on Monday afternoon, and the pool is sized at 200 connections, and the workers each open 12, and with the autoscaler allowed to go to 24 replicas that is 288 connections against a 200 connection pool, so once the queue got deep enough to trigger a scale up the workers started failing to get a connection, and the failure path retries with a two second backoff, and that is what the lag graph was actually showing. It was never the consumer logic. Nobody caught it in review because the pool size lives in the Terraform module and the replica ceiling lives in the Helm values file and the two numbers have never been in the same pull request.

At 22:05 Priya noticed the connection refused count in the Postgres logs and that is when the direction changed. We set the replica ceiling down to 16 by hand, which brings it to 192 connections, and the lag started draining at about 22:11 and was flat by 22:34. The queue never lost a message, which is worth saying clearly in the write up because two people in the channel assumed we had dropped data and that is now in three different threads. The dead letter queue has 41 messages in it from that window and every one of them is a schema validation failure unrelated to this, they are the usual malformed vendor payloads and they were already there on Monday.

The thing I want to argue about in the review is the alerting, not the pool. We have an alert on consumer lag and an alert on pod restarts and no alert at all on the pool utilisation, and Kubernetes restarting a pod is treated as routine so those restarts do not page anyone and they do not even show on the main dashboard, you have to go and look at the events. If we had a panel showing pool connections in use against the pool ceiling this would have been a two minute incident. So the action items I want are, one, put pool utilisation on the main dashboard with a page at 85 percent, and two, move the replica ceiling into the same module as the pool size so the arithmetic is visible in one file, and three, write the actual number down in the runbook, because right now the runbook says scale the workers if the lag is climbing, which is exactly the advice that made this worse.

I also want to note the human side of it, because Priya was on call for the third night in a row and found the cause at 22:05 after the rest of us had been in the wrong file for eighteen minutes, and the reason she found it is that she has read those Postgres logs before during the migration in March. That is not a process, that is one person's memory, and it is the second incident this quarter that resolved because she happened to be awake for it. I do not want to write an action item about that but I do want it in the narrative.

One more thing before I forget it. The rollback question came up at 22:18 and we decided not to roll back 4.2.1, and I still think that was right, because the release also carries the fix for the duplicate delivery bug and rolling it back would have brought that back, and by 22:18 we already had the replica ceiling change in and the lag was draining. But the reason we could make that call in two minutes is that Kubernetes had not been touched by the release at all, the release only changed where PgBouncer runs, and if it had changed the scheduling as well I do not think we would have been able to reason about it that fast. So the write up should say that we got away with the decision rather than that we made a good one.

Right, notes from the model sync so I can paste this into the thread. Laura is running the eval sweep this week and she wants the results table by Friday morning her time, which is Thursday evening for us, so anything we want in it has to be merged by Wednesday night. She has the harness set up on the two A100 box and she said she will not add any more configurations after Wednesday because the sweep takes about nine hours per configuration and she wants a day of slack before the review.

We agreed on five configurations. The base model with no adapter at all as the control, then rank 8, rank 16, rank 32, and then the rank 16 one again with the projection matrices frozen for the first 200 steps, which is the thing Dev wanted to test. Laura pushed back on the rank 64 configuration because she has run it twice on the smaller dataset and both times it was worse than rank 16 and she does not want to spend nine hours proving it a third time. I think she is right. If somebody wants it they can run it themselves after the review.

The thing that is still open is the eval set. We have 56 held out cases and Laura's point is that 56 cases cannot separate two configurations that are three points apart, and she is right about that, so she is proposing we report the per category breakdown instead of a single number and just say out loud that the differences inside a category are not significant. I would rather do that than pretend the single number means something. She also asked whether we can get the eval set to 200 cases before the sweep and the honest answer is no, not by Wednesday, because every case is hand written and reviewed and we are adding maybe eight a day at the moment.

Two smaller things. First, she found that the harness was loading the adapter twice on the first case of every run, which added about forty seconds and did not change any output, and she has a one line fix for it sitting on a branch waiting for someone to look at it, so if you have ten minutes please review that because it is holding up her sweep. Second, she wants the checkpoint naming changed so that the rank is in the directory name rather than only in the config file, because she has three checkpoints on disk right now that she cannot tell apart without opening the config, and that is a completely reasonable complaint and it takes one line in the training script.

For the review itself Laura is presenting the sweep results and I am presenting the data audit, and we should keep the two separate because the audit conclusion is that 180 rows were defective and that is going to generate a long conversation on its own and I do not want it to eat the sweep discussion. If it runs over we push the sweep to the following week and Laura is fine with that as long as nobody asks her to rerun anything in the meantime.

Last thing, she asked me to say in the thread that the two A100 box is booked for her until Thursday noon, so if you need it for anything else ask her first rather than just starting a job on it, because somebody did that last month and both runs got slower and it took an afternoon to work out why.

So the peering request from the analytics team is going to be a problem and I want to explain why before the meeting rather than in it. Their VPC is 10.0.0.0/16 and ours is 10.0.0.0/16 as well, because both of them were created from the same starter template about four years ago and nobody changed the default, and you cannot peer two VPCs with overlapping address space, so this is not a permissions question or a quota question, it is arithmetic. The peering connection will accept the request and then every route you try to add will fail.

There are three ways out of this and none of them are cheap. We can renumber our VPC, which means every subnet, every security group rule that references a cider block by hand, and the two on premise firewall rules that were written by someone who has left, and I would guess that is three weeks of work and one outage. Or we can put a private link in front of the four services they actually need, which is my preference, because it is about two days of work and it does not touch anything else. Or we can proxy through the shared services account, which works but adds a hop and means the analytics team's queries get billed to us.

I am going to argue for private link. Can you pull the list of what they are actually querying before Thursday so we can say the number of services out loud rather than guessing at it.

Quick note on the offline mode bug before I lose it. What the user reported is that if they open the app on the train, edit two notes, and then close it before they get signal, one of the two edits is gone when they come back. I reproduced it this morning with the network conditioner and it is not random, it is always the second edit, and it is always the one made after the first save attempt failed.

What is happening is that the failed save leaves the record marked as pending, and the second edit writes over the same record and clears the pending flag, because the flag is set on the record rather than on the individual change, so the second edit's success clears the first edit's failure and the queue never retries it. That is a one record one flag design and it needs to be a queue of changes instead.

The fix is not small. We either move to a change log per record, which is the correct thing and about a week, or we keep the flag and refuse the second edit while the first is pending, which is horrible for the user but takes an afternoon. I want the week. The reason I want the week is that the sink is going to get worse when we add shared notebooks and a per record flag cannot express two people editing the same record at all.

Memo for the file on the Thapa matter. The client came in on Monday with a demand letter about work that was invoiced in March 2022, and the first thing I checked is the statue of limitations, because on a written contract in this jurisdiction it is six years and on an oral one it is three, and the whole question is which of those two this is. There is no signed agreement. There is an email from the client's operations manager saying go ahead and start, and there are eleven invoices, all paid except the last two.

My view is that the email plus the invoices is enough to make this a written contract for these purposes, which puts us inside the six years comfortably, but I want to be careful about saying that to the client as though it is settled, because the email does not contain the price and the argument on the other side is going to be that the price was agreed on a call. If the price was agreed orally then they will say the contract is oral.

Two things I need before I advise. The phone records for the week of 14 March 2022, which the client says they can get, and the original scope document if it exists, because the operations manager's email refers to the scope we discussed and if there is a document with that name attached anywhere this gets much easier.

Okay I am recording this for myself so I do not forget where I got to tonight. The docker build is finally working on the laptop, and the reason it was failing for three days is nothing to do with the Dockerfile, it is that the base image I copied from the tutorial is amd64 only and this machine is arm, so every apt install step was running under emulation and timing out at exactly 300 seconds which looked like a network problem, and I spent two evenings changing the mirror. So the lesson is check the architecture first. I changed the base image to the slim bookworm one and the build is now 90 seconds.

Next thing is the dataset loader. Right now it reads the whole 400 megabyte json into memory before the first batch, which is fine on the laptop but the college server has 2 gigabytes per user and it gets killed. I need to switch to reading line by line, and the file is already jsonl so that is not hard, but the shuffle is the problem because you cannot shuffle a stream, so I will do the shuffle buffer thing where you keep 10000 lines in memory and pick randomly from those. Prof said that is good enough for this and I should not spend a week on it.

Then the evaluation. I have the accuracy number working but it is not the number I want, because it counts a whole output as wrong if one token is different, and for this task most of the output is copied from the input, so the accuracy is 94 percent and it looks amazing and it means nothing. What I actually want is the accuracy on the tokens that changed, which needs me to align the input and the output first, and I have not written that yet. That is tomorrow.

The thing I am stuck on and want to ask about in the lab meeting is the pile pat handling, because when the input has a Windows style path in it the model keeps turning the backslashes into forward slashes, and I do not know if that is the tokenizer or the training data. I checked twenty examples and none of them have a backslash in them at all, so my guess is the training data, but I want somebody to tell me if there is a way to check that properly instead of guessing.

Small things. The wandb logging is off because I ran out of the free tier, so right now I am printing to a text file and reading it with tail, which is bad but working. The checkpoints are 1.2 gigabytes each and I have deleted everything except the last three. And I need to email the lab about the GPU booking for next week before Friday because last time I forgot and got Sunday night.

Also the tutorial I have been following is from 2023 and the API has changed twice since then, so about a third of what it says does not work any more, and I keep discovering that the hard way. If anyone in the lab knows a current one that would save me a lot of evenings.

One more. I want to write the report as I go this time instead of at the end, so I am going to keep a file with one paragraph per day, and even if the paragraph is I did nothing today, I write it, because last semester I lost two weeks of detail by trying to remember it in April.

Right, bug triage notes for the standup. Century flagged 340 instances of the same null pointer overnight and all of them are on the checkout page and all of them are Safari 16, which is the version we said we would stop supporting in March and then did not. The stack trace points at the payment button handler and what is happening is that the optional chaining we added last month compiles fine but the polyfill is not in the Safari bundle, so the property access throws instead of returning undefined.

The fix is one line in the build config and I have it ready, but I want to check something before I push it, because the 340 instances came from 41 users, which means most of those users tried more than once, and if they tried more than once and it failed every time then we have lost 41 checkouts and that number should go in the ticket, not the 340. I will get the exact figure from the analytics before standup.

The other thing is that this should have paged somebody. The alert rule is set on error rate as a percentage of sessions and Safari 16 is under one percent of our traffic, so 340 errors in one browser never crosses the threshold. I do not know what the right rule is yet but percentage of sessions is clearly not it on its own.

Notes on the login work before I forget the order. The email and password path is done and the reset email is going out through the new provider, and I tested it on three accounts this morning including one with a plus in the address because that broke last time. The session cookie is set to 14 days and it is httpOnly and secure, and there is still no refresh rotation, which is on the list but not this week.

What is not done is the Google button. The button exists and it opens the consent screen and it comes back with a code, and then the token exchange fails with an invalid redirect, and the reason is that the redirect we send includes the port number in development and the console entry does not have it. I fixed it for localhost:3000 by adding that exact entry, but the preview deploys get a random subdomain every time and you cannot register a wildcard there, so preview deploys will keep failing until we put a stable proxy in front of them.

So the honest status is that the oath flow works on my machine and on production and nowhere in between, and I do not want to tick it off in the sprint board while that is true because somebody will find out the hard way on a review deploy.

So the reason the pricing page is showing last week's numbers for some people is the CDN, not the database, and I want to be clear about that because two people have now gone looking in the pricing service.

The page is served as a static asset with a one week max age, which was set two years ago when the prices changed twice a year, and the prices now change on the first of every month, so for up to a week after a change some fraction of users see the old ones. It is not a cash invalidation bug, there is no invalidation at all, nobody wired one up, the header just expires eventually. Which also means the fix is not a code fix, it is a purge on deploy plus a much shorter max age, and the shorter max age is the part that needs a decision because it costs us origin requests.

My suggestion is five minutes and a purge on the pricing deploy specifically, and leave everything else at a week. The pricing page is one file and five minutes of staleness on a price is survivable, whereas a week is a support ticket and arguably worse than that if somebody screenshots it.
output:
So the reason the pricing page is showing last week's numbers for some people is the CDN, not the database, and I want to be clear about that because two people have now gone looking in the pricing service.

The page is served as a static asset with a one week max age, which was set two years ago when the prices changed twice a year, and the prices now change on the first of every month, so for up to a week after a change some fraction of users see the old ones. It is not a cache invalidation bug, there is no invalidation at all, nobody wired one up, the header just expires eventually. Which also means the fix is not a code fix, it is a purge on deploy plus a much shorter max age, and the shorter max age is the part that needs a decision because it costs us origin requests.

My suggestion is five minutes and a purge on the pricing deploy specifically, and leave everything else at a week. The pricing page is one file and five minutes of staleness on a price is survivable, whereas a week is a support ticket and arguably worse than that if somebody screenshots it.

Test suite status, because I said I would write it down after the last time this came up in retro. The unit tests are 1,240 and they run in 40 seconds and they are fine and nobody complains about them. The integration tests are 180 and they take eleven minutes because each one spins a fresh Postgres container, and about six of them are flaky in a way that goes away on rerun, which means everybody reruns everything and nobody investigates.

I have looked at the six. Four of them share a fixture that seeds a user with a fixed email and they collide when the suite runs in parallel, and that is a real fix, one afternoon. The other two are timing on a webhook and I do not understand them yet.

The browser tests are the ones I want to talk about. We have 22 of them, they run headless in CI with the trace on first retry, they take nineteen minutes, and they have not been touched since the redesign in February, so nine of them are skipped and the other thirteen only cover the login page and the settings page. Either we invest in play right properly and cover the checkout flow, which is the only flow where a break costs money, or we admit that the browser tests are decoration and delete them. I would rather have four good ones than 22 like this.

This is the platform update for the Friday note, and it is mostly about the state file mess, so bear with me because the order matters.

We have four terror form repos and they all share one state bucket, which was fine when there was one team and it is not fine now. The billing module is in the platform repo, the network module is in the platform repo, the ECS services are in the app repo, and the DNS is in a repo nobody has touched since the person who made it left. Three of those four write records into the same hosted zone, so a plan in the app repo shows changes to resources the network repo owns, and everybody has learned to ignore the diff, which is exactly how you delete a production record by accident.

What I want to do is move the hosted zone into its own repo with its own state, and have the other three consume it as a data source rather than a resource. That is about two days of moving state entries around, and it is boring, and it is the highest value thing on my list this quarter, because right now the only thing stopping a bad apply is that people are being careful, and people stop being careful in December.

The second problem is version drift. The app repo pins the provider at 5.31 and the platform repo is on 5.72 and the DNS repo has no pin at all, so whatever terra form downloads on the day is what runs, and last Tuesday that turned into a plan that wanted to recreate the load balancer, which is the kind of surprise that ends an afternoon. I want a shared version file and a lock committed in all four, and I want CI to fail if the lock changes without somebody saying why in the pull request.

Third, and this is the one I need agreement on rather than time for, nobody can run apply locally any more except me and Dinesh, because the role trust policy lists two ARNs and adding a third needs a change through the security board. That is good for safety and it means the queue for infra changes is two people deep and both of us are also on call. My proposal is that apply runs only in CI, from a role no human holds, and local runs are plan only for everyone including us. That is more work up front and it removes the person shaped bottleneck.

Small things after that. The old bastion is still running and costs about 90 dollars a month and nothing has connected to it since April. There are eleven security groups with no attachments. And the tear a form docs we wrote in 2024 describe a directory layout we abandoned, so anybody following them creates files in the wrong place, and I would rather delete that page than leave it.

The one thing I am not proposing is a rewrite into modules that we publish internally, because we tried that at the last place and it turned into a team maintaining a module registry nobody wanted, and I do not think we are big enough for it.

Recording this for the board pack so somebody can turn it into slides, and I will be specific about numbers because last time the summary lost them.

Cash position first. We closed October with 1.4 million in the operating account and 300,000 in the reserve, and the reserve has not been touched since it was set up, which I want to keep saying out loud because two people keep treating it as runway. Burn was 210,000 in October, which is up from 185,000 in September, and the whole increase is the two engineering hires plus the annual insurance renewal, so it is not a trend, it is a step and then flat.

On the facility, the second trench of the loan is available from 1 December and the covenant is the same as the first, which is the revenue test measured quarterly, and we passed it in Q3 with about 12 percent of headroom. My recommendation is that we do not draw it in December. The interest starts on drawdown, we do not need the money before March on current burn, and drawing early to feel safe costs us about 4,000 a month for nothing. If the March number looks different we draw then.

Revenue. 96,000 recognised in October against a plan of 110,000, so we are 14,000 light, and the reason is one customer who signed on 28 October instead of 1 October, which is a timing miss and not a lost deal, and it lands in November. Underneath that, renewals are running at 91 percent by value and the two that did not renew are both under 500 a month, so the churn number looks worse as a count than it is as money, and I want the board pack to show both, because showing only the count invites the wrong question.

Receivables are the problem I want help with. We have 240,000 outstanding and 60,000 of it is over 90 days, and it is four customers, and three of them always pay eventually and one of them I am not sure about. I have stopped chasing by email because it does not work and I am calling instead, and I would like one of the non executives to make one call to the largest of them, because a call from a board member changes the answer in a way my fourth email does not.

Payroll and compliance are clean. The quarterly filings went in on 12 October, the pension contributions are current, and the audit letter has no open items from last year.

One risk I want minuted rather than solved. Our largest customer is 31 percent of recurring revenue and their contract renews in June with 90 days notice, so we know in March. Nothing in the relationship is bad. It is simply a number that would be irresponsible not to say in a board meeting, and I would rather it be in the minutes now than raised for the first time in April.

Last thing on the forecast. The model in the pack assumes November revenue of 130,000, which is October's plan plus the delayed signature, and it assumes burn flat at 210,000, and it does not assume the facility. On those numbers we end December at about 1.3 million and we do not cross the reserve at any point in the next nine months.

Quick one on the batch job cost before I forget the numbers. The nightly aggregation runs on one easy too instance that we launched by hand in 2023 and never touched, and it is an m5 dot 4 xlarge, and it runs for about forty minutes and then sits idle for twenty three hours. So we are paying full time for a machine that works for three percent of the day, and it is about 550 dollars a month.

Two options. Either the job moves to a scheduled task that starts a spot instance, runs, and terminates, which is maybe a day of work and takes the cost to under 40 dollars, or we move it into the existing cluster as a cron job, which is half a day but the memory ceiling in the cluster is 8 gigabytes per pod and the job peaks at 11.

I would rather do the spot instance version, and the reason is not the cost, it is that the current machine has three years of packages installed by hand and nobody knows what is on it, so rebuilding it from a script is the actual win and the saving is a bonus. If we lift it into the cluster we still do not know what is on it.

This is my note before the meeting with HR on Thursday and I want to be careful about how I put it, so I am going to say the facts and not the conclusion.

Two people on the team have separately told me the same thing about the same person, and neither of them wants to be named, and both of them asked me whether saying it would get back to him. That is the part I keep thinking about, because if two people are asking that question then the answer they expect is yes, and that tells you something about the team regardless of what happened.

What I plan to say on Thursday is only what I saw myself, which is the two meetings in October where he talked over her and then repeated her point as his own, and I said something afterwards in one of those and not the other. I am not going to repeat the second hand accounts, because they are not mine to bring and because the two people who told me were being discreet with me and I should be the same with them.

What I want from HR is process advice, not a decision. Specifically, whether there is a way for those two to raise something without it landing on his desk with their names on it, because as far as I can tell there is not, and if there is not then the policy page is misleading.

Training run notes, day four. The loss curve is finally behaving and I think the fix was the learning rate warmup rather than anything I did to the data, which is annoying because I spent two days on the data.

Loss at the end of the third epic was 0.41 and it is 0.33 now on the same held out split, and the shape is the one you want rather than the cliff we had on Monday, so I am going to let it run to eight and stop there rather than twelve, because the last three runs all got worse after eight and I have no reason to think this one is different.

The thing I am watching is the no op rate, because at the moment the model changes something in 78 percent of cases and the target is closer to 60, and that gap is the whole problem with this task. It edits when it should hold still. I do not think more steps fixes that, I think it is a data problem, which is why I spent the two days on the data.

Checkpoints are on the box at 2.1 gigabytes each and I am keeping four. The eval takes nine minutes so I am only running it at the end of each pass, not per thousand steps like the tutorial says.

Handing the prototype over so here is everything in one go. The front end is on Vercel and the database and auth are both super base, and I picked that because the free tier does row level security and I did not want to write an auth layer for a prototype.

The tables are three. Users, which is mostly the auth table with a display name on it, projects, and entries, and entries has a foreign key to both, which is redundant but it made the queries readable and there are four hundred rows in the whole thing so it does not matter yet.

The row level security policies are the part to read first, because they are where the bugs will be. Every policy checks the owner column against the session user and there is one exception, the shared project read, and that one is written as a view rather than a policy and I am not sure that is right.

What is not done is email. The signup confirmation goes out through the supper base default sender, which means it lands in spam about half the time, and for a real launch that needs a proper provider and a verified domain. I would do that before anything else on the list, because a signup flow that silently fails is worse than a missing feature.

input: I have rewritten the getting started page and I want to explain why it is now three pages instead of one, because I know that is going to come up in review. The old page tried to do the install, the first project and the troubleshooting all in one scroll, and the analytics say people bounced at the point where the install stopped and the concepts started, which is about a third of the way down. So the install is its own page now, and it only has the commands, nothing about why the tool works the way it does. The second page builds one project end to end, and I have kept the sample project small on purpose, it is a two file project, because the old one used the plugin system and people were debugging plugins before they had run anything successfully. Troubleshooting is the third page and it is mostly the errors from our support inbox, in the order we actually get them, which means the path error is first and not the version error. I called the whole thing a walkthrough rather than a tutorial, and a walkthrough here is the thing you read with the terminal open, which is also roughly what the design team means when they say guided flow. There is a fourth page I have not written yet for the migration path off version 1, and I would rather ship three good pages and add that next week than hold all of it back.

So the install is its own page now, and it only has the commands, nothing about why the tool works the way it does. The second page builds one project end to end, and I have kept the sample project small on purpose, it is a two file project, because the old one used the plugin system and people were debugging plugins before they had run anything successfully. Troubleshooting is the third page and it is mostly the errors from our support inbox, in the order we actually get them, which means the path error is first and not the version error. I called the whole thing a walkthrough rather than a tutorial, and a walkthrough here is the thing you read with the terminal open, which is also roughly what the design team means when they say guided flow. There is a fourth page I have not written yet for the migration path off version 1, and I would rather ship three good pages and add that next week than hold all of it back.

input: This is my note from the site visit this morning so that I do not lose it before the design meeting. The foundation trench on the east side is open along the full length now and the depth is roughly what the drawing says, but the width is the problem, because the drawing has 600 and what has actually been dug is closer to 750, and that changes the concrete order more than it changes anything structural. The rebar arrived on Tuesday and it is the right grade, it is stacked at the north end under sheeting, and there is enough of it for the east and south sides but not the west, so we need the second delivery before the pour. The pour is still pencilled for the 12th. The other thing I noticed is the standing water at the low corner, and it has been dry for three days, so that is groundwater and not rain, which means the pump stays on site and somebody has to log the readings every morning. The level dropped 30, that is centimetres, between yesterday and today, which is encouraging but it is one reading and I do not want to draw a line through one reading. I have photographs of the trench and of the water, and I will put them in the shared folder with today's date on them. Ahmad is meeting the concrete supplier tomorrow and he already knows about the width, so the only thing the design meeting has to decide is whether we are widening the whole run or just the section that is already dug.

input: Okay, this is my working note on the Halloran file before I ring them back, and I am dictating it because I have three years of statements in front of me and I will lose the thread if I stop to type. The position as I understand it is that the company has been treating the workshop rent as a business expense since the 2023 year, the rent is 1,450 a month, it has been 1,450 a month the whole time, and the landlord is the director's brother in law, which is the part nobody mentioned to me until last week. The 2023 return went in on the 14th of January and it claimed the full twelve months, so 17,400 for the year, and the 2024 return did the same thing, and the 2025 return is the one sitting on my desk unsigned. Now, none of that is automatically a problem, a related party can be a landlord and the rent can still be deductible, but it has to be at market rate and there has to be an actual agreement, and what I have been sent is a single page with no dates on it and no signatures, which is not an agreement, it is a note. So the first thing I need from them is whatever the original arrangement was in writing, and if there is nothing in writing then we say so plainly rather than pretending the note is a lease. The second thing is the market rate question, because the unit next door on the same estate is advertised at 1,100 a month and it is the same footprint, and if the revenue ever looks at this they will look at that advert before they look at anything I write. The gap is 350 a month, which is 4,200 a year, which across three years is 12,600, and 12,600 is not a rounding error on a company this size. My reading is that we disclose the related party in the 2025 accounts properly, we do not restate the earlier years unless they tell us to, and we get the arrangement documented from here forward at whatever the number actually is. If they want to keep it at 1,450 then they need something supporting 1,450, an agent's letter would do, and if they cannot get that then the sensible thing is to bring it down and take the smaller deduction, because the smaller deduction they can defend is worth more than the bigger one they cannot. The other loose end is the insurance. The policy is in the brother in law's name, the company pays it, and it has been going through the same expense line as the rent, which is why I did not see it separately at first, and that is 96 a month. It is small enough that on its own I would not raise it, but it is in the same relationship and the same expense line, so it goes in the same conversation. I would rather have one awkward call than two. On timing, the 2025 return is due at the end of the month and I am not signing it until the rent question is settled, and I am going to say that on the call in those words, because the last time I softened a deadline on this client we ended up filing on the last day. If the paperwork comes back this week we are fine. If it does not, we file on the numbers we can support and we amend later, which is ugly but it is not a disaster. Going back to the date I gave for the 2023 return, that is the wrong date, it went in on the 14th of February, not January, and I only know that because the submission receipt is in the file and I have just looked at it. Everything else in this note is as I have it. I will draft the letter after the call and put the market rate advert in as an appendix so the whole thing is in one place, and if they ask why we are being careful I am going to tell them the truth, which is that the brother in law is not the problem, the missing paperwork is the problem, and paperwork we can fix in a week.

input: This is the note for the ethics amendment and I want to get the reasoning down before I fill the form in, because the form asks for the change and not the reason and the reason is the part I will forget. The original protocol says we recruit adults who have used a voice interface in the last six months, and we set that window because we wanted people with current habits rather than people remembering an assistant they gave up on in 2019. What has happened in practice is that the six month window is doing something we did not intend. The people who pass it are overwhelmingly people who use dictation for work, because work is what makes you use a thing every week, and the people we are actually interested in are the ones who use it because typing is difficult for them, and that group turns out to be much more intermittent. Somebody with a wrist injury might use dictation heavily for two months and then not at all for a year. Under the current wording we screen that person out, and they are close to the centre of the population we said we were studying. So the amendment narrows the criterion. Instead of used in the last six months we want used for at least four weeks continuously at any point in the last three years, and I have written it that way round on purpose, because the thing we need is a period of real use, not recency. That does widen the recall problem, and I am not going to pretend otherwise, somebody recalling a period from two years ago is a worse informant about specifics than somebody describing last week. My answer to that is that the interview already asks for specifics about a single recent session and we simply drop that section for the retrospective participants, rather than asking them to invent detail. The second change is smaller. We currently exclude anyone who has taken part in a study run by this group in the last twelve months, and that was a fair rule when we had one study a year, but we have three running now and the exclusion is removing people twice over. I want to narrow that to studies on the same interface, so somebody who did the reading study last spring is eligible for this one, and I will say in the form that we will record any prior participation and control for it rather than screening on it. Nothing changes about consent, storage or the recording protocol, and I have not touched the sample size, which stays at 24, although if the wider criterion brings in more people than expected I would rather stop at 24 than quietly grow the study. Marieke is reviewing the wording tomorrow and she has the original protocol open in the other window, so between us we should catch anything that contradicts itself.

input: This is the escalation note for the ticket from the Rotterdam account and I am dictating it because support wants it before the shift ends and I have the whole thread open. The customer contact is Dhruv Raghunathan, and I have had that name wrong in two earlier emails so I am going to spell it, R A G H U N A T H A N, and it would be worth somebody fixing it in the CRM as well because whatever is in there is what our templates pull from. The problem itself is not complicated once you see it. Their integration posts to our webhook endpoint, they retry on any non 200, and our endpoint has been returning 202 for accepted since the March release, so every single successful post is being retried up to five times, and they have been running that way for eleven days. Nothing broke because we deduplicate on the idempotency key, which is why nobody noticed, but their rate limit dashboard has been red the whole time and they think we are dropping their traffic. We are not dropping anything. I have counted the duplicates for the 4th and there are 31,200 posts for 6,240 unique events, which is exactly five times, so the retry logic is doing precisely what it was told to do. What I want to say to them is three things, and I want to say them in this order because the last time we led with the fix they thought we were dodging the cause. First, their traffic is arriving and nothing has been lost, and here is the count for one day as evidence. Second, the 202 is intentional on our side and it is documented, but it changed in the March release without a migration note, and that is our fault and I am happy to say so in writing. Third, the change on their side is one line, they treat 2xx as success rather than 200 exactly, and if they would rather not touch it then we can put them behind the compatibility path that returns 200, but I would push for the one line because the compatibility path is going away. On our side there are two follow ups. The release note for March needs the status code change added retroactively, and somebody should check whether any other account is retrying on 202, because if Rotterdam did this then others have, and the way to find that is to look for accounts whose post volume is a clean multiple of their event volume. I would start with the four biggest webhook consumers. I am going to send the customer note tonight in English, and I will flag to the account manager that Dhruv has been asking for a Dutch summary for his own team, which we do not do, but he should hear that from her and not from a support ticket.
