input: This is the handover for the winter menu and I am talking it through rather than writing it because the chef who takes this over is going to want the reasoning and not just the numbers. We are dropping four dishes and adding five, and the reason there is one more is the bread, which was never on the menu properly and is going on it now at 4 euros because people were asking for it every service and we were giving it away. The four coming off are the sea bass, the veal, the courgette flowers and the panna cotta. The sea bass goes because the price has doubled since September and I am not putting a 34 euro fish on a menu in this room. The veal goes because it takes eleven minutes and the pass cannot hold eleven minutes on a Saturday, and every time we are late it is the veal. The courgette flowers go because it is winter. The panna cotta goes because the new dessert is better, and I will come back to that. Coming on, we have the pumpkin ravioli, the beef cheek, the sardines, the winter salad and the chocolate tart. The ravioli is the one I care about. The filling is roast pumpkin, ricotta and a lot of nutmeg, and the ratio matters, it is 400 pumpkin to 150 ricotta, and if you go heavier on the ricotta it tastes of nothing. Roast the pumpkin dry, no oil, no foil, until it colours at the edges, because the water is the enemy and every batch we lost last year was too wet. The pasta is the same dough we already make, we are not changing the dough in December. The beef cheek is the low risk one, it is four hours and it holds, and we can prep the whole weekend on Thursday. Two per portion, and the sauce is the braising liquid reduced by half, nothing added, because the last thing that menu needs is another sauce with butter in it. The sardines are the cheapest thing on the menu and they are the dish I expect the reviews to talk about, which is usually how it goes. They come in on Tuesday and Friday, they are gone within a day, and if they look tired we do not serve them, we run the salad as a second starter and nobody dies. The winter salad is radicchio, pear, walnut and the blue cheese from the same supplier as last year, and it exists so there is something on the menu for the table that arrives at nine and does not want a project. The chocolate tart is the panna cotta's replacement and it is better in every way that matters to us, it can be made in the morning, it cuts cleanly, it sits at room temperature for three hours, and it costs about a third of what the panna cotta cost once you count the waste. The pastry is the sweet one we already do for the lemon tart. The filling is 300 chocolate, and that is grams, 200 cream, two eggs, and the only difficult part is not overbaking it, so it comes out when the middle still moves. On ordering, the pumpkin is the thing to watch. We need 12 kilos a week if the ravioli sells the way I think it will, and our supplier can do 8 without notice, so the standing order goes up now and not in the second week of December when everybody else has had the same idea. The chocolate we buy in 5 kilo boxes and one box is roughly nine tarts, so two boxes a week to start. On the pass, the ravioli and the sardines are both fast and both fragile, so they do not go to the same section, and I have put the ravioli with the pasta station where the water already is. Service notes for the front of house. The bread is 4 euros and it is not optional to mention it, the ravioli is not vegan because of the ricotta and somebody will ask every single night, and the beef cheek is the dish to push at eight thirty when the kitchen is drowning, because it is already cooked. If the ravioli runs out we do not extend it with more ricotta. We take it off and we say it has gone.

input: Right, notes on the newsletter rewrite before I forget what I decided in the shower, because this is the third time I have started this and the first two attempts died because I tried to make it a strategy document. It is not a strategy document. It is a list of things I am going to stop doing. I am stopping the round up section. It takes me two hours a week, it is the section nobody clicks, and it exists because every newsletter I read when I started had one. The click data on the last twelve issues is brutal, the round up gets about 1% of clicks and it is a third of the words, and I have been keeping it out of habit and a vague fear that it is the professional thing to include. I am stopping the Tuesday send. We moved to Tuesday in March because of a post I read about open rates and our open rate did not move at all, but the reply rate dropped, and replies are the only metric I actually care about because replies are how I know anybody is on the other end. Thursday, Thursday is what we are going back to. I am stopping the intro paragraph where I explain what the issue is about, because the subject line already did that and the intro is where people leave. And I am stopping the practice of writing the whole thing on the day, which is not a section but it is the reason the last four issues were late. What replaces all of that is one long piece and one short recommendation. The long piece is the thing I would tell a friend about if they asked what I had been thinking about, and if I cannot answer that question on the Wednesday then there is no issue that week and I am going to say that out loud rather than shipping something thin. The short recommendation is one thing, one paragraph, and it can be a tool or a book or a person to follow, and it goes at the bottom because the people who want it will scroll. On length, I think the target is somewhere around 900 words, which is roughly half of what the current issue runs, and I would rather be short and finish than long and late. I am not going to redesign the template. The template is fine, it is boring, boring is correct for a newsletter, and every hour spent on the template is an hour not spent on the piece. The one design thing I will do is make the reply prompt visible without scrolling, because if replies are the metric then the invitation to reply should not be at the very bottom under the unsubscribe. Growth I am deliberately not thinking about for three months. We are at about 4,000 people, which is more than enough people to write for, and the thing that has always grown this list is somebody forwarding an issue, and nobody forwards a round up section.

Thursday is what we are going back to. I am stopping the intro paragraph where I explain what the issue is about, because the subject line already did that and the intro is where people leave. And I am stopping the practice of writing the whole thing on the day, which is not a section but it is the reason the last four issues were late. What replaces all of that is one long piece and one short recommendation. The long piece is the thing I would tell a friend about if they asked what I had been thinking about, and if I cannot answer that question on the Wednesday then there is no issue that week and I am going to say that out loud rather than shipping something thin. The short recommendation is one thing, one paragraph, and it can be a tool or a book or a person to follow, and it goes at the bottom because the people who want it will scroll. On length, I think the target is somewhere around 900 words, which is roughly half of what the current issue runs, and I would rather be short and finish than long and late. I am not going to redesign the template. The template is fine, it is boring, boring is correct for a newsletter, and every hour spent on the template is an hour not spent on the piece. The one design thing I will do is make the reply prompt visible without scrolling, because if replies are the metric then the invitation to reply should not be at the very bottom under the unsubscribe. Growth I am deliberately not thinking about for three months. We are at about 4,000 people, which is more than enough people to write for, and the thing that has always grown this list is somebody forwarding an issue, and nobody forwards a round up section.

input: This is my note after the home visit, dictated in the car, and I will tidy it into the record this evening. The patient is 84, she lives with her daughter, and the reason for the visit was a fall on Sunday which she did not report and the daughter rang about on Tuesday. There is no fracture that I can find. She is weight bearing, there is no pain on rotation, and the bruising is on the left hip and forearm and is the pattern you would expect from going down sideways against furniture. What concerns me is not the fall itself, it is the third fall since June and it is the second one she has not mentioned. Her blood pressure sitting was 138 over 82 and standing it was 106 over 64, which is a drop of over 30 systolic, and she takes the amlodipine in the morning, so the postural drop and the morning falls are almost certainly the same story. I want to halve the amlodipine and review in two weeks, and I want a standing and sitting reading written down by the daughter three mornings running, because one set of readings from a district nurse visit tells me less than three mornings at home. The other thing in the house is the rug in the hallway and the light on the stairs, and the daughter and I talked about both, and she is going to deal with the rug this week. She was clear that her mother will refuse a rail on the stairs, and I believe her, she knows her better than I do, so I am not going to make that the fight this month. The cognitive picture is unchanged as far as I can tell. She knew the day, she knew why I was there, she was irritated that I was there, which is normal for her, and the daughter has not noticed anything new. The reason I am recording that is that the underreporting of the falls is easy to read as memory and I do not think it is memory, I think she does not want a conversation about moving. On the medication list more broadly, she is on four things and the only one I would touch today is the amlodipine. The bisphosphonate stays, the statin stays, and the sertraline stays, and I am not going to unpick three drugs on the day I am also asking her to accept a change she does not want. I will speak to the daughter again after the readings and if the drop is still there at the lower dose then it is a referral rather than another adjustment from me.

input: This is my write up of the phishing wave from last week and I am dictating it because the timeline is the part that matters and the timeline is easier to say than to type. It started on the Monday, the 3rd, with eleven messages to eleven different people in finance, all of them claiming to be from the payroll provider, all of them asking the recipient to confirm bank details through a link. The link went to a domain registered on the Saturday, two days before, and the domain was one character off the real one, it used a capital I where the real domain has a lowercase l, and in the font our mail client uses those are the same shape. That is the whole trick. There was no malware, no attachment, nothing clever in the mail itself, and the page it landed on was a copy of the provider's login page pulled down with a tool anybody can install. Nine of the eleven people did nothing. Two of them clicked. One of those two typed a password and then rang the help desk about ninety seconds later, unprompted, because the page redirected to the real site and she thought that was strange, and she was right, it is strange, and that instinct is the reason this is a small incident and not a large one. The other one clicked, looked at the page, closed it, and mentioned it the next morning. We reset the password that was typed within four minutes of the call, we checked the sign in logs for that account going back a week, and there is one failed sign in from an address in a hosting range about three minutes after she typed it, and nothing after that, which lines up with the reset landing first. So the account did not fall. What did happen is that the same eleven people got a second wave on the Wednesday, and the second wave is the interesting one, because it was not a copy of the first. The second wave referenced the help desk call. The body said that the security team had flagged an issue with their payroll record and asked them to verify through a link, and the link went to a different domain registered on the Tuesday. That means somebody on the other side learned that we had responded, and there are only a few ways they learn that, and the one I believe is the simplest, which is that the first page logged the redirect and they could see we had killed the session. I do not think there is an insider. I want to be plain about that because it is the first thing people ask and the evidence does not support it. Nobody clicked on the Wednesday. Two people forwarded it to the help desk within the first ten minutes, which is what we asked for after Monday, and that is the part of our response I would call a success. The blocks went in on the Wednesday afternoon for both domains and for the hosting range, and I have asked the mail team to alert on any inbound domain that differs from a known good domain by a single character, which is a rule we should have had before this and did not. On the payroll provider, I have been careful about what we say to them, because their name was used and their login page was copied and none of that is their fault. They should know, and I sent them both domains and the page source on the Thursday, and they replied the same day, which is better than I expected. The recommendations are short. First, the single character domain rule, which is the only technical control that would have stopped this at the door. Second, we stop treating a click as a failure in the reporting, because the woman who typed the password and rang the help desk did more for us than the nine people who deleted the mail silently, and our current numbers count her as the failure and them as the successes, and that is backwards. Third, and this is the one that will get argued about, we should be able to reset a password and kill every session from one action, because four minutes was fast and four minutes was still slower than it needed to be. On the two people who clicked, I have been writing this as she and the other one, and to be clear the one who typed the password and rang us is Farida, so Farida is the one whose account we reset, and the second click was Tomas, who closed the page without entering anything. Neither of them did anything wrong and I am naming them because the write up is going to be read by people who will otherwise guess, and guessing is worse.

input: These are my notes for reworking the second half of the methods lecture, which has been the weak part of this course for three years and I have finally worked out why. The first half is fine. The first half is about measurement, and measurement has objects in it, so students have something to hold. The second half is about validity, and validity as I have been teaching it is four terms and a diagram, and the diagram is the problem, because the diagram implies the four kinds of validity are parallel and they are not. What I want to do instead is teach it as a single question asked at four points in a study. The question is whether the thing you are claiming is the thing you measured. At the level of the instrument that question is construct validity. At the level of the comparison it is internal validity. At the level of the population it is external validity, and at the level of the statistic it is statistical validity, and every one of those is the same question with the pronoun pointing somewhere else. If I say it that way I can drop the diagram entirely, and I suspect the diagram has been doing most of the damage, because it is the thing the students photograph and it is the thing they reproduce in the exam without understanding. The example I want to build the whole hour around is the reading study from the department, and I have permission to use it, which took two emails. It has a real construct problem, they measured reading with a comprehension test that has a heavy vocabulary load, so a child with a small vocabulary and perfect decoding scores badly, and the paper claims a decoding result. That is one slide and it is the only slide about construct validity that has ever produced a question from the back of the room. Then the same study has an internal problem, the control group got the intervention two weeks late rather than not at all, and the external problem is that it is one city and one year group. So one study carries three of the four, and I can use the fourth on the power calculation, which they did badly and reported honestly, and I want to praise them for the honesty while pulling apart the number, because that is the tone I want in the whole course. The assessment has to change with it. The current exam question asks students to define the four types, which rewards the photograph of the diagram, and the replacement asks them to read a short methods section and say at which of the four points the claim breaks, and I will need to write three of those and they will take a morning each. I am not changing the reading list. The reading list is fine and the students do not read it anyway, which is a separate problem and not one I am solving in November.

input: Notes on the rollback we did last night, and I want this written down before the retro because the retro is going to focus on the wrong thing. The deploy went out at 19:40, the alert fired at 19:52, and we were rolled back by 20:05, so twenty five minutes end to end and about thirteen minutes of user impact, which is the best rollback we have done and nobody is going to remember that. What broke was the checkout page for customers paying in a currency other than euros, and the reason is a config change that got merged in the same release as the feature, which is my fault because I approved both in one review. The config moved the currency list from the service to the edge, and the edge cache was still holding the old list, so for about thirteen minutes anybody selecting pounds or zloty got a 500 on the confirm step. Euro customers saw nothing at all, which is why the error rate only went to about 4% and why the alert took twelve minutes to fire rather than two. That 4% is the number people will argue about and it is the least interesting number here. The interesting number is thirteen minutes at 100% failure for the affected group, because a customer does not experience an error rate, they experience their own checkout not working. On what we change, the obvious one is that config and feature do not ship in one release, and I will write that into the release checklist rather than saying it in a meeting. The second one is the alert. The threshold is on the global error rate and it should be per currency, or at least per path, because a failure that only touches a tenth of traffic is invisible to a global threshold until it is not, and we got lucky that this one was loud enough. Everybody should redo their alert thresholds, and by everybody I mean the two teams that own a checkout path, not the whole platform group, because the platform alerts are already per service and making them redo an exercise they have done will get the whole thing ignored. Third, the edge cache needs an explicit invalidation step in the deploy, which we thought we had and we have for assets and not for config. On timing, I would rather we do the alert work before the currency launch in December than after it, and the alert work is about two days for one person. I am not asking for a freeze. The last freeze cost us three weeks and prevented nothing.

input: Quick note on the crash before I lose it, because it only happens on one machine and that machine belongs to the artist, so I get one attempt at reproducing it per day. The build crashes on level load, not on startup, and only when the save file has a completed run in it, which is why none of us saw it. The log line before the crash is the asset loader failing to find a texture, and the texture name in the log is not a texture we ship, it is Karnak underscore wall, and I could not find it anywhere in the project because I have been searching for it with a C. It is spelled with a K, K A R N A K, which is a folder from the old prototype that somebody referenced from a prefab and the prefab is still in the level. So the fix is not in the loader. The loader is doing the right thing, it is telling us a thing does not exist, and then something downstream dereferences the null and takes the whole process with it, and that downstream part is worth fixing separately because it will happen again with a different asset. For tonight I am going to strip the reference out of the prefab and get the artist a build that does not crash, and then tomorrow I want to make the loader failure loud instead of fatal, because a missing texture should be a pink square and a warning, not a crash on a machine I cannot get to.

input: This is the note on the churn number for the board pack, because the number in the draft is 6% and I am not comfortable with it going in without a sentence about what it means. The 6% is monthly, and the pack from last quarter had 18% in the same box, and that 18% was quarterly, and nobody changed the label. So the two numbers in the two packs describe roughly the same business and one of them looks three times worse than the other, and somebody on the board is going to notice that before we do. My preference is that we report monthly and we say monthly in the label, every time, and we restate the last four quarters on the same basis in a footnote so the trend is readable. The second thing is the denominator, which is customers and not revenue, and for us those give different answers because the churn is concentrated in the small accounts. Revenue churn last month was about 2%, which is a much better number and also the honest one for a board that is thinking about the revenue line, so I would put both in with both labels rather than choosing the flattering one. If we only have room for one, use revenue churn and say so plainly, and be ready for the question about customer churn, because it will come and the answer is that we are losing small accounts and keeping large ones, which is a real thing and not a spin.

input: Right, this is the thing I want to raise at the leads meeting and I want to say it once, properly, rather than in pieces over three weeks. Our cycle time is not the problem. Cycle time, and I mean first commit to production here, not ticket creation to production, has been steady at about four days for two quarters and nobody complains about four days. The number people are actually unhappy about is the time before the first commit, which is sitting somewhere between two and three weeks depending on the team, and we do not measure it, and because we do not measure it every conversation about speed lands on the four days that are already fine. What happens in those two to three weeks is mostly waiting for a decision that three people could make in a meeting, and I have gone back through the last twenty tickets to check that rather than asserting it, and fourteen of them were blocked on a decision and not on capacity. So what I want out of the leads meeting is not a process. It is a named person per area who can make the call, and a rule that if a ticket has been in the ready column for five days somebody escalates it rather than waiting politely, because the waiting is currently invisible and the escalation feels rude, and both of those are cultural and both are fixable. I am not proposing we track anything new in the tool. We can see the ready column dates already.

input: This is the note for the trustees ahead of Thursday and I am dictating it on the bus so forgive the shape of it. The grant application went in on the 6th and we hear back in eight weeks, which means the earliest we know anything is the second week of December, and that is after the point where we have to decide about the January programme. So we are deciding without knowing, and I would rather we did that deliberately than by drifting. The ask was 48,000 over two years, which is the full cost of the outreach worker plus the room hire, and the funder has been clear in their guidance that they do not part fund posts, so it is that number or nothing. If we get it, the January programme runs four days a week from the middle of the month and we advertise the post in December so somebody starts in February. If we do not get it, we run two days a week out of reserves, which we can afford for one year and not two, and we do not advertise anything. What I do not want is the middle version where we advertise on the hope and then withdraw it, because we did that in 2023 and it cost us a candidate and some goodwill with the college. On reserves, we are at 61,000, and the two day version spends about 22,000 of that across the year, which leaves us above the three month floor the policy sets, so it is within our own rules and I have checked that rather than assuming it. The room hire is the part I would push back on if we are running two days, because the community centre wants the same annual figure whether we use it twice a week or four times, and I think there is a conversation to have there that nobody has had. Sorry, going back to the amount we applied for, that is wrong, it was 42,000 and not 48,000, the 48 was the figure in the first draft before we took the training budget out. The rest of the numbers are as I said. On Thursday I want a decision on the two day version as the default, so that we are not waiting for December to start planning, and if the grant lands we upgrade rather than starting from nothing. I will bring the reserves policy and the funder guidance so nobody has to take my word for either.

input: Okay, this is the timeline for the incident on the fourteenth and I want to get it down before the review, because Marek is going to ask for exact times and I will not remember them by Monday. At 02:14 the first alert came in from the eu-west-1 collector, and it was the same alert we saw in June, disk pressure on node ip-10-0-14-22. At 02:14 nobody was paged, because the routing rule sends that class of alert to the low priority channel, and that is the part I want the review to look at, the routing rule, not the disk. At 02:31 Kasia acknowledged it from her phone and she cordoned node, which was the right call, and at 02:33 the pods rescheduled onto ip-10-0-14-9 and ip-10-0-14-31. Then between 02:33 and 03:10 nothing happened, and I mean nothing, no alert, no page, because the second node was already at 84 percent and the collector had stopped reporting by then. At 03:10 the checkout service started returning 502s and that is when the customer noticed, which is forty-six minutes after the first alert. Kasia drained the second node at 03:22 and the error rate came down by 03:29. So the whole thing is fifty-five minutes from the first alert to recovery, and the failure is not the disk, the failure is the routing rule that sent a disk alert to a channel nobody watches at two in the morning. I will write the action items separately but the first one is that routing rule.

input: This is the handover note for the ingest service, because I am on leave from Friday for two weeks and Sujata is taking it. First the shape of the thing. There are three moving parts, the poller, the queue and the writer, and they all live in the same repo under services slash ingest, but they deploy separately, which is the first thing that confuses people. The poller runs every five minutes on a cron and it asks the vendor API for anything changed since the last watermark, and the watermark is stored in Redis under the key ingest colon watermark, and if that key is missing the poller does a full pull, which takes about forty minutes and doubles the vendor bill for that day, so please do not flush Redis. I am saying it again, please do not flush Redis, because last time somebody did it on a Friday evening and we found out on Monday. The queue is just SQS, nothing special, but the visibility timeout is 300 seconds and the writer sometimes takes longer than that on a big batch, and when that happens the message comes back and the same batch is written twice. It is idempotent on the order id so the duplicates do not corrupt anything, but they do show in the metrics as a spike, and every time somebody sees that spike they open a ticket, so if you see the spike on the ingest dashboard, first check the timeout before you believe the ticket. The writer is the part I would not touch. It is Go, it is about 900 lines, and the batching logic in there is the reason the p99 is under two seconds, and I know it looks like it could be simpler but the last person who simplified it took the p99 to eleven seconds. There is a comment above the flush function that explains why, and the comment is longer than the function. Read it before you change anything there. Now the things that are broken and that I did not have time to finish. One, the retry counter is not reset after a successful write, so a batch that failed twice last week still shows two failures, and the alert threshold is three, which means one more failure and it pages somebody at night for nothing. The fix is one line in writer dot go, near the end of the flush function, but I did not want to deploy it on a Thursday. Two, the vendor sometimes returns the same order id with two different updated timestamps in the same page, and we take the last one, which is wrong maybe once a month, and I do not have a good answer for that, so I just wrote it down in the doc. Three, the staging environment is pointing at the production vendor key, which is my fault, and it should be moved to the sandbox key before anybody runs a load test. If something breaks and Sujata cannot reach me, the person who knows the writer second best is Ram, not me, and he sits on the platform side.

input: Site note for the Erdem job, the villa on the ridge, and this is the version I want the fabricator to work from, not the one from last week. The main span is 6.4 metres and the client wants it without a visible post in the middle, so we are going with the box section, 200 by 100 by 8 wall, hot rolled, and I checked the deflection twice, it comes to 18 millimetres under the full load which is inside the limit but only just. The finish is the part that changed. Last week we said galvanised and painted, and the client has now seen the sample and she does not like the texture, so it is now hot dip galvanised only, no paint, and that changes the lead time from nine days to fourteen. Fourteen days from the order, and the order is not placed yet, so somebody has to tell her that the balcony is not going to be up before the twenty-ninth. The brackets are still the same, ten millimetre plate, four bolts each, M16, and the bolt holes at 22 millimetres because the last set we drilled at 18 and the tolerance on site was not enough. Twenty-two, not eighteen, that is written in the drawing now. On the timber, the decking is the same iroko as the ground floor and it comes from the same supplier in Izmir, and they have enough in stock for both floors, I called them Tuesday and the man told me it is in the warehouse. The one thing I still do not know is the balustrade fixing, whether it goes on the top of the box or on the side of it, and that depends on the glass thickness which the glazier has not confirmed. So do not send the balustrade detail to the fabricator with the rest, hold it back until I have the glass thickness, and everything else can go today.

input: Right, thinking out loud about the caching layer before the design review, and I do not have a conclusion yet so treat this as notes. The problem is that the profile lookup is called four times per page render and each one is a round trip to the database, and the database is fine with it now at our size but it will not be fine at ten times the traffic. So the obvious answer is a cache in front of it, and the question is where the cache lives and how we invalidate it. If it lives in the process then each of the eight app instances has its own copy and they will disagree with each other for as long as the TTL, and for a profile name that is probably acceptable, but for the entitlement flags it is not, because a user who loses access should lose it now and not in sixty seconds. If it lives in Redis then everybody agrees but we have added a network hop and a new thing that can be down, and the failure mode when Redis is slow is worse than the failure mode we have today, which is that the database is slow. And there is the third option which is that we. Actually the third option is that we stop calling it four times, because two of those four calls are in components that already have the profile passed down as a prop and they are calling it again out of habit, so before we build anything we should just delete those two calls and see what the graph looks like. That is a day of work instead of a sprint, and it might be enough on its own.

input: This is the description for the pull request that splits the parser, and I want it to read properly because the reviewers on this one are going to be Dana and Theo and they both read descriptions. So, context first. The parser has been one file since 2023 and it is now a bit over four thousand lines, and the reason nobody has split it is that the tokenizer and the expression walker share a mutable state object, and every time somebody tried to pull them apart they hit that object and gave up. What this change does is make that state explicit. Instead of one struct that both halves mutate, the tokenizer now returns a token stream and the walker takes the stream as an argument, so the state goes across the boundary as a value and not as a shared field. That is the whole idea, and everything else in the diff follows from it. Concretely, there are four commits. The first one is pure movement, it takes the tokenizer out into its own file with no changes to the logic at all, so it should read as a rename plus a cut and paste and nothing else, and if you see a logic change in that commit please flag it because it is not intentional. The second commit introduces the token stream type and has the tokenizer produce it, and the walker still reads the old struct at that point so the tests pass on both. The third commit switches the walker over and deletes the shared field, and that is the commit that matters, it is about three hundred lines and it is the one to read carefully. The fourth is cleanup, unused imports and a couple of comments that were describing the old flow and are now lying. On testing. The existing parser tests all pass unchanged, which is the point, and I added nine new tests around the stream boundary, mostly for the cases where the tokenizer hits end of input in the middle of a construct, because that used to be signalled by a flag on the shared struct and is now an explicit end token. The list of tests that cover the error paths are in parser stream test dot go, and there is one I could not write, which is the case where a nested expression exceeds the depth limit, because the depth limit is checked in the walker and I need a fixture that is three hundred levels deep and generating it in the test file made the file unreadable. I will do that in a follow up. Risks. The behaviour should be identical and the tests say it is, but this touches every code path in the parser, so if something regresses it will regress everywhere at once rather than in one corner, and that is worth knowing when you decide how long to leave it on the canary. I would leave it a full day rather than the usual couple of hours. There is no config flag and no migration, it is a straight swap, and reverting it is a clean revert of the four commits.

So, context first. The parser has been one file since 2023 and it is now a bit over four thousand lines, and the reason nobody has split it is that the tokenizer and the expression walker share a mutable state object, and every time somebody tried to pull them apart they hit that object and gave up. What this change does is make that state explicit. Instead of one struct that both halves mutate, the tokenizer now returns a token stream and the walker takes the stream as an argument, so the state goes across the boundary as a value and not as a shared field. That is the whole idea, and everything else in the diff follows from it. Concretely, there are four commits. The first one is pure movement, it takes the tokenizer out into its own file with no changes to the logic at all, so it should read as a rename plus a cut and paste and nothing else, and if you see a logic change in that commit please flag it because it is not intentional. The second commit introduces the token stream type and has the tokenizer produce it, and the walker still reads the old struct at that point so the tests pass on both. The third commit switches the walker over and deletes the shared field, and that is the commit that matters, it is about three hundred lines and it is the one to read carefully. The fourth is cleanup, unused imports and a couple of comments that were describing the old flow and are now lying. On testing. The existing parser tests all pass unchanged, which is the point, and I added nine new tests around the stream boundary, mostly for the cases where the tokenizer hits end of input in the middle of a construct, because that used to be signalled by a flag on the shared struct and is now an explicit end token. The list of tests that cover the error paths is in parser stream test dot go, and there is one I could not write, which is the case where a nested expression exceeds the depth limit, because the depth limit is checked in the walker and I need a fixture that is three hundred levels deep and generating it in the test file made the file unreadable. I will do that in a follow up. Risks. The behaviour should be identical and the tests say it is, but this touches every code path in the parser, so if something regresses it will regress everywhere at once rather than in one corner, and that is worth knowing when you decide how long to leave it on the canary. I would leave it a full day rather than the usual couple of hours. There is no config flag and no migration, it is a straight swap, and reverting it is a clean revert of the four commits.

input: Dictating the discussion section for the van der Meer paper, first pass, and I will tidy the references later. The main finding is that the effect we report survives when we control for the size of the firm, which is the objection the second reviewer raised on the previous version, and it survives in both specifications, so we can say that with some confidence. What we cannot say, and I want to be careful here, is that the mechanism is the one we propose. The correlation between the adoption year and the productivity change is consistent with the learning story, but it is also consistent with a selection story where the firms that adopt early are the firms that were already improving, and our data does not let us separate those two. The instrument we use, the distance to the nearest supplier, is weaker than we would like, and the first stage F statistic is 9.1, which is below the conventional threshold, and I would rather write that plainly than bury it in a footnote. So the honest statement of the contribution is that we document the association across a much longer panel than the earlier work, twenty-two years instead of six, and that we rule out the two most obvious confounders, but the causal claim stays a conjecture. That is a smaller claim than the one in the abstract, and the abstract has to come down to match it. Then the limitations, and there are three that matter. The first is the coverage of the small firms, because the register only includes firms above ten employees, so everything we say is about medium and larger firms and the extension to the small ones is an assumption. The second is the measurement of the productivity itself, which is value added per worker, and that is the measure the register gives us, but it moves with the price of the output and we do not have firm level prices, so a firm that raised prices looks more productive in our data. Van der Meer made this point in the 2019 paper and we should cite him on it rather than pretending we noticed it ourselves. The third is that the last two years of the panel overlap with the energy price shock, and the shock hits the sectors in our sample unevenly, and although we include the year effects, the year effects cannot absorb something that is sector specific. We could drop the last two years and show that the result holds, and I think we should, as a robustness table in the appendix rather than in the main text. For the future work paragraph, the obvious thing is the supplier level data, which exists but is not linked, and the linking is the whole project rather than a paragraph, so I will phrase it as a direction and not as a promise.

input: Reading notes on the distillation paper, arXiv 2604.19883, and I want to write down what is actually new in it before I forget, because the abstract oversells it in the usual way. The setup is a teacher of seven billion parameters and a student of six hundred million, and the task is instruction following, and the claim is that the student recovers ninety-four percent of the teacher on their own benchmark. The first thing to say is that ninety-four percent is on their benchmark, and their benchmark is built from the same distribution as the training data, so it is telling us about interpolation and not about generalisation, and the number I care about is the held out one, which is in the appendix and is seventy-nine percent. Seventy-nine is still good for a model that is eleven times smaller, but it is a different sentence than the one in the abstract. Second, the actual method. They do not distil the logits, they distil the intermediate hidden states, which people have done before, but the new part is that they select which layers to align with a small search instead of aligning every layer, and the search is cheap because it runs on a subset of two thousand examples. The ablation in Table 3 in page 7 is the one that convinced me, because it shows that the selected alignment beats the uniform alignment by four points and beats the last layer only baseline by nine, and the gap is stable across three seeds, which is more seeds than most of these papers report. Third, and this is the part relevant to our own adapter, they freeze the student's embedding layer during distillation and they say in one line that unfreezing it made the training unstable. That is a single sentence with no experiment behind it, and it is exactly the choice we are about to make, so I would not treat it as evidence, but it is a hint and it is cheap for us to test both ways. Fourth, the things they do not report. There is no latency measurement anywhere in the paper, so the six hundred million parameter student is a parameter count and not a speed claim, and for us the whole point is the speed. There is also no comparison against just fine tuning the small model directly on the same data, which is the obvious baseline, and its absence is the weakest part of the paper, because if direct fine tuning gets to seventy-five the whole distillation apparatus is buying four points for a lot of complexity. I looked for it twice and it is not there. So the summary for our purposes. The layer selection idea is worth borrowing, it is simple and the ablation supports it. The embedding freeze is unsupported and we should test it ourselves. The headline number should be read as seventy-nine and not ninety-four. And the missing direct fine tuning baseline means we cannot use this paper to justify distillation over plain fine tuning, which is unfortunately the exact question we wanted an answer to.

input: Okay, notes for the migration guide, the section about the config file, and I will write the code fences in properly later, I just want the prose down. So the headline is that the config moves from the flat file to the layered one, and there is three things a reader needs to understand before any of the examples make sense. The first is that the layers are merged and not replaced, so a key in the local file does not throw away the block it sits in, it overrides that one key and leaves its siblings alone, and this is different to the old behaviour and it is the thing that surprises everybody. The second is precedence, which is command line, then environment, then local file, then project file, then the defaults, and I want that written as a list in the guide because people will look it up rather than read it. The third is that the defaults are now visible, there is a command that prints the fully merged config with the source of every key annotated, and honestly that command is the answer to most of the support questions we get, so it should be near the top and not buried in a reference section. Then the examples. I want less examples than the old guide had, because the old one had eleven and nobody reads eleven, and the four that matter are the plain upgrade with no local overrides, the upgrade where the user has a local override that used to replace a whole block, the multi environment case, and the case where somebody is generating the config from a template. The second one is the migration risk, because under the old rules their override replaced the block and they may be relying on the siblings being absent, and under the new rules those siblings come back from the defaults. That needs a warning box and it needs the exact command to check, which is the annotated print. There is also the question of who I write this for, and the answer is somebody who has a working setup and does not want to think about config at all, so the first line of the guide should tell them whether they need to do anything, and for most of them the answer is no. Data is on my side there, about eighty percent of the configs we see in support tickets have no overrides at all. One more thing and then I will stop. Do not let me invent a deprecation timeline in this guide. I do not know when the flat file stops being read and neither does anybody else yet, so the guide says the flat file is still read and links to the issue where the timeline will be decided, and that is all it says.

input: Release notes for 3.8.0, draft, and I will cut it down before it goes out because it is too long for a patch audience. The headline is the offline queue. Until now, if the app lost the network in the middle of a sync it kept the changes in memory and lost them when the process was killed, and the number of support threads about exactly that is the reason this release exists. Now the changes go to a local store first and the sync drains the store, so killing the app is safe and the changes go out when the network comes back. The store is capped at fifty megabytes and when it is full the oldest entries are dropped, and the app tells the user when that happens, which is a compromise, and I want that written honestly in the notes rather than hidden. Second thing is the conflict dialog. Before, when the same record changed on two devices, the later write won silently, and now the user gets a dialog with both versions and a choice, and the choice is remembered per record type so you are not asked forty times. The dialog is not pretty yet and the design team knows. Third, performance. The list view was rendering every row on every keystroke in the search box and now it renders the visible window only, and on a list of ten thousand records the search went from about nine hundred milliseconds to about sixty, measured on the test device, which is a three year old mid range phone and not my machine. I want the test device named in the notes because a benchmark on the newest phone is not useful to anybody. Fourth, and this one is small but people will notice it, the export file name now includes the date, so you stop getting export dot csv, export dot csv one, export dot csv two in your downloads folder. Fixes. There are eleven of them and most are one liners, but three are worth calling out. The crash when opening a shared link while logged out is fixed, and that one accounted for about a fifth of all crash reports. The wrong timezone on the weekly summary is fixed, and it was using the server timezone and not the user's, which meant everybody in Asia got the summary with Sunday's data on it. And the duplicate notification when a comment was edited is fixed. Known issues, because we should list them. The offline queue does not cover attachments yet, only the record changes, so an attachment added offline still fails and the user sees the old error, and that is the next release. The conflict dialog cannot show a diff for the rich text fields, it shows both versions in full, which for a long note is a wall of text. And on the tablet layout the dialog is centred wrongly in landscape, which we know about and did not want to hold the release for. Upgrade notes, there is nothing to do, the local store is created on first launch and no migration is needed, and downgrading to 3.7 the store is simply ignored and the pending changes stay in it, so a downgrade does not lose data, it just delays it.

input: Rationale for the connection pool change before I open the pull request. We are running one pool per worker process at 20 connections and with 12 workers that is 240 sockets against a Postgres box configured for 200, so under load we get connection refused rather than queueing, which is the worst version of this failure because it surfaces as a 500 instead of latency. I want to drop the per worker pool to 8 and put pgbouncer in transaction mode in front of it, which gives us the same throughput headroom without pretending the database has capacity it does not have. The migration risk is prepared statements, so that needs checking before we ship.
output: Rationale for the connection pool change before I open the pull request. We are running one pool per worker process at 20 connections and with 12 workers that is 240 sockets against a Postgres box configured for 200, so under load we get connection refused rather than queueing, which is the worst version of this failure because it surfaces as a 500 instead of latency. I want to drop the per worker pool to 8 and put pgbouncer in transaction mode in front of it, which gives us the same throughput headroom without pretending the database has capacity it does not have. The migration risk is prepared statements, so that needs checking before we ship.

input: Note on the save bug before I forget how it happens. The crash is in SaveManager.WriteSlot when the player quits during an autosave, because we open the stream with FileMode.Create and never dispose it if the serializer throws, so the next write hits an IOException and the slot ends up zero bytes. The fix I want is a using block around the FileStream in Assets/Scripts/Persistence/SaveManager.cs plus writing to slot_3.tmp and renaming it, and it should go on the branch fix/save-atomic-write. Do not change the JSON shape, because the version 4 saves already in the wild parse fine.

input: This is me thinking out loud about the consultation response before I start writing it, so it will ramble a bit. The department's own figures say uptake in the pilot areas was 34% against a target of 60%, and the interesting thing is that they never publish the denominator, so we cannot tell whether that is 34% of everybody eligible or 34% of the people who were actually contacted, which are very different claims. What is the real population they are measuring against? I want to ask that in the response rather than assume it, because if I guess wrong the whole second section falls over. The other thing is timing. The scheme opened in September and closed to new applicants in January, which is four months, and nobody in the evaluation seems to have adjusted for the fact that the January cohort had no time to complete anything at all. I would rather make two arguments properly than five in passing, so the shape is probably the denominator problem first, the truncated cohort second, and everything else in an annex if there is room.

input: Review notes on the caching change, and I will leave these as a comment but I want to say them out loud first. The decorator in src/api/cache.py keys on the request path only, so two users hitting /v1/profile get each other's payload, which is a correctness bug rather than a performance one and it needs the tenant id in the key before this goes anywhere near staging. Second, the TTL is read once at import time from settings.CACHE_TTL_SECONDS, so changing it in the config does nothing until a restart, and that will confuse whoever tries to tune it at three in the morning. The redis client itself is fine. I would also drop the try except around cache.get that swallows ConnectionError, because a silent cache miss storm looks exactly like a database problem and we lost two days to that in March.

# Failover: read this before touching anything

1. Confirm the primary is actually down. Check the health endpoint twice, thirty seconds apart.
2. Promote the standby with `pg_ctl promote`. Do not edit recovery.conf by hand.
3. Repoint the pgbouncer config and reload it. Connections do not need to be drained first.

If step 2 fails, stop and page Rafael. Do not attempt a second promote, because two primaries writing is a worse day than an hour of downtime.
output:

1. Confirm the primary is actually down. Check the health endpoint twice, thirty seconds apart.
2. Promote the standby with `pg_ctl promote`. Do not edit recovery.conf by hand.
3. Repoint the pgbouncer config and reload it. Connections do not need to be drained first.

If step 2 fails, stop and page Rafael. Do not attempt a second promote, because two primaries writing is a worse day than an hour of downtime.

input: Viewing report for the flat on Fenwick Road, 41B, seen this afternoon, I got there at 2:15 and the agent was late so we did not actually go in until about 2:30 and I was out again by 3:40, and I am doing this in the car while it is fresh because I have got the Kentmere one at six and after that they all blur into each other. So 41B is the top floor of a converted terrace, the conversion was 1974 by the look of the joinery and the building itself is much older, and the agent said the roof was done in 2019 which I half believe because the felt at the back looked newer than the rest of it. Layout is better than the photos, you come in and the hall is narrow, properly narrow, I would say under nine hundred wide, and that matters because the only way the sofa is getting in there is through the front window, and then it opens out into the living room which is the whole width of the building and gets light from both ends. North facing at the back. It is north facing at the back which is the thing I keep coming back to, because the kitchen is at that end and it will be dark by three in the winter, and that is not a dealbreaker for me but it is a price point. Two bedrooms, the second one is a box room and the agent called it a double, which it is not, you would get a bed in it and then you would get nothing else in it. Bathroom has been redone recently and cheaply, the tiling is fine and the extractor is not connected to anything, I checked, and there is the beginning of a stain in the corner of the ceiling above the shower which she said was historic. Service charge is the thing that worried me, she said 1,420 a year and then later when I asked for it in writing the figure on the sheet said 1,240, and I do not know which of those is right but I want it in writing before anything else happens because that is a two hundred pound gap on a flat I am going to hold for ten years. What is the ground rent, actually, because she talked about the service charge twice and never once said the ground rent, and that is the first thing I ask her tomorrow. EPC is band D. Lease has eighty one years on it which is under the eighty five where lenders start getting difficult, so that is either a negotiating point or a reason to walk. Their reference for it is FEN-41B-2 and there is a second listing for the ground floor flat in the same building at a lower price which she did not mention until I mentioned it. Overall I liked it more than I expected to and I trust the agent less than I expected to, and those two things are going to have to be resolved separately.

input: It is twenty to one and I am doing this instead of sleeping, which is on brand. Today was fine. It was fine. I got up late, I missed the lecture I said I would definitely not miss, and then I sat in the library from two until about half six and did maybe forty minutes of actual work in that time, which somehow feels worse than doing none. I said I would start at nine. I said I would start at nine and I started at two, and the four hours in between were not restful either, they were just four hours of knowing I was not starting. The essay is due Friday and it is not close, and every time I open the document I read the same first paragraph and decide the whole framing is wrong, and then I close it. input: Ok so this is the speech, or it is the shape of the speech, and I am saying it out loud because I have written it three times now and every version reads like a wedding card. Right. Good evening everyone, for those who do not know me I am Marcus, I have known Callum since 2014 when we shared a flat in Sheffield that had eleven separate things wrong with it, eleven, I counted, and the landlord fixed one of them, and it was not the boiler. And that is the thing about Callum. He lived in that flat for two years without complaining once, not because he is a saint but because he genuinely did not notice. I once watched him make a cup of tea in a kitchen that had no ceiling. Anyway. So the way Callum and Priya met is not romantic and I have been asked not to tell the full version so I am going to tell about sixty percent of it. They met at a work thing, a leaving do for somebody neither of them liked, and Callum spent the first hour talking to Priya about a documentary on shipping containers, an hour, and Priya let him, and if you want to know what kind of person Priya is, that is it, that is the whole thing, she let a man she had just met talk about shipping containers for an hour and then she gave him her number. Priya, on behalf of everyone who has ever had to sit through the shipping container thing, thank you. Then there is Alicante, and I have to be careful here because Priya's mother is in the room and she has already looked at me twice. What I will say about Alicante is that four of us went out, four of us came back, and one of us came back with a tattoo he does not remember getting and cannot explain, and it is not on his arm. And that is the thing about Callum, he owned it immediately, he did not hide it, he showed everyone in the departure lounge, which is the same instinct that makes him a genuinely good friend, he has never once in eleven years told me a version of something that made him look better than he was. Eleven years and not one flattering edit. I would not say that about many people and I would not say it about myself. What I actually want to say, and this is the bit I keep rewriting, is that I watched Callum get better after he met Priya. Not different. Better. He answered his phone. He remembered birthdays, which I want to stress he had never done, and he started turning up to things at 4:30 when he said he would turn up at 4:30 instead of what he used to call flexible time, which meant somewhere between 4:30 and Thursday. And that is the thing about Callum, he does not do things by halves once he has decided, and he decided about Priya very fast and he has not wavered once. Priya, I have known Callum a long time and I have never seen him look at anything the way he looks at you when you are telling a story he has already heard four times. He is doing it right now. He has been doing it all day. So, and then I need something to land this on, I do not have the ending yet, but the shape of it is something about the flat with no ceiling and how the two of them are going to be fine wherever they live, which is true and also a bit neat, so I might come at it a different way. Something about how the eleven things wrong with the flat all got fixed eventually, just not by the landlord. That might be it. That might actually be it. Then, please raise your glasses, to Callum and Priya. That is the shape. It is about six minutes at the speed I say things and probably eight at the speed I will say them on the day, so I am going to have to lose either the shipping containers or the tattoo, and I know which one Priya's mother would prefer.

input: Right, Sunday, and I want to talk about the Samaritan again even though we did it two years ago, because I have been reading it differently since the winter and I think the way we usually tell it is too comfortable. So the text is Luke chapter 10 verse 33, and the shape of it everybody knows, a man is beaten and left, and two respectable men walk past him, and then the one who stops is the one nobody in the room expected to stop. And what I want to sit with is what the Samaritan did not do. He did not ask them anything. He did not ask the man what he was doing on that road at that hour, which is the first thing we ask, is it not, we ask what were you doing there. He did not ask him anything. He did not check whether the man deserved it, he did not ask which village he came from, he did not ask whether he would have stopped if it had been the other way round, and I think if we are honest most of us would want the answer to at least one of those before we got off the donkey. And then the question that starts the whole thing, the lawyer stands up and asks it, and who is my neighbour, and notice that he already knows the law, he quotes it correctly, he gets it right, and he asks the question anyway, because knowing the answer and wanting a smaller version of the answer are two different things. That is the bit I want to land on. He wanted a boundary drawn. He wanted somebody to tell him where the edge of the obligation was. And the answer he gets is not a boundary, it is a story about a man on a road who is not asked any questions. Now I want to bring it to the food bank, carefully, because I do not want it to sound like a fundraising appeal in the middle of a sermon, and I am aware that is exactly what it will sound like if I do it badly. But the thing Ruth said in the meeting has stayed with me, that the hardest part of the work is not the money, it is the forms, and every form is a version of the lawyer's question, where is the edge, who qualifies, prove you are my neighbour. He did not ask them anything. He put the man on his own animal, he walked, and he paid two days wages to a stranger to look after him and said he would come back and settle the rest. He did not ask them anything and he came back. Then I close on that, and I think the hymn after is 411 which works because of the verse about the road, and I need to check with Gareth whether the choir know it, because last time we picked something they did not know and it was a long two minutes. Twelve minutes maybe. It wants to be twelve and it will want to run to eighteen, and I would rather cut the food bank part than rush the ending.

input: Ok, this is the material for the complaint, not the letter itself, do not send anything yet, I want to read it once more when I am less annoyed. So the sequence. That is the first thing that goes in, that they lost it in their own system for sixteen days. Then on 6 March I got an email saying the repair was outside warranty because the fault was, and I am reading this off the screen, consistent with operator misuse, and there is no engineer report attached to that email and when I asked for the report I was told it would follow within 48 hours. They have had the machine for six weeks, they have quoted me 1,340 euro for a repair they originally accepted as a warranty claim, and the part they say has failed, 0K-3155, is the same part that was replaced under warranty on the previous unit in 2023, which I can prove because I still have that paperwork. Keep this firm but polite, I do not want it to read like a rant, because the person who opens it is not the person who did any of this and if I insult them I get nothing. input: Ok, handover for the day team, I am going bed by bed but not in order because bed 11 is the one you need to hear first. Bed 11, the gentleman who came up from A and E yesterday evening, MRN 4471902, he spiked at 02:10, temperature 38.2, and I did the full set of obs, sats were 96 percent on air and the blood pressure was 88 over 52 which is low for him because he was sitting at about 130 systolic all evening. I gave the paracetamol 1 gram at 02:10 as charted and he came down to 37.4 by 04:40, but the pressure did not really come back up, it was 94 over 58 at 04:40 and 96 over 60 at 06:15, so he is not right and I have flagged it twice. I have not been able to get hold of the medical registrar. I bleeped 2213 at 02:20 and again at 03:00 and again at about half four and got nothing, and the switchboard said he was in theatre, so bed 11 has not been reviewed since he came up, and that is the first job of the morning, please do not let it slide into the ward round because the ward round is not until eleven. His cannula in the left hand tissued overnight, I resited it in the right forearm at 04:40, and the antibiotics went through fine after that. Were the family told he was admitted, because there is a next of kin number in the notes and nothing documented about anybody ringing them, and he keeps asking, so that needs checking before you get busy. Bed 4, the lady post op day two, comfortable all night, slept from about midnight through to five which is the best she has had, pain score 2 at 06:15, and the drain output was 30 mils for the whole shift which is a lot less than yesterday. She wants to know when the drain comes out and I said the surgical team would say on the round. She mobilised to the chair at 06:15 with one person and managed it without much trouble. Bed 7 is the confused gentleman, and he has been up most of the night, he was trying to get out of bed at about one and again at three, and I found him standing at the end of the bay at 04:40 with no idea where he was, so he needs eyes on him. He is not aggressive at all, he is frightened, and he settles completely if you sit with him for two minutes and talk about the farm, so if you have a student put them with him rather than in the treatment room. He had the 500 milligrams at 22:00 and nothing since. Sensor mat is on and it has gone off twice. Bed 14 is the discharge, she is medically fit, she has been fit since yesterday lunchtime, and she is still here because the pharmacy did not send the take home medicines up, and I have not been able to get hold of pharmacy either because out of hours you get the on call and the on call said it was a day team dispensing issue. So bed 14 is a phone call at nine and she could be gone by ten if somebody chases it, and she is getting upset about it now, understandably, because she has been told twice she is going home today and today has become tomorrow twice. The rest of the bay is stable. Bed 2 and bed 6 both slept, obs all within range, nothing to report. The fridge temperature log has not been signed since Sunday and I have written it in the book but somebody senior needs to look at it. And we are two down for the day shift, they know, the coordinator was ringing round at about five and had found one. So the priorities, bed 11 needs a medical review before the round and the pressure is the reason, bed 14 needs pharmacy chasing, and bed 7 needs somebody near him. Everything else can wait until after the drug round. I have documented all of it in the notes but bed 11 is the one I would want said out loud, which is why I said it first and I am saying it again now. One more thing and then I am off. The night coordinator asked me to write in the incident book about bed 7 standing at the end of the bay at 04:40, and I have not done it, because by the time I had him settled it was time for the 06:15 obs and I would rather hand over accurately than write it up badly at the end of a twelve hour shift. So that is outstanding and it is mine, I will do it when I come back tonight, but if anybody asks today, it happened at 04:40, he was found standing, he was not injured, and he went back to bed with one person assisting. And please tell whoever takes bed 11 that the pressure is the reason, not the temperature, because if you say he spiked overnight the reg will treat it as a fever that has already settled and it will go to the bottom of the list again.

input: Right, this is the full picture on the Djibouti consignment so that when Selam asks tomorrow there is one version of it and not four. The container is MSKU4471820, it came in on the Northern Diligence, and the booking reference is 218-99417 which is the number the freight forwarder uses, not the number the customs broker uses, and half the confusion this week has been people quoting one at the other. It discharged on 11 April. It has been sitting since 11 April, which is thirteen days now, and the reason it is sitting is not what we were told at the start. What we were told at the start was that it was a documentation hold and that the broker was resolving it. What actually happened is that the commercial invoice went over with the HS code 8471.30 on it, and the goods in the container are not all 8471.30, there is a pallet of accessories that should have gone under a different heading, and because the invoice value is 46,800 dollars in one line item the customs officer would not split it himself, and so the whole container is held rather than the one pallet. Nobody signed anything. That is the part I want to be very clear about because it changes who pays. Nobody signed anything on our side accepting the amended classification, the broker's man says he was told verbally by somebody at the counter to submit an amendment, he did submit it, and the amendment has been sitting in a queue since 24 April. 24 April is when it went in. 24 April, and today is the twenty fourth day of the container being on the ground counting from discharge, so we are into demurrage either way and the demurrage clock does not care whose fault the classification was. I spoke to the port clearance office twice. The first time I got a very helpful woman who found the amendment in the system and said it needed an officer's signature and that officers were signing Tuesdays and Thursdays. The second time I got a man who told me the amendment was not in the system and asked me to resend it, and I asked him to check under the booking rather than the container and he found it, and then he said it needed an officer's signature. So it is the same answer twice with an argument in the middle. The address to send everything to is clearance at portservices dot com, and I have sent the packing list and the amended invoice to that address twice, on the nineteenth and again yesterday, and I have read receipts for neither. Now the money. The demurrage is running at a daily rate and I do not have the exact figure in front of me because the forwarder quotes it in a different currency to the one we get invoiced in, but on thirteen days it is already more than the duty difference we are arguing about, which is the absurd part, we are holding 46,800 dollars of goods over a classification difference smaller than what the waiting is costing. Do not release the payment to the forwarder. Their invoice came in on Tuesday with the demurrage passed straight through as a disbursement and I am not accepting it as a disbursement until somebody tells me in writing why the classification went in wrong, because if their broker keyed it then it is theirs, and if our supplier's invoice was wrong at origin then it is ours, and right now nobody has said. Tell Yonas to hold the trucks. He has two booked for Thursday morning on the assumption it clears Wednesday, and if it does not clear Wednesday we pay for two trucks to sit at the gate, and we have done that once already this year. What I need for tomorrow is a straight answer from the broker on whether the amendment is with an officer or in a queue, because those are different things and he has used both words, and the honest position for Selam is that the goods are not lost, they are not damaged, they are eleven kilometres from the warehouse behind a signature, and the cost of that signature is going up every day nobody chases it. And one last thing that nobody has raised and somebody should. The supplier has done this to us twice now, the same single line commercial invoice with one HS code covering mixed goods, and the first time it cost us four days at origin and we told them then, in writing, in February, that the accessories had to be on a separate line. So when I write this up for Selam I am going to say plainly that the classification problem is a supplier problem that we have already flagged once and that the demurrage is a consequence of it, and that the forwarder's broker made it worse by amending without telling us rather than calling. Both of those are true and they point at different invoices, and if we do not separate them now we will end up absorbing the whole thing again the way we did in February, which is exactly how a supplier learns that a single line invoice is fine.

input: Ok, playtest debrief for build 0.4.2, six players, and I am going to say the bad news first because the bad news is the whole session. They all died at wave 3. Six out of six, and not spread out either, they all died at wave 3 within about forty seconds of each other in real time, and two of them died twice at wave 3 after we let them retry. So whatever we did between 0.4.1 and 0.4.2 has made wave 3 a wall, and my first guess was the new enemy but I do not think it is the new enemy. I think it is the wave timer. In EnemySpawner the wave underscore timer is still set to 3.5 seconds between spawns, which was fine when wave 3 had four enemies in it, and now wave 3 has twelve, and 3.5 seconds times twelve means the tail of wave 3 is still walking in while the player is trying to deal with the front of it, so it stops being a wave and becomes a constant stream with no gap to breathe in. 3.5 seconds. It was tuned for four enemies and nobody retuned it when the count went to twelve, which is my fault because I changed the count in Assets slash Prefabs slash Wave03 dot prefab and never opened the spawner. The other thing, and this one is more interesting, is that nobody used the dash. Nobody. Six players, one of them has played every build since the first prototype, and none of them dashed more than twice in the whole session. And when I asked afterwards, two of them said they forgot it existed and one said he tried it early on and it felt like it did nothing, so I went and looked at PlayerController dot Dash and the recovery is 0.8, which means after you dash you are standing still for most of a second, and in a stream of twelve enemies standing still for most of a second is how you die. So the dash is technically in the game and functionally not in the game, and that is worse than not shipping it, because the whole difficulty curve from wave 3 onward assumes people are dashing. Should the dash cancel the recovery if you land a hit during it, because that is the obvious fix and it is also the fix that turns this into a completely different game, so I am not deciding that on my own. The good news, such as it is, is that everybody understood the resource system without being told. Nobody asked what the blue meter was, four of them figured out that spending it early is a trap, and one of them worked out the overcharge thing on his own in about six minutes, which took me an hour to explain to the publisher. So the systems reading is fine, it is the moment to moment that is broken. Numbers I want to try before the next session, and these are guesses not decisions. Wave timer down from 3.5 seconds to something like 2.2 but with an actual gap between waves, a real pause, three or four seconds where nothing spawns, because right now the waves are only conceptually separate. Dash recovery from 0.8 down to about 0.35 and see whether it becomes overpowered, which it might, and if it does that tells us something too. And drop wave 3 from twelve enemies to eight and move the other four into wave 4, which is empty enough to take them. One process thing. They all died at wave 3 and I did not know that until I watched the recordings, because in the room it felt like they were doing fine, and I sat there for forty minutes thinking the session was going well. So we need the death position logged automatically, wave number and timestamp, because my read of the room was 40 percent wrong and I am not going to trust it again. Last thing, on the room itself, because I want to write it down while I am annoyed enough to remember it. Two of the six were friends of mine and they were being kind, and kind testers tell you the build is good and then die at wave 3 and apologise for dying. The one who was not being kind, the woman from the Thursday group, said the game was unfair rather than hard, and unfair is the word that matters, because hard is a tuning number and unfair is a design mistake, and she said it in the first five minutes and I did not write it down. So for the next session I want strangers, or at least people who do not know me, and I want a recording of what they say in the first two minutes rather than what they say at the end when they are being polite about it.

input: Review comments on the retry patch. The backoff in internal/queue/retry.go is doing jitter after the cap instead of before, so a maxed out backoff has no jitter at all and every consumer wakes at the same time. Line 88 or thereabouts. Second thing, RetryConfig.MaxAttempts is an int and it is compared against attempt which is a uint32 further down, that compiles but it will bite. Third, the test only covers the happy path, there is no case where the context is cancelled mid sleep. Why did we not put the cap in the config struct in the first place? Not a review comment, just thinking aloud. Otherwise it is good, ship it after those three.
