Those are the normal numbers and I test alkalinity twice a week with the same kit and the same person doing it, which matters more than which kit it is. What happened. On the Tuesday I did a 20 litre water change, which is a sixth of the volume and slightly more than usual, and I mixed the new water the night before as always and I checked the salinity of the mixed water, 1.026, no issue. On the Wednesday morning two of the acropora had lost colour at the tips, not tissue, just colour, and I did nothing because colour comes back. On the Wednesday evening the same two were pale halfway down and a third one had started, and I tested and alkalinity was 7.6, which is 0.8 down, and that is a bigger single drop than I have ever recorded in this tank. Alkalinity was 7.6. I retested with the same kit and got 7.6 again, and then I made the mistake, and I want it in the log because the mistake is the useful part. I dosed to bring alkalinity back to 8.4 in one go. In one go, in the evening, into a tank that had been dropping all day, and by Thursday morning the three pale corals were bleached at the top third and two more were pale, and the alkalinity read 8.9, so I had overshot as well. What I should have done, and what everybody says and what I know perfectly well, is raise it slowly over three or four days and accept the low number in the meantime, because the corals do not mind 7.6, they mind going from 7.6 to 8.9 in twelve hours. They do not mind the number. They mind the change. Thursday I did nothing except turn the lights down to 60% and stop all dosing, and Friday I tested everything and the only other thing out was nitrate at under 2, which is lower than it should be and is probably why the colour went in the first place, because a 20 litre change on a tank that was already lean will pull nitrate down and pale tips after a big water change on a lean tank is the oldest story in this hobby and I walked straight into it. So the actual cause was not the alkalinity at all, the alkalinity drop was consumption on top of a change, and my response to it is what did the damage. Where it stands now, eleven days later. The three worst are dead at the tips and holding tissue on the lower two thirds, and one of them has started to encrust again at the base which I am taking as a good sign. The two that went pale later have coloured back up completely. Nitrate is at 6 because I have been feeding heavier and stopped running the reactor, phosphate is 0.08, alkalinity has been at 8.2 to 8.4 for a week without me touching it, which tells me the demand dropped because there is less coral to feed. Lights are back to 80% and I will leave them there for another fortnight. Rules for myself, and this is the part I will actually read again. Never correct alkalinity by more than 0.2 in a day, no matter what the number says. Test before a water change as well as after, because I only test after and that is why I did not see the tank was lean. And keep the water change at 15 litres, which is what it was for two years, and stop being clever about it. One more note for whoever reads this if I ever post it, the kit I use reads consistently about 0.2 high against the reference solution, so my 8.4 is somebody else's 8.2, and comparing my numbers to a forum thread without that offset is meaningless.

input: Right, tech rehearsal notes for the panto, and I am doing this in the hall while they clear the stage because if I wait until tomorrow it turns into a list of complaints instead of a plan. Overall it is closer than I thought it would be. The cast know it, the band know it, and what does not work is entirely the transitions, which is what always does not work, so nobody should panic on Thursday. Lighting first. The general wash is fine for act one but it is too warm for the forest, and Ciaran is going to put the blue front wash on a separate submaster so we can drop the warm without losing the faces, because at the moment when we go to the forest the whole stage goes murky and you lose Dolores completely, and Dolores is the one person who cannot be lost because she has three quarters of the plot. You lose Dolores completely. That is the note. The follow spot from the box is unusable, and I am saying that as a decision not as a complaint, because the operator cannot see the stage left third at all from up there and we have had two rehearsals of him hunting for people, so we are cutting the follow spot and putting a warm special on the down stage right corner instead and Rory walks into it. Sound. The band is too loud for the songs and exactly right for the walk down, which suggests the answer is not the band, it is that the vocal mics are too far downstage and the singers are behind the speakers on half the numbers. Ciaran and I will move the two floats upstage by about a metre and see whether that fixes it before we start turning the band down, because the band being loud is half the reason the room feels alive. If it is still bad we will turn the band down for the two ballads only. Radio mics, we have four and we need six, and I have asked twice, so if the answer is still no then the two smallest parts lose theirs and I will accept the drop in the second half. Set. The flat on stage left is not going to survive twenty performances, the hinge has gone at the bottom, and either it gets a proper repair on Saturday morning or it comes off and we play that scene with the tabs in. I would rather it were repaired but I am not spending Thursday's rehearsal on it. The trap is fine, it is safe, it has been checked, and the only rule is that nobody stands on the lid while it is unlatched and I have said that to every single one of them individually and I will say it again on Thursday. The staircase unit needs the tape renewed because the glow tape has gone dull and in the blackout at the top of act two there are eleven people coming down it. Now the transitions, which is the whole problem. Act one into the kitchen scene takes forty seconds and it should take twelve, and it takes forty because we are trying to move the whole kitchen on with three people while the front cloth is up. So either the cloth comes in and we do it properly behind it, which costs us the joke about the pudding, or we cut the kitchen table and set it with just the chairs and the pot. I want to try the chairs and the pot on Thursday. The other bad one is the transformation, obviously, and that one is not a set problem, it is that the smoke takes eleven seconds to reach the middle of the stage and the cue is written for four, so the smoke goes on at the start of Dolores's line and not at the end of it. Eleven seconds. Whoever wrote the cue sheet wrote it for a smaller room. Cast notes I will give individually tomorrow, but the general one is that they are all playing to the front row and the hall goes back twenty two rows, and I will say the thing I say every year about the back wall, which is that if the person at the back cannot hear you the joke does not exist. Thursday, then. We start at half six with the two transitions, not with a full run, and we do them until they are dull, and then we run act two only, and if there is time at the end we do the walk down because it is still ragged and it is the last thing the audience sees so it is worth more than it looks. And somebody please find the second pudding.

input: Wheel build notes for the rear on the touring bike, and I am recording the numbers because I will build the front next week and I want the same wheel twice rather than two wheels. Rim is the Ryde Sputnik, 36 hole, ERD 599, and the hub is the old Deore, 36 hole, and the flange measurements I took myself with the calipers rather than trusting the chart, because the chart for this hub is wrong and I found that out the hard way last year. Drive side, flange diameter 45, centre to flange 20.5, and non drive side, flange diameter 45 as well, centre to flange 32. Three cross, so the spoke length comes out at 290 on the drive side and 292 on the non drive side, and I ordered 290 and 292 and I ordered four spares of each because a bent spoke on a Sunday is a wasted Sunday. Lacing took an hour and I did the drive side pulling spokes first, all nine of them, before anything else, which is the only way I can keep the pattern straight in my head. Tension. I brought it up in quarter turns going round twice, then in half turns, and the drive side is sitting at about 110 kilograms force on the meter and the non drive side is at about 70, which is the ratio you would expect from those flange numbers. Lateral is within half a millimetre all the way round, radial is within a millimetre at one spot by the join and I am leaving that because chasing it will cost me tension balance and nobody feels a millimetre. Stress relieved twice, squeezing pairs, and it lost almost nothing the second time, which is the whole point of doing it twice. Dish is centred, checked both ways round in the frame and with the gauge. The thing to remember for the front. Measure the flanges. Measure the flanges, do not read the chart, because the chart cost me two spokes of the wrong length and a week of waiting.

input: Right, the quiz league thing, and I am sending this to the committee rather than arguing in the pub because in the pub I will lose my temper. Round four, question six, the answer on the sheet was plaice and we wrote plaice and the marker gave it to the Ferrymen and not to us, and when I asked, he said our spelling was the place you go to and not the fish. It was not. I have the sheet, our handwriting is bad but the word is plaice with an i, and the marker had already marked the two sheets either side of ours as right, so I think he stopped reading properly. That is one point. The bigger one is round six, the music round, where the tie break was whether the band were bare or bear, and I know how that sounds, but the question was about a song title and the title has bare in it, and the Ferrymen wrote bear and got the point, and we wrote bare and did not, and the answer sheet the league sends out has bare on it, so that is not a judgement call, that is just wrong. Two points, and the final margin was one point. The final margin was one point. So what I am asking for is not a rerun, because nobody wants a Tuesday in February replaying a quiz, I am asking for the two points to be corrected on the league table and for the marking to be swapped next time we play them, because they have marked us twice now and both times it has been close and both times it has gone their way, and I am not saying anybody cheated, I am saying it is a bad system and it would be a bad system even if we had won.

input: Stock note for the food bank before the trustees meeting, and I am walking the shelves as I say it so it will jump about a bit. Tinned tomatoes, we are drowning in tinned tomatoes, roughly 400 tins and the harvest festival collections have not come in yet, and the oldest date on the shelf is best before March 2027 so there is no urgency, but we should stop asking for them and I will change the wording on the board outside. Tinned meat is the opposite, 22 tins across everything, and that is under a week at the current rate, which is 61 parcels last week and 58 the week before. Sixty one parcels. That is the highest week we have had and I want the trustees to hear the number rather than the word busy. Long life milk, 90 litres, fine. Cereal, low, about 30 boxes, and we go through 40 a week. Nappies, size 5 and size 6 only, nothing smaller, and the requests are almost all for size 2 and 3, which is the mismatch I raised in July and again in September. Toiletries are fine because of the church collection. Two things that are not stock. The freezer in the back is running at minus 12 rather than minus 18 and it has been for a fortnight, and if it goes we lose about £300 of donated meat, so that is a call to the engineer this week and not next. And the delivery slot from the supermarket has moved from Tuesday morning to Thursday afternoon, which sounds small and is not, because the Thursday afternoon volunteers are the two who cannot lift, so either the slot moves back or the rota changes. I have emailed about the slot twice, on 4 and 11 October, no reply.

input: Ok, camp kit and the stuff the parents keep asking about, and this is going in the newsletter so somebody tidy it after me, but the content is right. Friday to Sunday, we leave from the church car park at 17:30 on the Friday and we are back there at about 15:00 on the Sunday, and about means about, because it depends on the traffic on the ring road and last year we were an hour late and I got four phone calls. Tent groups are already sorted and no, they cannot be changed at the car park. Kit list, the same as always, and the two things people forget are a second pair of shoes and a torch that works. A torch that works. Not a torch, a torch that works, because half of them arrive with a torch that has been in a drawer since last year. Sleeping bag, mat, warm layers even though it is June, waterproof, refillable bottle, and no phones is not a rule I am going to pretend we enforce, so bring it if you must but it lives in the tent and there is no charging. Food is provided, all of it, including Saturday's cooked breakfast, and if your child has an allergy I need it in writing by Wednesday even if you told me in person in March, and yes I know you told me in March. Money, five pounds maximum for the shop on the Saturday, and anybody with twenty pounds will be looked after by me and given back on the Sunday. The activity on the Saturday is the river, so they will get wet, all of them, plan for wet. Old trainers for the water, not sandals, and not the good trainers. Last thing, the one question I get every single year, and the answer is yes, they can ring home if they are homesick, and no, we do not ring you at eleven o'clock at night to tell you they were homesick for ten minutes and then went to sleep.

input: Fitting note for Mr Whelan, second appointment, and I am doing this now because he is coming back on the 26th and whoever sees him needs to know what we tried. Both ears, receiver in canal, and the audiogram is unchanged from January, moderate sloping to severe above 2 kilohertz on the right and slightly better on the left. First fit was too bright and he said so straight away, and he was right, so I came down 4 decibels across the top two channels and the sibilance stopped bothering him. He does not want the programme button explained again. He has asked me not to explain it again and I am writing that down so nobody explains it again, because he only ever uses the default and he is happy, and every time somebody walks him through the four programmes he goes home worried he is using it wrong. The real problem is the right dome. He is losing it in his ear canal, twice now, and both times his daughter had to take him to the walk in, and that is not a comfort issue, that is a safety issue, so I have moved him to the closed dome one size up and put the retention tail on, and I have shown him and his daughter how to check it is seated. Show the daughter, not just him. Battery, he is on rechargeable and he manages the charger fine, and he told me the case is easier than the little doors on his old ones, which is worth knowing because he is 84 and his hands are not good. For the 26th, check the right dome first before anything else, ask about the television because he mentioned it and then changed the subject, and do not touch the gain unless he complains, because he has been comfortable for three weeks and comfortable is what we are after.

input: Winterisation note for the boat, and I am dictating it in the shed because last year I did it from memory in the spring and found out in June that I had missed the raw water side. Engine is the Beta 43, hours are 2,180 as of today. Oil and filter done warm, 5 litres of 15W40, and the filter is the short one not the tall one, and I have written that on the shelf label as well because I have bought the wrong one twice. Gearbox oil changed, 1.2 litres, and the level goes to the top of the mark and not above it. Fuel filters, both, the primary with the water trap and the secondary on the engine, and the primary bowl had about 10 millilitres of water in it which is normal for a season. Antifreeze in the fresh water circuit tested to minus 25 and I left it alone. Now the raw water side, which is the part I missed. Impeller out, and it had two vanes cracked, not broken off, cracked, and I have the old one in the bag as a spare which is exactly the mistake that ends with a cracked vane in the heat exchanger, so I am throwing it away instead. Throwing it away. Then the seacock closed, the hose off, and antifreeze drawn through until it came out of the exhaust pink, which took about 4 litres. Batteries, both off the boat and on the shelf on the charger, and the domestic bank is 5 years old and holding 12.6 volts overnight which is fine for another season. Seacocks all closed and greased except the cockpit drains which are open. Water tank drained, calorifier drained, and the shower pump run dry for a second. Sails off, dried in the barn, not in a bag. For the spring, the two jobs are the impeller which is now on order, and the anode on the shaft which is at about half and will not last two seasons.

## Rotating the signing key

Rotate the key before the certificate expires on 2026-11-04. The old key stays valid for 30 days after rotation.

1. Generate the new key with `keygen --alg ed25519 --out signing-2026b.pem`.
2. Upload the public half in the console under Settings > Signing.
3. Wait for the fleet to pick it up, which takes up to 15 minutes.
4. Revoke `signing-2026a.pem` only once the dashboard shows zero requests against the old key.

If step 4 happens early, every unattended installer fails and there is no way to roll it back.

input: Incident timeline for INC-3312 while it is still fresh. First alert was the p99 latency page at 04:12 and the on call acked it at 04:14. The obvious suspect was the deploy that went out at 03:58, but the rollback at 04:26 did not help, and that is where we lost twenty minutes because everybody kept staring at the deploy. The actual cause was the connection pool on the orders replica, which had been sitting at 190 of 200 since about 02:00, so the deploy only pushed it over the edge. We drained the replica at 04:51 and latency came back inside two minutes. Going back to what I said about the rollback, it was not useless, it ruled the deploy out, but we should have looked at saturation first and the runbook does not tell you to. Two follow ups from me. The pool size alert does exist but its threshold is 195, which is far too late to be useful, and the replica has no dashboard of its own so nobody thought to go and look at it. Total customer impact is 49 minutes on checkout, not the 63 minutes the status page currently says.

input: Test report notes for the bracket, revision D. The fatigue rig ran to 2.1 million cycles at 4.5 kilonewtons and stopped with a crack at the root of the weld, which is where we expected it, so the geometry change has done what it was intended to do. Revision C failed at 780,000 cycles under the same load, so this is not a marginal improvement. The crack initiated on the inboard side and not the outboard side, which is the opposite of what the simulation predicted, and I have no explanation for that yet. The report from the laboratory says 4.5 kilonewtons peak and that is wrong, it was 4.5 kilonewtons amplitude with a mean of 0.5, and I have asked them to reissue it. Should we run a second specimen before we sign the release? My own view is yes, because one specimen is not a population, but that is a programme decision and not mine to make. The strain gauge data is on the shared drive under Projekte/Halterung/RevD.

input: So for the ragu that goes on the menu in October, before I forget again, what actually went in today. 400 grams of coarse ground beef shoulder. 200 grams of pancetta from Renzo and not the supermarket one. 100 grams of chicken liver, cleaned properly. The soffritto goes in first though and it has to cook much longer than the boys think, 25 minutes at least, until the carrot has gone sweet and lost its edge, because if it is still crunchy when the meat goes in then the whole thing tastes raw at the end no matter how long it sits. Then the milk before the wine, which is how it is done here and I am not arguing about it with Marco again, and the milk has to go in warm or it will split on you. input: I am writing this up before I push because the change is bigger than the ticket made it sound. The ticket was only about the date picker not opening on iOS Safari but the actual cause was the focus trap we added in March, it was calling preventDefault on touchstart which kills the tap on the button that opens the picker, so fixing the picker without touching the focus trap was never going to work and that is why this touches more files than you would expect from the title. I kept the trap behaviour for keyboard users because that is the entire point of it and the accessibility audit called it out by name, so what actually changed is that touchstart is no longer swallowed and the trap now intercepts keydown only. I tested on a real iPhone and not the simulator, because the simulator does not reproduce it at all, and then on Android Chrome to make sure I had not broken the thing the trap was added for in the first place. The files I touched. The focus trap hook in shared hooks. The date picker component itself. The touchstart test in the picker suite. I would rather this went in as one commit than three, because splitting it leaves the trap broken in the middle of the history and somebody bisecting next month will land right on it.

input: Okay, what this change does. Moves the webhook retry off the request thread. Adds a dead letter queue for anything that fails five times. Deletes the sleep loop in the notifier that everybody has been complaining about since I got here. The reason all three are in one change instead of three is that they are the same bug wearing three hats, the retry was on the request thread so a slow customer endpoint held a worker, which is why somebody added the sleep loop to spread the load out, and once the retry is off the thread the sleep loop is not just unnecessary, it is actively making the tail latency worse. I had Devika look at the queue part because I have not written one of these here before and the naming conventions are not obvious from the outside, and she pointed out that the existing consumer already handles poison messages, so the dead letter queue is thinner than it was when I started. Rollout is the part I want a second opinion on. My plan is to ship it behind the existing flag off by default, turn it on for the internal tenant on Monday, and then go to 10% of the fleet on Wednesday if the retry metric looks the way I expect, which is fewer retries but each one taking longer. If anybody wants to argue about the sleep loop I am very happy to have that argument, but I would like to have it before Monday and not after, because backing it out afterwards means backing out the queue too.

input: I went out to the Jabal Amman site this morning before the concrete arrived because I wanted to see the formwork myself rather than take a photograph of it on the phone from somebody else. The formwork is fine, better than the last pour actually, the ties are at 600 centres the way we asked and the props are all on the base plates, which was the thing I was worried about after what happened on the second floor. What is not fine is the rebar cover on the north edge, it is nowhere near 40 millimetres in places, I could see the bar through the release agent in two spots, and I stopped the pour on that bay because once the concrete is in there is nothing anybody can do about it and it is my name on the inspection sheet. So before Thursday I need three things and Sami knows about all of them already. The revised bar bending schedule for the north edge only. The spacer count for that bay signed off by the steel foreman. A photograph of the corrected cover before the formwork closes. The rest of the slab can go ahead on Wednesday as planned, and I have told the concrete supplier that the volume is smaller than the order so there is no argument about it on the day, and if the north bay slips to the following week that is better than pouring it wrong and coring it out in August.

input: I finished the triage on the report that came in through the disclosure address on Friday and I do not think it is what the reporter thinks it is. The claim is unauthenticated remote code execution in the export service, and the proof of concept does run, but it runs because the reporter had a valid session cookie in the request, and when I strip the cookie the same request comes back 403 from the edge before it ever reaches the service. So it is authenticated, which moves it down a lot, and it is authenticated as a user who already has the export permission, which moves it down further. What is actually wrong is that the template parameter is passed into the renderer without a whitelist and then the renderer resolves it against the filesystem and then the error page reflects the resolved path back to the caller, so a user with export rights can read any template on the box and can confirm whether an arbitrary path exists. That is a real bug and I am not dismissing it, it just is not the bug in the title. I have reproduced it on 4.11.2 and on the 4.12 release candidate, the hash of the payload I used is in the ticket, and I have not tried it against 4.10 because we do not support it any more. I want to give this a CVE and pay the reporter, but at high and not critical, and I would rather have that conversation with Marek before I reply to them because the last time we downgraded something the thread went sideways in public within a day.

input: Dear Nomvula, thank you for your call yesterday afternoon and for the time you gave me at short notice. I said I would put the position in writing so that both of us are working from the same set of facts, and this is that letter. On the deliveries themselves, our records show that of the 14 consignments scheduled between the second of June and the end of July, four arrived on the agreed date, six arrived between one and three days late, and four have still not arrived at all. The four outstanding are the ones I am most concerned about, because two of them contain the cold chain items for the Gqeberha depot and we have been buying those locally at roughly double the contract price since the middle of June. I am not raising that to open an argument about the invoice, I am raising it because the local purchase is now the larger of the two costs and I have to explain it to my board on the eighth. On the cause, I accept what you told me about the driver shortage and I have no reason at all to doubt it. What I do not accept is that we were not told. Your team knew on the fifth of June that the June schedule was not achievable and we found out on the nineteenth, when the depot manager in Gqeberha rang me directly, which is two weeks in which we could have arranged cover at a sensible price instead of an emergency one. If the only thing that changes out of this letter is that your planner picks up the telephone on the day a schedule slips, that would be worth more to us than any credit note. On the way forward, and I want to be constructive here, because we have worked together for six years and I would far rather fix this than tender it out. I would like a revised schedule for August and September by Friday, with the four outstanding consignments named in it and dated. I would like the weekly call reinstated, the one we dropped in March when everything was going well. And I would like a short written note of what your planner will do differently when a schedule slips. On the penalty clause, I have taken advice and I am told that we are entitled to invoke it. I am not invoking it at this stage. I would rather have the revised schedule and the call, and if the August schedule holds then as far as I am concerned this letter is the end of the matter. If it does not hold then I will invoke it, and I am telling you that now so that it is not a surprise to you later. Perhaps you would confirm receipt of this and let me know whether Friday is achievable for the schedule. If it is not, tell me what is, and I will work with it rather than around it. Kind regards, Thandiwe Mokoena, Operations Director.

input: This is me thinking out loud about the read path before I write the actual document, so none of it is settled. The problem we have is not that the queries are slow, the queries are fine, the problem is that we issue about 40 of them to render one board and the client waits for all 40 because the last one to come back determines when the spinner stops. So the obvious answer is a cache and I have been resisting the obvious answer for about three weeks now, because every caching layer I have worked on in the past became the thing that was hardest to reason about within a year, and the reason is always the same, which is that the invalidation is written by whoever is shipping the feature that needs it and nobody owns the whole picture. What I would rather do first is reduce the 40 to something like five, because most of those queries are the same query with a different identifier and they are being issued from four different components that do not know about each other. If we batch at the transport layer rather than at the query layer then the components do not have to change at all, which matters because two of them are owned by the mobile team and they are mid release. I did a rough measurement on my laptop against a copy of last Tuesday's data and batching alone took the render from about 900 milliseconds to about 340, and that is without any caching whatsoever, and 340 is under the threshold where people describe an interface as sluggish. If that holds up in staging then the cache conversation becomes a much smaller conversation about the two queries that are genuinely expensive rather than an architecture. The part I am least sure about is ordering. Right now the components render as their own data arrives, so the board fills in progressively and people have told us in interviews that they like it, even though it looks unfinished, because they can start reading the top of the board while the rest lands. If we batch, everything arrives at once and the board goes from empty to complete, and I genuinely do not know whether that feels faster or slower to a person, and I do not trust my own opinion on it because I know what the number says. So I want to ship it behind a flag and put it in front of maybe 20 people with the old behaviour on the other side, and ask them which one they think is faster rather than which one they prefer, because those are different questions and the second one gets you a design argument instead of an answer. The other thing I keep coming back to is that none of this helps the first load, because the first load is dominated by the bundle and not by the data, and there is a version of this project where we spend a quarter on the read path and the number people actually complain about does not move at all. I do not think that is what happens here, because the complaints we have are specifically about switching boards rather than about opening the app, but I want that written down at the top of the document so that in six months nobody thinks we forgot about it. I will write the real version on Thursday once the staging numbers are in, and if the staging numbers look nothing like my laptop numbers then the document is going to be much shorter and it is going to say we should look at the bundle instead.

input: Right, incident write up for last night while it is still fresh, and the timeline first because that is the part I will get wrong if I leave it until Monday. The first alert was the checkout latency one at 02:14 and it went to Kasia because she was on call, and she acknowledged it at 02:17 which is well inside the target. At that point latency was about 4 seconds at the 99th percentile and error rate was flat, which is why it did not look like an outage to begin with, it looked like the batch job we run at two o'clock, and honestly on any other night that is exactly what it would have been. What made it different is that the connection pool on the payments service started refusing at 02:31 and that is the alert that woke me up. Between 02:31 and about 02:50 we were both looking at the wrong service. Kasia was on the database because the pool was refusing, and I was on the load balancer because the latency graph had the shape of an uneven backend, and neither of those was it. The actual cause was the certificate on the internal token service expiring at 02:30, which is a number I will never forget now, and every service that talks to it started retrying, and the retries are what filled the pool. Nobody was paged for the certificate because the expiry monitor is on the external certificates only. Recovery was quick once we knew. We rotated the certificate manually at 02:58, the pool drained by 03:04, and checkout latency was back under a second at 03:07, so the customer visible window is about 36 minutes although the payment failures are concentrated in about 12 of those. I have the failed payment count from the finance side as 214 and I am waiting on Aleks to confirm whether the retries on their end recovered any of those, because if they did the number we report is much smaller and if they did not we owe some people an email. What I want to come out of this, and I have put these in the order I think they should happen rather than the order they occurred to me. Step one, put the internal certificates into the same expiry monitor as the external ones, which is a configuration change and could be done this week. Step two, make the payments service fail fast when the token service is unreachable instead of retrying into the pool, which is the real fix and is not a week of work. Step three, add the pool saturation metric to the checkout dashboard so that the next person looking at a latency graph can see in one place that the two are related. There is a fourth thing which I am deliberately not putting on that list because I do not think it is an action, which is that both of us went to the service we know best rather than to the dependency graph, and I do not know how you fix that with a runbook. Maybe you do not. Maybe you just say it out loud in the review and everybody nods and the next person does it anyway.

The actual cause was the certificate on the internal token service expiring at 02:30, which is a number I will never forget now, and every service that talks to it started retrying, and the retries are what filled the pool. Nobody was paged for the certificate because the expiry monitor is on the external certificates only. Recovery was quick once we knew. We rotated the certificate manually at 02:58, the pool drained by 03:04, and checkout latency was back under a second at 03:07, so the customer visible window is about 36 minutes although the payment failures are concentrated in about 12 of those. I have the failed payment count from the finance side as 214 and I am waiting on Aleks to confirm whether the retries on their end recovered any of those, because if they did the number we report is much smaller and if they did not we owe some people an email. What I want to come out of this, and I have put these in the order I think they should happen rather than the order they occurred to me.

1. Put the internal certificates into the same expiry monitor as the external ones, which is a configuration change and could be done this week.
2. Make the payments service fail fast when the token service is unreachable instead of retrying into the pool, which is the real fix and is not a week of work.
3. Add the pool saturation metric to the checkout dashboard so that the next person looking at a latency graph can see in one place that the two are related.

There is a fourth thing which I am deliberately not putting on that list because I do not think it is an action, which is that both of us went to the service we know best rather than to the dependency graph, and I do not know how you fix that with a runbook. Maybe you do not. Maybe you just say it out loud in the review and everybody nods and the next person does it anyway.

input: Note for the file on the gearbox housing samples that came in from Bregenz on Wednesday. I measured all six of them myself on the bench comparator rather than on the CMM, because the CMM is booked out for the turbine work until Friday and the tolerance we care about here is 20 microns, which the comparator resolves perfectly well. Four of the six are inside the drawing tolerance and two are not, and the two that are not are both from the same cavity, which tells me this is a tooling problem and not a process problem, and that is the useful part of the result. The bore diameter on the two bad ones is 60.048 and 60.051 against a drawing figure of 60.000 plus 0.030, so we are talking about 18 and 21 microns over the upper limit, which in a housing of this size is not catastrophic on its own. The reason it matters is the interaction with the bearing seat, because if the bore is 20 microns large and the seat is at the top of its own tolerance band then the press fit is close to nothing, and a press fit close to nothing on a housing that runs at 85 degrees is how you get the noise complaint we had from the Slovakian customer in 2024. So the three things I want from Bregenz before we accept the next batch. The cavity numbers stamped or etched on every part, not written on the box. The bore measurement from their own final inspection for each cavity. The tool maintenance record for cavity three since the last service. I have deliberately not asked them to scrap the two parts, because I would like to keep them here as reference samples, and if they want them back for their own analysis then they can have them after I have measured the bearing seats on both. On the wider question of whether we tighten the drawing, I am against it. The drawing figure has been the same since the 1990s and the parts we have run for 30 years against it have been fine, and tightening a tolerance because one cavity is drifting is solving a supplier problem with a specification, which costs us money on every part we ever buy afterwards. What I would rather do is add the bore to the incoming inspection sampling plan at a higher frequency for the next three deliveries, and then drop it back once we have seen a clean batch. I will speak to Herr Vogel on Monday and I will copy the measurement sheet to purchasing so that nobody agrees a price for the next batch before this is settled, because that is what happened with the seals last year and I am still hearing about it.

input: This is my referee report for the manuscript on retrieval augmented summarisation, and I am dictating it because I have read the thing three times now and I still cannot decide what I think, so I am hoping that saying it out loud will settle me. My overall position is a major revision rather than a rejection, and I want to explain why it is not a rejection first, because the reasons to reject are the ones that will be obvious to the other referees and I do not want the editor to think I missed them. The experimental section is thin. There is one dataset, the evaluation is automatic only, and the baselines are two years old, and if I read that list back to myself in the abstract of somebody else's review I would assume the paper was weak. But the contribution is not the experiment. The contribution is the observation in section 3, which is that the retrieval step and the generation step are being trained against objectives that disagree about what a relevant passage is, and that the disagreement grows with the length of the generated summary, and I have not seen that stated cleanly anywhere else. The authors do not seem to know that this is the interesting part of their own paper, because they spend two pages on it and eleven on an architecture that I do not think anybody will adopt. If the revision moves section 3 to the front, gives it the space it deserves, and treats the architecture as one instantiation rather than as the point, then this becomes a paper I would want to cite. On the experiments, and I want to be specific here rather than saying that more experiments are needed, which is the least useful sentence in our field. The claim that the objective disagreement grows with summary length is measured at three lengths, 64, 128 and 256 tokens, and the trend across three points is not a trend. I would want at least six lengths and I would want the longest of them to be well past the point where the retrieval budget stops mattering, because the alternative explanation for their figure 4 is simply that longer summaries exhaust the retrieved context and the model starts inventing, which is a different phenomenon with a large existing literature. If that alternative can be ruled out by an ablation on the retrieval budget then the paper is much stronger and the ablation is a day of compute. On the evaluation, I accept that human evaluation is expensive and I am not going to demand it as a condition. What I will say is that the automatic metric they use is known to reward extractive overlap, and their method produces more extractive summaries than the baselines, which the authors themselves note in a footnote on page 7 and then do not follow up. A referee who wanted to be unkind could stop reading at that footnote. I would ask them to report at least one metric that does not reward overlap, and to say plainly in the text what the footnote currently says quietly. On the writing, the paper is clear and I had no trouble following it, which I mention because it is rarer than it should be and because the revision I am asking for is structural rather than linguistic. Section 5 is the exception, where the notation changes halfway through without warning, the retrieval scoring function is called s in equations 6 and 7 and then r from equation 8 onwards, and I assume that is an artefact of two authors writing two halves. On related work, they have missed the line of work on query and document objective mismatch in dense retrieval, which predates their observation and does not diminish it, but which they should engage with rather than have a reviewer point out. I am not going to list references in a review because it identifies me, but the editor can pass on that the relevant papers are from the 2021 and 2022 retrieval literature rather than the summarisation literature, which is probably why they missed them. Two smaller things. Table 2 reports standard deviations for their method and not for the baselines, which I assume is an oversight, and if it is not then the comparison is not sound. The code link in the footnote on page 9 is a private repository and returned a 404 for me, and I would like it to be live before this is published rather than after. To summarise my recommendation, major revision, with the essential changes being the promotion of section 3, the retrieval budget ablation, and a metric that does not reward extractive overlap, and with the notation and the missing related work as straightforward corrections. If the authors do the first three properly I would be happy to see it again and I would expect to recommend acceptance. If they do only the corrections and leave the structure as it is, then I think the paper gets published somewhere, gets read by nobody, and the good idea in section 3 waits another two years for somebody else to have it.

input: Okay, notes from the vendor call before I lose them, and some of this is me thinking rather than reporting so read it that way. The three things we did not get answers on. Whether the SLA covers the regional endpoints or only the primary. What happens to our data if we terminate inside the first year. Who actually owns the fine tuning artefacts we produce on their platform. Their solutions engineer was good, genuinely, better than the last two we have spoken to, and he did not pretend to know things he did not know, which is why I have three open questions instead of three vague answers. On the SLA, the contract language says 99.9% and their status page shows 99.94% over the last year, and both of those are fine, but the number is measured at the primary and we would be serving Bengaluru and Singapore from regional endpoints, and he could not tell me whether those are inside the measurement or outside it. If they are outside it then the 99.9% is not a commitment about anything our users would experience, and I would want that in writing before we sign rather than discovering it during an incident. On the exit, the standard agreement has a 90 day export window and a 30 day deletion certificate, which is normal, but there is a clause that makes the export format their own JSON schema rather than anything portable, and Rohit's point in the room was that if the export is in a format only they read then a 90 day window is decorative. He is right and I should have caught that myself. On the artefacts, this is the one that worries me most and the one their engineer was most honest about, which is that he did not know and said so and offered to get us legal language by Thursday. My read is that the platform terms as written give them a licence to the artefacts, not ownership, but the licence is broad enough that it does not matter very much which word you use. Separately from all that, the pricing is better than I expected and better than the incumbent by roughly 30% at our volume, and the finance case is not close if you only look at the invoice. I do not think we should decide on the invoice. If the answer to the artefacts question is unfavourable then the 30% is buying us a switching cost we cannot pay later, and I would rather stay where we are and be slightly poorer. I said none of that in the room. What I want to do is get the three answers in writing, put them next to the incumbent's renewal terms which land in November anyway, and take a recommendation to the steering group in the first week of December rather than trying to force it before the quarter closes. Nobody is asking us to decide this month and I would like to stop behaving as though somebody is.

input: So the churn number in the Monday deck is wrong and I would rather say that myself than have somebody find it, and the explanation is boring but I need to write it down properly because I have already confused two people by explaining it badly in the standup. The definition we agreed in March was that a customer churns in the month their last active subscription ends, and the query I inherited implements something slightly different, it takes the max of ended_at across the subscriptions table grouped by account_id, which sounds like the same thing and is not, because accounts that downgrade to the free plan do not get an ended_at at all, they get a plan_id change and the row stays open. So every downgrade has been counted as a retained customer since the query was written, and the churn number we have been reporting is lower than the real one by however many downgrades there were. I have run the corrected version against the last 18 months and the gap is not as bad as I feared in most months, between 0.3 and 0.6 points, but in February it is 2.1 points because of the pricing change, and February is the month everybody quotes. The uncomfortable part is that the corrected number makes the retention improvement we announced in April look like about half of what we said it was. It is still an improvement. It is just a smaller one, and I would rather we restate it ourselves in the Monday deck with a footnote than have the board ask about it in the quarterly, because the quarterly is the wrong room to explain a group by in. I have kept both versions of the query and I have written the difference between them in the comment at the top, and I would like somebody who is not me to read it before Monday, because I have been staring at it since Thursday and I am no longer a reliable reader of my own SQL. The other thing this exposes is that we have no test on any of these definitions, and a definition that lives only in a query is a definition that changes whenever somebody edits the query. To fix it properly I need three things from the data team. A test fixture with one account per lifecycle path, including the downgrade path that broke this. The agreed definition written down somewhere that is not a query comment. A named owner for the churn metric who has to approve a change to it. None of those are big pieces of work and all three of them would have caught this in March, and I am aware that saying so now is easier than saying so then.

input: Long note on Mr Halloran because the referral needs to carry the whole story and the specialist will not have the old file. He first came to me in 2019 with intermittent left sided chest discomfort on exertion, which at that time settled with rest inside five minutes, and the stress test that year was normal, so we managed it as reflux and he did well on 40 mg pantoprazole for about two years. The pattern changed in the winter of 2023, and this is the part I want the specialist to read carefully, because it did not change in the way you would expect. The discomfort stopped being exertional. He now describes it at rest, most often in the early morning, lasting 10 to 20 minutes, not related to meals, not relieved by the pantoprazole which he has continued to take, and not accompanied by breathlessness or sweating on any occasion he can recall. He is a poor historian about severity and tends to say everything is fine, and his wife gives a rather different account, which I have recorded separately with her permission. On examination today he is comfortable at rest, blood pressure 148 over 88 in the left arm, 144 over 86 in the right, pulse 72 and regular, no murmur, chest clear, no ankle oedema, and the ECG I did in the room is unchanged from the one in 2022 apart from a slightly longer PR interval which I do not think is significant on its own. His bloods from last Thursday show total cholesterol 6.2, LDL 4.1, HbA1c 6.4%, and eGFR 68 which is down from 79 two years ago and is the other reason I am writing. Current medications are pantoprazole 40 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte which he started in March and says he takes most nights, and perindopril 5 mg which was started by the after hours service in January and which nobody has reviewed since. He also takes over the counter ibuprofen for his knee, more often than he tells me, and I have gone over that again today in the context of the eGFR. He has never smoked. His father died at 61 of a myocardial infarction and his brother had a stent at 58, and he knows both of those numbers very well and mentions them at every visit. My concern is that the change from exertional to rest symptoms in a man of 63 with that family history and an unimproved lipid profile deserves a cardiology opinion rather than another trial of acid suppression, and I have told him that plainly today and he has agreed, which is a change from last year. I am not calling this unstable angina because the episodes have been stable in character for 18 months now and he is not having them more often, but I would not want the referral triaged as routine on the basis that the stress test was normal in 2019. He is aware that if the discomfort lasts longer than his usual 20 minutes or comes with breathlessness he is to call an ambulance and not the surgery, and his wife is aware of that too, and I have written it down for them because he will not remember it. I have asked him to keep a simple diary of the episodes with the time and the duration until he is seen. Repeat bloods in eight weeks unless cardiology wants them sooner, and I will review the perindopril and the ibuprofen at that visit rather than changing two things at once now.

input: Commit message for the focus trap fix and I want the body to say why, because the diff looks enormous for what is basically a bug fix and Jiwon is going to ask me about it in review. The summary line is fix focus trap escaping the settings dialog on save. Then the body. The original implementation only guarded the tab key on the dialog root, which was fine back when the dialog was a single form, but we have been adding things into it for four months and every one of them turned out to be a new way out. I spent most of yesterday finding them rather than fixing anything, and the fix itself is maybe thirty lines. The three places it was actually leaking. The close button, once it goes disabled during the save request. The date picker portal, rendering outside the dialog in the DOM. The success toast, taking focus the moment the save resolves. The toast is the one users actually noticed, because after saving you would press tab expecting to be back in the form and instead you were somewhere in the page behind it, and on Safari with VoiceOver on you were simply gone. I have written a test for each of the three but the toast test is flaky on CI while passing locally every single time, so I have marked it skip with a comment pointing at ticket 2291 rather than leaving a red build for everybody else. Reviewers should look at useFocusTrap.ts first and the portal change second, the rest of the diff is test setup and it reads fast.
output:

The summary line is fix focus trap escaping the settings dialog on save. Then the body. The original implementation only guarded the tab key on the dialog root, which was fine back when the dialog was a single form, but we have been adding things into it for four months and every one of them turned out to be a new way out. I spent most of yesterday finding them rather than fixing anything, and the fix itself is maybe thirty lines. The three places it was actually leaking.

- The close button, once it goes disabled during the save request.
- The date picker portal, rendering outside the dialog in the DOM.
- The success toast, taking focus the moment the save resolves.

The toast is the one users actually noticed, because after saving you would press tab expecting to be back in the form and instead you were somewhere in the page behind it, and on Safari with VoiceOver on you were simply gone. I have written a test for each of the three but the toast test is flaky on CI while passing locally every single time, so I have marked it skip with a comment pointing at ticket 2291 rather than leaving a red build for everybody else. Reviewers should look at useFocusTrap.ts first and the portal change second, the rest of the diff is test setup and it reads fast.

input: This is for the literature note and I want it structured with headings so I can navigate it later with the screen reader, so put headings in. What I have read this week on the childcare subsidy question, and none of it changes the direction of the chapter, it just fills in the middle. The Norwegian evaluation is the strongest thing I have found and it is also the least useful to us, because they had a register that let them follow the same households for eleven years and we have a survey that changed its sampling frame twice in that period. The Chilean paper is closer to our situation, same problem with the frame, and they solve it by simply not claiming anything about the level and only claiming things about the direction, which I think is the honest move and I want to say so in the chapter rather than pretending our data is better than it is. Three things I need to go back for. The 2019 administrative note that the Chilean authors cite twice. The unpublished appendix Kjersti mentioned in the seminar. The subsidy take-up numbers by region, which are on the ministry site somewhere but not in the statistical yearbook. The take-up numbers are the ones that actually matter for the argument, because if take-up is as uneven as the seminar suggested then the national average is doing a lot of hiding, and the whole chapter is about what the average hides.

input: PR description for the queue change and I am going to talk through it in the order a reviewer should read it, because if they start in the worker they will not understand why any of it is there. First read the migration, because it adds the attempt count and the visibility timeout columns and everything else depends on those two. Second read the enqueue path, where the only real change is that we no longer trust the client to give us an idempotency key. Third read the worker, which is where the retry logic actually moved to. The reason this is one PR and not three is that the intermediate states do not work, and I did try: if the migration lands without the worker change then every job that fails once sits in the queue forever, and if the worker lands first it reads a column that is not there yet. So it is one PR and it is 900 lines and I am sorry about that, but splitting it would mean shipping two broken states to production and then a third commit that fixes them. Testing, and this is the part I want someone to be unhappy with rather than me finding out on Friday. I have run the new path against a copy of last Tuesday's queue dump, which had the pathological case in it, the 4,000 jobs from the same tenant, and it drained in about nine minutes against forty something before. What I have not tested is what happens when the database fails over mid-drain, because I do not have a way to do that outside production, and Piotr thinks the answer is that we double-process anything in flight. If he is right that is a follow-up, not a blocker, but I would like it written down in the ticket before we merge rather than after.

input: Okay this is the debrief from the Halvorsen visit, I am on the 35 heading back so if it cuts out I will pick it up again. Short version is that it went better than the last one and worse than I told Priya on the phone, and the difference is entirely about who was in the room. So I expected Karl and I got Karl plus their new procurement person, and the procurement person had clearly read the contract properly, which nobody on their side had done in two years, and about twenty minutes in she asked why the platform fee is on a separate line from the per-seat number when the per-seat number already says it includes support. Which is a fair question and I did not have a good answer for it because there is not one, it is just how we have always quoted, and I said I would come back to her rather than making something up on the spot, which I think was the right call but it did cost us the momentum for the rest of the hour. Karl was on my side the whole time, that has not changed. He wants this renewed, he said twice that the team would riot if we took the scheduling piece away from them, and at one point he pulled up the usage dashboard himself without me asking, which is the single best thing that happened in that room. The procurement person was not hostile either, I want to be clear about that, she was just doing her job properly for the first time in the history of this account. What she wants is a single number, one line, three years, and she said she does not care whether that number is bigger than what they pay now as long as she can put it in a spreadsheet and forecast it, and honestly if that is the trade then we should take it, because the thing that has killed this account twice is the annual argument about the fee line. On the technical side there was nothing new. Same two complaints, the export takes too long and the mobile view drops the room column, and I said the same thing I said in October about the export which is that it is on the roadmap, and she looked at me exactly the way you would expect someone to look at a person saying it is on the roadmap for the second time. So I would like an actual date on the export before I go back in there, even a bad one, even the third quarter, because a bad date is a fact and the roadmap is not. Next steps as I see them, and I want to talk this through with Priya before anything goes in the CRM, are that we rework the quote as one line over three years and we see whether the discount that implies is something we can live with, and separately somebody senior needs to ring Karl and thank him properly, because he has carried this internally for two years and he has never once asked us for anything. I am going to write the quote tonight and sit on it until Priya has looked at it, because the last time I sent a reworked number the same week as a meeting it read as desperate and it probably was. And tell whoever picks up the export question that the person asking is procurement and not engineering, because the answer they need is a date and not an explanation of why it is slow.

input: This is the first pass at the search extraction doc and I am dictating it because I have been staring at an empty page for two days, so it is going to be rough and I will tidy it after. The problem statement is not that search is slow, everybody says search is slow and that is not the interesting part. The problem is that search is slow in a way that takes the checkout with it, and it has done that four times since January, and every one of those four times the on-call story is the same, which is that somebody in the admin tool ran a query with an empty filter against the orders table and the connection pool filled up and then checkout could not get a connection either. So the thing I want the doc to argue is not that we need a search cluster because search clusters are nice, it is that search and checkout are sharing a failure domain that nobody chose deliberately, and the cheapest way to stop sharing it might not even be a search cluster. I want to write the alternatives down honestly before I write the recommendation, because the last three design docs on this team already knew the answer in paragraph one and everybody could tell. Background first. The orders table is 340 million rows and it is the same table the admin tool searches, the customer service tool searches, the finance export reads on the first of the month, and checkout writes to on every single order. It has eleven indexes, four of which exist only for the admin tool's search screen, and two of those four are on columns that the search screen no longer shows because we redesigned it in March and nobody dropped the indexes. Sofia found that last week while she was looking at something else entirely and it is worth saying out loud that dropping those two indexes might buy us more write headroom than any of the big options in this doc, for a day of work and no architecture at all. The three failure modes I actually want us to design against. The unbounded admin query that fills the connection pool. The finance export on the first of the month that competes with the morning traffic peak. The reindex after a schema change, which currently takes the write lock for about eleven minutes and we have just been doing it at four in the morning and hoping. Those are the three, and I think the useful test for every option below is whether it fixes all three or only the first one, because the first one is the one that pages us and the other two are the ones that will page us next year when the table is twice the size. Option one is a read replica for the admin and service tools, nothing else changes. It is about a week of work, mostly plumbing and a config flag, and it fixes failure mode one properly and failure mode two accidentally, because the export can read the replica too. It does nothing at all for the reindex problem and it does not make search any faster, it just stops search taking checkout down with it, which is honestly most of what I want. Option two is a real search index, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, populated from the write-ahead log. This is the one everybody assumes we are going to do and it is the one I am least comfortable with, not because it does not work but because it means we own a second stateful system and a pipeline that can silently fall behind, and the failure mode of a search index that is four hours stale is worse than a search that is slow, because a slow search looks broken and a stale one looks correct. If we do this we need staleness monitoring before we need anything else, and I want that written into the doc as a requirement and not a follow-up. Option three is to bound the admin queries and leave the architecture alone. Force a date range, cap the result set, put a statement timeout on the admin connection pool, and put the admin tool on its own pool so that when it fills up it only hurts the admin tool. Sofia and I sketched this on Thursday and it is two days of work, it fixes failure mode one, it does not fix two or three, and it makes the admin tool worse to use for the four people who use the wide queries deliberately, and one of those four people is the person who runs the fraud reports. My recommendation is going to be option three now and option one in the same quarter, and option two written down as the thing we do when the replica is not enough, with the trigger being written down as an actual number rather than a feeling. Sofia disagrees with me on the ordering and thinks the replica is the thing to do first because it is the one we would not regret, and she may well be right, so I am going to write both orderings into the doc and let the review settle it rather than pretending we agree.

This is the first pass at the search extraction doc and I am dictating it because I have been staring at an empty page for two days, so it is going to be rough and I will tidy it after. The problem statement is not that search is slow, everybody says search is slow and that is not the interesting part. The problem is that search is slow in a way that takes the checkout with it, and it has done that four times since January, and every one of those four times the on-call story is the same, which is that somebody in the admin tool ran a query with an empty filter against the orders table and the connection pool filled up and then checkout could not get a connection either. So the thing I want the doc to argue is not that we need a search cluster because search clusters are nice, it is that search and checkout are sharing a failure domain that nobody chose deliberately, and the cheapest way to stop sharing it might not even be a search cluster. I want to write the alternatives down honestly before I write the recommendation, because the last three design docs on this team already knew the answer in paragraph one and everybody could tell. Background first. The orders table is 340 million rows and it is the same table the admin tool searches, the customer service tool searches, the finance export reads on the first of the month, and checkout writes to on every single order. It has eleven indexes, four of which exist only for the admin tool's search screen, and two of those four are on columns that the search screen no longer shows because we redesigned it in March and nobody dropped the indexes. Sofia found that last week while she was looking at something else entirely and it is worth saying out loud that dropping those two indexes might buy us more write headroom than any of the big options in this doc, for a day of work and no architecture at all. The three failure modes I actually want us to design against.

- The unbounded admin query that fills the connection pool.
- The finance export on the first of the month that competes with the morning traffic peak.
- The reindex after a schema change, which currently takes the write lock for about eleven minutes and we have just been doing it at four in the morning and hoping.

Those are the three, and I think the useful test for every option below is whether it fixes all three or only the first one, because the first one is the one that pages us and the other two are the ones that will page us next year when the table is twice the size. Option one is a read replica for the admin and service tools, nothing else changes. It is about a week of work, mostly plumbing and a config flag, and it fixes failure mode one properly and failure mode two accidentally, because the export can read the replica too. It does nothing at all for the reindex problem and it does not make search any faster, it just stops search taking checkout down with it, which is honestly most of what I want. Option two is a real search index, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, populated from the write-ahead log. This is the one everybody assumes we are going to do and it is the one I am least comfortable with, not because it does not work but because it means we own a second stateful system and a pipeline that can silently fall behind, and the failure mode of a search index that is four hours stale is worse than a search that is slow, because a slow search looks broken and a stale one looks correct. If we do this we need staleness monitoring before we need anything else, and I want that written into the doc as a requirement and not a follow-up. Option three is to bound the admin queries and leave the architecture alone. Force a date range, cap the result set, put a statement timeout on the admin connection pool, and put the admin tool on its own pool so that when it fills up it only hurts the admin tool. Sofia and I sketched this on Thursday and it is two days of work, it fixes failure mode one, it does not fix two or three, and it makes the admin tool worse to use for the four people who use the wide queries deliberately, and one of those four people is the person who runs the fraud reports. My recommendation is going to be option three now and option one in the same quarter, and option two written down as the thing we do when the replica is not enough, with the trigger being written down as an actual number rather than a feeling. Sofia disagrees with me on the ordering and thinks the replica is the thing to do first because it is the one we would not regret, and she may well be right, so I am going to write both orderings into the doc and let the review settle it rather than pretending we agree.

input: Note for the pastry section before service, because I am not going to be here Thursday and Rafa will get this wrong if it is not written down. The tart shells for the weekend. 250 grams of flour, the weaker one in the blue sack and not the bread flour. 150 grams of the cold butter, cut small, straight from the fridge. 80 grams of icing sugar, sifted, because it will not come out smooth otherwise. One yolk and a spoon of cold water at the end and no more than that. The butter is the whole thing here, if it goes soft while he is working it then the shells shrink in the oven and we lose two out of every twelve and I am not paying for that twice in one week. So he should make it in two batches rather than one big one, and put the second batch of butter back in the fridge while he does the first, which sounds slow and is faster than remaking them. Rest it properly, an hour minimum and overnight is better, then roll it cold and dock it and freeze the shells in the tins before they go in, and blind bake from frozen at 170 for about eighteen minutes until the edge is the colour of the ones I left in the box as a reference. Tell him the reference shells are the ones in the box marked with the tape, not the pale ones on the rack, the pale ones are underbaked and that is what I am trying to stop.
output:

- 250 grams of flour, the weaker one in the blue sack and not the bread flour.
- 150 grams of the cold butter, cut small, straight from the fridge.
- 80 grams of icing sugar, sifted, because it will not come out smooth otherwise.
- One yolk and a spoon of cold water at the end and no more than that.

The butter is the whole thing here, if it goes soft while he is working it then the shells shrink in the oven and we lose two out of every twelve and I am not paying for that twice in one week. So he should make it in two batches rather than one big one, and put the second batch of butter back in the fridge while he does the first, which sounds slow and is faster than remaking them. Rest it properly, an hour minimum and overnight is better, then roll it cold and dock it and freeze the shells in the tins before they go in, and blind bake from frozen at 170 for about eighteen minutes until the edge is the colour of the ones I left in the box as a reference. input: This is the referee report for the manuscript on subsidy take-up, and I want to be careful with it, because I think the paper should be published and I also think the current draft would embarrass the authors if it went out as it stands. So the tone matters more than usual and I would rather spend a paragraph explaining a criticism than make it in a sentence and have them read it as dismissal. The contribution is real and I want to say that first and clearly. They have assembled a household panel for a country where nobody has had one, they have documented how they built it in enough detail that somebody could rebuild it, and the descriptive section alone is worth publishing, because the existing literature on this question has been arguing about a level that nobody had actually measured. The estimate in table four is the paper as far as most readers will be concerned, and I believe it, roughly, within a factor that I will come to. My main concern is the identification and it is not the concern the authors seem to expect, because they spend four pages defending the exogeneity of the eligibility threshold and I have no quarrel with any of it. My concern is upstream of that. The panel loses eighteen percent of households between the second and third waves, the attrition is concentrated in exactly the group the subsidy targets, and the appendix handles it with an inverse probability weight estimated on the variables that are available rather than the variables that plausibly drive attrition. That is standard practice and it is also, in this specific case, the weakest link in the paper, because the households that leave the panel are the ones that moved, and moving is the outcome the subsidy is supposed to affect. I do not think this is fatal and I do not think it is fixable with a better weight. What I would like is for the authors to say it out loud in the main text rather than in appendix C, and to give the reader a bound: if every household that left the panel had taken up the subsidy, and if none of them had, what does the estimate in table four become. If the answer is that the sign survives both, which I suspect it does, then the paper is stronger for having said so, and if the sign does not survive then the reader has to know that. On the modelling, section five is doing too much and I would cut it rather than expand it. The structural exercise sits awkwardly against the reduced form results, it requires assumptions about the discount rate and the cost of applying that are not defended anywhere, and the paper's own descriptive evidence contradicts one of them, because the application cost cannot be as small as the calibration assumes if take-up is as uneven across regions as figure three shows. My honest reading is that section five was written for a different referee, possibly a real one at a different journal, and the paper would be shorter and better without it, and I say that knowing how unwelcome it is to be told to delete twelve pages. The writing needs a pass but not from me. The English is fine, better than mine in places, but the paper is organised as a chronology of what the authors did rather than as an argument, so the reader meets the data construction before they know why it matters, and the result arrives on page twenty two. Moving the headline estimate forward would cost nothing and would change how the paper is read entirely. Two smaller things that I noticed and that are easy. The regional deflator is described in the text as the national one in one place and the regional one in another, and I could not tell from the appendix which was actually used. The standard errors in table six are clustered at a level that is not stated, and given the sampling design I would want them clustered at the enumeration area, which may well be what they have done. My recommendation is a major revision, and I want the letter to the editor to say clearly that I expect to recommend acceptance after it, because a major revision from me has been read as a rejection before and this is not that. If it helps the authors I am happy for my identity to be disclosed to them and I would be glad to look at the attrition bound informally before they resubmit, rather than making them guess at what would satisfy me.
