input: Right, first draft of the upgrade page for 4.2, dictating it because I write faster this way and I will clean up the prose in the editor afterwards. Heading, before you upgrade. There are two things worth doing before you start and neither of them takes long. Take a copy of the config directory, because the upgrade rewrites it in place and there is no undo, and check which storage backend you are on, because the SQLite path and the Postgres path diverge halfway through this page and following the wrong one wastes an hour. If you are not sure which backend you are on, the answer is in the first ten lines of the server log at startup. Heading, upgrading on Postgres. This is the path we test and it is the one that works. Stop the server, run the migration command with the dry run flag first and read what it says it is going to do, then run it for real, then start the server and watch the log until you see the schema version line. The dry run is not optional in my opinion even though the flag says it is, because it is the only place you will see the estimate for how long the index rebuild takes, and on a table over about ten million rows that estimate is the difference between a five minute maintenance window and a fifty minute one. If the migration fails partway it is safe to run it again, it is idempotent by design, and if it fails twice in the same place then stop and open an issue with the log rather than trying the force flag, which exists for us and not for you. Heading, upgrading on SQLite. Same three commands, one extra problem. The rebuild holds a write lock on the whole file, so anything that talks to the database while it runs will get a locked error rather than waiting politely, and that includes the backup timer if you have it enabled, which is enabled by default and which nobody remembers. Disable the timer, upgrade, enable it again. On a file over about two gigabytes the rebuild is slow enough that you want to do this out of hours, and I would take a copy of the file first rather than trusting the migration to be reversible, because on this path it is not. Heading, after you upgrade. Check the schema version, check that the workers reconnected, and look at the deprecation warnings in the log, because 4.2 warns about three config keys it will drop in 4.3 and the warning is the only notice you get. The old keys keep working for this release. They do not keep working in the next one, and the migration will not rename them for you, so this is the moment to do it while you are already in the file. Heading, if it goes wrong. Roll back by restoring the config copy and the database copy you took at the start, in that order, and start the old binary. There is no downgrade command and there will not be one, because the schema change is not reversible without losing the attempt history, and we decided that silently losing history was worse than making you restore a backup.
output:
Right, first draft of the upgrade page for 4.2, dictating it because I write faster this way and I will clean up the prose in the editor afterwards.

## Before you upgrade

There are two things worth doing before you start and neither of them takes long. Take a copy of the config directory, because the upgrade rewrites it in place and there is no undo, and check which storage backend you are on, because the SQLite path and the Postgres path diverge halfway through this page and following the wrong one wastes an hour. If you are not sure which backend you are on, the answer is in the first ten lines of the server log at startup.

## Upgrading on Postgres

This is the path we test and it is the one that works. Stop the server, run the migration command with the dry run flag first and read what it says it is going to do, then run it for real, then start the server and watch the log until you see the schema version line. The dry run is not optional in my opinion even though the flag says it is, because it is the only place you will see the estimate for how long the index rebuild takes, and on a table over about ten million rows that estimate is the difference between a five minute maintenance window and a fifty minute one. If the migration fails partway it is safe to run it again, it is idempotent by design, and if it fails twice in the same place then stop and open an issue with the log rather than trying the force flag, which exists for us and not for you.

## Upgrading on SQLite

Same three commands, one extra problem. The rebuild holds a write lock on the whole file, so anything that talks to the database while it runs will get a locked error rather than waiting politely, and that includes the backup timer if you have it enabled, which is enabled by default and which nobody remembers. Disable the timer, upgrade, enable it again. On a file over about two gigabytes the rebuild is slow enough that you want to do this out of hours, and I would take a copy of the file first rather than trusting the migration to be reversible, because on this path it is not.

## After you upgrade

Check the schema version, check that the workers reconnected, and look at the deprecation warnings in the log, because 4.2 warns about three config keys it will drop in 4.3 and the warning is the only notice you get. The old keys keep working for this release. They do not keep working in the next one, and the migration will not rename them for you, so this is the moment to do it while you are already in the file.

## If it goes wrong

Roll back by restoring the config copy and the database copy you took at the start, in that order, and start the old binary. There is no downgrade command and there will not be one, because the schema change is not reversible without losing the attempt history, and we decided that silently losing history was worse than making you restore a backup.

input: Okay so this is my own note after the roadmap review, not the summary I have to send out, that one I will write tomorrow when I am less annoyed. The review went for two hours and twenty minutes and we made one decision, and the decision we made was not on the agenda, so I want to write down what actually happened while I still remember the order of it. The context is that we went in to get a yes or a no on shipping the merchant dashboard in the same release as the payout changes, and I had built the whole deck around that question, twelve slides, and we never got to slide four. What happened instead is that Ravi asked in the first ten minutes why the payout changes need a release at all when they are behind a flag, and nobody in the room could answer it, including me, and by the time we had worked out that the flag only covers the API and not the reconciliation job, forty minutes had gone and the question on the table was a completely different question. Which was the right question, that is the annoying part. I cannot be cross about it because if the flag does not cover reconciliation then the thing I was asking them to approve was not the thing I thought it was, and I would have found that out in staging next week instead of in a room, which would have been worse. So the decision, and I want it written the way it was actually said rather than the way it will look in the summary, is that the payout changes go out on their own next Thursday with the reconciliation job still on the old path, and the dashboard waits for the release after, and Ravi's team does the flag work on reconciliation in between. Priya was not in the room and Priya owns the reconciliation job, so that third part is not actually a decision, it is a thing three people agreed to in her absence, and I need to talk to her before it goes in any summary as agreed. That is the sentence I am most likely to get wrong when I write this up nicely, so I am flagging it to myself now. On the things that did not get discussed, and this is the part I want to carry into the next one, we did not talk about the dashboard scope at all, we did not talk about whether the merchant onboarding copy needs legal review before it ships, and we did not talk about the support load, which is the thing that actually worries me, because the last dashboard we shipped generated about two hundred tickets in the first week and support found out about it from the tickets. Any one of those could eat another two hour meeting and I would rather do them as three short conversations with the right two people in each than another room with eleven people in it. Eleven people, for a yes or no question. That is on me, I invited them. On tone, because I have to be careful here, the meeting was not hostile and it would read as hostile if I wrote it up literally. Ravi was doing his job, and doing it better than I did mine, and the reason it felt bad is that I had spent a week on a deck for a question that turned out to rest on an assumption I had not checked. The summary should say what we decided and what is still open and it should not narrate the forty minutes, because the forty minutes were useful and they will read as chaos. For next time, and this is the actual lesson rather than the process complaint, I should have written the assumption on slide one. Payout changes are fully behind a flag. One line, and either somebody corrects it in the first two minutes or the rest of the deck stands. Every review I have taken in that has gone better and I keep not doing it because it feels like padding, and it is the opposite of padding, it is the only slide that does any work. Also I should stop putting the ask on slide four. Nobody has ever reached slide four.

input: These are my notes from the trustees meeting on the ninth, and they are notes rather than minutes, I will turn them into minutes at the weekend when I have the papers in front of me. Present were myself, Gareth, Rhian, the new trustee whose name I am going to spell wrong so I will check it, and Mr Prosser from the accountants for the first half only. Delyth sent apologies and she had sent her comments on the reserves paper in writing beforehand, which I read out, and I want to record that she did that because it made a difference to the discussion and she was not in the room to get any credit for it. We started with the reserves policy because Mr Prosser had to leave at half past seven and it is the item he actually needed to be there for. The position, as I understand it and somebody should check me on this, is that we are holding about eleven months of running costs in unrestricted reserves and the policy we adopted in 2019 says six, and the reason for the gap is not that we have been careful, it is that the two legacies came in the same year and we have never made a decision about them. Mr Prosser was very clear that there is nothing improper about the position and equally clear that we would be asked about it, and Gareth's point, which I think is the right one, is that being asked about it is not the problem, the problem is that we do not currently have an answer beyond saying that it happened by accident. So the decision, and this one was unanimous, is that Rhian and I will bring a paper to the January meeting setting out what the money is for, and if the answer is that some of it should be spent then we say so in the paper rather than waiting to be pushed. Delyth's written comment was that she would like the paper to consider the building before it considers new services, and nobody disagreed with that, although Gareth said, and I am recording this because he asked me to, that he does not want the building to become the answer to every question about money the way it was between 2014 and 2019. On the safeguarding review we are behind and it is my fault. The policy was due for review in June, it has not been reviewed, and the reason is that I was waiting for the new guidance which then came out in August and which I have not read properly. I told the meeting I would have a revised policy for January alongside the reserves paper and Rhian offered to read the guidance and mark the bits that have actually changed, which is a much better use of her time than mine because she does this professionally. Two trustees have still not done the online training and I am not going to name them in the minutes but I am going to email them separately, and if it is not done by January then it goes in the minutes, because that is the sanction we agreed last year and there is no point having it if we never use it. On the funding position, and this is where the meeting became difficult, the county council grant is confirmed at the same cash amount for a third year, which with the wage rise we agreed in April means the service is actually being funded about seven percent less than it was, and the coordinator post is the thing that gives. Rhian asked directly whether we are heading for a redundancy and I said I did not know, which was true, and Gareth said we should be honest with Ceri about the position now rather than in March, and I agreed to speak to her before the end of the month. That is the hardest thing in these notes and it is the thing most likely to get softened when I write the minutes, so I am writing it plainly here so that I can hold myself to it. Nothing has been decided about the post. Ceri needs to know that nothing has been decided and also that the question exists. The volunteer recruitment went better than we expected and I want to say so because we spend every meeting on the difficult items. Fourteen people came to the open evening, nine have filled in the form, and seven have started their checks, which is more than the last three open evenings put together, and the difference appears to be that we held it on a Saturday morning instead of a Tuesday evening. Rhian's suggestion, which we should act on, is that we do the next one the same way and stop treating the Tuesday evening as a fixture just because it always has been. Any other business was short. The photocopier lease ends in February and Gareth will look at it. The AGM date is fixed for the sixteenth of May and the room is booked. Present were myself, Gareth, Rhian, the new trustee whose name I am going to spell wrong so I will check it, and Mr Prosser from the accountants for the first half only. Delyth sent apologies and she had sent her comments on the reserves paper in writing beforehand, which I read out, and I want to record that she did that because it made a difference to the discussion and she was not in the room to get any credit for it. We started with the reserves policy because Mr Prosser had to leave at half past seven and it is the item he actually needed to be there for. The position, as I understand it and somebody should check me on this, is that we are holding about eleven months of running costs in unrestricted reserves and the policy we adopted in 2019 says six, and the reason for the gap is not that we have been careful, it is that the two legacies came in the same year and we have never made a decision about them. Mr Prosser was very clear that there is nothing improper about the position and equally clear that we would be asked about it, and Gareth's point, which I think is the right one, is that being asked about it is not the problem, the problem is that we do not currently have an answer beyond saying that it happened by accident. So the decision, and this one was unanimous, is that Rhian and I will bring a paper to the January meeting setting out what the money is for, and if the answer is that some of it should be spent then we say so in the paper rather than waiting to be pushed. Delyth's written comment was that she would like the paper to consider the building before it considers new services, and nobody disagreed with that, although Gareth said, and I am recording this because he asked me to, that he does not want the building to become the answer to every question about money the way it was between 2014 and 2019. On the safeguarding review we are behind and it is my fault. The policy was due for review in June, it has not been reviewed, and the reason is that I was waiting for the new guidance which then came out in August and which I have not read properly. I told the meeting I would have a revised policy for January alongside the reserves paper and Rhian offered to read the guidance and mark the bits that have actually changed, which is a much better use of her time than mine because she does this professionally. Two trustees have still not done the online training and I am not going to name them in the minutes but I am going to email them separately, and if it is not done by January then it goes in the minutes, because that is the sanction we agreed last year and there is no point having it if we never use it. input: Writing up the incident while the timeline is still fresh, and this is my own notes, the postmortem doc comes later. The alert fired at 02:14 and it was the p99 on the checkout endpoint, and I want to say at the start that the alert was correct and it fired on the right thing at the right time, because the last three times we have had this conversation the alert was the problem and this time it was not. I got to a laptop at 02:19 and the graphs looked like a database problem, which is what everybody's graphs look like at two in the morning, so I spent from 02:19 to about 02:35 looking at the wrong system, and I want that written down honestly because the postmortem is going to say sixteen minutes of investigation and the truth is sixteen minutes of investigating something that was fine. What it actually was is that the connection pool on the checkout service was exhausted, and it was exhausted because a deployment at 01:52 had rolled out a change to the retry policy that retries on any 5xx including the ones we return deliberately when a cart is stale, and stale carts are a thing that happens all night at low volume and never during the day, so the change looked completely clean in staging and in the canary. The interesting part is that it took twenty two minutes from the deploy to the alert, which is about how long it takes for the retries to accumulate at overnight traffic levels, and at daytime traffic it would have been about ninety seconds and it would have been obvious. So an overnight deploy of this specific change was the worst possible time to catch it and also the best possible time to have it happen, and I do not think that is a coincidence worth building policy on. I rolled back at 02:41, the pool recovered on its own within about two minutes, and the p99 was back under the threshold at 02:46. Nothing was lost as far as I can tell, the failed requests all returned a 503 and the client retries, and Marek is going to check the payment provider's side in the morning to be sure that nothing was double-charged, because the retry policy is exactly the kind of change that could do that and I would rather he looked than assumed. Things I need to do before the postmortem on Wednesday. Pull the 5xx breakdown by reason code for the whole window, not just the totals. Ask Marek for the provider reconciliation for the two hours either side. Write down what the pool saturation graph looked like before anybody edits the dashboard. The dashboard one is genuinely urgent because somebody always tidies a dashboard after an incident and then the evidence is gone, and I have lost that argument twice.

input: Draft of the advisory for the gateway bug and I want to be careful with the wording because the last one we published got picked up and half-quoted and the half that got quoted was the scariest sentence in it. So the summary should be boring and accurate and the detail can be alarming if it needs to be. The issue is in the session handling on the admin interface of firmware 3.8.2 and 3.8.3, and it is not in 3.7 and it is not in 4.0, which matters because most of the fleet is on 3.7 and most of the noise will come from people who are not affected at all. What happens is that the session token is regenerated on privilege change but the old token is not invalidated, so a token captured before an operator elevates continues to work afterwards with the elevated rights, and it keeps working until the absolute timeout, which defaults to seven days. I have reproduced it on a 3.8.3 unit on my own bench and Katarzyna has reproduced it independently on 3.8.2, and we have not tested any of the OEM rebadged versions, which I want stated as not tested rather than not affected. On severity, and I expect to argue about this internally, I would call it high rather than critical, because it needs an already-captured token and it needs an operator to elevate during the window, and the admin interface should not be reachable from outside in any correct deployment. The reason I would not go lower than high is that the interface is reachable from outside in a great many real deployments, we have the scan data, and 'should not be' has never once protected anybody. The mitigation, in the order I would actually do it. First restrict the admin interface to the management VLAN, which most people think they have already done and about a third of them have not. Second reduce the absolute session timeout from seven days to something under an hour, which is a single setting and costs you nothing but re-logins. Third upgrade to 3.8.4 when it ships on the fourteenth, which invalidates the old token properly. The reason the upgrade is third and not first is that the upgrade requires a reboot and a maintenance window, and the first two do not, and I would rather people did the two free things this week than scheduled the reboot for next month and did nothing in between. On disclosure, the vendor was notified on the second of last month, they acknowledged in four days, they have been genuinely good to deal with, and the fix date slipped once by a week for reasons they explained. I want to say that in the advisory because it is true and because the last three advisories I have read from anybody make the vendor sound obstructive by default. Credit goes to Katarzyna for the independent reproduction and to the operator who reported the odd session behaviour in the first place, who has asked not to be named and whose employer I am also not naming.

input: Patient note for Mr Whitaker, second visit, and I want the plan written properly this time because the last note just said continue as before and neither of us could remember what before was. He is four weeks post the right shoulder, the right shoulder repair, and the range has come back further than I expected, he is getting to about 140 degrees of flexion actively which is ahead of where the protocol says he should be. He is doing the home exercises, I believe him, the scapular ones look clean when I watch him do them and that is usually where people cheat. What we are changing today. Review in three weeks, and if the front of shoulder pain is still there at that point I want him to see Dr Okafor before we load him any further, because I would rather ask the question early than find out I have been loading something structural for six weeks.

input: Reading notes on the retrieval paper before the group tomorrow, and I want to be fair to it because I think the criticism I am going to make is the obvious one and they probably know it. What they do is train the retriever and the reader jointly with a single objective, which is not new, but they do it at a scale where the retriever index has to be rebuilt during training and their contribution is really the schedule for when to rebuild it, how stale they let it get, and what happens to the gradients in between. That is a real engineering contribution and the paper is honest that it is one. The results are on three benchmarks, two of which are the ones everybody uses and the third is their own filtered subset, and the gain on the two standard ones is about one and a half points, and on their own subset it is nine, which is the number in the abstract. I am not accusing them of anything, they describe the filtering clearly, but the nine is doing a lot of work in the framing and the one and a half is the number I would quote. The ablation I actually wanted is not there. They vary the rebuild interval, the index size, and the number of retrieved passages, but they never hold the compute fixed, so I cannot tell whether the schedule is better than simply training the baseline for the extra hours the rebuilds cost. That is the question I will ask tomorrow and I suspect the answer is that they did run it and it was close, because that is usually why an ablation is missing.

input: Notes on the parser work before I forget where I got to, and this is going to ramble because I have been in it all afternoon. The importer is fine on the happy path, it reads the header, it maps the columns, and it writes rows in batches of 500, which is the number we settled on last quarter and nobody has argued with it since. The problem is the files that come from the old till system, because every one of them has a new line in the middle of the address field, and the reader treats that as the end of the record, so a shop with a two line address turns into two customers and the second one has no name. I tried the quoted reader and it fixes about half of them, the other half fail because whoever exported them put a tab inside the field as well, and the tab order in the source spreadsheet was changed at some point so the columns do not line up between two files from the same week. So the plan is two passes. New line. First pass joins any record that has fewer fields than the header and does not end in a closing quote, and it writes what it joined to a side file so we can eyeball it before it goes anywhere near the warehouse. Second pass runs the normal mapping and refuses anything that still looks short, and it refuses loudly rather than skipping, because the silent skip is how we lost the March data and I am not doing that again. I would rather have a failed import than a quiet one, and Priya said the same thing when we talked about it on Tuesday, so I am going to write it up that way and put the side file path in the runbook next to the old one.

input: Design note on the export job, written down because we have had this conversation twice and both times it evaporated. Right now the job reads every order from the last 30 days, joins the customer record, and writes one flat file per region, and the whole thing takes about 40 minutes, most of which is the join because the customer table has no index on the column we join by. That column is snake case last seen at, and it was added in a migration nobody reviewed, so it is nullable and about 8% of rows have nothing in it, which means the join quietly drops those orders and the regional totals have never matched the finance figures. Finance noticed in April, we told them it was a rounding thing, and it was not a rounding thing. So the fix has three parts and they have to land in this order, because doing them the other way round takes the table offline in the middle of the day. Backfill the null rows from the login history first, since the login history goes back further than the orders do. Then add the index in a transaction we can cancel, on the replica first so we can time it. Then change the join to an inner join and let it fail loudly if a row is missing, rather than dropping it, which is the part Priya cares about and she is right. I will do the backfill tonight because the write volume is lowest then, and if the backfill runs long I will stop it and we do it in two nights instead of one.

input: Right, this is the migration writeup and it is going to be long because there are four systems involved and I want it all in one place for once. The starting point is that the booking service still talks to the old inventory database directly, over a connection string that lives in an environment file on the box, and that box is the last one on the old image, so every time security patches the fleet we get a page from the booking service at about two in the morning. We have known about this since the audit in February and it has been on the board since then with nobody's name on it. What has changed is that inventory is being rewritten anyway, so there is finally a reason to do the work now rather than argue about who owns it. The new inventory service exposes the same three reads we need, availability by date, availability by room type, and the hold that we take when somebody starts a checkout, and the hold is the interesting one because the semantics are not the same. In the old database a hold was a row with an expiry column and a background job cleaned it up, and if the job did not run the row sat there forever and the room looked booked. In the new service a hold is a lease with a time to live, and it expires on read, which means we cannot rely on the count of holds being accurate unless we touch every one of them, and nobody wants to touch every hold to count them. So we need to change how the checkout page asks the question, and instead of asking how many holds are there we ask can I have one, and we handle the no. That is a bigger change to the page than it sounds, because the page currently shows a number, and product will ask us to keep showing the number, and the honest answer is that the number was never right. On the actual cutover, I want to do it in shadow mode for a fortnight first, so the booking service calls both, uses the old answer, and logs where they disagree, and we look at the disagreements every morning rather than at the end. Then a percentage rollout by region, starting with the region that has the fewest bookings, and I want the switch to be a config value rather than a deploy so we can turn it back in seconds. The rollback plan is literally that config value, plus the old connection string stays in the environment file until the last region is done, and I know we normally rip those out immediately, and I am saying explicitly that we are not doing that this time. Two things I still do not have answers for. The first is the reporting job that reads the old inventory tables at midnight, which nobody claims to own and which finance definitely uses, and the second is whether the new service is happy with our request rate, because our peak is Sunday evening and the load test they ran was flat. Sequence for the runbook. Indent. Enable shadow mode and leave it for ten working days. Outdent. Then we review the disagreement log together and only then do we start the regional rollout, and if the log is still noisy after ten days we extend rather than pushing on, because the whole point of shadow mode is that it is cheap to wait.

input: Long one, sorry, this is the whole picture on the clinic scheduling problem and I would rather say it once properly than answer the same question six times this week. The referral letters arrive by post and by the portal, and the portal ones are fine, they come in as structured records and they land in the right list, and the postal ones get scanned by the front desk and then somebody types the details into the same list by hand. The typing is where all of this goes wrong. The person doing it is also the person answering the phone, so it happens in gaps, and a letter that arrives on Monday can sit in the tray until Thursday, and the clock on the referral target starts from the date on the letter, not the date we typed it in, so we are losing three days on a target we are already failing. Everyone knows this. What nobody has written down is that the scanning itself is fine, the scanner is fast and the images are readable, and if we could get the details out of the image we would not need the typing at all. I asked the vendor and they do have a reader, and it costs about what one bank shift costs per month, which is not nothing but it is not the number people are afraid of either. There is a new line of equipment coming in the next contract cycle anyway, so the timing is not terrible. The objection I keep hearing is accuracy, and I think that objection is half right. The reader will get the name and the date of birth and the referring practice, and it will get them right more often than we do at four in the afternoon with the phone ringing. What it will not get reliably is the free text at the bottom of the letter where the general practitioner explains why they are worried, and that free text is the thing the consultant actually reads when they triage, so we cannot have a system that drops it. So the shape I would propose is that the reader does the structured fields, a human checks them against the image on one screen, side by side, and the free text is attached as the image rather than transcribed. That last part is the bit I want people to argue with, because it means the free text is not searchable, and somebody will say we need it searchable for audit. I do not think we do, and I would like to be shown where that requirement is written down rather than repeated. On the estate side there is no space left in the records room, which is a separate problem that this makes slightly better, since we would keep fewer paper copies, though I am not going to pretend that is the reason to do it. The tab order on the form the front desk uses is also wrong, it jumps from surname to postcode and back up to first name, and that is a ten minute fix somebody should have done years ago. If we do nothing else this quarter I would like that one done, because it costs nothing and it is the thing the staff mention every single time we ask them what is annoying, and small things being ignored is why nobody fills in the survey any more.

The referral letters arrive by post and by the portal, and the portal ones are fine, they come in as structured records and they land in the right list, and the postal ones get scanned by the front desk and then somebody types the details into the same list by hand. The typing is where all of this goes wrong. The person doing it is also the person answering the phone, so it happens in gaps, and a letter that arrives on Monday can sit in the tray until Thursday, and the clock on the referral target starts from the date on the letter, not the date we typed it in, so we are losing three days on a target we are already failing. Everyone knows this. What nobody has written down is that the scanning itself is fine, the scanner is fast and the images are readable, and if we could get the details out of the image we would not need the typing at all. I asked the vendor and they do have a reader, and it costs about what one bank shift costs per month, which is not nothing but it is not the number people are afraid of either. There is a new line of equipment coming in the next contract cycle anyway, so the timing is not terrible. The objection I keep hearing is accuracy, and I think that objection is half right. The reader will get the name and the date of birth and the referring practice, and it will get them right more often than we do at four in the afternoon with the phone ringing. What it will not get reliably is the free text at the bottom of the letter where the general practitioner explains why they are worried, and that free text is the thing the consultant actually reads when they triage, so we cannot have a system that drops it. So the shape I would propose is that the reader does the structured fields, a human checks them against the image on one screen, side by side, and the free text is attached as the image rather than transcribed. That last part is the bit I want people to argue with, because it means the free text is not searchable, and somebody will say we need it searchable for audit. I do not think we do, and I would like to be shown where that requirement is written down rather than repeated. On the estate side there is no space left in the records room, which is a separate problem that this makes slightly better, since we would keep fewer paper copies, though I am not going to pretend that is the reason to do it. The tab order on the form the front desk uses is also wrong, it jumps from surname to postcode and back up to first name, and that is a ten minute fix somebody should have done years ago. If we do nothing else this quarter I would like that one done, because it costs nothing and it is the thing the staff mention every single time we ask them what is annoying, and small things being ignored is why nobody fills in the survey any more.

input: Incident writeup for last night, and I am going to go through it in the order it happened because that is the only way it makes sense. At about half past nine the alerting for the payments queue went quiet, which nobody noticed, because a quiet alert looks exactly like a healthy service. At twenty past ten a partner rang the support line to say their callbacks had stopped, and support opened a ticket at the normal priority, because the partner said stopped and not down and the script keys off the word down. I picked it up at about eleven because I was awake anyway and I saw the ticket go past in the channel. The queue was not down. The queue was fine and it was accepting messages and the depth was flat, and the consumer was running, and the consumer had been running for nine hours without processing anything, which is the state we have no alert for. The reason it stopped is that the credential the consumer uses to read from the queue was rotated at nine, on schedule, by the rotation job that we asked for and built and are pleased with, and the consumer reads that credential once at startup. It does not reread it. So the rotation succeeded, the old credential kept working for the grace period, the grace period ended at half past nine, and from then the consumer was making calls that failed with a permission error which it logged at debug level and retried forever. Debug level, on that service, is not shipped anywhere. So there was a perfect record of the failure sitting in a container nobody was reading, and no signal at all anywhere that a human looks. I restarted the consumer at ten to midnight and it drained the backlog in about twenty minutes, and the partner has all their callbacks now, in the original order, which is the one thing that went right. Three things need to change and only one of them is the obvious one. The obvious one is that the consumer should reread the credential on a permission error, and that is a small change and I will do it tomorrow. The second is that retry forever with no ceiling and no alarm is the actual bug, because it turned a loud failure into a silent one, and we have that pattern in at least four other services that I can name. The third is the alert itself, and this is where I want a decision rather than a discussion. We alert on queue depth, and queue depth was flat because the producer traffic was low overnight, so a stalled consumer and a quiet Sunday night look identical. What we should alert on is time since last successful process, per consumer, and that is a metric none of our services emit today. Put caps on stalled consumer caps off in the ticket title so the on call rota can filter for it, because I want the next person who sees this to find last night's writeup in one search rather than working it out again from scratch at midnight.

input: Follow up on the on call rota conversation, and this is the long version because the short version keeps being misheard as me asking for more people. The rota has six names on it and it covers three services, and two of those services were added last year without anybody adding a name, so the load per person has gone up by something like half while the headcount has not moved at all. That is the actual complaint and it is not about pay. What happens in practice is that the same two people take most of the night pages, because they are the two who know the payments path, and everyone else pages them anyway when they get something they do not recognise, so a night on call for the other four is really a night of forwarding. The fix everyone reaches for first is documentation, and I want to say clearly that I do not think documentation is the fix, because we wrote runbooks in March and they are good runbooks and the forwarding did not change. The reason it did not change is that at three in the morning nobody reads a runbook they have never read before, they ring the person whose name is on the last commit. So what would actually change it is shadowing, where the person who is not confident takes the page with the person who is, in the daytime, on purpose, on a real incident, twice, and then they are on the rota properly. That costs daytime hours and it is the only thing on this list that costs anything real. On the alerting side there is a smaller thing that would take a fortnight, which is that eleven of our alerts do not say what to do, they say a threshold was crossed, and a threshold with no action is a page that has to be interpreted from scratch every time. Fixing the text on those eleven is boring work that somebody could do in gaps. I have gone back and forth on whether to write the caps on part of this up formally or just say it here, and I have landed on saying it here first, because the moment it becomes a document it becomes a negotiation with people who were not on the rota. The typography of the thing matters less than people think, so I am not going to make the heading bold, that never helped anybody read a proposal, and I am not going to underline that either. What I want is a decision on the shadowing hours by the end of next week, and if the answer is no then I want the no written down so that the next time we have this conversation we start from it rather than from the beginning.

input: Right, notes on the pricing page rewrite while it is fresh, and this is the part I need somebody else to look at because I have read it too many times. The page has three plans on it and the middle one is the one we want people to take, and at the moment it does not look any different from the other two, so people either take the cheapest one or they leave. The thing I want to change is not the design, it is the order of the sentences. Right now each plan leads with the price and then lists what you get, and every competitor page does exactly the same thing, so a person comparing four tabs is comparing four identical shapes and the only variable left is the number. If we lead with who the plan is for, in one line, then the number is read as a consequence rather than as the whole story. The heading on the middle plan should be bold that, and the same line needs the word team in it rather than the word pro, because pro means nothing and team tells a person whether it is them. On the copy itself, the feature list is thirty one items long and nobody reads thirty one items, and about a third of them are things every plan has, so they are not differentiators, they are reassurance, and reassurance belongs lower down the page in smaller type. I would cut the visible list to the six things that actually differ and put the rest behind a link that says everything included, which is honest and does not pretend the page is shorter than it is. The other change is the annual toggle. Today it says save twenty percent and the price silently becomes the monthly equivalent of the annual bill, which is the industry convention and is also mildly dishonest, and support gets a ticket about it most weeks. I would rather show both numbers than win the comparison and then explain ourselves. I have not touched the enterprise column because that is a conversation, not a price, and the current wording is fine for a conversation.

input: Case note for the flat sale, and I am recording it now because I have three of these running and I will not remember which is which by Friday. The buyer's solicitor has finally come back on the leasehold enquiries, six weeks after we sent them, and the answers are thin. They have confirmed the ground rent, which nobody was arguing about, and they have said the service charge accounts for the last three years are with the managing agent and they will forward them when they receive them, which is the same sentence they sent in July. The thing I actually need is the schedule of major works, because the building had scaffolding on it for most of last year and if there is a section twenty notice coming then my client is buying a bill she does not know about. I have asked three times. On the mortgage side the offer expires on the fourteenth of next month and the lender has said they will re-run the valuation rather than extend, and a re-run in this market is a risk we do not need, so the practical deadline is about ten days earlier than the paper deadline. My client knows that and she is being very patient, more patient than I would be. On the searches, the local authority came back clean apart from a planning application two doors down for a loft conversion, which is normal and which I will report but not make a fuss about. The drainage search is outstanding and that is us, not them, because it went to the wrong water company, and I would rather say that plainly in the file than let it look like a delay at their end. Next step is a letter to the managing agent directly rather than through the seller's solicitor, copying the seller's solicitor so nobody can say they were not told, and if the major works schedule is not with us in a fortnight I will advise my client to make the offer conditional on it and let the seller decide how badly they want to move.

input: Handover before I go on leave, and it is one long note rather than five short ones because they all touch the same service. The billing exporter runs at two every morning and writes one file per tenant into the bucket, and the file name is built from the tenant id and the run date, and nothing downstream reads the file name so do not spend time on it if it looks odd. The part that will page you is the reconciler, which reads yesterday's file and compares totals with the ledger, and it pages when the difference is over a pound. Almost every page you get from it is a tenant who changed plan mid month, because the ledger books the change on the day and the exporter books it at the end of the period, and the difference clears itself the next night. So the first thing to check is whether the tenant changed plan, and if they did, acknowledge it and go back to bed. The one that does not clear itself is when a refund is issued after the export has run, and then the difference persists and grows, and the only fix is to re-run the export for that tenant, which is a script in the ops repo. I have left the camel case reconciler run date parameter in the readme with an example, because I get it wrong every time myself and the error message when you get it wrong is not helpful. Second thing, the alerting for the exporter itself is on completion, not on duration, so a run that takes four hours instead of forty minutes will not tell you anything, and it has done that twice, both times because a tenant with a very large account was retrying. If you see the reconciler page for lots of tenants at once, that is the shape of it, and the exporter is probably still running rather than broken. Third thing, and this is the one I am slightly worried about, the certificate on the ledger connection expires on the ninth, and the renewal is manual, and the person who normally does it is also away, so I have written the steps in the same readme and I have asked Ana to be the backup. If the certificate does lapse, everything looks healthy and the reconciler simply stops pagng, which is the worst failure mode we have, so please check the dashboard on the tenth even if nothing has paged. I will have my phone with me and I would rather be asked than come back to a week of drift.

input: Okay, this is me talking through the whole allotment committee thing so that the minutes have something to start from, and I am going to include the bits that are awkward because leaving them out is how we got here. The waiting list is at forty one names and the average wait is now over three years, and two of the plots at the top end have been effectively abandoned for eighteen months, one of them since the winter before last, and both of those tenants have paid their rent every year, which is the whole problem. The rules say we can serve notice for non cultivation and the rules also say we send two warnings first, and we have never once served the notice, because the person who would have to knock on the door is the person who sees them at the shop. I understand that completely and I am not blaming anybody, but the effect is that somebody who wants a plot waits three years while a plot sits under bindweed, and when that comes up at the annual meeting, which it will, the answer cannot be that we felt awkward. So what I would like to agree is a process that takes the awkwardness off any single person. My suggestion is that the inspection is done by two people together, on a fixed date, twice a year, in June and in September, and the notes are written down on the same form every time with photographs, so a conversation later is about a form and not about somebody's memory. The first letter is a friendly one and it offers help, because in about half of these cases the reason is illness or a new baby or a job that moved, and a plot can be halved or paused for a season and we have done that before and it worked. The second letter is the formal one and it has a date on it. Only after that does anybody talk about reallocating, and by then it is the committee's decision and not one member's. On the money side, and this is the part I want written properly. New paragraph. Rent has not risen since 2019 and the water bill has nearly doubled, so we are quietly running down the reserve, which is now under six hundred pounds, and the shed roof will need doing within two years. A rise of five pounds a plot covers the water and puts a little back, and I would rather propose that openly with the numbers on the notice board than do a special appeal when the roof goes. I know one or two people will be unhappy and I think they will be less unhappy than they would be about a sudden levy. The last thing, and it is smaller but it keeps coming up, is the car parking at the bottom gate, where three people park across the turning space and the delivery lorry cannot get in, and the honest answer is that there is no space there for three cars and never was. If we paint the turning area and ask people to use the road, that is free and it might work, and if it does not work then we are back to a conversation nobody wants, which at least we will have had once already by then.

input: This is the long version of the thesis update for my supervisor, and I am dictating it because typing it takes me twice as long and I always end up writing less than I mean to. The second chapter is where I have been stuck since the middle of last term, and I now think the reason is not the writing, it is that the chapter is trying to do two jobs. It is supposed to be the literature review for the whole thesis and it is also supposed to set up the specific gap the experiment addresses, and every draft I write does one of those well and the other one badly. When I lead with the broad review, the gap arrives on page twenty and by then the reader has lost the thread. When I lead with the gap, the review reads like I am only citing the papers that agree with me, which is not true but it looks like it. So what I would like to do is split it, and make chapter two the review proper, organised by method rather than by year, because organising by year is what makes it read like a list, and then make chapter three a short chapter that does nothing except state the gap and the two competing explanations for it. That makes the thesis one chapter longer and I know the guidance says four, and I would rather ask now than find out in the viva that it mattered. On the experimental side the second run finished and the numbers are cleaner than the first run, and the difference is almost certainly the change to the calibration step rather than anything about the samples, which is slightly annoying because it means the first run is not directly comparable and I cannot pool them. I have both sets in the repository with the calibration constants recorded for each, and the analysis notebook regenerates every figure from raw, so nothing in the chapter is a number I typed by hand. There is one figure I am unsure about, the one with the two distributions overlaid, because the overlap is the finding and the way I have drawn it makes the overlap look like noise. I will try it as two panels instead and send you both. The thing I actually need from you before the end of the month is a view on the split, because everything else follows from it, and I do not want to write another draft of the current shape and then throw it away, which is what happened twice already. If you would rather talk it through than read it, I can come to office hours on Thursday, and I will bring the two versions of the figure and the outline of the split rather than a full draft, so we are looking at the structure and not at my sentences, which is the conversation I think we need to have first. I have also asked the other two people in the group how many chapters they ended up with, and one of them had five and nobody minded, which is either reassuring or a sample of one, and I suspect it is a sample of one.

input: Notes on the rate limiter before the review, and I am saying it out loud because I keep rewriting the same paragraph and getting nowhere. The limiter is a token bucket per API key, refilled every second, and the bucket size is currently the same for every key, which is the thing I want to change, because a partner doing bulk imports overnight and a mobile app doing one call per screen are not the same shape of traffic at all. The size is read from screaming snake case default bucket size at boot, and it is never reread, so changing it means a rolling restart, and a rolling restart of the gateway in the middle of the day is not something I am going to do for a config change. So the first part of the work is making the value reloadable, and that part is small. The second part is the per key override, and that is where the actual design question is, because the override has to live somewhere the gateway can read cheaply on every request, and the obvious place is the key record we already fetch. That record is cached for five minutes, so an override would take up to five minutes to take effect, and I think that is fine, and I would much rather say so now than have somebody discover it during an incident. The bucket size in the docs is wrong by the way, it says sixty and it has been a hundred and twenty since March, and the page has been reviewed twice since then by people who did not check it against the code.

input: Follow up on the limiter conversation, and this is the part I did not put in the design note because it is opinion rather than fact. The default bucket size we have now was picked in a meeting in 2019 by somebody who no longer works here, and every argument since has been about whether the number is too small, and nobody has ever gone and looked at what the per key traffic actually looks like. I did look, last week, and the distribution is not what anybody assumes. Half of our keys make fewer than ten calls a day and will never touch any limit we set. About forty keys sit in a band where the limit matters and where a bad day genuinely hurts them. Three keys are so far above everyone else that they probably should not be on the shared gateway at all, and one of those three is our own mobile app, which is quietly the biggest consumer of our own API and has never once been counted as a partner. So the question is not what the default bucket size should be. The question is whether a single default is the right shape at all, and I think the honest answer is no, and I think we have known that for a while and kept adjusting the number because adjusting a number is easier than changing a model. I would rather we spent the sprint on the per key override and left the default exactly where it is, and if that means the number stays wrong for another quarter then at least it stays wrong on purpose.

input: Right, this is the whole story on the reporting export because three people have asked me separately and I have given three slightly different answers. Finance get a spreadsheet every Monday morning and it is produced by a job that runs on Sunday night, and the job has been running since long before I joined, and nobody has touched it because it works. What it does is read the transactions table for the previous week, group by cost centre, and write one sheet per cost centre into a shared folder, and then a second job zips the folder and mails it out. The trouble started when finance renamed two of the cost centres, because the sheet name is built from the cost centre name, and one of the new names has an ampersand in it, and the zip step silently skipped that sheet rather than failing. So finance got a mail with eleven sheets instead of twelve for three weeks running, and the missing one was the one that had just been renamed, which is also the one they were watching most closely. Nobody noticed at our end because the job reported success, and the zip tool treats a skipped file as a warning and warnings are not shipped anywhere. The fix I have put in is that the sheet name is now built from the cost centre code rather than the name, and the code is stable and has no punctuation in it at all. I have also made the zip step count the files and fail loudly if the count does not match the folder. One last thing, the archive itself has to be called no space weekly finance dot zip, because the mail rule finance set up matches on the exact filename and a space in it breaks the rule silently.

One last thing, the archive itself has to be called weeklyfinance.zip, because the mail rule finance set up matches on the exact filename and a space in it breaks the rule silently.

input: Draft of the letter to the members about the hall bookings, and I want the money part set apart from the rest so people actually read it. Blank line. So the sums only work if we either raise the hire charge or find a second regular booking midweek, and my own view is that we do both and do them modestly rather than doing one of them dramatically. On the hire charge, the current rate has not moved since before the pandemic and it is still eight pounds an hour, which is well under everything comparable in the town, and I do not think ten pounds would lose us a single group. On the midweek booking, the two obvious approaches are the adult education people, who asked us two years ago and were turned down because of the piano, and the toddler group who currently meet in a church that is being reroofed. I have spoken informally to neither, because I did not want to promise anything before the committee had seen the numbers, and I would like permission at the next meeting to have both conversations properly. If we do nothing at all we can cover the new rent from the reserve for about fourteen months and then we cannot.

input: Okay so this is the whole thing about search relevance, and I am dictating it because I have tried to write it three times and every time I get two paragraphs in and delete it. The background is that we replaced the old keyword search in November with the vector one, and on the demo queries it was obviously better, and on real traffic it is better for about two thirds of queries and noticeably worse for the rest, and the rest is the part nobody wants to talk about. The queries it is worse on are the short ones, one or two words, usually a product code or a surname, and for those the old search was exact and the new one is approximate, so somebody typing a code they know gets a page of things that are sort of near it. Which is the worst possible failure for a person who knows exactly what they want. I have looked at a week of logs and short queries are thirty eight percent of everything, which is much higher than anybody guessed in the planning meeting, and the reformulation rate on them is nearly double the average, meaning people search, do not find it, and search again with different words. That reformulation number is the one I would put in front of product, because it is the closest thing we have to a measure of frustration. What I want to do is not roll back. Rolling back loses the two thirds that got better and I do not think anybody would thank us for it. What I want is a cheap exact path in front of the vector path, so a query that looks like a code or a single token gets an exact lookup first, and if that returns anything at all we serve it and never call the vector index. That is maybe forty lines of code and one regular expression I will hate in a year. The bit I need a second opinion on is where the cutoff sits, because the vector path also has a score floor below which it returns nothing rather than returning rubbish, and that floor is camel case min score threshold in the config, and it is currently set to a value somebody picked from a blog post rather than from our data. If I lower it the approximate results get worse but we return something; if I raise it we return an empty page more often, and an empty page at least tells the truth. My instinct is to raise it and lean on the exact path to catch the short queries, and I am aware my instinct is the one that makes my own change look better, which is why I am asking. On timing, the exact path I can have behind a flag by the end of next week, and I would like a fortnight of it on ten percent of traffic before we argue about the floor, because arguing about the floor without the exact path in place is arguing about a different system. One more thing that is not really part of this but keeps coming up, the search box on the mobile layout loses focus when the keyboard opens, so people type the first character into nothing, and that is almost certainly inflating the short query count in ways I cannot separate out from the logs. Somebody should fix that regardless of anything I have just said.

input: Reading notes on the retrieval paper for the group meeting, and I am going to talk through all of it because the parts I do not understand are the parts I most need to say out loud. The setup is a two stage retriever, a cheap first stage that pulls a few hundred candidates and an expensive reranker that orders them, which is the standard shape and not the contribution. The contribution is what they do with the min score threshold, which in every system I have read about is a single number chosen once and then left alone, and here it is learned per query type, so a short lookup style query and a long descriptive query end up with different floors. The intuition they give is that a short query has less signal so the score distribution is flatter, and a fixed floor on a flat distribution either lets everything through or nothing, and I think that intuition is right and I have felt it in our own system without being able to say it that clearly. Where I get stuck is the training signal. They learn the min score threshold from click data, and click data on results the old floor never showed does not exist, so the thing they are learning from is shaped by the floor they are replacing. They acknowledge this in a footnote and say the effect is small, and the footnote is one sentence and there is no experiment behind it, and I do not think you can wave at a feedback loop with a footnote. The ablation table is good otherwise. They show the per query floor is worth about four points on their short query slice and roughly nothing on the long slice, which is honest, and a lot of papers would have reported the average and let you think it helped everywhere. input: Right, this is the long one, the whole state of the migration off the legacy job runner, and I am dictating it because it needs to exist as a document before I go on leave and I will not type nine hundred words tonight. Start from where we are. There are forty one jobs on the old runner and thirty of them are cron shaped, meaning they run on a schedule, do one thing, and either succeed or page somebody. Those thirty are boring and I have moved eleven of them already with no incident, and the pattern is well established now, so anybody on the team can do the rest by copying what is in the platform repo. The remaining eleven are the interesting ones and they break into three shapes that need different treatment, and I want to describe each shape properly rather than list them, because the shape is the whole point and a list would flatten it. The first shape is the jobs that talk to the old inventory database over the connection string in the environment file, and there are four of those, and every one of them assumes it can hold a transaction open for the length of the job. On the new runner a job gets a connection from a pool with a statement timeout of thirty seconds, so a job that holds a transaction for four minutes simply dies, and dies in a way that looks like a network error rather than like a timeout, which cost me most of a Thursday. The fix for those four is not a port, it is a rewrite into batches, and a batch rewrite needs somebody to decide what happens when batch seven of twelve fails, and nobody has decided that, and I am not going to decide it alone in a handover note. The second shape is the two jobs that write into the shared folder that finance read from, and the problem there is not technical at all, it is that finance have automation of their own pointed at that folder and nobody knows what the automation does. I have asked twice. Until somebody answers, moving those two jobs means possibly breaking a system we cannot see, so I have deliberately left them alone and I want that recorded as a decision rather than as an oversight. The third shape is the five reporting jobs that read yesterday's output from the job before them, so they are a chain, and the chain is currently held together by the schedule, which is to say job B runs at two because job A usually finishes by half past one. That is not a dependency, that is a hope, and it has failed twice this year, both times silently, because job B reads the previous day's file when the current one is missing and produces a report that is entirely plausible and entirely wrong. The new runner has real dependencies, which is the single best reason to do this migration at all, and converting the chain properly means the five jobs become one graph and the schedule becomes an input rather than the mechanism. That is the work I would most like somebody to pick up while I am away, and it is also the work most likely to reveal that one of the five has been quietly broken for a year. On the things that will page you while I am gone. The old runner's own health check reports the process, not the jobs, so a runner that is up with every job failing looks green, and the only real signal is the alert on job age which I added in March and which only covers the eleven jobs I have migrated. For everything still on the old runner, the signal is somebody noticing a missing report, and that somebody is usually finance on a Monday. If that happens, the runbook entry is in the platform repo under the old runner heading, and the first thing to check is disk, because the old box fills up about every six weeks and a full disk makes every job fail with an unhelpful message about temporary files. Do not resize the disk, clear the log directory, because resizing it needs a restart and a restart loses any job mid flight with no record that it ran. Last thing and then I will stop. Next line. The decision I want from the group when I am back is whether we finish this properly in one quarter with two people on it, or whether we accept that the last eleven jobs live on the old runner for another year and we make that survivable by moving the box onto the current image. I do not much mind which we choose, and I mind a great deal that we keep choosing neither, because the current position costs us a day every few weeks and produces exactly the kind of quiet wrongness that nobody puts on a roadmap.

input: Documentation review for the runner pages, and this is all editorial rather than technical, so nothing here blocks anybody. The overview page is in reasonable shape and the diagram is finally accurate, which took three attempts and a lot of patience from the platform team. My main problem with it is the ordering. It opens with the architecture and gets to how you actually schedule a job on page four, and almost everybody arriving at that page wants to schedule a job, so the architecture is between them and the thing they came for. I would put the scheduling walkthrough first and let the architecture be a page people choose to read. On the reference pages, the field descriptions are mostly copied from the code comments, which is fine as a starting point and is why several of them describe the type rather than the meaning. The timeout field says an integer in seconds, which is true and useless, and what a reader needs to know is that it starts when the job is dequeued rather than when it is submitted, which is the thing that surprises people. There is a similar gap on the retry field, where the docs say how many times and do not say that a retry reuses the original payload, and somebody built a whole workaround for a problem they did not have because of it. Formatting wise, the tables are inconsistent. Two of them have a description column that wraps and two have one that runs off the side on a laptop, and the tab order on the interactive example is wrong so keyboard users land in the output box before the input, which the accessibility audit already flagged in the spring and which is still open. On the same page there is a next line of example output that does not match the example above it, and I think that happened when somebody updated the input and not the output, and it is the kind of small wrongness that makes a reader distrust the whole page. The migration guide is the weakest of them. It reads as though it was written by somebody who had already done the migration, which of course it was, and it assumes you know which of the two runners you are on. A person arriving at that page frequently does not know, and there is no way to find out from the page itself. I would open it with two sentences telling the reader how to check, and I would say plainly that the old runner is being retired, because at the moment the page is neutral in a way that leaves people wondering whether they need to do anything at all. Last thing, there is no space left in the sidebar for another top level heading, which is why the migration guide is buried under reference where nobody looks, and that is a navigation problem rather than a writing one. I do not have a good answer for it and I would rather raise it than quietly leave the guide where it is.

input: This is the trip report for the office so somebody can put it in the file properly, and I am talking it through on the bus so it will not be tidy. The group was eight clients and two porters and we went in from Chame on the fourteenth, which is two days later than the plan because the flight from Kathmandu was cancelled twice and the road was closed at Besisahar for a day after that. The clients were good about it and only one of them was on a fixed return, and I moved her out a day early at the end rather than rushing everybody, which cost us one night's lodge money and was clearly the right call. The walking was fine for the first four days and the weather held. Two of the group were slower than their booking form suggested, which is normal and is why we plan the acclimatisation day at Manang rather than making it optional, and both of them were fine once they had the day. The oldest client was sixty eight and was stronger than two people in their thirties, which I say every year and nobody believes until they see it. Where it went wrong was the side trip. The lake is spell mode T I L I C H O and the path to it had a section washed out about forty minutes above the base camp, and the washout is new since last season, and nobody at the lodge mentioned it because the people who had come down that morning had gone across it before it slipped. I turned the group round there. Two clients were unhappy and one of them said so at length, and I would make the same decision again, because the alternative was eight people on a wet traverse with a drop and no fixed line. I have written the location down for the office and somebody should tell the other guides before the next group goes up, and it should go in the pre departure notes as well rather than only in the group chat, because the group chat is not a record. The rest of the trip ran normally. The pass day was cold and clear and we were over by eight in the morning, which is early even for us, and the descent to Muktinath took longer than the book says because one client's knee was bad and we went slowly on purpose. The lodges were as expected except the one at Yak Kharka, which has changed hands and is now noticeably worse, and I would not book it again this season. On the money side, the extra night from the flight delay and the moved return are both on the receipt I have photographed, and the porters were paid in cash on the last day as usual with the amounts on the same sheet. One thing for the office to decide, not me. Three of the eight have asked about the Manaslu circuit for next spring, and if we are going to run that we need the permit paperwork started now rather than in January, because last time it took eleven weeks and we nearly lost the booking.

input: Test round summary for the release candidate, and I will go through it as I found it rather than by severity, because two of the small things turned out to be the same bug as one of the big ones. Registration first. The form accepts an email with a trailing space and then the confirmation mail never arrives, and the reason is that the space survives into the send queue and the provider rejects the address silently, so the user sits on a page that says check your inbox forever. That is one line to fix and it has been there since the beginning, which I find slightly hard to believe and have checked twice. The name field has a spell mode toggle on it that the phone puts there, not us, and on my device it changed a Vietnamese name into an English word twice while I was typing, which means real users are almost certainly submitting names they did not intend and we have no way to detect that from our side. I do not think there is anything we can do about it and I am recording it because somebody will ask. On the payment step, the amount is right and the currency is right, and the receipt page is right, but the receipt mail rounds to two decimal places by truncating rather than rounding, so a charge that ends in a half cent shows a cent lower on the mail than on the card statement. That is small and it is also the sort of thing that generates a support ticket from somebody who thinks they have been overcharged. The bigger issue is the session. If you leave the checkout open for longer than thirty minutes the session expires, and the page does not know, so the next button you press does nothing at all with no message, and pressing it again does nothing again. Most people press it four or five times and then reload, and the reload loses the basket. I have reproduced that on all three browsers. Related to it, and this is the part I only worked out on the second day, the same expired session is why two of my earlier bug reports about the address book were wrong. The address book is fine. My session had gone and the failure looks identical from the outside, which is worth saying out loud because whoever picks up those two tickets will spend an afternoon looking at code that works. On the accessibility pass, the tab order on the payment form is wrong, it goes from the card number to the postcode and back up to the expiry, and the audit tool did not catch it because every field is reachable, just in a daft order. Nothing here is a release blocker on its own except the session one, and I think the session one is a blocker because the failure mode is a user losing a full basket with no explanation. Everything else I would ship and fix in the next patch, and I would rather say that plainly than mark six things critical and let somebody else decide which of them I meant.

Right, notes on the checkout bug before I forget the shape of it, because I spent most of yesterday on it and the fix is not where anyone thought it was. The staging build is fine and the production build fails, and the only difference between them is the domain, which should have been the first clue. What is actually happening is that the course policy on the API gateway lists the staging origin and the marketing site origin and it does not list the app origin, so the preflight comes back without the allow origin header and the browser drops the response before our code ever sees it. The network tab shows a 200 on the OPTIONS request, which is why nobody caught it, and then the actual POST just never resolves and our error handler reports it as a timeout, so every ticket about this says timeout and none of them say anything about headers.

I have a one line change to the gateway config that adds the app origin, and I have tested it against the staging gateway, and it works. What I do not want to do is add a wildcard, which is what the last person to hit this did in February, and it is still there on the internal admin gateway, and I am going to open a separate ticket for that rather than fix it quietly in the same change, because the security review should see it.

input:
Okay this is for the runbook, and I want it written down because the same question came up twice this week and both times I answered it in a thread that is now gone.

When a task in the batch cluster cannot read from the reports bucket, the problem is almost never the bucket policy. The bucket policy has been the same for two years. The problem is that the task definition and the task itself use two different roles, and people conflate them. The execution role is what pulls the image and writes the log stream, and the task role is what your code actually gets credentials for, so if your code is getting access denied on a GetObject then the thing to look at is the task role, and nine times out of ten somebody has attached the policy to the I am role that has the same name as the service instead of the one with the dash task suffix. The names are three characters apart and the console sorts them next to each other.

The way to check it in ten seconds is to call get caller identity from inside the container and read the ARN it prints back, because that tells you which role you are actually running as rather than which one you think you attached. If the ARN ends in dash task you are in the right place and the problem is the policy. If it does not, stop reading the policy.
