This is for the inventory meeting on Thursday and I want to get my thoughts down while I am driving so bear with me.

The count came out 340 units short on the summer range and I do not think we have lost 340 units. I think we have counted the same thing twice under two different labels. When we moved to the new till system in March the import brought over the product names but it did not bring over the old codes, so anything that had been discontinued and then brought back has two entries, one from the old system and one that Marie created by hand in April, and the till happily sells from either of them. The bestseller list has the linen shirt at number two and at number nine and they are the same shirt.

So before we order anything for autumn I want somebody to go through the export and find every pair of entries where the description matches and the skew numbers are different, and I would rather that was done by a person than by a clever formula, because there are only about 900 lines and the descriptions are not consistent enough for a formula to be trusted. Marie can do it in two afternoons. Then we recount the summer range against the merged list and I would put money on the shortfall being closer to 40 than 340.

When we moved to the new till system in March the import brought over the product names but it did not bring over the old codes, so anything that had been discontinued and then brought back has two entries, one from the old system and one that Marie created by hand in April, and the till happily sells from either of them. The bestseller list has the linen shirt at number two and at number nine and they are the same shirt.

So before we order anything for autumn I want somebody to go through the export and find every pair of entries where the description matches and the SKU numbers are different, and I would rather that was done by a person than by a clever formula, because there are only about 900 lines and the descriptions are not consistent enough for a formula to be trusted. Marie can do it in two afternoons. Then we recount the summer range against the merged list and I would put money on the shortfall being closer to 40 than 340.

Notes for the design review on Thursday. Please read this before the meeting, because the drawings alone will not tell you what changed.

The revision we are reviewing is C, and there are three changes from revision B. First, the mounting bracket is now 6 millimetres thick instead of 4, because the deflection under the 900 newton load case was 1.8 millimetres and the requirement is 1.0. Second, the two M8 fasteners on the lower face are replaced by four M6, which is the change I expect an argument about, and I will explain it in the meeting. Third, the bomb has been corrected, because the previous version listed the old bracket part number, 44 dash 0271, and the supplier quoted against that number for six weeks. That is the reason the quotation is wrong and it is not the supplier's fault.

The part I am not comfortable with is the tolerance on the bore. The drawing says H7, and the fit we actually need is a press fit, and H7 with the shaft we have specified gives a clearance fit at the upper limit. I would like to change the shaft to r6 and keep the bore as it is, because we already have the reamer for that bore and changing the bore means new tooling. Herr Brandt disagrees, and he has been building these for longer than I have, so I want it discussed rather than decided by drawing.

Notes from the site visit this morning, and I am recording this in the car so the order is not perfect.

The glazing on the north face is the problem and it is worse than the photographs suggested. The million between the second and third panes is out of plumb by something like 12 millimetres over the height of the opening, and you can see it from the street, and once you have seen it you cannot stop seeing it. The installer says the opening was out before they arrived and that may well be true, because the blockwork on that face was the part that got rushed in February, but the client is not going to accept an explanation, the client is going to accept a straight line.

So what I want to know from the structure people is whether the head can take a packing shim of that depth without a new lintel calculation, because if it can then this is a two day fix with the same subcontractor and nobody has to argue about who pays. If it cannot then we are into a conversation that involves the main contractor and the insurer and it will not be finished before the handover date on the twenty second.

The rest of the visit was fine. The stair balustrade is up, the finish on the terrazzo is better than the sample, and the lighting positions in the entrance follow the revised drawing.

Quick note on the book before the close because I do not want to explain this from memory tomorrow.

We are short the June 4200 calls against a long position in the September 4400s, and that spread has been fine for three weeks, and it is not fine this week because the June contract has eleven sessions left. The position is roughly delta neutral if you look at it once in the morning and that is exactly the trap, because the delta is only neutral at the current level and it stops being neutral very quickly in either direction now.

What actually matters is the grammar on the short leg. It is about four times what it was in April on the same notional, because the strike is close and the expiry is near, and that means the hedge has to be rebalanced intraday rather than at the open, and the desk is not staffed for intraday rebalancing on a Friday.

So my recommendation is that we roll the June leg out to July this week and accept the cost, which I have priced at about 18 basis points on the notional, rather than carry the position into expiry week and rely on somebody watching it. I would rather pay 18 basis points for a boring week than explain a good week that turned into a bad afternoon.

This is the post incident note for the 502s on Sunday morning, and the short version is that engine X was the thing that broke and the application was never involved at all.

At about six twenty on Sunday the checkout endpoint started returning 502 for roughly one request in nine, and it carried on like that for fifty minutes, and it stopped on its own before anyone deployed anything, which is why the first three people who looked at it found nothing. The application logs are clean for that window. There is no error, no restart, no memory pressure, nothing, because the application never saw those requests.

The proxy had a worker connection limit of 512 and we crossed it, and when it runs out of worker connections it does not queue, it fails the connection and logs one line at warning level that nobody alerts on. Sunday morning is the newsletter, which goes out at six fifteen, and this is the third month running that something has broken fifteen minutes after the newsletter and nobody has connected the two.

Two changes. Raise worker connections to 4096, which is one line and I will do it today, and add an alert on that warning line, which is the change that actually matters, because the limit will be wrong again the next time the newsletter list doubles and I would rather find out from a page than from a graph on Monday morning while I am reading it on my phone.

Okay this is my update for the standup tomorrow because I will not be online, so please read it out or just paste it.

The embedding job finished on the full catalogue on Saturday night, one point one million items, and it took nine hours on the single GPU box which is about what I estimated. The vectors are in the index and I have spot checked forty of them by hand against the product titles and they look right, and the two that looked wrong were both products where the title is in Bengali and the description is in English, so that is a data problem and not a model problem and I will write it up separately.

The part that is not finished is the incremental path. When a new product is added we need to embed just that one item, and right now that happens in the request, which takes about four hundred milliseconds and is the slowest thing on that page by a long way. It should be a background job, and we already have the salary workers running for the image resizing, so I want to put it on the same queue with a separate name rather than build anything new. I have the task written and it works locally and I have not deployed it because I do not want to deploy on a Friday.

Right, I am writing this down because I asked about it in the channel and I think the answer is useful to more people than me.

The century alerts for the mobile app are almost all coming from one place and it is not a real crash. When the app loses network mid request we throw and we catch it and we show the offline banner, which is correct behaviour, and then we also report the exception, which means every commute through the tunnel generates a report. Last week there were four thousand one hundred events and I looked at two hundred of them and every single one was that.

So the number that gets shown in the weekly report is meaningless right now, and worse than meaningless, because the two crashes that actually mattered last week were buried under it and nobody saw them until a user emailed.

What I want to do is stop reporting that one exception type and instead count it as a metric, so we still know how often people go offline but it does not sit in the same list as real crashes. I do not know if that is the right call so I would like somebody to tell me it is fine before I do it, because it feels strange to make an error stop being an error.

This is the build times thing, and I want to write it out properly because every time it comes up in a meeting I say something vague and then nothing happens.

A clean build of the server target takes eleven minutes on my laptop and about six on CI, and an incremental build after a one line change takes between forty seconds and four minutes depending on which file you touched. The forty second case is the common one and nobody is unhappy about it. The four minute case is what people complain about, and it happens when you touch anything under the shared proto directory, because everything depends on it, and there are two hundred and sixty targets that will rebuild.

The reason it is not eleven minutes for everyone all the time is the remote cache, and the reason people who have just joined complain more is that the cache is not configured in the template repo, so a new checkout is cold and stays cold. That is a documentation fix and I will do it this week.

The bigger thing is that the proto directory should be four packages rather than one, so touching one message does not invalidate the world, and whoever does that will spend most of the week arguing with basil about visibility rules rather than writing any code.

input:
Okay this is the write up for the rate limiter problem and I am going to talk through it in the order it happened rather than the order that makes sense, because the order it happened is the reason it took two days, and nobody said the word readies out loud until Tuesday night.

On Monday afternoon the support queue started filling with people saying the app said too many requests when they had done nothing at all, and the first thing we did was look at the limiter config, which says one hundred requests per minute per account, and nobody was anywhere near one hundred. The person who reported it most clearly was a merchant in Mombasa who had made four requests in the whole morning and got blocked on the fifth. So the config was not the problem, and we spent the rest of Monday convinced it was the client sending duplicates, which it was not.

What was actually happening is that the red is instance we use for the counters had failed over on Sunday night, and the replica it failed over to was about forty minutes behind, and the counters came back with keys that had no expiry on them, because the expiry is set when the key is created and the replica had the keys without ever having run the create path. So an account that had crossed the limit at any point in the previous week had a counter sitting at a number above the limit with no TTL, forever, and every request that account made from then on was rejected. It was not a rate limiter any more, it was a permanent ban list, and it had ninety one accounts on it.

The reason it took until Wednesday morning is that our dashboard reads the current count from the primary and the limiter reads it from the read replica, so the dashboard showed us a count of four for the merchant in Mombasa while the limiter was looking at a count of one hundred and six, and I stared at that four for most of Tuesday. Two different views of the same key. I want that written down somewhere permanent because it will happen again with something else and next time it will not be counters.

The fix on Wednesday was to delete the ninety one keys, which took a minute, and then set an expiry explicitly on every write rather than relying on it being set at creation, which is a four line change and is already merged. I also want the limiter and the dashboard reading the same endpoint, and that is a config change I have not made yet because it moves read traffic onto the primary and I want to see the numbers first.

The longer term thing is that the counters should not be in the same reddish as the session store. They have different failure requirements. If the session store fails over and loses forty minutes, people log in again and complain a bit. If the counters fail over and lose forty minutes, we ban ninety one merchants and nobody notices for two days. Separating them is half a day of work and I have put it on the board for next sprint, and I would rather do that than add monitoring on a thing that should not be shared in the first place.

input:
Right, notes on the documentation build before I forget where I got to, and this is mostly for me but Basil should read it too because half of it is his.

We have about a million words of published documentation across the two sites and the build takes fourteen minutes, and nobody would care about fourteen minutes except that the preview build takes the same fourteen minutes, so a one word typo fix is a fourteen minute wait before you can see it. Basil looked at this in April and his conclusion was that the slow part is not the rendering, it is the link checker, which walks every page and resolves every internal link against the full page list, and it does that from scratch on every build including preview builds.

His suggestion, which I agree with, is that preview builds should check only the links on pages that changed, and the full check runs on the nightly and on release. That is not perfect, because a change to page A can break an incoming link from page B and the preview would not catch it, and Basil's answer to that is that the nightly catches it within a day and a broken internal link for a day is not the end of the world. I think he is right and I want it recorded that it was a deliberate trade and not an oversight, because in eight months somebody will find a broken link and ask why the checker did not catch it.

The second thing is the API reference, which is generated, and which nobody has looked at properly since the two point four release. There are eleven endpoints in the reference that do not exist any more, and four that exist and are not in the reference, and the reason is that the generator reads a spec file that is maintained by hand and drifts. Of course the real fix is generating that spec from the code, which is a platform team change and not mine, and I have raised it twice and it is not going to happen this quarter, so what I would like to do in the meantime is add a test that fails when the spec and the route table disagree. That is a day of work and it converts a silent drift into a loud one.

Third, and this is the one I want a decision on rather than an opinion, the course we ran for new hires in March used the tutorial pages, and the feedback was that the tutorial assumes a working local environment and does not say how to get one. That is fair. The install page exists and it is good and it is not linked from the tutorial at all. I can fix the link in five minutes. What I cannot fix in five minutes is the deeper thing, which is that the tutorial was written for a version where setup was three commands and it is now nine, and the honest fix is a rewrite of the first section, which is a week.

One more thing, minor. The search index is rebuilt on every deploy and the first search after a deploy takes about four seconds while it warms, and if anybody asks, that is expected and it is not a bug.

So the link checker change is Basil's, the spec test is mine, and the tutorial rewrite needs somebody to tell me it is worth a week.

This is the bug report I said I would write properly instead of leaving it as three messages in the channel, and I want to describe what I did rather than what I think is wrong, because last time I guessed and I was wrong.

The app crashes on the second scan, not the first. On a fresh install I open the app, I scan a barcode, it resolves, I see the product page, and everything is fine. I go back and scan a second barcode and the app closes with no dialog and no message, and when I reopen it the session is gone and I have to sign in again. This is the handover note for the reporting migration because I am off for two weeks from Friday and if this stays in my head it will be redone badly while I am away, so it is long and I am sorry about that.

Where we are. The nightly load into the warehouse finishes at about four in the morning and the dashboards refresh at six, and that has been stable since March apart from two nights, the sixth and the twenty first, both of which were the upstream export failing and not us. The load is nine tables, seven of them small and two of them large, and the two large ones are the transactions table at about four hundred and ten million rows and the events table at about one point two billion, and everything that is slow or expensive in this project is one of those two tables and nothing else.

The migration is moving all of that off the old post grass box that lives in the office and into the managed instance, and about two thirds of it is done. The seven small tables are moved and reconciled and I have checked row counts and three sample aggregates on each of them and they match to the row. The transactions table is copied but not reconciled, and the events table is not copied, and that is deliberate, because the events copy takes about eleven hours and I did not want it running while I was away with nobody watching it.

The reconciliation script is in the repo under tools and it takes a table name and a date range and prints counts and three sums, and it does not write anything, so it is safe to run whenever. For the transactions table please run it a month at a time rather than the whole history, because the whole history holds a read lock long enough that the nightly load times out behind it, which I found out the hard way on the ninth and which is why there is a gap in the transactions dashboard for that one day. That gap is real data that was never loaded and it will need a backfill, and I have not done it, and it is on the board.

Two things about the new instance that are not obvious. The first is that the connection limit is 200 and the pooler is configured for 180, and the nightly load opens twelve connections per table in parallel, so if somebody runs the load and a large reconciliation and the dashboards refresh at the same time we will hit the limit and the failure looks like a permissions error rather than a limit error, which will send whoever sees it in the wrong direction for an hour. The second is that the timezone on the new instance is UTC and on the old post grease box it was set to local time by somebody in 2019, so any query that compares a stored timestamp to a date literal gives a different answer on the two machines, and that is the actual reason the revenue figure for the twenty first was out by about forty thousand when Priya checked it against the old dashboard. It was not a data problem. It was midnight in two places.

What I would like to happen while I am away is nothing, honestly. The seven small tables are done, the dashboards read from the new instance for those, and the transactions and events dashboards still read from the old box, and that split is ugly but it works and it is written down in the README next to the connection strings. If something breaks, the rollback is one line in the config that points everything back at the old box, and the old box is still running and still receiving the nightly load, which costs us about ninety dollars a month and is the cheapest insurance we have.

If somebody does have to touch it, the one thing I would ask is that nobody starts the events copy, because the copy script does not resume. If it dies at hour nine it starts again at zero, and it also holds enough disk on the old post crest box that a second attempt while the first one's temporary files are still there will fill the volume, and a full volume on that machine takes the nightly load down as well, and then we are explaining to finance why the dashboards are empty at quarter end.

When I am back the order is: reconcile transactions a month at a time, backfill the ninth, copy events over a weekend with somebody watching it, reconcile events, then move the two dashboards and delete the old connection strings. That is about a week of real work and three weeks of calendar, and I would rather it took three weeks and nobody was surprised than that it was rushed in the four days I am away.

Okay, this is my note on the equipment loan before the year end meeting, and I want it written down because I have explained it twice verbally and both times somebody left the room with the wrong number in their head.

The loan was taken out in June 2022 for one hundred and forty thousand over five years at 6.4 percent, and the repayment is two thousand seven hundred and thirty a month, and that figure has not changed and will not change because the rate is fixed. What people keep getting wrong is what that payment is made of. In the first year most of it was interest. Right now, in the middle of year three, it is about sixty forty the other way, and by the last year almost all of it is capital.

So when the operations report says the loan costs us thirty two thousand a year, that is true as a cash figure and it is wrong as a cost figure, because only part of it is an expense and the rest is repaying money we already spent. That distinction is the whole reason the profit line and the bank balance disagree, and it is worth ten minutes in the meeting because it comes up every quarter.

The number I actually need people to know is the principle outstanding, which at the end of November is ninety one thousand four hundred, and that is the number that matters if we refinance, and it is the number nobody has in front of them because the only place it appears is the lender's statement, which arrives as a PDF and goes into a folder nobody opens.

What I would like to do is put three figures on the monthly one pager. The balance outstanding, the interest paid so far this year, and the settlement figure if we paid it off early, which the lender quotes on request and which is not the same as the balance because there is a two month interest penalty in the agreement. Three numbers, one line each, and then nobody has to remember any of this.

The reason this is live now rather than in January is the new oven. If we buy it outright it is nineteen thousand and it comes out of cash, and our cash at the end of November is forty one thousand, which is thin but survivable. If we finance it we are adding a second agreement on top of one we are halfway through, and I would rather not do that until I have the settlement figure in front of me, because if the penalty is small then paying the first loan down early and starting clean is the better shape, and if it is large then it is not, and I cannot tell you which without the number.

Right, this is the operations note for the board pack and I want it in my words before it gets summarised by somebody else.

Three things are going well and one thing is not, and the one that is not is the depot in Port Elizabeth, so I will do that last.

Cash first, because it is the thing the board asks about before anything else. Cash at the end of the month is two point one million, which is up from one point eight, and the improvement is almost entirely that the two largest customers paid inside terms for the first time in a year rather than anything we did. I am not going to present that as an achievement. Debtor days are fifty one against a target of forty five, and the number that worries me is not the average, it is that four customers make up sixty percent of what is overdue, and one of them has been overdue three months running and is still being served.

Second, the fleet. We took delivery of six of the eight vehicles and the last two arrive in February. Fuel is nine percent under budget for the quarter, and about half of that is the route changes and about half of it is the fuel price, and I would not want the board to read the whole nine percent as something we earned. The maintenance line is over by eleven percent and that is the old vehicles being kept on longer than planned, which is the direct consequence of the delivery delay, so those two numbers should be read together and not separately.

Third, headcount. We are two under in the warehouse and I have stopped recruiting for those two deliberately until the new shift pattern has run for a month, because if it works we do not need them, and if it does not work I would rather hire against the real shape of the problem than fill the seats we happened to have.

Now Port Elizabeth. The lease is up in April and the landlord has come back with a thirty one percent increase, which is not a negotiation, it is a message that they want the space for something else. The site is the wrong shape for us anyway. It was chosen in 2018 when the mix was mostly pallets and the mix is now mostly small parcels, and the loading arrangement that made it cheap then makes it slow now. So my recommendation is that we do not renew, and instead we take the smaller unit near the airport, which is more per square metre and less in total, and we accept about six weeks of disruption in the move.

The principle I want the board to sign off on is that we stop treating depots as permanent, and that is worth saying out loud, because every one of these leases has been renewed by default since 2018 and none of them have been looked at against what we actually ship now.

Nothing in there is affected yet, but if it is still above 5 in the morning somebody has to move the contents, and that is a two person job with the log signed by both, so do not leave it to the person coming on at seven by themselves.

Okay, this is the writeup for the reconciliation gap on Tuesday night and I want to get it down while I still remember the order I did things in, because the order matters and the postmortem template is going to ask me for a timeline. At about twenty past eleven the settlement job for the mobile money leg finished and reported 412 successful transfers, and the ledger service showed 409, and that three transaction gap is what woke me up, because we alert on any non-zero difference on that pair of counters. The first thing I did was open the cabana dashboard that Wanjiru built for the settlement index, the one with the four panels, and I filtered it to the job run id, and the panel that counts outbound requests agreed with the settlement job at 412, so whatever we lost, we lost it after the request left us.

Then I went looking for the three. I did not have transaction ids at that point, only the count, so I widened the time range to the whole evening and grouped by response code, and what came back was 409 with a 200 and three with a 502, which is the gateway in front of the partner and not the partner itself. That is a good outcome for us and a bad outcome for the night, because a 502 on that endpoint is not idempotent from our side. We retry it, and the retry either lands on a request the partner already processed or it lands on nothing, and the only way to know which is to ask them, and their reconciliation file arrives at six in the morning.

So I did not retry. I want that written down clearly, because someone is going to ask why the gap was still open at six and the answer is that I chose to leave it open. I paged Wanjiru at half past midnight and she agreed. Between the two of us we went through the Havana panels for the gateway itself rather than for our own service, and the interesting thing there is that the 502s are not spread out at all. All three of them land inside a nine second window at 23:41, and in that same window the gateway's own error panel shows fourteen upstream connect timeouts, only three of which are ours, and the other eleven belong to the airtime top-up service, which does not alert on anything and therefore nobody noticed.

That changes the shape of the incident. This is not a payments bug, it is a nine second connectivity event at the partner edge that hit two of our services and only one of them was watching. I have asked the platform team for whatever they have on the link for that window and I expect them to come back with something about a route flap, and if they do, the real action item is not on my team at all, which is a slightly uncomfortable thing to write in your own postmortem but it is what the numbers say.

At six the reconciliation file came in and all three transactions are on it as settled on their side, so the money moved and our ledger was wrong, not the world. I posted the three references in the incident channel and the finance team booked them by hand at about half seven. The references are TRF-88214, TRF-88217 and TRF-88231, and I am putting them in this document as well as in the channel because the incident channel gets archived after ninety days and this document does not.

Now the follow-ups, and I want to be honest that only the first one is real work. The first is that our 502 handler should write the transaction id into the failure record before it gives up, because the reason the first hour of this was slow is that I had a count and not a list, and I had to reconstruct the list from log lines one at a time. That is a small change in the settlement client and I will do it this week. The second is that the airtime service needs the same alert on the same pair of counters, which is a copy of a rule that already exists and half an hour of work for whoever picks it up. The third is that the banana dashboard needs a panel for gateway response codes sitting next to the panel for our own response codes, because we had both of those numbers on two different screens and looking at them side by side is what actually broke this open, and Wanjiru said the same thing independently about ten minutes before I did.

The thing I do not want as a follow-up is automatic retry on 502 for this endpoint. It has been suggested twice before, it is in the notes from the March incident, and it is still wrong for exactly the same reason it was wrong in March, which is that we cannot tell a duplicate from a miss without the partner's file. I would rather book three transactions by hand once a quarter than double pay one, and I would rather Wanjiru and I lose a night than have finance find it in a monthly close.

Right, notes for standup because I will forget half of this by tomorrow. The cradle build on the release branch has been failing on CI since Thursday and passing on my machine every single time, which is the worst version of a build problem to have because you cannot iterate on it. What I found today is that it is not really failing, it is timing out. The step has a fifteen minute budget and the compile itself takes about 11 minutes on the runner, and on Thursday somebody bumped the plugin version and that pushed it to about sixteen and a half, so the runner kills it and we get a log that ends in the middle of a task with no error in it, which is why nobody could see what was wrong.

So the actual question is why the runner takes 11 minutes when my laptop takes 40 seconds, and the answer is that my laptop is warm and the runner is cold every time. The daemon is not reused between jobs, there is no dependency cache restored, and the arm64 image we switched to in June does not have a prebuilt toolchain for the native module, so it builds that from source on every run. Any one of those on its own is survivable. All three together are the sixteen and a half minutes.

I have three things I want to do and I want to do them in this order, because I think the first one alone might be enough. First, cache the dependency directory keyed on the lock file, which is a five line change to the workflow. Second, turn on the configuration cache, which we have been avoiding because the grader wrapper in this repo is on 8.7 and the two custom tasks in the game module are not compatible with it, so that one is real work and it touches the task graph. Third, and only if the first two do not get us under the budget, split the step so the native module builds in its own job and publishes an artifact the main job consumes.

What I do not want to do is raise the timeout, and I want to say why in advance because it is going to be the first suggestion in standup. Raising it hides the regression, and the regression is that we added twenty percent to every build for a plugin bump nobody has justified yet. If we raise the timeout we will be back here in two months with a twenty minute build and the same conversation.

One more thing while I remember it. The gradual cache on the runner is being written and then thrown away, because the cache path in the workflow points at the home directory and the container runs the job as a different user than the one the setup step used. That is almost certainly a one line fix and it might be the whole cache story on its own, so I will test that first thing tomorrow before I touch anything else. If it is, then the second and third items go away entirely and I will close the ticket about splitting the native module, which I opened myself and which I now think was the wrong instinct.

Also, unrelated, the release notes still say the Android build is unsigned. It has been signed since the June release. Somebody should fix that and it is not going to be me this week.

Notes after the coordination meeting this morning, mostly for Kaya so she has it before she talks to the contractor on Thursday. The clash report came back with sixty-one hard clashes and about forty of them are the same problem in different places, which is the main duct on level 2 running at the same height as the secondary steel. That is not a design change, that is somebody having federated the wrong revision. The beam model we issued is revision C and the services consultant is still working against revision A, which was superseded in March, and revision A has the steel 300 millimetres lower than it is now.

So before anyone redesigns anything, the beam coordinator needs to confirm which revision is in the federated model, and if it is A then most of this report evaporates and we are left with the eight or nine clashes in the plant room, which are real and which I do want to talk about on Thursday. The plant room ones are not a revision problem. The duct is 600 by 400 there and there is genuinely not enough space between the slab soffit and the door head, and either the duct goes flat and wide or the door moves, and I would rather the door moved because the duct going flat costs pressure and the contractor will come back for it later.

Also, Demir has asked twice now for the model to be issued weekly rather than at stages, and I keep saying no, and I want to explain the reason once in writing so I do not have to keep saying it in meetings. A weekly issue means the contractor is always building from something that has not been checked, and the whole point of issuing at a stage is that somebody signed it. If they want weekly, they can have a weekly view, but the issued model stays at stages and revision C stays revision C until we say otherwise.

This is for the file on the transfer level, and I am going to be careful with the numbers because the contractor is going to quote them back at me. The beam over the loading bay is deflecting more than the model said it would. We measured 22 millimetres at mid span yesterday afternoon and the design figure is 14, and the span is 8 metres, so 22 is inside the 1 in 360 check but it is well outside what we told them to expect, and the finishes subcontractor has already flagged that the ceiling grid will not sit flat against it.

The reason, I am fairly confident, is that the beam is carrying the block wall above it, which was not in the loading when it was designed. The wall went up in the week of the 14th, before the propping came out, and nobody told us it was going there because on the architect's drawing that line is a partition and partitions are not our problem. On site it is 140 blockwork, which is about 457 kilos a metre, and that is a beam problem.

What I want to happen is this. Leave the props under that beam until we have rechecked it, and I mean the props stay even if they are in the way of the pour next week, because a beam that is already deflecting past its design figure is not the place to be clever about programme. Then we recheck it with the wall load in, and if it fails we either take the wall off it and hang the wall from the slab above, or we plate the beam, and plating is the answer nobody will like because it means welding on a live floor.

I have asked Fadi to photograph the underside and the bearing at both ends before the props come anywhere near it, because if the bearing has moved at all then this is a different conversation and it happens on Monday, not Thursday. And to be clear, the pour can move. The propping cannot.

Right, this is the note for the board pack on the Nairobi office and I am going to dictate it rather than write it because I have twenty minutes before the airport and the pack closes on Friday. Overall position is that we are two weeks behind on the fit-out and on budget, and I would rather be in that order than the other way round.

On the lease. The lease is signed, it is a six year term with a break at three, and the rent free period is four months rather than the three we underwrote, which is the one commercial win of the whole exercise and it is worth about 4.2 million shillings. The lease is signed and registered, and I want that stated plainly in the pack because the last two board packs said it was about to be signed and one director has stopped believing that sentence.

On the paperwork. We needed two documents notarised for the registration and that took eleven days rather than the two we were told, because the honorary consul only sits on Tuesdays and Thursdays and the first Tuesday we went, the power was out in the building. That is not a complaint, it is the reason for a line in the timeline, and if anyone asks why the registration slipped, that is the answer. Grace has the stamped copies and the scans are in the shared folder under legal, second subfolder, not the one at the top level which is the old draft.

On the fit-out. The two week slip is the electrical first fix and it is our fault, not the contractor's, because we changed the desk layout after they had already set out the floor boxes. I signed that change and I am happy to say so in the room. Everything downstream of first fix has moved by the same two weeks, so the handover is now the second week of November rather than the last week of October, and the second week of November is still inside the fit-out period on the lease, which is the only date that actually has money attached to it.

On the cash handling, because this is the item I expect questions on. The office will take cash for the walk-in trade counter, which we did not originally plan for and which the country manager pushed for hard and I now agree with. That means a vault, and a vault means it is bolted through the slab, insured separately, and two people to open it, and none of that was in the original fit-out spec. It adds about six weeks of lead time on the unit itself and roughly nine hundred thousand shillings including the installation, and it is the single largest thing that was not in the paper the board approved in June. My recommendation is that we do it, because the alternative is a daily cash run to the bank through Nairobi traffic at 06:30 and I am not asking a two person team to do that five days a week.

On people. Grace is at the helm until the country manager starts in January, and she has been doing that job in addition to her own since July, which is not sustainable and is the reason I want the temporary admin hire signed off in this pack rather than the next one. It is a six month contract, it is small money, and if we defer it we will be having a retention conversation instead.

On the trade mission in February. The chamber has asked whether we want a place on the delegation, and the delegation is being led by a trade envoy rather than by a minister, which lowers the value of it considerably in my view. I have said we will take one place rather than the two they offered and that I will go myself if the office has handed over by then, and Grace will go if it has not. Either way it is two days and the chamber covers the room.

Risks, briefly. First, the vault lead time, which is the one that can actually move the handover again. Second, the power supply, because the building has one generator for six floors and our server room assumption was written for a building with two. Third, and this is the one nobody wants to talk about, we still do not have a signed data processing agreement with the local payroll provider, and until we do, nobody in that office gets paid through them and we are running payroll out of Cape Town by hand.

That is the note. Grace, if you are reading this before I land, the only thing I need from you today is the vault quote in writing so it can go in the pack as a number rather than as an estimate.

Notes for the file on the Hendricks contract before I forget where I got to, and this is the second time I have looked at it so I want it written down properly this time. They invoiced 180,000 in February for a twelve month support agreement that starts on March 31, and they have booked all of it in February because that is when the cash arrived, and that is the problem. Under gap the revenue follows the performance obligation, not the cash, so if the service runs for twelve months from March 31 then eleven months of that sits in deferred revenue at the year end and about 15,000 is earned.

I have been through the contract itself rather than the invoice, because the invoice is not the agreement, and the contract has a wrinkle in it. There is a three month onboarding phase that is separately priced at 30,000 and it is genuinely a distinct service, they deliver it, it has its own acceptance sign-off, and the client could have bought it without the support. So that 30,000 is arguably earned across three months rather than twelve, which is a different curve and it does change the year end number by a few thousand.

What I am not going to do is decide that on my own. I am going to write it up both ways, single obligation over twelve months and two obligations with the onboarding taken over three, and send it to the auditors with the contract attached and let them tell me which one they will accept. The auditors will have a view and I would rather have their view in writing in October than have it as an adjustment in February.

The conversation with the client is the harder half of this. Marcus is going to say that the cash is in the bank and the year has closed and why are we reopening it, and the answer is that what the bank shows and what gap requires are two different questions, and the second one is the one that gets audited. I have had this conversation with him before, about the Alderman job in the year before last, and it went badly for about a week and then he understood it and it has not come up since, so I am reasonably confident it goes the same way.

One more thing to check before I send anything. There is a termination clause at clause 9 that lets them cancel with sixty days notice and take a pro rata refund, and if that is real and not just boilerplate then the deferral is not merely correct, it is a liability, because we would owe cash back. I want to read clause 9 properly with the schedule next to it, and I want to do it before I write to the auditors rather than after, because if the refund is real it changes how the whole thing is presented and not just the number.

They invoiced 180,000 in February for a twelve month support agreement that starts on March 31, and they have booked all of it in February because that is when the cash arrived, and that is the problem. Under GAAP the revenue follows the performance obligation, not the cash, so if the service runs for twelve months from March 31 then eleven months of that sits in deferred revenue at the year end and about 15,000 is earned.

I have been through the contract itself rather than the invoice, because the invoice is not the agreement, and the contract has a wrinkle in it. There is a three month onboarding phase that is separately priced at 30,000 and it is genuinely a distinct service, they deliver it, it has its own acceptance sign-off, and the client could have bought it without the support. So that 30,000 is arguably earned across three months rather than twelve, which is a different curve and it does change the year end number by a few thousand.

What I am not going to do is decide that on my own. I am going to write it up both ways, single obligation over twelve months and two obligations with the onboarding taken over three, and send it to the auditors with the contract attached and let them tell me which one they will accept. The auditors will have a view and I would rather have their view in writing in October than have it as an adjustment in February.

The conversation with the client is the harder half of this. Marcus is going to say that the cash is in the bank and the year has closed and why are we reopening it, and the answer is that what the bank shows and what GAAP requires are two different questions, and the second one is the one that gets audited. I have had this conversation with him before, about the Alderman job in the year before last, and it went badly for about a week and then he understood it and it has not come up since, so I am reasonably confident it goes the same way.

One more thing to check before I send anything. There is a termination clause at clause 9 that lets them cancel with sixty days notice and take a pro rata refund, and if that is real and not just boilerplate then the deferral is not merely correct, it is a liability, because we would owe cash back. I want to read clause 9 properly with the schedule next to it, and I want to do it before I write to the auditors rather than after, because if the refund is real it changes how the whole thing is presented and not just the number.

This is the update on the Djibouti consignment for whoever picks up my inbox tomorrow, because I am on the road all day and this is going to get worse before it gets better if nobody chases it. Four containers landed on the 12th, two of them cleared and moved on the 16th and are at the warehouse, and two of them are still sitting at the port because the phytosanitary certificate for the coffee consignment names the wrong exporter. Not the wrong goods, not the wrong quantity, the wrong exporter, because the shipper's agent copied the details from an older document, and the certificate cannot be amended at this end, it has to be reissued at origin.

So the two boxes are stuck and the clock is running. We had seven free days from discharge and those expired on the 19th, and the mirage charges started on the 20th at 96 dollars per container per day for the first week and it steps up after that, and today is the 26th, so we are already looking at seven days on two containers and it is going to be more than that because the reissued certificate will not be here before Monday at the earliest.

Two separate things need to happen and they are not the same thing, which is the part that keeps getting confused on these calls. The first is the certificate, and that is the shipper's problem and I have been on it since the 20th with the agent in Addis and with the exporter directly since the 22nd. The second is the money, and that is ours whether or not the certificate was our fault, because the terms are what they are and the port does not care whose mistake it was.

On the money. We should claim the mirage on the two containers back from the shipper under the indemnity in clause 14, and I think we win that because the certificate defect is documented and it is theirs, but that claim takes months and the port wants paying before it releases anything. So we pay now and claim later, and I need somebody to say yes to that today.

Also, and this is separate again, the shipping line has raised a container detention charge of 41 dollars a day on top, which is for their equipment being off the terminal, and that one does not start until the box leaves the port, so it is currently zero and it becomes the expensive one the moment we move them to a warehouse and cannot strip them quickly. Which means when the certificate does come, we need the unloading crew booked for the same day and not for whenever suits them, or we swap one charge for another and gain nothing.

One last thing. This is the third certificate defect from this exporter this year, and after the second one I wrote a note saying we should ask for the certificate to be sent for checking before the vessel sails rather than after. Nobody actioned it, including me. It should be actioned now.

Incident notes, and this one is embarrassing so I want it accurate. At 14:02 the reverse proxy stopped serving the admin hostname and kept serving the app hostname, and both of those are behind the same instance, so my first assumption was a routing rule and my first assumption was wrong. The traffic container was healthy, it was answering on 80 and on 443, and the access log showed requests arriving for both hostnames. So the traffic was arriving, which took routing off the table within about four minutes.

What had actually happened is that the certificate resolver hit the rate limit at the certificate authority. We have the admin hostname and the app hostname on separate certificates, and the admin one came up for renewal, and the renewal failed five times in a row because the challenge could not complete, and after the fifth failure the resolver stopped serving that hostname rather than serving it with an expired certificate. Which is arguably correct behaviour and it is certainly not documented anywhere in our runbook.

The challenge could not complete because the entrypoint for the challenge is on 80 and somebody added a redirect from 80 to 443 in the router rules on the 19th, so every challenge request got a 301 and the authority does not follow redirects for that check. That change was made to fix a genuine problem, it was reviewed, and neither the author nor the reviewer knew the challenge rode on the same entrypoint.

Fix in the moment was to add an exclusion for the challenge path ahead of the redirect rule, which took two minutes once we understood it, and the certificate issued on the next attempt. Total impact was 51 minutes on the admin hostname only, no customer traffic affected at all, which is the one lucky part of this.

Follow-ups. The rate limit resets weekly, so if this recurs before the reset we cannot simply retry and we need the staging authority configured as a fallback, and that is a real piece of work rather than a config line. And the runbook needs a section on certificate renewal failures, because the current runbook covers what to do when traffic stops arriving and says nothing about what to do when traffic arrives and gets dropped on purpose. The labels on the container are also carrying nine rules now, which is more than anyone can read at a glance, and I think they belong in a file rather than in labels, but that is a preference and not an action item, and the certificates expire every 90 days so there is no urgency.

input:
Capacity note before the sale, because we get one shot at this and last year we got it wrong in a specific and avoidable way. Baseline traffic on the API is about 12k requests a minute at the weekday peak, and during last year's sale it went to 40k in the first eleven minutes and then sat around 28k for two hours. So the shape is a spike and then a plateau, and the spike is roughly three and a half times baseline, and the plateau is a bit over double.

What fell over last year was not the application. The application scaled out fine. What fell over was the read replica, because the traffic that arrives during a sale is not the same mix as ordinary traffic. Ordinary traffic is mostly writes to the cart and reads of a single product. Sale traffic is almost entirely reads of the same twelve products, over and over, and those reads went to the replica and the replica was on a smaller instance than the primary because that had never mattered before.

So the plan this year. First, we pre-warm rather than react, which means the replica goes up two sizes on the Friday and comes back down on the Tuesday, and that is about 3.1 thousand dollars for the four days and it is the cheapest item on this list. Second, we shift the product read path to the edge for the twelve sale products only, with a short lifetime, so most of that traffic never reaches the database at all. Third, we split the traffic at the load balancer so that checkout and browsing do not share a target group, because last year browsing traffic starved checkout and the only thing that actually loses money is a failed checkout.

I want to be honest that the third item is the one I am least sure about. Splitting the traffic means two sets of health checks, two scaling policies and a rule at the proxy that has to be right on the day, and if the rule is wrong we shed the wrong traffic. Sao Paulo and the Virginia region both have to carry it identically, and they are not identical today. If we only get two of these three done, I would do the first and the second and leave the split for next year with a proper test behind it.

This is for the trustees ahead of the meeting on the 14th, and it is a summary rather than the full paper because the full paper is forty pages and nobody reads it. Position on the reserves is that we are at 41,000 free reserves against a policy minimum of six months of running costs, which is about 6,800 a month, so we are at roughly six months exactly and the policy says six months minimum, which means we have no headroom at all and any unbudgeted spend takes us below policy.

The reserves policy was set in 2019 and it has not been revisited since, and I think revisiting it is a legitimate thing to do, but I want to be clear that revisiting a policy because you are about to breach it is not a good look in an annual report, so if we are going to change it we change it in the spring and not on the 14th.

What I am actually asking the meeting to do is reign in the discretionary spend for the rest of this financial year, which means the two conference places, the away day and the new laptops all go to the spring, and the only exception I would make is the safeguarding training because that one is not really discretionary whatever line it sits on. That is about 4,200 held back, which gets us to about seven months of cover by the year end if the grant lands when it is supposed to.

On the grant. It was submitted in June, we were told eight weeks, it has been eleven, and the officer we were dealing with has left. I chased on the 2nd and again last Tuesday and I have had no reply to either, so the paper assumes it lands and the paper also has a paragraph on what happens if it does not, and the trustees should read that paragraph specifically. If it does not land we are having a different meeting in January.

Okay so the bug report from design is real but it is not what they think it is. They say the preview link shows the old header, and it does, and the reason is not caching. The vessel preview for the feature branch is building from a commit that is four days old, because the branch was pushed with the header change but the change is in a file that is not in the build output at all, it is in a component that nothing imports any more. So the preview is correct, it is just previewing a header that is dead code, and design has been reviewing a component that no user will ever see.

How it got that way. When we split the layout in the redesign branch there were two header components, the old one and the new one, and the plan was to delete the old one once the new one shipped. The new one shipped in June. The old one is still there, and it is still exported from the index file, and design's bookmark points at a route that still imports the index rather than the component directly. So the route renders the old header, and it renders it fast, 1.4 seconds to first paint, because it is a much simpler component, which is probably why nobody questioned it.

What I want to do is delete the old header rather than fix the route. If I fix the route we have two headers again and this happens again in six months to somebody else. If I delete it, three routes break, and all three of those routes are behind the internal flag and are not in the product, and I can fix them in the same change. That takes the bundle down by about 340 kilobytes too, which is not the reason to do it but I will put it in the description because it makes the change easier to approve.

Separately, and this is the thing that actually needs a decision from somebody other than me, the parcel dashboard shows twelve preview deployments still live for branches that were merged in July, and every one of those is serving from an environment where the analytics key points at production. Which means every time somebody opens an old preview link, we get events in the production dataset from a build that is two months stale. Nobody has noticed because the volume is tiny, but it is wrong, and the fix is either to expire previews after a branch merges or to scope the analytics key per environment properly, and the second one is the right answer.

The environment variable is the part I keep getting stuck on, so I want to write it down. The environment variable is set once at the project level, which is why every preview inherits the production value, and to scope it per environment we have to set it three times and remove the project level one, and the moment we remove the project level one, anything we forgot breaks immediately rather than quietly. So it needs doing on a Tuesday morning and not on a Friday afternoon.

One more thing. The rehearsal project still has the old domain attached as a redirect and design's bookmark goes through that redirect, which is a fourth reason the link behaved oddly and it is the only one I have already fixed.

This is the note on the bearing housings from the second batch, and I want to be precise because we are going to have to reject some of them and the supplier will want reasons.

The drawing calls the bore 62 millimetres H7, which is plus 0.03 minus zero, and we are measuring between 62.00 and 62.05 across the twenty pieces I have checked so far. So five of the twenty are outside, and they are outside by 0.02, which is small but it is outside, and an H7 bore that is 0.02 oversize on a bearing seat gives a loose fit and the bearing will creep in service. It will not fail on the test bench. It will fail in a year in the field, and that is worse.

The measurements themselves I am confident about. I checked the bore gauge against the setting ring twice, once cold at the start and once after two hours, and it read the same both times, and Herr Vogel repeated six of the twenty independently and got the same numbers to within 0.005.

What is interesting is which five are out. They are not random. They are all from the same fixture position, and I have the position stamped on the flange, so I sink the tolerance problem is a fixture problem and not a process drift problem, because a drift would walk through the batch in order and this does not. It is one of four positions and it is consistently the same one.

The supplier's certificate says every piece was inspected and every piece was in tolerance, and that certificate cannot be correct, because five pieces from one fixture position are 0.02 oversize and no inspection that actually happened would have passed them. The certificate says every piece was inspected. I am not going to accuse anybody of anything in writing, but the certificate and the parts disagree and somebody has to explain that.

So my recommendation. Reject the five, keep the fifteen, and ask for the fixture to be re-shimmed and for the next batch to be delivered with the fixture position stamped on every piece rather than on some of them. The clamping torque should also be recorded, because at 120 Newton metres on a thin walled housing you can distort the bore during machining and get exactly this reading pattern, and if that is what is happening then re-shimming will not fix it and we will be here again in October.

And I sink we should hold the assembly build until this is settled, because putting bearings into five housings we already suspect and then taking them out again damages the housings, and then we own the scrap rather than the supplier. I think that is the whole decision, really. Hold the build, reject five, ask for the fixture data.

Clinical note, Mr Ellery, review in clinic today, and copy to the cardiology registrar please.

He is 74, came in with three days of palpitations and mild breathlessness on the stairs, no chest pain, no syncope. He has had atrial flutter before, twice, first documented in 2019 and again last March, and both times it converted with rate control alone and did not need cardioversion. Today the ECG shows flutter again at a ventricular rate of about 150, and the sawtooth is clear in the inferior leads, so this is not a new diagnosis and it is not fibrillation, and I want that distinction in the letter because the last discharge summary said fibrillation and it was not.

Examination. He is comfortable at rest, chest clear, no murmur, no ankle oedema, blood pressure 138 over 84 sitting. He was quite mute for the first few minutes of the consultation, which is not like him, and his daughter said he has been low since his wife's funeral in June, and I think that is worth a separate conversation and possibly a separate appointment rather than being squeezed into a cardiology review.

Plan. Continue the bisoprolol, and increase it to 5 milligrams once daily rather than 2.5, and I have explained that this may make him feel more tired for the first week or two and that this usually settles. Continue the apixaban at the current dose, and I have checked the renal function, which is stable, so no dose adjustment. Bloods today for potassium, magnesium, thyroid function and a full blood count, and please chase the potassium specifically, because his potassium was 3.4 in March and nobody acted on it and low potassium in a patient with recurrent flutter is a treatable contributor.

He asked directly whether this will keep happening and I said honestly that it might, and that if it does then ablation is a reasonable conversation to have with cardiology, and that flutter in particular responds well to ablation, better than fibrillation does. He said he would rather take a tablet than have a procedure and I have documented that preference without pushing it either way.

On the injection site from his shingles vaccine three weeks ago, which he raised at the end and which is why this consultation ran over. The site is a little firm and slightly pink over about two centimetres, not hot, not spreading, not tender to any real degree, and he has no fever. I am confident that is a normal local reaction at three weeks rather than an infection, and I have said so, and I have also said that if it becomes hot or painful or spreads beyond the mark I drew on his arm today then he comes back the same day rather than waiting.

Safety netting given verbally and in writing. Come back immediately with chest pain, fainting, or breathlessness at rest. Otherwise review in two weeks with the blood results, and please chase the potassium.

Continue the apixaban at the current dose, and I have checked the renal function, which is stable, so no dose adjustment. Bloods today for potassium, magnesium, thyroid function and a full blood count, and please chase the potassium specifically, because his potassium was 3.4 in March and nobody acted on it and low potassium in a patient with recurrent flutter is a treatable contributor.

He asked directly whether this will keep happening and I said honestly that it might, and that if it does then ablation is a reasonable conversation to have with cardiology, and that flutter in particular responds well to ablation, better than fibrillation does. He said he would rather take a tablet than have a procedure and I have documented that preference without pushing it either way.

On the injection site from his shingles vaccine three weeks ago, which he raised at the end and which is why this consultation ran over. The site is a little firm and slightly pink over about two centimetres, not hot, not spreading, not tender to any real degree, and he has no fever. I am confident that is a normal local reaction at three weeks rather than an infection, and I have said so, and I have also said that if it becomes hot or painful or spreads beyond the mark I drew on his arm today then he comes back the same day rather than waiting.

Safety netting given verbally and in writing. Come back immediately with chest pain, fainting, or breathlessness at rest. Otherwise review in two weeks with the blood results, and please chase the potassium.

input:
Design review notes on the service discovery change, and I want to push back on part of it before it gets built.

The proposal is that every service reads its own configuration from the council cluster at boot rather than from the file baked into the image, and I understand why, because right now a configuration change means a rebuild and a redeploy and that is slow. But it makes the registry a hard boot dependency for every single service, and today it is only a soft dependency, because a service that cannot reach it still starts and still serves traffic with whatever it already knows.

That difference matters more than the proposal admits. We lost quorum in the Oregon datacentre in April, three of five nodes, for about eleven minutes, and nothing customer facing broke, and the reason nothing broke is exactly that services did not need the registry to start. If this change had been in place in April, every pod that restarted during those eleven minutes would have crash looped, and pods restart constantly, so we would have had a real outage instead of a graph nobody noticed.

What I would rather do is keep the file as the fallback. Read the registry at boot, with a 10 second timeout, and if it does not answer, start with the baked file and log loudly. That gives us the fast configuration change in the normal case and it keeps the April behaviour in the bad case, and the cost is that a service can start with stale configuration, which I think is clearly better than not starting.

The health check and deregistration half of the proposal I have no argument with at all and I think it should go ahead independently, because the current deregistration is manual and we have had stale entries for dead nodes twice this quarter. Split it into two changes and I will approve the second one today.

Right, site note for Monday and somebody needs to read this before the lads turn up at 07:30.

The council have put a notice on the hoarding about the working hours. It says 8 to 6 weekdays and no work at all on Sunday, and we have been starting at half seven all month because that is what the last job round the corner allowed, and it is not what this one allows. So from Monday nobody starts before eight, and I mean nobody, not even the sparkies doing quiet work inside, because the notice does not distinguish and the neighbour who complained is standing at her window at half seven with her phone out.

The skip is the other thing. The skip licence runs out on the 14th and the council will not extend it while the notice is live, so the skip comes off the road on the 13th and everything that is going in it goes in it before then. I am not chasing anybody about this on the 13th. If it is not in the skip it stays on site and it is somebody's problem for another three weeks.

I have spoken to the planning department twice and they are sending an officer out on Wednesday, and when he comes I want the wheel wash working and the mud off the pavement, because the mud is the thing he will actually write down. The hours we can argue about. The pavement we cannot.

The council closed the road at the far end for the resurfacing and the closure is longer than they told us, until the 22nd, so deliveries come in from the crescent end only and the concrete lorry on Thursday needs telling because he came the other way last time and had to reverse two hundred yards. Ring him Wednesday, not Thursday morning.

Cutting list notes for the Prentice job before I start, because I got this wrong on the Hallam order in the spring and it cost me a board.

The boards are 2.4 metres by 300 wide and I need four shelves at 580 and a pair of uprights at 1180, and if you just add those up it looks like one board does the shelves and one does the uprights with plenty spare. It does not, and the reason is that every cut takes material away. The curve of the blade on the panel saw is 3.2 millimetres, and three cuts across a 2.4 metre board to get four shelves at 580 loses nearly ten millimetres, and four times 580 is 2320, so 2320 plus the waste is over 2330 and the board is 2400, which is fine, but only just, and that is with a square end to start from. If the factory end is not square, and it usually is not, I lose another five to ten before I begin.

So I am cutting the shelves out of one board and the uprights out of a second, and the offcut from the second board is 1220 by 300, which is enough for the back rail and the two cleats, and I want to cut those from that offcut rather than opening a third board.

The grain is the other thing. The grain runs the length of the board and the shelves want the grain running along the length of the shelf, not across it, so the shelves come out of the board the long way and I cannot nest them cleverly to save material. The grain runs the length of the board, which means the layout is fixed and there is no optimising to do.

One last thing for the quote. Mrs Prentice asked for a shelf at 620 rather than 580 and I have priced 580, and at 620 four shelves is 2480 plus the waste, which is a second board for one shelf's worth of extra length. So either she takes 580, or she takes three shelves at 620, or the price goes up by the cost of a board and I would rather she heard that from me now than from the invoice.

Retro notes, and I want to bring one thing back that we tried in the spring and abandoned, because I think we abandoned it for the wrong reason.

The board has nine cards sitting in review right now. Nine. Two of them have been there for 14 days. Our cycle time on the cards that actually finish is about 4.5 days, and of that 4.5 days, roughly three of them are the card sitting in review waiting for somebody, and less than two are anybody writing anything. So the bottleneck is not development capacity, it has never been development capacity, and every conversation we have had about capacity for the last two quarters has been about the wrong column.

In April we put the whip limit on the review column and it lasted nine days. What happened is that the column filled, nobody could move a new card into it, and instead of that being the signal to go and review something, three people opened new cards in the column before it, because the board was blocked and they wanted to look busy. Then somebody raised it in standup as the limit not working and we took it off.

My read now is that the limit worked exactly as designed and we did not like what it told us, which is that we would rather start something new than finish something old. That is a preference, not a process problem, and taking the limit off did not fix the preference, it just hid it again, and the nine cards in review are the proof.

So what I want to propose is the same thing with two changes. First, the limit goes on review and it is agreed by the team rather than announced by me, because in April I announced it and that is half of why it failed. Second, and this is the part we did not do at all, we agree in advance what you do when the column is full, and the answer is that you review something, and if there is genuinely nothing you can review, you say so in standup and we look at why together rather than you finding other work.

I would start with a whip limit of three on review, which is roughly one per pair, and I would leave every other column alone for a month so we only change one thing and can actually tell what it did. And I would agree up front that we keep it for four weeks whatever happens, because the failure mode in April was that we removed it on day nine, before it had shown us anything except discomfort.

The thing I do not want is for this to turn into a conversation about individuals, and it will if we are not careful, because the two cards that have been in review for 14 days both belong to the same person and everybody knows that. It is not about them. If it were about them, the other seven cards would not be there.

Attendance note of my telephone call with Mrs Ashworth this afternoon, and then instructions for Nadia on the next steps, and I will deal with the note first.

I explained to her that the position on the deposit has not changed since March and that the landlord's agents are wrong in law about the deduction for the carpet, because the inventory at the start of the tenancy describes the carpet as worn in two places and the schedule of dilapidations at the end describes it as worn, which is the same condition and not damage. I said that in my view the deduction of 480 pounds for the carpet falls away entirely and that the deduction of 95 pounds for the cleaning is arguable and that I would not fight it, and she agreed with that approach.

I also explained the timetable, which she has found frustrating and I think reasonably. The scheme has 28 days to respond and they took the 14 day extension, so we are at day 39 with no substantive answer, and the only thing we can do about that is chase, which I have done twice.

On the second matter, the commercial lease. She has asked whether she needs her own solicitor for this or whether the company's in house council can act, and I have explained the difficulty, which is that the company's interests and her interests as guarantor are not the same interests, and that the moment she signs a personal guarantee she needs advice that is hers rather than the company's. She understood that immediately, which not everybody does.

Instructions for Nadia. Please chase the scheme in writing tomorrow, copy to the landlord's agents, and put the day count in the first line rather than in the third paragraph, because the last letter buried it. Then please pull the lease and look specifically at clause 22, which is the break clause, and tell me whether the break is conditional on vacant possession, because if it is then the advice on the guarantee changes and I want to know before I write to her rather than after.

On the correspondence generally. The letter from their side dated the 11th of March is headed without prejudice and most of it is plainly not without prejudice at all, it is simply their position, and I want to be careful about that when we come to costs, because we may want to put parts of it in front of the tribunal. The letter is headed without prejudice and I am not going to argue the label with them now. I would rather raise it once, properly, at the point it matters.

One further thing. If their council will not engage on the carpet point by the end of the month, my advice to Mrs Ashworth will be to take the 95 pound cleaning deduction on the chin, accept nothing on the carpet, and let the scheme adjudicate, because the adjudication is free and the correspondence is not.
