Notes towards the methods section, dictated on the train, so I will tidy the citations later.

The sample is 1,400 responses collected between February and April, of which 62 are unusable because the respondent skipped the entire second block, and I want to be explicit in the paper that those 62 are excluded rather than imputed, because the second block is where the outcome measure lives and imputing an outcome would be indefensible.

There is a gap in the coverage that I have to address head on rather than in a limitations paragraph at the end. We have almost nothing from respondents aged over 70, 31 responses in total, and the recruitment was online, so that gap is a recruitment artefact and not a finding about the population. It would be easy to write a sentence that makes the gap sound like an incidental feature of the sample and I do not want to do that.

On the instrument. Items 9 through 14 were adapted from the 2019 questionnaire and items 15 through 22 are new, and the new items are the ones that carry the argument, so the reliability of that subscale matters more than the reliability of the whole thing. The alpha on the new subscale is acceptable and the alpha on the adapted items is better, which is unsurprising and slightly annoying.

Two of the reviewers on the earlier paper asked for a gap analysis against the national survey and I have now done it, and the honest answer is that our sample and the national sample seem comparable on income and education and do not seem comparable on household composition, because we have far more single occupant households than the national figure. So the gap analysis supports the argument for two of the three covariates and undermines it for the third, and that goes in the paper as it is.

On the pilot. The pilot was 40 respondents in December, and the reason the pilot matters is that it is where we found the wording problem on item 17, which respondents were reading as being about the previous month rather than the previous year. We fixed it before the main collection. The pilot data are not pooled with the main data and the paper should say so plainly, because a reviewer will ask, and because pooling them would be wrong.

One small thing I keep forgetting and want written down. In the appendix, the photograph of the field kit has a whip and a set of scales in it, because the field task involved preparing a standard portion, and a reviewer on the earlier paper thought the photograph was from a different study entirely. Caption it properly this time.

And the gap between the pilot in December and the main collection starting in February is nine weeks, which seems longer than it was because of the wording revision and the ethics amendment, and I should say why in one sentence rather than leaving the reader to wonder.

input:
Notes from the usability session this morning, six participants, and the headline is that the sign-up screen tested fine and the consent screen did not.

On sign-up, nobody hesitated, everybody typed a real address, and the average time from landing to submit was under thirty seconds. Two people commented that the button label is friendly, which I did not expect anybody to mention at all.

On consent, four of the six read the checkbox text out loud, which in my experience means they did not understand it, and two of those four asked me what it meant before they clicked. The text says that we correct the email addresses so that we can contact you about the trial, and the problem is the sentence is doing two jobs, the purpose and the permission, and neither one lands. One participant asked whether she was agreeing to marketing. She was not, and the fact that she had to ask is the finding.

What I would change. Split the sentence in two, say plainly what we store and for how long, and move the trial contact permission to its own line with its own checkbox, because right now one click covers both and that is the part that will not survive a legal review anyway.

We have 340 people on the waiting list and the plan is to open sign-up on the 11th, so if the consent copy is going to change it has to change this week, and I would rather delay by a few days than open with a screen that four out of six people had to read twice.

Bug triage notes for the flaky test problem, and I think I have it, so I want to write it down before I lose it.

The gist suite has 812 tests and three of them fail intermittently, always the same three, and always when the whole suite runs and never when you run that file on its own. That pattern is almost always shared state, and it is shared state here, but not the kind I was looking for.

The three tests all touch the date formatter, and the date formatter reads the timezone once at module load and caches it. One other test file, the invoice export one, sets the timezone to UTC to make its own assertions stable, and it does not set it back. So whether the three tests pass depends entirely on whether the invoice file happened to run before them, and the runner picks the file order by how long each file took last time, which changes.

So it is not really flaky, it is deterministic given an order nobody controls. The fix I want is to make the formatter read the timezone at call time rather than at load time, which is a real fix and takes about 40 seconds of typing, and then the invoice file can do whatever it likes.

The fix I do not want is to set the timezone globally in the setup file, which is what the last person to look at this suggested in the ticket, because that makes all 812 tests pass under one timezone and hides the fact that the formatter is broken for everybody else in the world.

Separately, gist is configured with the snapshot directory outside the test folder, which is why the snapshots never show up in review diffs properly, and I think that is worth changing but it is a different change and a different pull request. The snapshot directory should sit next to the tests.

Right, thoughts on the Ferrers draft before I send it back, and I want to be careful how I put this because the client wrote the second paragraph himself and he is quite attached to it.

The piece is 900 words and it wants to be about 650, and the cut is almost entirely in the middle, where there are three examples doing the work of one. Keep the first example, which is specific and has a number in it. Lose the second and third, which are the same point in different clothes.

The second paragraph is the problem. It opens with a joke about the industry, and the joke is fine in a room and does not survive on a page, because in a room you can hear that it was said in jest and on a page it reads as a genuine complaint about their own customers. I am not going to tell him it is a bad joke. input: Writing up the incident from last night while it is still fresh, and this is my recollection rather than the timeline from the alerting, which I will reconcile in the morning. The first page came in at 01:14 and it was the latency alert on the checkout path, not the error rate one, which is why nobody treated it as urgent for the first ten minutes. I acknowledged it, looked at the dashboard, saw the p99 sitting around four seconds against a normal of two hundred milliseconds, and started walking the request path from the edge inwards. The load balancer was healthy and the application pods were healthy, and the connection pool on the primary database was saturated at two hundred connections with a queue behind it. My first theory was the nightly reindex overrunning, so I checked and it had finished at 00:52 as usual. What actually happened is that the migration we shipped at 18:00 yesterday added an index on the orders table but the query planner did not pick it up until it saw enough traffic, and by then it was choosing a sequential scan on a table with eleven million rows. I bounced the pooler at 01:41 and ran an analyze on the orders table, and the p99 came back inside two minutes. Going back to what I said about the first page, it was the error rate alert and not the latency one, which matters because the latency alert is the one routed to the channel nobody watches overnight. Actions for me are to fix that routing, to add an analyze step to the migration runner, and to write the customer facing note before standup.

input: Site instruction for the retaining wall on the north boundary, and this supersedes what I said on the phone this morning. The wall is 24 metres long and it steps down in three bays following the fall of the ground, so the top of each bay is level and the base follows the slope. Excavation goes to 1.2 metres below the existing ground level at the low end and the base slab is 400 thick with the reinforcement in the bottom face, mesh A252, with 50 of cover to the earth face. The stem thickness at the base is 300, sorry, 350, and it tapers to 200 at the top, and the vertical bars are at 200 centres in the earth face with the starter bars projecting 600 above the slab. Drainage behind the wall is a 100 perforated pipe wrapped in geotextile bedded in single size aggregate, and it discharges to the existing gully at the north east corner rather than to the road. Do not backfill against the wall until the concrete has reached seven days, and backfill in 300 layers compacted with the plate rather than the roller, because the roller will push the top of the wall out of plumb before it has any load on it. The movement joints are at 6 metre centres with a compressible filler and a debonded dowel across each one. I want a photograph of the reinforcement in place before every pour and I want the concrete tickets kept on site, because the last job we did with this supplier had two loads at the wrong strength and nobody noticed until the cubes came back at 28 days.

input: Handover for the search reindex work because I am out from Thursday and it should not sit still for a week. The tracking issue is PLATFORM-4471 and everything I have written down is in there, including the two dead ends, so read that before you read anything I say here. The reindex itself is driven by the job at services/search/reindex.py and it takes a shard argument, and the safe way to run it is one shard at a time with the checkpoint file on the shared volume, because if you run all of them together the cluster hits its merge throttle and the whole thing takes longer than doing it serially. Shard three is the one that failed twice, and both times it failed on the same document, a listing with a description field of about two megabytes that somebody pasted an entire spreadsheet into. I have not fixed that document and I do not think we should, because the next one will look different and the job needs to survive it either way, so the fix is a size guard in the mapper with a log line and a skipped counter. The staging cluster is a fair copy of production for this purpose, three data nodes and the same mapping, and the only difference is the replica count. If you need to start over, delete the checkpoint file rather than the index, and never delete the alias, because the alias is what the application reads and recreating it takes a deploy. Earlier I gave the wrong issue number. It is PLATFORM-4417, not PLATFORM-4471. Ping me if shard three fails a third time and I will look at it from wherever I am.

input: Recording the decision on the pilot rollout so it is written down somewhere other than the thread. We are starting with the accounts in the enterprise tier that already have SSO configured, because they are the ones whose admins will actually read a change notice, and that is about thirty accounts depending on how you count the ones mid migration. The pilot runs for three weeks, no, four weeks, actually let me say three weeks and we extend if the ticket volume is flat, because a fixed four weeks means we sit through two quiet weeks before anybody is allowed to make a decision. Success is not a usage number. It is that support does not see a rise in tickets tagged permissions, and that at least five admins give us something written about the new flow, good or bad. Rahul owns the comms and he is sending one notice at the start and one at the end, nothing in between, because the last pilot had four emails and two of them contradicted each other. I own the flag and the rollback, and rollback is a flag flip that takes effect on the next request, not a deploy. The thing I am least comfortable with is that we have no way to tell whether an admin saw the notice, so if the feedback is thin we will not know whether the flow is fine or nobody noticed it changed. I would rather ship it and find that out than spend another sprint building notice tracking that nobody asked for.

input: Notes on the reconciliation for the March close, because two numbers in it look like a mistake and they are not. input: This is the handover for the distribution side while I am on leave, and it is long because there are three things running at once and none of them can wait three weeks. Start with the Epping depot, because that is the one that will page you. The lease runs to 31 March next year and we have already told the landlord we are not renewing, so everything in that building has to be somewhere else by the middle of February, which gives you six weeks of moving while the depot is still shipping. The racking is being bought by the tenant who is taking over, which is why we are not dismantling it, and the only things going on a truck are the stock, the two forklifts and the office contents. Thandi has the stock plan and it moves in four waves by product line, slowest moving first, and the reason for that order is that if the plan slips we want the slippage to land on the lines nobody is waiting for. The forklifts are on a maintenance contract that transfers with them and the certificates are in the folder on the shared drive, and do not let them go on a truck without the certificates because we will not be able to use them at the new site until they are re-inspected. Second thing is the packaging supplier. We moved to Verwoerd Packaging in October and the quality has been fine, better than fine on the boxes, but the lead time they quoted us was ten working days and what we are actually seeing is closer to fifteen, and twice it has been twenty. That is the whole reason the December backlog looked as bad as it did. I have a meeting booked with their account manager for the second week of January and if you can take it, take it, and if you cannot then move it rather than sending somebody who has not seen the numbers. What I want out of that meeting is either a written commitment to ten days with something behind it, or permission from them to dual source the boxes without losing the pricing on the rest of the range. Third thing is the returns process, which is the one I care about most and the one that has no deadline attached to it, so it is also the one that will quietly not happen. Every return currently goes back to Epping, gets inspected, and then either goes back into sellable stock or gets written off, and the inspection is done by whoever is free, which means the standard moves around and we have stock going back on the shelf that should not be there. Sipho has drafted a one page inspection sheet with photographs and I think it is genuinely good, and all it needs is somebody with authority to say it is the standard from a given date. That somebody can be you. Going back to what I said about the packaging lead time, the quote was twelve working days, not ten, which matters because they will have the signed quote in front of them and I do not want you arguing from a number they can disprove in the first five minutes. Everything else is in the shared drive under the same folder names as last year, and if something is not there it is because it does not exist, not because I have hidden it somewhere clever.

input: This is the runbook and the reasoning for the certificate rotation next week, and I am recording it rather than writing it because I want the reasoning in it and I never write the reasoning down. The short version is that the wildcard certificate for the internal domain expires on 9 February and it is used in more places than the inventory says, so we are rotating early and we are doing it in an order that lets us stop halfway. The certificate is issued by the internal CA and the private key lives in the vault at secret/pki/internal-wildcard, and the only people who can read that path are the two of us and the CI role. That CI role is the reason this is not a five minute job, because three pipelines pull the certificate at build time and bake it into an image, so rotating the secret does not rotate what is running until those images are rebuilt. Order of work is as follows. First the load balancers, because they terminate TLS for everything public facing and they read the certificate from disk at start, so they can be done one at a time behind the health check with no traffic impact. Second the internal ingress, which reads from a Kubernetes secret and needs the pods restarted, and a rolling restart there is safe because the readiness probe is honest. Third the three baked images, which need a pipeline run each and about twenty minutes of build time each, and those can run in parallel because they do not share a build agent. Fourth and last the two legacy services on the old VMs, which have the certificate in a directory next to the binary and need a systemd restart, and those are the ones that will go wrong, because one of them reads the certificate once at boot and holds it in memory forever, and the other one has a hardcoded path to a file that has been a symlink since before I joined. The rollback for the first three is to put the previous certificate back and repeat the same restarts, and it works because the old certificate is still valid until 9 February. The rollback for the legacy pair is a snapshot restore, which is slow and which I would rather not do on a Friday, which is why they are last and why we are doing this on a Tuesday. Monitoring is the part people skip. There is a blackbox probe that checks certificate expiry on the public endpoints and it alerts at fourteen days, and it does not check the internal endpoints at all, so during the rotation the only signal from the internal side is application errors. I am adding internal probes as part of this work rather than after it, because after it means never. The certificate expires on 19 February, not 9 February. One more thing that is not in any document. The old certificate has the wrong subject alternative name for one of the legacy services and that service works only because its client does not verify the hostname, so when we put a correct certificate in front of it, it will start failing verification if anybody ever fixes the client. I have written that down in the ticket rather than fixing it, because fixing it needs the owning team and they do not know they own it yet.

input: This is my dictated first pass at the section on consultation, and I want it kept exactly as it comes out because I will edit it on paper tomorrow and I lose things when I edit on screen. The claim I want to make is narrow. It is not that consultation improves policy, which is asserted everywhere and demonstrated almost nowhere, and it is not that consultation is a democratic good in itself, which is an argument I am happy to leave to other people. The claim is that the way a consultation is timed determines what it can possibly change, and that most of the consultations in our sample were timed such that they could not change anything material even in principle. Take the twenty three consultations on the transport side. In seventeen of them the consultation opened after the funding envelope had been set and after the preferred option had appeared in a published document, which means the only questions genuinely open were questions of implementation. That is not a criticism of the officials running them. An official who opens a consultation before the funding is settled is inviting the public to express a preference the department cannot deliver, and the reputational cost of that lands on the same official. So the timing is rational at the level of the individual decision and irrational at the level of the system, which is a pattern that appears throughout this literature and which I will come back to in the discussion. The counter example is the one case in the sample where consultation preceded option development, the coastal defence review, and it is instructive precisely because it went badly. The consultation produced three broad directions rather than a preference, the department had to develop options for all three, the process took nineteen months instead of the planned seven, and two of the three directions were abandoned late, which left a group of participants who had been told their view was being taken seriously and then watched it disappear without explanation. If I only had that case I would conclude that early consultation is worse. What the other twenty two cases tell me is that early consultation is expensive and late consultation is empty, and that the interesting question is not when to consult but what a department is willing to leave undecided while it does. I want to be careful here not to overstate what a sample of twenty three tells us. These are all English transport and infrastructure cases from a seven year window, they are all cases where a consultation actually took place, which excludes the decisions taken without one, and I have no access to the internal advice that shaped the timing, only to the published documents and the dates. So the mechanism I am describing is inferred from timing and outcome, not observed, and I will say so in the limitations rather than in a footnote, because a claim about mechanism belongs next to its own weakness.

input: I am going to talk through the whole settlement integration before the call tomorrow, because the document we sent them is accurate and useless, and the people on the call need the reasoning and not the field list. The counterparty is Ashanti Rail Credit and they are a small lender, about forty thousand active loans, and everything they do today is a nightly batch file dropped on an SFTP server that somebody logs in and collects. Our side of the work is to take that batch, break it into individual settlement instructions, push each one to the payment rail, and then reconcile what the rail tells us against what the batch said. None of that is hard. What is hard is that their batch is not idempotent, and I want to spend most of the call on that. Start with the shape of the file. It arrives between 23:00 and 01:00 depending on how long their end of day takes, it is a fixed width text file, and the record layout has been the same since 2019 apart from one field that was widened. Each record has a loan reference, a borrower reference, an amount in cents, a value date, and a status flag, and the loan reference is the only thing in the file that is stable across days. The borrower reference is regenerated by their core system on every export, which they did not tell us and which we discovered by diffing two consecutive files, so it cannot be used as a key for anything. The amount is in cents and it is unsigned, and the direction is carried by the status flag rather than by the sign, which means a refund and a collection look identical apart from a single character. Now the idempotency problem. If their end of day fails partway and they rerun it, we receive two files for the same business date, and the second file is not a delta, it is a full replacement that includes every record from the first one with the same loan references and the same amounts. There is nothing in the file itself that says which one it is. The filename carries a sequence number that resets weekly, and we have seen the sequence number repeat inside a single day twice this year, so the filename is evidence and not proof. Our defence is a hash of the record content plus the business date, held for ninety days, and any record whose hash we have already seen and already settled is skipped with a log line and a counter. That is why the counter matters and why I do not want it hidden behind a debug flag. The webhook for settlement results goes to https://api.ashanti-rail.co.ke/v2/settlements and they have asked us to include the loan reference in every callback, not the borrower reference, for the reason I explained a moment ago. Their endpoint is authenticated with a bearer token that they rotate quarterly, and the rotation has broken twice, both times because the new token was issued but the old one was revoked before we deployed. So for this integration the rotation procedure is that they issue the new token, we confirm in writing that it is live in our configuration, and only then do they revoke the old one. I want that written into the contract schedule and not just agreed on a call, because the people who revoke tokens are not the people on this call. Reconciliation runs at 09:00 the following morning and it compares three things, the count and total of the batch as we parsed it, the count and total of the instructions we pushed, and the count and total of what the rail confirmed. If all three agree we send a green report and nobody reads it, which is fine. If the first two agree and the third does not, the difference is in flight and we wait an hour and check again. If the first two disagree, we stop, because that means we parsed the file differently than we settled it, and there is no safe automatic response to that. The report goes to their operations mailbox and to ours, and it names the file we processed and the hash of it, so that a disagreement three weeks later can be traced to a specific file rather than to a date. Two open items before I forget them. Their test environment shares a database with their production reporting, which we found out when a test settlement appeared on a live report, so all testing from now on is against files they hand us rather than against their environment. And they have asked for a same day file in addition to the nightly one, which I am not agreeing to until the idempotency work is in production, because a second file per day doubles the chance of the exact failure we spent this call talking about. Going back to the webhook address, it is https://api.ashantirail.co.ke/v2/settlements with no hyphen in the hostname, and I want somebody to read that back to me on the call, because I have now given it wrong in two documents and the hyphenated one belongs to a parked domain.

input: Dictating the letter content for the orthopaedic referral, and this is the clinical detail, not the letter itself. Mr Okonkwo is 63 and he has had right knee pain for about eighteen months, gradually worsening, now waking him at night two or three times a week, which is the change that brought him back in. He can manage about two hundred metres on the flat before he has to stop, and stairs are worse going down than going up. There is no history of injury, no locking, and no giving way. On examination there is a fixed flexion of about ten degrees, crepitus through the range, and tenderness over the medial joint line, and the lateral side is unremarkable. He is otherwise well. He takes amlodipine 5 milligrams for hypertension and nothing else, no anticoagulants, and his BMI is 31. Weight bearing films from November show medial compartment joint space loss with subchondral sclerosis and no evidence of inflammatory change. He has completed twelve weeks of physiotherapy with the community team and reports no benefit, and he has tried paracetamol and topical anti inflammatories, which take the edge off during the day and do nothing at night. He is keen on surgery and he understands it is not a decision that gets made today. I have that the wrong way round. Stairs are worse going up than going down. His daughter will be at the appointment and she is the one who chased the last referral, so any letter should go to him and copy her, and she is aware he minimises symptoms when he is asked directly.

input: This is the escalation summary for ticket 88421 so the next shift does not start from the beginning. The customer is Northgate Dental, they have twelve sites, and the problem is that appointment reminders stopped sending on Tuesday afternoon for four of those sites and are still sending normally for the other eight. They noticed because a patient turned up on the wrong day and complained, so the first thing I did was check whether the reminders were being generated at all, and they are, the records are there with a queued status and a timestamp. So it is not generation. The send, the sending step is where it stops, and the four affected sites all share one thing, which is that they were migrated to the new messaging provider in the batch on 14 January and the other eight are still on the old provider. I have not proved that is the cause but I would be surprised if it is not. input: Notes for the newsletter draft, and this is me thinking out loud rather than copy, so do not paste any of it in. The theme for this issue is the pricing change, and the hard part is that we are raising prices on the two cheapest plans and leaving the expensive one alone, which is the opposite of the story people expect. So the order matters. Lead with what is changing, put the numbers in the second paragraph rather than the fifth, and do not open with a paragraph about how much we value our community, because everybody who has ever received one of these knows that paragraph means the price is going up. Second section is the reasoning, and the honest reasoning is that the cheap plans cost us more to support than they bring in, scratch that, the honest reasoning is that the cheap plans were priced in 2021 and our infrastructure bill has roughly doubled since. Third section is what nobody is losing, and that is the part people will actually read, so it goes above the fold on mobile. The grandfathering is six months for anybody on an annual plan and three months for monthly, and both dates should be spelled out rather than described, because relative dates in an email are read weeks later. Last thing, the reply address has to be a real inbox that somebody is watching for the first week. Last time it went to the noreply address and the complaints ended up on social media instead, where they stayed.

input: This is the note on the Djibouti corridor for the quarterly review, and I want to describe what actually happens rather than what the process document says happens, because the two have not matched for about a year. A container lands at the port and the clock we are measured on starts when the vessel is discharged, not when the container clears, and that single definition is why our numbers look worse than the operation is. Discharge to gate out is running at about nine days on average, and the average is a bad number here because the distribution has two humps. Roughly two thirds of containers move in four to five days and they are the ones where the paperwork was complete before the vessel arrived. The remaining third sits for two to three weeks, and in almost every case the reason is a single missing document, usually the certificate of origin, and usually because the supplier sent a scan of a scan that the authority would not accept. So the operational problem is not trucking capacity, which is what everybody assumes because trucking is the visible part. We have enough trucks. The trucks are idle waiting for releases. I have the figures for the last quarter and they are in the sheet, but the one to remember is that we paid demurrage on forty one containers and thirty six of those forty one were document delays, not transport delays. On the road leg, Djibouti to Addis is between two and three days depending on the queue at the border post, and the queue is worse on Mondays for reasons nobody has ever explained to me. Our drivers do the run with two drivers per truck on the long leg, which costs more and which I am not proposing we change, because the alternative is an overnight stop at a place where we have lost cargo twice. Warehousing at the Addis end is the bit that is genuinely fine. We have the space, the yard has been resurfaced, and the handover to the customer teams works because Meseret rebuilt the appointment system last year and it is the only part of this chain where nobody is guessing. What I want from the review is a decision on one thing, which is whether we are allowed to refuse a booking when the documents are not complete at the point of booking. Today we accept it, the container arrives, and we absorb the delay and the demurrage, and the commercial team counts the booking as a win in the month they took it. If we can refuse, the operational numbers improve immediately and the commercial numbers get worse for a quarter, and somebody more senior than me has to be willing to say that out loud. Going back to the demurrage figure, it was thirty two of the forty one that were document delays, not thirty six. The other nine were transport, and four of those nine were the same broken trailer, which we have since sold.

input: Recording the findings for the client report on the staging environment assessment, in the order I found them rather than by severity, and I will reorder when I write it up. First thing, and this is the one that matters, the staging environment is reachable from the internet on port 8443 with no network restriction, and it holds a copy of production data that was taken in March. So this is not a staging finding. It is a production data exposure with a staging label on it, and I will write it that way in the report because calling it a staging issue is how it gets deprioritised. The application on that port requires authentication, and the authentication is a shared account whose credentials are in the repository history, in a file that was deleted eight months ago but never purged, and I found it in about four minutes with a tool that anybody has. Second, the session cookie is issued without the secure flag and without an expiry, so it persists until the browser is closed, and on the staging host it is also issued for the parent domain rather than the host, which means it is sent to every other service on that domain including two I was not asked to test and did not touch. Third, the file upload accepts any content type and stores the file under the web root with the original filename, and I was able to retrieve my own upload over HTTP, which means the only thing standing between that and code execution is whether the server is configured to execute what is in that directory. It is not, today, on this host. I want to be precise about that in the report, because a finding that overstates itself gets argued about instead of fixed. Fourth, and this is the one the developers will not like, there are eleven dependencies with known advisories, and I checked every one against the actual code paths, and nine of them are not reachable in this application. Two are. I am reporting those two as findings and the other nine as an inventory note, because handing somebody eleven advisories they cannot triage is how the whole list gets ignored. Fifth, error responses include a full stack trace with absolute filesystem paths and the framework version, which is minor on its own and useful to an attacker in combination with everything above. On the positive side, the database is not reachable from outside the host, the backups are encrypted and I verified that by trying to read one, and the deployment pipeline requires a signed commit, which is better than most of what I see. Remediation order in the report will be the network restriction first, because it is one firewall rule and it removes the exposure entirely while everything else is being fixed, then the credentials in the repository history, which needs a rewrite and a rotation and not just a rotation. The application is reachable on port 8843, not 8443, and I want that right in the report because the client will test it themselves and a wrong port number will make them doubt the rest of it.

input: I am dictating the methods narrative for the resubmission, and I want it verbatim, because the last time somebody tidied my dictation the tidying removed the two places where I hedge, and the reviewers read the unhedged version as overclaiming, which cost us the grant. So please leave the hedges. The study is a within subject design with three sessions per participant, and the reason it is within subject and not between is the effect size we are chasing. In the pilot the difference between conditions was about a fifth of a standard deviation, and a between subject design at that effect size and eighty percent power needs something in the region of eight hundred people per arm, which we cannot recruit and could not afford if we could. Within subject with three sessions gets us to a usable number, and the cost of that choice is order effects, which is what the counterbalancing is for and what reviewer two did not believe we had handled. So let me be explicit about the counterbalancing, because being explicit is the whole point of this revision. There are three conditions, which I will call quiet, babble and music, and with three conditions there are six possible orders, and we assign participants to orders in blocks of six so that at any point in recruitment the orders are balanced to within one participant. That is not the same as randomising the order per participant, which is what the previous version said, and randomising per participant is exactly the thing that leaves you with an unbalanced design when recruitment stops early, which it always does. It always does. Every study I have ever run has stopped early for one reason or another, and a design that only balances in expectation is a design that does not balance. The sessions are seven days apart, with a tolerance of plus or minus two days, and the tolerance is in the protocol rather than being an accident, because participants have lives and a rigid seven days is how you lose a third of your sample to attrition. Attrition in the pilot was eleven percent by session three, which is lower than I expected, and I think the reason is that we pay per session rather than on completion. We will keep paying per session. The measures are the same three at every session, and the order of the measures within a session is fixed rather than counterbalanced, which is a deliberate asymmetry and I want to defend it rather than hide it. The comprehension task has to come first because it is the one that is sensitive to fatigue, the working memory span comes second, and the questionnaire comes last because a questionnaire is the only thing on the list a tired participant can still do honestly. Fixing that order means any fatigue effect is constant across conditions, which is what we care about, rather than being balanced away into the error term. Analysis is a mixed effects model with condition as a fixed effect, participant as a random intercept, and session number as a covariate, and I want to say plainly that session number is in there because we expect practice effects and not because we are interested in them. The comparison of interest is quiet against babble and quiet against music, two comparisons, specified in advance, and we are not testing babble against music because we have no hypothesis about it and testing it would just be a third chance to find something. Reviewer three asked for a Bonferroni correction across all three pairwise comparisons and I am going to push back on that politely, because correcting across a comparison we are not making is not conservatism, it is arithmetic applied to the wrong set. The exclusions are specified before we look at anything. A session is excluded if the participant's accuracy on the practice trials is below chance, if the noise level in the room exceeded the calibration by more than three decibels, or if the participant reports having taken the test in a language other than the one they were tested in, and that last one sounds strange until you have run this with bilingual participants and seen what happens. A participant is excluded entirely only if two of their three sessions are excluded, and if that leaves us short we recruit replacements in blocks of six for the reason I gave earlier. Where I am genuinely uncertain, and this is the hedge I want kept, is whether three sessions is enough to separate a practice effect from a condition effect at this effect size. It might not be. If it is not, the honest outcome of this study is a better estimate for the next one rather than an answer, and I would rather say that in the proposal than discover the reviewers saying it for me.

input: Notes toward the data management section, and also a decision I need to record because I keep changing my mind about it in conversation and then forgetting what I settled on. The dataset is interview transcripts from forty two participants across three institutions, and the sensitivity is not in the topics, which are ordinary questions about workload, it is in the fact that in a department of nine people a transcript is identifiable from its content no matter what you redact. That is the whole problem and everything below follows from it. Recording and transcription happen locally, the audio never leaves the encrypted volume, and the audio is destroyed after the transcript is checked, which is at most fourteen days, no, thirty days, let me say fourteen days after the interview and I will hold myself to it, because the reason to hold audio at all is to correct a transcription error and if I have not checked it in two weeks I am not going to. Transcripts are pseudonymised at the point of transcription rather than afterwards, and the key linking pseudonym to participant lives in a separate encrypted file that only I hold, and the retention on that key is the end of the project plus one year for query handling, after which it is deleted and the transcripts become genuinely anonymous rather than pseudonymous. Whether they are genuinely anonymous is arguable given what I said about departments of nine people, and I will say so in the section rather than claiming anonymity I cannot guarantee. Sharing is the part reviewers will ask about and the part where I am going to disappoint them. I am not depositing the transcripts, not even under controlled access, because controlled access at a repository means somebody else decides who is trustworthy, and I promised participants that I would make that decision. What I will deposit is the interview schedule, the coding frame with definitions, the codebook with frequencies, and a set of illustrative quotations that participants have individually approved for release, and that last part is work, about an hour per participant, and it is in the budget. Requests for access to the full transcripts come to me and I answer them, and if I am not contactable the answer is no, which is a worse outcome than a repository and is still the promise I made. Ethics approval is in place from the lead institution and the two partner institutions have accepted it by reciprocal agreement rather than reviewing it separately, and I have the correspondence for that in the appendix because a reviewer asked for it last time and I could not find it. Consent is written, it covers secondary analysis by me but not by others, and participants can withdraw up to the point of anonymisation, which is a real limit and is stated in the information sheet in the same words I have just used.

input: This is for the group arriving on the fourteenth, seven people, four from Australia and three from Germany, and the German three have done Kilimanjaro so they think they know about altitude. The itinerary is the standard Ghorepani loop with the extra night at Tadapani, and the extra night is not negotiable even if they feel fine, because feeling fine on day three is not information. Permits I will do in Pokhara on the twelfth, and I need passport copies before then, not on the day, because the office closes at four and the queue does not care about our flight. The porter arrangement is. Two of them have said they do not want porters and I am not going to argue about it in the office, so we take three porters instead of five and whoever changes their mind on day two pays the difference, which I will tell them clearly at the briefing rather than letting it become an argument on the trail. Food and water is the usual, teahouse meals, and I will say at the briefing that the water from the taps at Tadapani has made people ill twice this season, so tablets or boiled, no exceptions. One of the Australians has mentioned a knee and has not said which knee or how bad, so I will ask at the briefing in front of the others, because people are honest about injuries in a group in a way they are not on the phone.

input: Working notes on the Marchetti contract translation, source Italian, target French, deadline the twenty second. The document is fifty one pages but only about thirty of them are real translation, because the annexes repeat the definitions clause almost verbatim and I have a memory match on nearly all of it. The client's terminology list is the problem. They have supplied a glossary that renders comodato as pret a usage throughout, which is defensible in ordinary usage and wrong in this document, because clause 4.2 makes the arrangement gratuitous and the French legal term for that distinction matters if this is ever read by a court. I have flagged it in a comment rather than overriding it, and I will not deliver an override without their written agreement, because the last time I corrected a client glossary silently they assumed the inconsistency was mine. There is one genuine ambiguity in the source, in clause 9, where the Italian could mean either party may terminate or only the lender may terminate, and the Italian is ambiguous rather than badly written, so I am delivering both readings in a note and letting their lawyer decide. I am not resolving it in the target text. The formatting is theirs, I keep their numbering, and I do not renumber anything even where the source skips a number, which it does between 12 and 14. input: This is my synthesis from the eight sessions we ran on the onboarding flow, and I am recording it before I make slides, because when I make slides first I end up defending the slides instead of the findings. Eight participants, all new to the product, four on desktop and four on mobile, and every session was the same task, get to the point where you have created your first project and invited one person to it. Nobody failed the task. That is worth saying first, because the last round of research we presented sounded like the product was broken and it was not, and the team stopped trusting the research for a while afterwards. Everybody got there. The question is what it cost them. The first thing all eight of them did was skip the introduction screens, and I mean skip in the strong sense, they tapped through three screens in under two seconds without their eyes settling on any of them. So whatever we put on those screens is not being read, and the honest response to that is either to delete them or to put something there that survives being skipped, like a single sentence that is also visible later. Six of the eight then tried to create a project from the empty state illustration rather than from the button, and I want to be careful about what that means. It does not mean the illustration should be a button, scratch that, it means the illustration is where their attention landed and the button is not, and the fix could be either moving the button or changing where the illustration sits. The invite step is where the real cost was. Five participants looked for invite inside the project settings, which is where it used to be in a competitor most of them had used, and three of those five gave up looking and used the share link instead, which works and which produces a different permission level than an invite does, and not one of them noticed that. That is the finding I care about most, because it is silent. Nobody was confused, nobody complained, and three out of eight ended up with a collaborator on the wrong permission. On mobile specifically, the invite field opened the keyboard over the confirm button on two of the four devices, and both participants scrolled, found the button, and carried on without comment, which is exactly the kind of thing that never appears in a support ticket and shows up as a drop off number nobody can explain. I have video timestamps for all of it in the sheet. What I want out of the review is a decision about the invite discoverability and nothing else, because if we open the introduction screens and the empty state and the mobile keyboard in one meeting, we will discuss all three and decide none of them. The other findings are written up and they will keep. And I want to say plainly that eight sessions is eight sessions, so the five out of eight on the settings path is a strong signal about where people look and a weak estimate of how often, and I am not going to put a percentage in the slides.

input: Progress note on the ablation runs so I have something written before the meeting. The baseline is reproduced, and by reproduced I mean within half a point of the reported number on the same split, which took four days and most of that was finding out that their tokenizer strips accents and ours does not. Three ablations are done. Removing the auxiliary loss costs 2.1 points, which is more than the paper claims and I have run it twice with different seeds to be sure. Freezing the lower six layers costs almost nothing, 0.3, which is inside seed variance so I would not report it as an effect at all. Reducing the context from 2048 to 512 costs 4.8, which is the biggest single effect and also the least interesting because everybody already knows it. The one I am still running is the data ordering ablation, and it is slow because it needs a full retrain per ordering rather than a fine tune, so it is three days for four orderings on the two GPUs I have. What I want to ask in the meeting is whether the data ordering result is worth three days of the cluster, given that we already have a plausible story without it, and I think the answer is yes but I would rather be told no now than on Friday. Everything is logged under the runs directory with the config hash in the folder name, and the seeds are 0, 1 and 2 everywhere so nothing is cherry picked. The context ablation costs 4.2 points, not 4.8.

input: Assessment note for Mr Halvorsen, second visit. Presenting complaint is right shoulder pain, onset about six weeks ago, no specific injury, and it came on over a few days after he started swimming again after a long break. Pain is worst on overhead reaching and on lying on that side at night, which is what wakes him. On examination the passive range is full and the active range is limited in abduction from about ninety degrees, painful arc between ninety and one twenty, and empty can is positive. Cervical screen is clear and there is no neurological deficit in the arm. Strength in external rotation is reduced compared to the left but not markedly. First visit we did scapular setting and isometric external rotation, three sets of ten, twice daily, and he has done them, which I can tell because the isometric hold is noticeably stronger today. Today I have progressed him to banded external rotation and added a wall slide, and I have told him to stop swimming freestyle for two weeks and use backstroke instead. Sorry, not backstroke. Stop swimming freestyle and use breaststroke for two weeks, because backstroke has the same overhead position that is provoking it. Review in two weeks and if the painful arc has not narrowed by then I will write to the GP about imaging.

input: Retro summary for the board, and I am writing it as what we are changing rather than what people said, because the board does not need the transcript. Two things came up that everybody agreed on and one that split the room. The agreed ones first. Estimation is not working and nobody in the room defended it, so we are stopping story points and switching to counting items, and I expect the throughput number to be noisier and more honest than the velocity number was. Second agreed thing is that the definition of done does not include anything about the runbook, which is why the last two features shipped without one, so the runbook goes in the definition of done and the team wrote the wording themselves rather than me writing it. The thing that split the room is the standup. Four people want it asynchronous in the channel and three want to keep it as a call, and the arguments are both about the same underlying thing, which is that the call is the only time the two people working on the migration talk to each other. So the compromise we landed on is asynchronous four days a week and a call on Wednesday, and I want to be clear in front of the board that this is a compromise and not a decision anybody was happy with, and we will look at it again in six weeks. Six weeks, not four.

input: This is the note for the protocol amendment on the shift work cohort, and I am dictating it before Thursday so Marieke has something to work from while I am in Groningen. The study reference is METC 2024-1187 and it has to appear on the front page of every version we submit, because the committee sent the last one back for exactly that and it cost us five weeks. The recruitment target stays at 240 participants across the three sites, and the split is 100 at Utrecht, 80 at Nijmegen and 60 at Maastricht, which is not even, but it follows the number of night shift staff each hospital actually employs rather than the assumption we made when we wrote the design. The substantive change in the amendment is the actigraphy device. We specified the GENEActiv units in the original protocol and we are moving to the Axivity AX3, and the reason is not that the GENEActiv is worse, it is that the AX3 gives us thirty days on a charge instead of seven, and with a shift pattern that runs four on and four off, a seven day battery means a participant has to come back to the site in the middle of their own rotation, which is the single thing every one of the pilot participants complained about. So the burden argument is the one to lead with in the amendment and not the data quality argument, because the committee is much more interested in burden, and because on data quality the two devices are close enough that I would not want to be cross examined on it. The sampling rate we are asking for is 100 hertz, and that matters for the storage estimate, which is the second thing the committee will ask about, and the answer is about 700 megabytes per participant per wear period, so the whole study fits in under 200 gigabytes and the secure share has room for that three times over. Data goes to the pseudonymised area on the research share, the path is /research/shiftwork/wave2, and the linkage file stays exactly where it already is, which is the encrypted volume that only Marieke and I can open, and nobody else gets a key, not the students and not the statistician, because the statistician does not need it and asking for it in writing would slow the amendment down for no gain at all. On consent, we are not reconsenting the people who are already enrolled, and I want to be careful how we word that, because the device change does not alter what we collect or how long we keep it, it alters the object strapped to somebody's wrist, so the position is that this is a non substantial amendment with an information sheet update, and the updated sheet goes out with the next scheduled contact rather than as a separate mailing. If the committee disagrees and calls it substantial we lose about six weeks, and we should say now that we would accept that rather than argue, because arguing about substantiality is how the sleep group down the corridor spent most of last year. Marieke is drafting the amendment text itself and I am doing the burden section and the storage numbers, and we want a version with track changes to circulate on the 14th, so the internal deadline is the 12th, and that is tighter than it sounds because the 13th is a holiday. Two smaller things while I am talking. The first is that the pilot data, the fourteen participants from last spring, are not in the amendment at all and should not be, they are their own protocol, and somebody will ask, so have the answer ready before the meeting rather than during it. The second is that the wear compliance definition needs to go into the amendment even though it has not changed, because our original wording said at least four valid days and never defined a valid day, and a reviewer picked that up informally and we never fixed it, so we fix it now while the file is open, and a valid day is at least twenty hours of non zero movement in any twenty four hour window starting at noon. One thing I have the wrong way round at the start of this. It is 60 at Nijmegen and 80 at Maastricht, not the other way about, because Maastricht is the one with the two intensive care units. Everything else stands. Send me the draft as a PDF rather than as a document, because I am reading it on the train and tracked changes on my phone are unreadable in the document format, and if anything in the storage section looks wrong to you, change it and tell me afterwards rather than waiting to ask me first.

input: Right, this is the handover on my renewals book because I am out from the 3rd and I do not want anyone finding out about these accounts in week two. There are four that matter and the rest can wait for me. Ravensmoor Logistics is the big one, they are at $184,000 and the renewal date is 31 August, and the thing to know about Ravensmoor is that the person who bought us has gone, Aidan left in April, and the woman who inherited it does not know why she is paying us, so that renewal is not a renewal conversation it is a first sales call wearing a renewal hat, and if you treat it as paperwork we will lose it. Her name is Denise Oyelaran and she is in procurement, not in operations, which is why she looks at the line item and not at the product. Her direct line is 512 555 0148, no, 512 555 0184, and she answers that rather than email, and the last two times I emailed her I got a reply eleven days later from somebody else on her team. Kepler Dental Group is smaller, $61,000, and they are on a co-term with the practice management module which means the whole thing lands on one date, and that date is 30 September, and there is nothing hard about them except that they always ask for twelve percent and they always accept eight, so open at nothing and let them ask. Truvine Foods is the one I am worried about for a different reason, which is that they are using about a third of what they bought and they know it, and their finance director said out loud on the last call that they would be looking at seat count at renewal, so the play there is to get in front of it and propose the reduction ourselves, because a customer who proposes it feels clever and a customer who has it proposed to them feels handled. Their renewal is on 30 June and they will want a two year term to justify the smaller number, and I think that is a good trade for us. The fourth is Halden Precision, $38,000, renewal 15 October, and honestly they are fine, they renew, they have renewed three years running and they have never once asked for a discount, so do not go and remind them that discounts exist. Everything is in the CRM but the notes field is where I keep the real detail, so read the notes field on all four and not just the summary, and where I have written a date in the notes it is the date somebody said something rather than the date it happened. Hold on, I said Truvine is on 30 June and it is not, it is 30 July, because they moved it last year when they added the second site. I have not touched the pricing approvals, so anything over ten percent still needs Marcus, and Marcus is genuinely fine about it if you ask him the day before rather than the hour before. If Ravensmoor goes quiet in the last two weeks, the escalation is not to chase Denise harder, it is to go back through Aidan's old contact in operations, a man called Paolo, who still uses the product every day and who is the only person in that building who would notice if we turned it off. That is the whole book. Call me if Ravensmoor moves, do not call me about Halden, and if Truvine come back asking for a three year term rather than two, say yes and take the win.

input: These are my working notes on the terminology setup for the Vasquin infusion pump manual, and I am recording them because the agency will ask me to justify the hours and I would rather have written the reasoning down while I still remember it. The source is 412 pages of English, the targets are French, German and Spanish, and the deadline for the French is 28 February with the other two following at two week intervals, which sounds generous and is not, because the regulatory annex has to be re-checked against the current directive rather than translated freely, and that annex is only nineteen pages but it is the nineteen pages that can stop the product shipping. The first decision is that we build the glossary before anybody translates a sentence, and we build it from the client's own existing material rather than from the source manual, because they have eleven years of approved French documentation and the words in it are the words their regulator has already accepted. Extracting from their old files gave me 1,240 candidate terms, which is far too many, and after I removed everything that is ordinary language and everything that appears once, the working glossary is 380 terms, and that is the number to quote to the agency. Of those, about sixty are the ones that will actually cause an argument, and they fall into two groups. The first group is the device parts, where the client has an internal name and the market has a different name, and the rule there is that the internal name wins in the maintenance chapters and the market name wins in anything a nurse reads, which is not elegant but it is what their own old manuals do and consistency with themselves matters more than consistency with the industry. The second group is the verbs in the warnings, and here I am being strict: prime, purge, flush and bleed are four different actions on this device and three of them are commonly translated the same way into French, so every one of them gets a locked entry with a usage note, and the usage note is in French rather than in English so the reviewer cannot claim she misread it. Now, on process. Everything goes through the translation memory we already have from the 2023 job, and the match rate is going to look impressive, about 47 percent at 85 percent and above, but I do not trust the segments from the 2023 job in the alarms chapter, because that chapter was done under time pressure by somebody who is no longer at the agency, so we treat alarms as new work and I have said so in writing. The reviewer for French is Madame Guérin, who is a clinical pharmacist rather than a linguist, and that is deliberate, because on the last job the linguistic reviewer changed correct terminology to elegant terminology and we spent three rounds putting it back. Scratch what I said about the second reviewer, we are not adding one for German. The QA pass is two people and not three, and if the German comes back weak we deal with it then. Files come to me as XLIFF and not as a Word export, and if they arrive as Word I am sending them back the same day rather than fixing the tags, because the last time I fixed tags by hand it took nine hours that nobody paid for. The deliverable for the client is the translated set plus the glossary as a bilingual file per language, and I want the glossary delivered whether or not they ask for it, because it is the thing that makes them come back to us instead of to whoever quotes fifteen percent cheaper next year. Budget wise, I am quoting the glossary work separately as 22 hours, and the reason to itemise it rather than bury it is that it survives the project and they should see that. If they refuse to pay for it I will still do it, but they will see the line. One last thing for me rather than for them, which is that I should look at whether the 380 terms can be loaded into the checker so the term violations come out as warnings during translation rather than as corrections after it, because catching prime and purge at the point somebody types them is worth more than catching them in review, and I have never actually set that up on a job this size.

The source is 412 pages of English, the targets are French, German and Spanish, and the deadline for the French is 28 February with the other two following at two week intervals, which sounds generous and is not, because the regulatory annex has to be re-checked against the current directive rather than translated freely, and that annex is only nineteen pages but it is the nineteen pages that can stop the product shipping. The first decision is that we build the glossary before anybody translates a sentence, and we build it from the client's own existing material rather than from the source manual, because they have eleven years of approved French documentation and the words in it are the words their regulator has already accepted. Of those, about sixty are the ones that will actually cause an argument, and they fall into two groups. The first group is the device parts, where the client has an internal name and the market has a different name, and the rule there is that the internal name wins in the maintenance chapters and the market name wins in anything a nurse reads, which is not elegant but it is what their own old manuals do and consistency with themselves matters more than consistency with the industry. The second group is the verbs in the warnings, and here I am being strict: prime, purge, flush and bleed are four different actions on this device and three of them are commonly translated the same way into French, so every one of them gets a locked entry with a usage note, and the usage note is in French rather than in English so the reviewer cannot claim she misread it. Now, on process. Everything goes through the translation memory we already have from the 2023 job, and the match rate is going to look impressive, about 47 percent at 85 percent and above, but I do not trust the segments from the 2023 job in the alarms chapter, because that chapter was done under time pressure by somebody who is no longer at the agency, so we treat alarms as new work and I have said so in writing. The QA pass is two people and not three, and if the German comes back weak we deal with it then. Files come to me as XLIFF and not as a Word export, and if they arrive as Word I am sending them back the same day rather than fixing the tags, because the last time I fixed tags by hand it took nine hours that nobody paid for. The deliverable for the client is the translated set plus the glossary as a bilingual file per language, and I want the glossary delivered whether or not they ask for it, because it is the thing that makes them come back to us instead of to whoever quotes fifteen percent cheaper next year. input: Okay, notes to myself about the press and about December, because I keep going round in circles on this and I want it written down before I talk to Ellen. The quote from Kaplan is $28,400 for the used Heidelberg, delivered and installed, and that includes the first service but not the ink system flush, which they want another $900 for and which I think we should just pay because doing it ourselves means a day of Marco's time and Marco is the only person who can run the folder. The order reference is KP-70412, wait, KP-74012, and I need that right because their invoices come through with the reference and nothing else and Ellen has already had one payment go to the wrong job because of that. Lead time is six weeks from deposit, the deposit is a third, and if I put the deposit down this week the press lands in the second week of January, which is exactly wrong, because January is when we have nothing on and December is when we are drowning. So the real question is whether paying the deposit now buys us anything at all this year, and the answer is no, it buys us a machine sitting in the back in January. What it does do is lock the price, and Kaplan's man was clear that the price holds for thirty days and after that it goes to whatever the auction market is doing, and that is the only reason to move now rather than in three weeks. On December itself, we have the Harlow catalogue, which is 12,000 copies and is the biggest single job we have taken all year, and it has to be on a truck by the 18th. That job on its own fills the back half of the month. Then there is the usual December work, the cards and the calendars and the two restaurant menu reprints, and none of it is hard but all of it is fiddly and all of it comes in late. Staffing is where I am stuck. Marco is off from the 22nd and that is not negotiable, he asked in March. Priya can do extra days but not Saturdays because of her course. That leaves the week of the 15th thin, and the Harlow job is in that week, so either I bring somebody in for four days or I move Harlow earlier and tell them the truck goes on the 16th instead. I think we ask Harlow. They moved their own deadline twice on us last year and they know it, and a customer who has moved a date twice has spent their right to be surprised. If they say no, then we pay for four days of agency help and it comes out of the margin on that job, and the margin on that job is thin enough that I want to know now rather than on the 14th. Last thing, and it is the thing I will forget, the old Ryobi has to be gone before the Heidelberg arrives, and the scrap merchant wants a week's notice, so whatever I decide about the deposit, I ring him the same day. Talk to Ellen about the flush money, ring Harlow about the 16th, and do not sign anything at all until both of those are answers rather than hopes.

input: This is my write up of where the regression suite actually is, ahead of the planning session, and I am dictating it because writing it in the ticket takes me twice as long. We have 1,412 automated cases and the honest position is that about 300 of them are load bearing and the rest run because nobody has been brave enough to delete them. Last week's nightly failed on 41 cases and 34 of those were the same root cause, a fixture that expects the seed data to have exactly two saved addresses, and somebody added a third saved address to the seed set in October, so those 34 have been failing for five weeks and everyone has learned to ignore the red. That is the real problem, not the count. A suite that is red every night is a suite nobody reads, and once nobody reads it we are paying for the runtime and getting nothing. So what I want out of the planning session is agreement on three things. First, we fix the fixture, which is an hour of work, and I have already written it and not merged it because I wanted the count in front of people first. Second, we quarantine anything that has failed more than three nights running and has not been looked at, and quarantine means it moves to a separate job that does not gate the pipeline, not that it is deleted, because deleting is what I would like and it is not what I will get. Third, and this is the one that will cause an argument, we stop writing new UI cases for anything that has an API level equivalent, because I went through the failures for the last two months and the UI cases found four real bugs and cost us about thirty hours of triage, and the API cases found eleven real bugs and cost us maybe six hours. The checkout flow is the exception. I would keep full UI coverage there and I would keep it even if the numbers said otherwise, because that is the one place where a broken button is money and where our users are on browsers we do not test in. On the flaky ones, I do not think, actually the honest answer is that I have not measured flakiness properly, I have been going on which ones annoy me, so before the session I will pull the pass rate per case over thirty days and bring the list. Runtime is 52 minutes on a good night and 70 when the parallel workers fight over the database, and if we quarantine what I am proposing it comes down to about 35, which matters because at 35 minutes people run it before merging and at 70 they do not. That is the whole argument really. Everything I am asking for is in service of somebody actually looking at the result.

input: This is me thinking through the on call rebuild before I put a proposal in front of the group, and I want the reasoning captured because the proposal will get pushed back on and the reasoning is the part that survives. Where we are now is that eleven engineers share one rotation, one week each, primary only, no secondary, and the escalation path when primary does not answer is a phone tree that ends at me. That has held for two years and it is not holding now, for three reasons that are all the same reason underneath, which is that we have more services and the same number of people. First, page volume is up. We took 214 pages last quarter against 130 the quarter before, and the increase is almost entirely from the two services we inherited from the data team in June, and about a third of those pages are the same disk alert on the same two hosts, which nobody has fixed because fixing it belongs to whoever is on call and whoever is on call is too busy being on call. Second, the one week rotation means a person is on call five or six times a year and never gets good at it, so every incident starts with somebody reading a runbook for the first time. Third, we have no secondary, so a person who is at their kid's thing simply does not answer, and the phone tree exists to launder that fact rather than to fix it. So the proposal is that we go to two week rotations, no, one week, actually let me say two weeks with a handoff on the Wednesday, and the reason for the Wednesday handoff is that it stops the person carrying a live incident across a weekend boundary into their own week off, which happened to Devi in August and was the single worst on call experience anyone has reported to me. Two weeks also means five rotations a year per person rather than six with a secondary added, and it means the person has time to actually finish the alert cleanup work that the rotation is supposed to include. Because that is the other half of the proposal and it is the half that will get cut, so I want it written down first. On call is not just answering. Every rotation ends with a written handoff and at least one alert either fixed, tuned or deleted, and the deleted option is not a joke, because we have 34 alerts that have fired more than twice and led to action zero times. If we do not take something out every fortnight then the volume argument I just made gets worse on its own. On the secondary, I want a real secondary with a real expectation, which is a fifteen minute acknowledgement rather than five, and I want the secondary drawn from a different service area than the primary, because the failure mode we keep hitting is that both people who understand the ingest path are unreachable at the same time. That is going to be unpopular with the platform group because it means they carry pages for services they did not write, and the honest answer to that objection is yes, and the runbooks are how we make that survivable, and if a runbook is not good enough for a stranger to follow at 3 in the morning then it is not a runbook it is a note to self. Compensation I am deliberately not putting in this proposal. It comes up every time and it drags the conversation to a place I cannot deliver from, so I am going to ask for the rotation shape and the alert budget, get those, and take compensation to Yusuf separately. Timeline is that I want this agreed by the end of the month and running from the first Wednesday in the new quarter, and the migration is that the current rotation finishes its cycle and we do not try to switch mid week for the sake of starting sooner. If it goes badly, the failure signal is not page volume, it is whether people are trading shifts, because trading is what people do when the shape is wrong and they are being polite about it.

input: Care plan review for Mrs Halina Oduya, 82, seen at home this morning with her daughter present. Background is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, and a fall in February that did not fracture anything but has changed how she moves around the house. She is on apixaban 5 milligrams twice daily, bisoprolol 5 milligrams once daily, and furosemide 40 milligrams in the morning. Weight this morning was 71.2 kilograms, which is up 1.4 kilograms from the district nurse's reading a fortnight ago, and her ankles are worse than they were, so the plan is to increase the furosemide to 60 milligrams in the morning for five days and then review, and I have asked the district nurse to weigh her on Thursday and to ring me the same day rather than putting it in the notes for me to find. Blood pressure sitting was 118 over 68 and standing was 104 over 62, which she did not feel, but the postural drop is the thing I am watching because of the fall, so no change to the bisoprolol today even though the rate is a little quick. Bloods are due, and I have asked for renal function and potassium before Friday rather than next week, because that is the pair that matters if we are moving the diuretic. On the house itself, the daughter has already moved the bed downstairs, which was sensible, and the problem now is the step into the bathroom, which is a single step with nothing to hold, and she is using the towel rail, so the referral to occupational therapy is urgent rather than routine and I have said in the referral that she is using a towel rail as a grab rail, because that sentence gets referrals moved and a description of the step does not. Correction to the furosemide, earlier I said 60 and it should be 80 milligrams in the morning for five days, because she was already on 60 through the winter and came off it in March. The daughter's main worry is not the heart, it is that her mother is not eating much, and on questioning she is eating twice a day and drinking tea all afternoon, which is not nothing, and I do not want to medicalise appetite in an 82 year old who has just had her tablets increased. So we watch it and we ask again in a fortnight. She has an appointment with cardiology on 14 April and my view is she should keep it rather than being seen sooner, because there is nothing new structurally and being taken to hospital costs her two days of being unsettled. If the weight is not down by Thursday, or if she is more breathless at night, the daughter has my number and knows to use it, and I have written that on the front of the folder in the kitchen rather than telling her, because telling people is not the same as them being able to find it at 9 at night.
