input: Draft of the release note for 4.9, and this is the narrative part rather than the changelog, so the bullet list of fixes is already generated and I am not dictating that. The headline for this release is the new import path, and the thing to say about it plainly is that imports no longer run in the web process, which means an import of a hundred thousand rows no longer takes the site down for the people who are not importing anything. That is the whole story from a user's point of view and I want it in the first two sentences, not in the third paragraph after a discussion of the queue architecture, because our release notes have a habit of explaining the plumbing before the benefit. Second thing is the migrate migration step, which is the part people will actually get stuck on, and it is one command, it is reversible, and it takes about four minutes on a database of our reference size. What it does is move the existing import history table into its own schema, and the reason that matters to a reader is that anybody who has written their own queries against import history will need to change them, so that gets its own subheading with the old and the new table name side by side rather than being mentioned in passing. Third, we are deprecating the legacy CSV endpoint, and deprecating in this release means it logs a warning and keeps working, with removal scheduled for 5.1, and I want the removal version stated even though it is two releases away, because the last time we deprecated something without naming the removal version we had people still using it eighteen months later and a support argument about whether we had warned them. On the upgrade order, and this is the bit I always get wrong when I write it quickly, the workers have to be upgraded before the web tier, not after, because the new web tier enqueues jobs in a format the old workers cannot read. If somebody does it the other way round the symptom is imports that sit in queued forever and no error anywhere, which is the worst possible symptom, so that sentence needs to be a warning box and not a paragraph. Known issues, there are two. Imports that were already in flight when you upgrade are not migrated and have to be restarted, and there is no way around that, so people should drain the queue first. And the progress indicator on very large imports stops updating past about half a million rows while the import itself carries on fine, which is a cosmetic bug that looks exactly like a real one, and I would rather name it than have four support tickets about it. Credits at the bottom, and check the contributor list against the actual commits this time rather than against the last release's list, because we missed two people in 4.8 and one of them noticed publicly.

input: I am going to talk through the packaging change end to end so that there is one version of it written down, because right now it lives in four threads and two spreadsheets and everybody believes a slightly different thing. The change is that we collapse the three paid tiers into two and we move seat based pricing to a hybrid of seats plus included usage. Today we have Starter at $12 per seat, Growth at $29 per seat and Scale which is negotiated, and the problem is not the prices, it is that Growth exists mainly as a place to put people who need one feature from Scale, so half our Growth accounts are there for a single reason and each of them thinks that reason is worth $29. The new shape is Team and Business. Team is $18 per seat with 5,000 included operations per seat per month, Business is $40 per seat with 25,000 included, and overage is billed at four dollars per thousand operations in both, which is deliberately not cheap, because the overage is a signal to upgrade rather than a revenue line. Everything currently in Scale stays negotiated and is untouched by this, and I want that said early in every conversation because the enterprise team hears packaging change and assumes their contracts are being reopened. Migration is the part that actually matters. Existing customers keep their current pricing for twelve months from launch, and this is not a discount, it is a promise, and it goes in writing on the pricing page rather than only in the email, because the last time we changed packaging we said it in an email and then spent a quarter proving to people that we had said it. At the twelve month point, an account that would pay more on the new packaging moves to whichever is lower, which sounds like we are giving away money and is actually about twenty accounts, and I would rather lose that than have twenty angry renewal calls in the same week. The launch date is 6 May and the work in front of it is three streams. Billing needs the metering to be trustworthy at the account level, which today it is not, because we count operations for internal dashboards where being ten percent out does not matter and we are about to count them for invoices where it does. That is the critical path and it is the one thing that will move the date. Second stream is the pricing page and the in product upgrade flow, and third is enablement, which is the sales team, the support macros and the reseller documentation, and the resellers need six weeks of notice under the agreement, so their notice goes out at the end of this month regardless of whether anything else is ready. What I do not want is a launch where the page is beautiful and support cannot answer a question about overage. Risks, honestly. The first is that the metering is wrong at launch and we invoice somebody for usage they did not have, which is the only failure here that damages trust rather than revenue, so the mitigation is that the first billing cycle runs in shadow mode, we generate the invoice, we do not send it, and finance compares it against what the old packaging would have produced. input: Notes on the rate limiter before I put it in the ticket, because I want somebody to tell me if this is wrong before I merge it. The limit is per API key and the window is sixty seconds, and the cap I have set is 300 requests, wait no, 600 requests, because I checked what the busiest integration actually does and it does about 420 in its worst minute, so 300 would break a paying customer on day one. The store is Redis and the key is the API key plus the minute, which means a client that sends everything in the last second of one window and the first second of the next gets double the allowance briefly, and I know that is what a sliding window would fix, and I am not doing a sliding window in this change because the fixed window is four lines and I would rather ship the protection and improve it than argue about the algorithm for two weeks. When a client goes over we return 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds, and we do not silently drop, because a silent drop is what the old proxy did and it took somebody three days to work out why their sync was incomplete. The thing I am not sure about is the internal services, because they use API keys too and two of them poll hard, so either they get exempted by a flag or somebody raises their limits, and exempting internal traffic feels like the kind of decision that is fine until an internal service is the thing that takes us down. I would rather give them a higher number than an exemption. Metrics are in, so we will be able to see who is being limited before they email us about it, and I have added a log line with the key prefix and not the whole key.

input: Right, this is everything about assessment week and the parents evenings, and I am talking it through rather than writing it because I have twenty minutes in the car park and I will not get another twenty until Thursday. Assessment week is the week beginning 9 February, and the first thing everybody needs to understand is that it is four days and not five, because the Friday is the in service day that got moved from November, and every year somebody plans an assessment for the Friday and every year we find out about it on the Tuesday. So four days, Monday to Thursday, and the timetable is collapsed on the Monday and Tuesday and normal on the Wednesday and Thursday. Second year sit maths and English on the Monday, both in the sports hall, maths in the morning and English after lunch, and we need eighty desks in there which means the hall is set up on the Sunday afternoon, and I have asked Brendan whether the caretaking overtime is approved and I have not had an answer, so if it is not approved then it is set up on the Monday morning at seven and the PE department loses their first two periods, which they will accept once and complain about for a term. Third year sit science on the Tuesday morning, and science is the awkward one because the practical element needs the labs rather than the hall, so that is three labs running simultaneously with three invigilators who are not the science teachers, because the science teachers are needed to set up the next room, and that means I am short two invigilators on Tuesday morning specifically. Fiona has said she can do one of them. The other one I do not have and I am not going to pretend I do, so the fallback is that we run the practical in two sittings on Tuesday morning and Tuesday afternoon, which is not ideal because the afternoon group will have heard what is in it, and my honest view is that at this level that matters less than people think. Now the parents evenings, and this is where it gets tangled, because they were originally the week after assessment week and they have been moved to the week before, so the parents are coming in before anybody has any results, which changes what teachers can usefully say and nobody has told the teachers that yet. First year parents are on the Tuesday, second and third year parents are on the Thursday, both from half four until seven, and the booking system opens a fortnight before and closes at noon on the day, and last year we left it open until four o'clock and three teachers had appointments they did not know about. Ten minute slots, and I want a five minute gap built in after every six slots, because without it everybody runs half an hour late by the end and the parents who booked the last slot are the ones who sat in a corridor. Rooms are the usual, first year in the assembly hall in rows, second and third year in the classrooms, and the signage is the thing that always fails, so Marie is doing signs with room numbers and teacher names and she is doing them the week before rather than on the day. On what teachers say, and this is the part I actually want to make a point about, if a parent asks how their child is doing in a subject and there is no assessment yet, the answer is what the child is doing in class and what they should be doing at home, and it is not a prediction of a grade. I have heard predicted grades handed out in October before now and they follow a child around for two years. Wait, I have the parents evenings the wrong way round. First year parents are on the Thursday and second and third year are on the Tuesday, because the second and third year ones need the classrooms and the classrooms are free on the Tuesday. Then the practical arrangements. Tea and coffee at the back of the hall, and somebody needs to be on the door from four o'clock, because the door is how parents who have not booked get seen at all, and we do see them, we just do not promise them ten minutes. Any parent who needs an interpreter, I need to know by the Friday before, and there are two families I already know about and probably a third. And the last thing, which is the thing I will be asked about at the staff meeting, is whether the reports go out before or after the parents evenings. After. They go out on the 27th, they are written in the week after assessment week, and I am not moving that, because a report written the same week as four days of assessment is a report written at midnight and it reads like one.

input: Sir, this is the note for the Manaslu group so we have it in writing before I send the money. Seven trekkers, arriving Kathmandu on 3 October, and the permit is the restricted area one, which is the expensive one, and it is per person per week. For the first week it is $100 per person, oops, $75 per person, sorry, the hundred dollars is the old rate before they changed it in the spring, and after the first week it is ten dollars per person per day. So for seven people and eight days inside the restricted area, I need the money in the office two days before we file, because they will not file on the same day, and the office needs the passport copies and the visa page and not just the passport number. Two of the group are on visas they got at the airport and one is on a thirty day visa that expires on the 27th, and the trek finishes on the 24th, which is fine but only just, so if we lose two days to weather at Larke La then that person is out of visa in Kathmandu, and extending in Kathmandu takes a full day of somebody sitting in an office. I would rather she extends now while we are still in the city. Guide is me, one assistant guide, and three porters for seven trekkers, and that is tight but the group is walking light and two of them have done Everest base camp before. The insurance certificates, I have five of seven, and I will not walk without all seven, so please tell the two of them again, and tell them it must say helicopter evacuation and it must say the altitude, because a policy that says trekking and stops at 4,000 metres is no policy on this route.

input: Working notes on the disclosure before I write the advisory properly. The finding is in the export endpoint on the reporting service, and it is an authorization gap rather than an injection: a member of one workspace can request a report for another workspace by changing the workspace ID in the request body, because the handler validates the session and then trusts the body. Impact is read only, but the report includes email addresses and role names for every member, so it is personal data in volume and it is not a low severity finding no matter how the vendor prefers to score it. I have reproduced it on two accounts I control, three times each, and the working proof is a curl with a copied session cookie, nothing exotic. Forget that last part about the cookie. It works with a bearer token from the normal login flow, which matters because a cookie based proof invites the argument that the tester was doing something unusual. Timeline so far, I reported on the 4th through their security address, got an automated acknowledgement the same day and nothing since, and their policy says ten business days for a substantive response, which expires on the 18th. I am not going to publish on the 19th out of spite, but I am going to send one more email on the 17th, to the security address and to their CTO on LinkedIn, because in my experience the second channel is what produces the reply. When they do reply, the thing I want in writing is whether the fix is a check in the handler or a change to how the token scope works, because a check in one handler tells me the other nine export endpoints are still wrong and I would rather test that than assume it.

input: Test notes for the pump rig, run 14. Inlet pressure was held at 2.4 bar and the flow was stepped from 20 to 90 litres per minute in ten steps, with two minutes at each step and the temperature logged at the outlet. The vibration reading at the 70 step is the interesting one, 4.1 millimetres per second against 1.8 at the step below, and it drops back to 2.0 at 80, so it is not a trend, it is a band, and a band that narrow usually means a resonance rather than a bearing. I would like to, the sensible next run is to approach 70 from both directions in smaller steps and see whether the peak moves, because if it moves with the direction of approach then it is mechanical play and not resonance. The instrumentation held throughout, no dropouts in the log, and the outlet temperature rose four degrees over the whole run which is normal for this duration. One thing to note for the report is that the coupling was replaced before run 12, so runs 1 to 11 are not comparable on vibration and should not be plotted on the same axis, and somebody will plot them on the same axis unless it says so in the caption. The rig is left assembled and the sensors are still in place, so run 15 can happen on Monday without a setup day, provided nobody borrows the accelerometer over the weekend, which has happened twice.

input: Handover for the Djibouti to Addis leg while I am away, and I am recording it because two of these consignments have documents in three places and the drivers ring at night. The pharmaceutical consignment is the priority. It is 18 pallets, temperature controlled between 2 and 8 degrees, and the reefer unit on that trailer is the older one, so the driver checks the temperature log at every stop and photographs it, and if the reading is outside the range even once, he rings me before he moves, not after. The clearing agent is Bekele and his number is in the shared sheet, and he is good but he does not volunteer information, so ask him specifically whether the health certificate has been endorsed rather than asking whether the file is complete, because he will say the file is complete either way. The second consignment is the packaging materials, 26 pallets, no temperature requirement, and it can wait a day without anyone caring. Third is the spare parts for the bottling line, small, three crates, and those matter more than their size because the line is down until they arrive. On the parts, the duty exemption letter is the whole game. Without it we pay and then spend four months getting it back. Earlier I said the pharmaceutical consignment is 18 pallets and it is 16 pallets, because two were held back at origin for the next sailing. Trucks are with Hailu's company for the first two and with our own for the parts, and the reason the parts go on our own truck is that Hailu's drivers will not do the run overnight and the parts need to move overnight. If anything is held at the border, the escalation is Selam at the head office and not me, because she can call the customs supervisor directly and I cannot.

input: Rollout plan for the new session store, writing it down because I want somebody to argue with the percentages rather than with the design. The flag is session_store_v2 and it is evaluated per user and not per request, because a user whose session bounces between two stores gets logged out and then writes a support ticket that takes an hour to understand. Day one is internal staff only, which is about 200 accounts, and it stays there for two days because the first thing we are looking for is whether anybody gets logged out at all rather than anything statistical. Then 5 percent, hold on, 2 percent, and I want to start low specifically because the failure mode here is invisible in aggregate, a small number of people repeatedly logged out looks like nothing on a graph of session errors. From there 10, 25, 50 and 100, with at least a day at each and two days at 50, and the thing that moves us to the next step is not the clock, it is the logout rate on the cohort inside the flag compared to the cohort outside it. Rollback is a flag flip and it takes effect on the next request, but the sessions already written to the new store are not migrated back, so anybody in the flag at the time of a rollback gets logged out once. That is acceptable at 2 percent and it is not acceptable at 50, which is the real reason to spend a second day there. The one thing I am unsure about is the mobile clients on the old app version, because they hold a token for thirty days and I do not know whether the refresh path reads the store directly. I will find out before we go past 10 rather than assuming, and if it does read the store directly then the mobile users come last and they come with a forced token refresh, which is a different conversation.

input: Notes from the restore drill, and the honest summary is that we passed on the number we advertise and failed on the one that matters. Target recovery time is four hours. We restored the primary database from the nightly snapshot into the standby account in two hours and fifty minutes, so the four hour figure holds, and that is the number in the customer facing document. What did not hold is the rest restore drill on the object storage side, because we have never actually tested it, and when we tried, the bucket replication had been configured with the wrong lifecycle rule since March, so objects older than ninety days are in the archive tier and come back in twelve hours rather than minutes. Nobody knew that. So a full recovery today is four hours for the database and up to twelve hours for anything a customer uploaded more than ninety days ago, and that is the sentence I am putting at the top of the report. The fix is a lifecycle change and a re-run of the drill, and the lifecycle change is not free, it is about 340 dollars a month more, and I would rather pay it than discover this during an incident. Two smaller findings. The runbook says to restore into the standby account and does not say which region, and we picked the right one by luck. And the credentials in the runbook are for a role that was rotated in January, so the first fifteen minutes of the drill were spent on access rather than on restoring, which in a real incident is fifteen minutes of everybody watching one person.

input: Progress note for Danny Reyes, sixth session, right ankle, inversion sprain from the eleventh of last month. Single leg balance is up to forty seconds on the eyes open and about twelve on the eyes closed, which is the one I care about, and there is still a clear difference side to side. Calf raises are 20 repetitions in a row with good height and no compensation through the toes, and hopping is not started yet. Pain is what he calls a two at worst and it is at end range only. Plan is to progress the balance work to the foam pad and to add a hop and stick this week, and I have told him the hop and stick is the point where people reinjure by doing it on the driveway in trainers at eleven at night, so it stays in the clinic until next week. Home programme stays as it is, three times a day, and he is actually doing it, which is not always true. Correction on the balance number, I said forty seconds eyes open and it is thirty. Discharge is realistically three more sessions and the criteria I am using are symmetrical single leg balance eyes closed, 25 calf raises both sides, and hopping without hesitation, and I said all three to him out loud so he knows what he is working towards rather than waiting for me to decide he is done. He plays five a side and he will ask about going back, and my answer is after the hopping, not before, and I would rather say that now than negotiate it in three weeks.

input: Caveats for the retention report before anybody quotes a number from it in a deck. The cohorts are monthly by first paid invoice and not by signup, and that choice matters because we have a fourteen day trial and a signup cohort mixes people who never paid with people who did. Retention is measured as logged revenue in the month, so a customer who downgrades stays retained, and if anybody wants logo retention rather than revenue retention that is a different query and it gives a worse number. The window is January 2024 through last month, so 26 cohorts, and the last three are immature and I have marked them on the chart, which nobody will notice, so say it out loud in the meeting. Two data problems the reader should know about. The billing migration in August 2024 changed how annual plans are recognised, so anything spanning that month has a step in it that is an artefact and not behaviour, and I have not smoothed it because smoothing hides it. And about 40 accounts have manual invoices raised outside the billing system, mostly the early enterprise deals, and those are excluded entirely rather than partially counted, which is defensible and which also means the enterprise story in this report is not the whole enterprise story. Going back to the cohort window, it is January 2023 and not January 2024, so there are 38 cohorts and not 26. My own view of what the report says is that month 3 is where we lose people and month 1 looks fine, and that the interesting cohorts are the ones acquired through the partner channel, which retain better and which nobody talks about because they are a small share of new revenue.

input: Thinking out loud about the spring campaign before the call, so this is not copy, it is me working out what the campaign is actually about. The brief says awareness and the budget says performance, which is the usual problem, and if we split it we will do both badly on 18 thousand pounds. My instinct is to spend it all on the one thing we can actually prove, which is the comparison page, because that page converts at nearly four percent and nothing else we own gets close. The creative idea I keep coming back to is, maybe I should start with what the audience already believes. They already believe the cheap option is a false economy, they have been told that by everybody, and repeating it makes us sound like everybody. What they do not believe is that switching is easy, and that is where the money should go, because that is the objection that stops the four percent being six. So the campaign is about the switch and not about the product, three assets, a fifteen second video of the import running, a page that shows the import with real timings and not a marketing number, and one email to the people who started a trial and stopped. Channels, I would put nothing into display, and I know that is where the agency will want to go because it spends the budget cleanly. Timing is April, and the thing to check before the call is whether the import feature actually ships in March, because the whole campaign is a lie if it does not.

input: Decision on the depot cover for the peak weeks, recorded so that we are not relitigating it in November. Volumes from the 24th to the 6th run at about 2.4 times normal, that is what last year did and the year before was 2.2, so we plan to 2.4 and we accept that some days will be quieter than the plan. Cover is two extra pickers per shift, sorry, three extra pickers per shift, actually two, and the reason it is two rather than three is that the constraint is not picking, it is the single wrap station, and a third picker just builds a longer queue in front of it. So the money that would have gone to a third picker goes to a second wrap station, which is a hire and it is available from the 20th. Shifts change as well. We go to two shifts of nine hours rather than three of eight, because the handover between shifts costs us about twenty minutes each time and two handovers cost less than three. Deon is running the early and Chantelle the late, and both of them know they are not covering each other's absence, because that is how we ended up with somebody doing sixteen hours last December. Agency staff are booked for four days only, the 27th to the 30th, and they are booked now rather than in November because in November they cost forty percent more and are worse. Last thing, the returns pile is what beat us last year, not the outbound, and nobody is assigned to it in this plan, so that is the open question for the meeting.

input: Logging what I actually ran, because the results table in the shared doc says something slightly different and I want the record to be right. Base model is the 1.5 billion parameter checkpoint, LoRA on the attention projections only, rank 16, alpha 32, learning rate 1e-4 with cosine decay and 40 warmup steps. Batch size is 8 with gradient accumulation of 4, so an effective batch of 32, and sequence length 2048, which is the thing that constrained everything because the longer examples in the set get truncated at 2048 and about 6 percent of them are longer than that. Three epochs, and the loss curve is flat after the second, so if I run it again I run two. Eval is the held out 200 examples and I am reporting exact match and not any similarity score, because a similarity score on this task rewards a model that keeps most of the text and changes the wrong thing. Actually I need to correct the rank, I said 16 and it was 8, which matters because the parameter count in the doc is computed from it. Result is 71 percent exact match against 58 for the base model with the same prompt, and the failures are concentrated in the long examples, which is the truncation showing up rather than a reasoning failure, and the honest next step is to fix the sequence length before touching any hyperparameter.

input: This is the note for the evidence annex, and it is dictated so please treat the wording as provisional, but the structure is what I want. The annex has three parts. The first is the survey, which is 1,180 responses from a panel weighted to the working population, fielded in March, and the response rate is worth stating because reviewers ask, it was 31 percent. The second is the administrative data, which covers claims made between April 2021 and March 2024, and the caveat there is that the recording practice changed in 2022, so a rise across that boundary is partly a recording artefact and we say so in the text rather than in a footnote, because footnotes are where inconvenient things go to be ignored. The third part is the qualitative work, 22 interviews, and I want the sampling described honestly, which is that they were recruited through two advice organisations and are therefore people who sought help, and that is a real limitation and also the only practical way to reach them. On the ordering, I want the qualitative material first in the narrative even though it is third in the annex, because the numbers do not explain why anybody made the choices they made. Earlier I said 22 interviews and it is 27, because the final five were completed after the interim report went out. What I do not want is a section that reconciles the survey and the administrative data, because they are measuring different things and a reconciliation would imply otherwise. If a reviewer asks for it, the answer is a paragraph explaining the difference, not a table pretending it away.

input: Playtest notes from the six sessions on the second level, and these are observations rather than decisions. Nobody found the side route. Not one of the six, and two of them walked past the entrance twice, so either the lighting cue is too subtle or the corridor reads as scenery, and my guess is the second one because it has no floor detail and everything walkable in the game so far has floor detail. Time to first death is between forty seconds and four minutes, which is a huge spread, and the four minute player was the one who had played the first level twice. The boss took an average of five attempts and the failure was almost always the second phase, specifically the moment the arena floods, and three players said out loud that they did not know they could climb. Scratch what I said about the checkpoint. So the climbing affordance is the real problem, not the boss timing, and I would rather add one prop that is obviously climbable early in the level than lower the boss health. Two smaller things. The pickup sound plays twice when you collect during a dash, and one player quit the session at nineteen minutes because of motion sickness during the flood phase, which is a camera shake amount and not a design decision, so that is a straightforward fix and it goes ahead of everything else on this list.

So the climbing affordance is the real problem, not the boss timing, and I would rather add one prop that is obviously climbable early in the level than lower the boss health. Two smaller things. The pickup sound plays twice when you collect during a dash, and one player quit the session at nineteen minutes because of motion sickness during the flood phase, which is a camera shake amount and not a design decision, so that is a straightforward fix and it goes ahead of everything else on this list.

input: Notes on the payout failures before the postmortem, so people can disagree with the facts separately from the conclusions. Between 09:40 and 11:05 we failed 1,342 payouts, all to one bank, and all with the same downstream code that we map to a generic failure. The mapping is the first problem: their code means the beneficiary account is dormant and ours means try again later, so our retry logic retried each one three times, which is 4,026 requests to tell us the same thing. The second problem is that the retries went out at ten second intervals rather than with backoff, and their side rate limited us at about the twenty minute mark, which is when payouts to other banks started failing as well, so a data quality issue at one bank became an outage for everybody. Correction on the window, it was 09:40 to 12:05 and not 11:05, the last failure is in the log at 12:03. Nothing was lost, all 1,342 are in the failed state with a reason and none were double sent, and I have checked that specifically because a double send is the only version of this that costs money. What I want out of the postmortem is agreement on two changes, mapping their dormant account code to a terminal state rather than a retryable one, and putting backoff on the retry path regardless of the mapping, because the mapping will be wrong again for a different code.

input: Incident notes for the certificate expiry, written up while it is fresh. At 04:12 the internal API started returning TLS errors to the mobile gateway and to nothing else, and the reason it was only the gateway is that everything else talks to the API through the mesh and the gateway does not. The cert expired at 04:00 exactly. It was issued for a year, it was renewed by hand last year because the automation did not cover internal names at the time, and the calendar reminder for it was on the account of somebody who left in November. That is the actual root cause and I want it written that way rather than as an expired certificate, because an expired certificate is a symptom of an ownership gap. Recovery took 38 minutes and most of that was finding who could issue for that name, not the issuing itself. The change I am proposing is that the auto automation covers internal names, which it now can, and that we alert at 30 days and at 7 days on every certificate we can see, and the second half of that sentence is the important half, because we did not know this certificate existed. There is a second certificate on the same host expiring in April and nobody has claimed it either, so I have raised that separately rather than fixing it quietly, because fixing it quietly is how the ownership gap survives.

input: Okay this is the handover for the payments integration because I am off from Thursday and I do not want anybody rediscovering all of it from scratch. The state of it is that the sandbox side works end to end and the live side works for cards but not for the bank transfer flow, which fails somewhere between our callback and their ledger, and I have not been able to prove which side is dropping it. The runbook I have been keeping is at ops dot internal slash payments dash handover and there is a longer set of notes with the actual request bodies in it at gist dot internal slash tomas slash transfer dash trace, and that second one needs the VPN, it will look empty until you are on it. The thing to know before you touch anything is that their sandbox and their live environment disagree about the field order, so the signature check passes in one and fails in the other for the same payload, and the fix on our side is that the comparison has to be timing safe, so use hmac dot compare underscore digest not double equals, I found that out the hard way on Monday afternoon. Marisol pushed back on the retry window and I think she is right, she gave the whole approach a star for effort and then pointed out that it would page somebody at three in the morning, which it absolutely would. She wants the summary in dot points for the steering group, so somebody will have to write that. One more thing, the ledger reconciliation is a plus for us because we get the daily matching for free out of it, so do not rip that part out just because the transfer flow is broken. I will leave the branch pushed and unmerged and the tickets are all linked off the epic.

input: This is my write up of the emoji study for the design review, and I am recording it rather than typing it because the deadline is tomorrow and my hands are done. We tested six reactions with fourteen participants across two age groups and the short version is that the reactions do not mean what the product team assumed they mean. The red heart emoji was the clearest split. Everybody over forty read it as warm and sincere, and four of the younger participants read it as either sarcastic or, in one case, passive aggressive, which is not a range you want on a support ticket. The thumbs up emoji was worse. Three people described it as the thing your manager sends when they have not read your message, and one person said it ends a conversation rather than continuing it. The sparkles emoji did not have that problem, probably because nobody has been managed with it yet. On the star rating question, participants ignored the middle of the scale almost entirely, which is the usual finding, and two of them told us a three star review feels crueller than a one star review because it looks considered. One thing I did not expect is that people described the temperature of a reaction, and two of them used degrees to do it, as in the heart runs hotter than the thumbs up. That is a plus for the visual language work if we can make it deliberate rather than accidental. Recommendation is that we keep three reactions and cut the rest, and I will bring the transcripts to the review.

input: Right, this is the long version of the scanner crash for the ticket, and I am going to talk through it in the order I found it rather than the order it makes sense in, because the order I found it in is the part that took three days. The symptom the support team gets is that the app closes with no message when somebody scans a document, and the first thing everybody assumes is that it is the camera, and it is not the camera. It only happens on the second document in a session and never on the first, and that is why nobody in the office could reproduce it, because we all scan one thing and put the phone down. Tuyen was the one who noticed it, she was scanning a stack of receipts for her expenses and it died on every second one, and she mentioned it in passing in the standup like it was normal. So the steps are, open the app cold, scan anything, wait for the preview to finish rendering which is about a second and a half on my phone, then scan a second thing, and it goes. If you do not wait for the preview it does not crash, which is the bit that made me think it was the camera to begin with. The crash log is on the shared box at qa dot internal slash scanner slash crash dash session dash two and there are four runs in there, the two that crashed and two that did not, so you can diff them. The interesting part is about forty lines in where the buffer that holds the page image gets released while the preview is still reading it, and on the runs that do not crash it is released after. Our Android lead reckons it is a race in the release path and not a leak at all, and if she is right then the fix is ordering and not memory. I have not opened a PR because I do not trust myself in that file. The other thing worth knowing is temperature. On the test bench at about 22 degrees it crashes maybe one time in three, and on the phone that has been sitting in the sun on the windowsill, which was 41 degrees on the surface when I measured it, it crashed every single time out of ten attempts. So it is a timing thing and heat makes the timing worse, which fits the race theory. If somebody wants the raw numbers I put them in a sheet and shared it, and the device list with the OS versions is at qa dot internal slash scanner slash devices. If you cannot get on the VPN, mail dinh at brightpath dot io and he will send you the two files directly, he did that for me on Monday when I was locked out. Two things I want to say before somebody asks. This is not the same bug as the one from March, that one was the camera permission and it had a message. And I am not convinced the retry the app does is helping, because it retries with the same released buffer, so the second attempt fails the same way, and swapping that check to a not equals instead of a truthy check would at least make it obvious in the log. Tuyen has been a star about testing this on her own phone with her own receipts, and the fact that she reported it at all is a plus, because most people just stop using the feature. She wants the summary in dot points for the release notes and I will do that separately.

input: Okay, this is my account of the warehouse move for the board pack, and I would rather dictate it while it is fresh than write it up next week when I have started being reasonable about it. The move happened over the long weekend as planned and the short version is that we are operating out of the new site and nothing was lost, but it cost us two days more than the plan said and the reason is not the reason anybody expects. The plan was three trucks running a loop, load at the old site, drive the forty minutes, unload, come back. That part worked. input: Attendance note, and this is for the file rather than for the client, so I will speak plainly. I met Mr Ellery at the property this morning for about an hour and a half and we walked the boundary together, and I want to record what he told me while I can still remember which parts he was sure about and which parts he was guessing at. The fence on the eastern side open paren the one in the photographs at tab four close paren was put up by his predecessor in title and he does not know the year, he thinks late nineties. That matters because the deposited plan shows the boundary running behind it, and he has been maintaining the strip on the far side of it for as long as he has owned the property, which is fourteen years this June. He described the arrangement with the previous neighbour as, quote, we have never had a cross word about it, unquote, and he was keen that I write that down, so I have. The difficulty is that the neighbour has now sold. The new owner has put in a planning application semicolon the drawings show a garage footprint that crosses the line on the deposited plan by about a metre. Mr Ellery's position is that he does not want a fight and he would rather agree a line and have it recorded, and I have advised him that a boundary agreement open paren as opposed to a determined boundary application close paren is quicker and cheaper and does not require the Land Registry to accept anything. He understood the distinction and he asked twice about cost, so put a fee estimate in the letter. Two points of caution for whoever picks this up after me. First, he told me the hedge was replanted at some point and he does not know by whom, and a replanted hedge is not evidence of anything, so it does not go in a letter as though it were. Second, he mentioned a period of about three years when the property was let and he was not living there, and adverse possession arguments have a habit of turning on exactly that sort of period, so we need the tenancy dates before we say anything at all about continuous use. He is going to look for the paperwork this week. On the practical side he wants everything by email and not by post, and the address is d dot ellery at northgate dash mills dot co dot uk, which he spelled out for me twice because people get the dash wrong and it bounces. He was a star about digging out the old photographs, he had them in a shoebox in the garage and he found four of them while I was standing there, and the fact that they are dated on the back is a plus for us because it puts that fence in place before the current owner bought. Diary it for two weeks, and if the tenancy dates have not arrived by then chase him by telephone rather than by email, because he answers the telephone and he does not answer email.

input: These are my notes for Thursday's seminar and I am talking them through rather than writing them because I want to keep the argument in the order it occurred to me. The topic is punctuation as social history, which sounds like a joke until you look at what the marks were actually for. Start with the comma, because everybody thinks they know what a comma is and almost nobody can state the rule they are using. The honest answer is that the comma began as a breathing mark for reading aloud, and the reason students find it arbitrary is that it is arbitrary, or rather it stopped being about breath and became about syntax somewhere in the eighteenth century without anybody announcing the change. Then the semicolon, which is the mark my students are most frightened of, and I want to spend real time on it, because a semicolon is not a decorated comma and it is not a weak full stop, it is a claim that two complete thoughts belong to each other. Ask them to find one in something they have read for pleasure in the last month. Half of them will come back and say they could not find a single one, and that is the finding, not a failure of the exercise. The colon is easier and I will not linger, it points forwards and it promises something, and the test is whether what follows pays the debt. The dash is where the seminar will get interesting, because the dash is the mark of speech, and every student in that room writes in dashes when they text and takes them out when they submit an essay, which tells you they have absorbed a rule nobody taught them explicitly. I want to ask them who taught it to them. On the asterisk, my one point is that it is a mark that has changed jobs more than once, it was a reference mark, then it was a footnote, then it became a way of censoring a word without deleting it, and now it marks a correction in a chat window, which is a genuinely new function and not a decayed old one. That is the argument of the whole seminar in one mark, so put it near the end. A period of roughly two centuries separates the punctuation my grandmother was taught from what my students actually use, and neither of them was ever taught that the marks have a history at all. Sara has been a star at finding the primary sources for this and she turned up a printer's manual from eighteen twenty four that argues about the comma in exactly the terms my students do, which is a plus for the argument because it stops it being a story about decline. Read that section aloud to them. End on the question rather than an answer, because the reading for the following week does the answering, and if they leave irritated they will actually do it.

input: This is the trip report for the Manaslu group and I am sending it to the office as a voice note because I am still in Samagaun and typing on this phone in the cold is not happening. Fourteen clients, nine days, everybody home safe, and the short version is that it went well and the two problems we had were both weather and neither was anybody's fault. Day three we sat at Jagat because the trail above the bridge was closed after the rain, and the group took it better than I expected, mostly because the lodge there has hot water and one of the Australians turned out to play cards for money. We made the day back on day six by leaving at four in the morning instead of six, which I would not do with a slower group. The older couple from Denmark were slower than the booking form suggested and I want that in the file properly, not as a complaint but so whoever takes the next Manaslu group knows to ask a second question at booking. They were fine on flat ground and they were fine going up, but coming down from Larke La they were very slow and we came into Bimtang in the dark, which I do not like doing with clients who are already tired and cold. Nothing happened. But it could have, and the file should say so. Pemba was a star on that descent, he stayed at the back the whole way with the two of them and he never once made them feel like they were holding anybody up, and the husband said as much to me at dinner in front of the group, so please tell Pemba that the client mentioned him by name. On kit, three of the fourteen arrived without proper gloves, which is normal, and the rental in Kathmandu was a plus this time because the office had actually checked the sizes before we left instead of us finding out at Deng. The thing I want to raise for next season is the arrow at the junction above Bihi. Somebody has painted a new one and it points up the old trail that washed out two years ago, and two groups ahead of us went the wrong way and lost an hour, and we only did not because I have walked that junction thirty times. Either the office reports it to the committee or we tell every guide at the briefing, but it needs saying before the spring season starts. Also the toilet block at Dharapani is finished and it is better than the one at the teahouse we usually stop at, so we can stop apologising for that stop. Money side, I am over on the porter budget by the two extra days and under on the lodge budget because of Jagat, and it roughly cancels out, and the receipts are all in the envelope with the names on the back. One client asked for a photo album afterwards and I told her the office would email her about it, so somebody should actually email her this week.

input: Site note on the retaining wall on the east side, and I am recording it in the truck before I forget the numbers because I left the pad on the scaffold. The panel spacing on the drawing is wrong. It says 2.4 metres and what is actually built out there is 2.1, and I measured it three times in three different places so it is not me, somebody changed it on site and nobody marked it up. That matters because the load case in the calculation was 12 kilonewtons divided by 3 panels, which is fine at 2.4 spacing and is not fine at 2.1, so the calculation has to be redone before anybody pours the next section. The slope behind the wall is steeper than the survey shows as well. I put the level on it in two places and it is closer to 34 degrees than the 30 the drawing gives, and 4 degrees at that height is not nothing, it changes the surcharge. Two other things while I am here. The drain outlet is 150 millimetres times 150 and it is sitting one course too high for the fall, and the mason told me he was put there by the foreman, so I am not blaming him for it. And the anchor spacing is correct, which I want written down, because the last time I raised something on a wall like this everybody assumed the whole thing was wrong and we lost a week. Ahmad has been a star chasing the as built dimensions for me and having the survey team still on site was a plus. Nobody pours on Sunday until the calculation comes back.

input: Notes before the menu meeting on Monday, and I am saying this out loud in the walk in because it is the only quiet place in the building. The autumn menu is too long. We are carrying nine mains and four of them do not sell, and every one of those four ties up a prep list and a section of the fridge, so I want to cut it to six and I want the meeting to be about which six and not about whether. The duck stays. The rabbit goes, and I know Marco will fight me on the rabbit, but we sold eleven portions in a month and we bin the trim. On the dressing, we changed it three times in three weeks over the summer and none of us can now remember which one the customers actually liked, which is my fault for not writing it down, so from now on any change gets written on the sheet with the date. The one we are using has a dash of the aged vinegar in it and that is the version I want to keep. Chiara has been a star this month, she has covered two sections on her own on a Friday twice, and the fact that she did not ask me for anything in return is exactly why somebody should give her something. Getting the new supplier for the shellfish was a plus, they deliver at six instead of nine so the fish sits an hour less. Nobody is talking about a star on the door yet and I do not want that conversation in this meeting.

input: This is for whoever picks up the flaky test suite after me, because I am on the other project from Monday and I do not want this to be folklore. There are three tests that fail maybe one run in eight and they are all in the checkout flow, and none of them fail locally, which is the whole problem. What I have worked out is that they share a fixture and the fixture does not wait for the animation to finish, so on a slow CI box the click lands before the button is in place. I have marked all three with at pytest dot mark dot slow for now, which keeps them out of the fast job, and that is a plaster and not a fix. To reproduce it you have to run the suite the way CI does, which is npm test ampersand ampersand npm run lint in one shell, because running them separately gives the box enough slack that it passes. The write up I did in the wiki is under the anchor hash flaky dash checkout if you want the screenshots, they are worth looking at because you can see the button mid transition. What I have not done is the actual fix, and I do not want to guess at the right wait condition at the moment because I have not read that component properly. Somebody should hash out with the design team whether that animation needs to be there at all, since removing it would kill the whole class of failure. Minji has been a star running the suite fifty times on her own machine to get me the failure rate.

input: This is my handover note on the Ferrand contract translation, and I am dictating it because the file is due tomorrow and I would rather talk than type at this point. The source text is worse than the client thinks it is. Whoever drafted the French version was working from an English original that we have not been given, and you can see it in the sentence shapes, so there are places where the French says something the English almost certainly did not, and I have flagged eleven of those in the margin rather than deciding them myself. The client and I need to hash out how they want those handled, because there are only two honest options, translate what the French says or ask for the original, and I am not choosing between them on their behalf. On terminology, they have used two different words for the same obligation throughout and I have kept both and noted it, which will look like an error to anybody skimming, so please do not let a reviewer quietly harmonise them. The glossary is fine at the moment and I have not added anything to it. Camille has been a star on this one, she read the whole thing cold and caught two numbers that had been transposed in the source, which is not her job at all. Having the deadline moved by a week was a plus and it is the only reason this is not a disaster. If the client comes back asking for a summary in dot points, somebody will need to write that from scratch, because nothing in the file is in that shape.

input: Notes on the phishing wave for the internal write up, and I am recording rather than typing because I want the shape of the argument before I clean it up. Twenty two people in the company got the message on Monday and four clicked it, and the interesting part is not the four, it is why the message was convincing. It copied our own vendor notification almost exactly, including the way we sign those emails off, and it used a lookalike domain that differs from ours by one character, which is the entire trick. When I showed it to people afterwards, nobody spotted it unread, and three of them told me they only realised because the greeting was wrong. That is worth writing down, because it means our training is teaching people to look at the wrong thing. On the domain, the registrar suspended it within about six hours of our report, which is faster than the last two we reported, and having a relationship with that registrar was a plus we did not have a year ago. Dato has been a star on this, he wrote the detection rule the same evening and it caught two later attempts from the same infrastructure. The recommendation I want in the write up is boring on purpose. Stop teaching people to hunt for a dot or a dash in a domain name, because they cannot do it reliably and neither can I, and teach them the one thing that does work, which is that we never ask for credentials in a message at all.

input: Okay this is my write up of the export timeout for the ticket because support want it in there before the handover call, and I am going to talk it through in the order it actually happened rather than the order it makes sense in. The first report came in on Tuesday afternoon from the Meadowbank account, and the user said the export button spins and then nothing arrives, no file, no email, nothing at all, and she waited about twenty minutes before she gave up and rang us. She also said the export being automated is a plus for her month end, which is why she chased it so hard. I could not reproduce it on my own tenant, which is the annoying part, so I asked her to send the browser console and she did, and I have read through the whole thing twice now. The thing that actually matters is the queue. If you open help dot brightpath dot io slash runbooks slash export dash queue you will see the drain step, and the drain step checks whether the row count double equals the batch size before it marks the job finished, and on the Meadowbank data the row count comes back one short every single time because one record is soft deleted and the count query does not filter it out, so the check never passes and the job sits there forever without ever failing. That is the whole bug. I have the trace saved at status dot brightpath dot io slash traces slash 90210 if you want to look at it yourself, and it is worth a look because the last line is the interesting one. Now the reason I have not just fixed it is that the count query is shared with the billing export and I do not want to touch it two days before month end, so my plan is to change the drain check rather than the query, and I will put a star next to it on the board so whoever picks it up knows that is deliberate. One more thing, the customer asked whether this is the same as the March incident and it is not, that one was a dash in the file name breaking the download header, completely different code path, and I have told her that already but she may well ask again, so if she rings while I am off that is the answer, and the point to make is that her data was never at risk at any stage.

input: Right, this is my note for the style guide argument we had this morning, mostly so I do not have to repeat it in the meeting, and I am dictating it while I walk so it will wander a bit. The disagreement is about how we write addresses in body copy, and there are three camps, which is two more than I expected for something this small. Priya wants everything spelled out in full because she says readers skim and a bare domain looks like a typo. Callum wants the shortest form that still resolves, and he made the point that nobody has typed a full address into a browser bar since about 2012, which I think is roughly fair. And then there is the group who care mainly about the screen reader behaviour, which is the argument I actually find convincing, because a slash read out loud in the middle of a sentence is genuinely hard to follow if you are listening rather than reading. We also spent far too long on the at sign in her handle, because the marketing draft has it in three different styles on the same page, and once you notice that you cannot unsee it. My own view, for what it is worth, is that we pick one form and stop having this conversation twice a year, and if that form is the long one then fine, I will lose gracefully. The one thing I do want to hold out on is the dot com question, because writing dot com in prose reads as an era rather than an address to anyone who was working in that era, and half our readers were. Callum also brought up whether we should ever write double equals in a customer facing help page and I said no, that belongs in the developer docs, and he agreed surprisingly quickly, so at least one thing got settled before the coffee ran out.

input: So this is the description for the retry pull request and I am saying it out loud because by the time the form is open I have forgotten what I actually did. The short version is that the upload retry was firing on every failure including the ones that will never succeed, so a bad file was hammering the queue for an hour before anyone noticed, and the fix is to narrow the condition rather than add another timer. The guard now reads if the attempt count is under three ampersand ampersand the error is retryable, and retryable is a small allow list rather than anything clever, so an authentication failure drops straight out instead of going round again. I also changed the health probe, because it was treating anything that came back as alive, and now it checks that status bang equals 503 before it reports healthy, which is the one line in here I would look at hardest in review. On the dependency side I pinned the client as caret 1.4 in the package file so patch releases still come through but the next major cannot land on a Friday afternoon without anybody choosing it. Brace yourself for the diff though, because the tests moved as well, and that is most of the line count. There is no behaviour change in the tests, they are the same assertions in a different file, and splitting them out is a net plus for whoever has to read this next. If you want a second pair of eyes on anything make it the probe change rather than the retry condition, because the retry condition is boring and the probe is the one that can take the service down if I have the comparison the wrong way round. I have run it locally against the staging bucket twice and both times the bad file dropped out after three attempts, which is what we want.

input: These are my notes from the tutorial on Thursday, and I am dictating them because I want to remember what actually confused people rather than what I planned to teach. The session was meant to be about comparison and it turned into a session about names, which was more useful anyway. Almost nobody in that room could say the operators out loud with any confidence, and once I started asking them to read the code back to me the problem was obvious. One student read every equals sign the same way regardless of how many there were, so double equals and triple equals came out identically, and she had no idea the two lines behind them did different things. Another one kept saying bang equals as not equals, which is fine and arguably better, except the documentation she was reading uses bang equals throughout, so she could not search for the thing she was looking at. We spent about ten minutes on ampersand ampersand, mostly on why the short circuit matters, and I think that landed. The caret came up because one of them had a dependency error and could not describe it to me over chat, and I realised none of them had ever been taught to read a version range aloud at all. My conclusion for the course notes is that we should teach the spoken names deliberately in week two rather than assuming they pick them up, and I want a glossary page that gives both readings where two exist. Brace yourself for the marking though, because if they cannot say it they cannot write it either, and that is going to show up in the coursework.

input: Site note on the second pour at the north end, and I am recording it in the cabin before I lose the numbers, so it will be in the order I wrote them down rather than any sensible order. The concrete arrived at half seven, which is earlier than the docket says, and the ambient was already climbing, so the first thing to flag is that the pour has to stay under 32 degrees at the face or we are into the curing problem we had in June. I have told the ganger twice and I will tell him again tomorrow. On the loading, the design figure works out at 40 divided by 3 per pile once you take the pile cap into account, and that is the number the checker will want to see written down rather than the one on the old drawing, because the old drawing has the cap in the wrong place. The fill quantity is 600 plus 250 for the access ramp, and the ramp figure is the one I am least sure about because it depends on whether the site office moves, so treat it as provisional. The point of the extra survey is the settlement monitoring rather than the levels, so if anyone asks why we are paying for it twice, that is why. Nothing here is urgent enough to ring anybody about tonight, but I would rather it was written down while it is fresh than remembered wrong on Monday.

input: Note for the faculty meeting about the marking moderation, and I am talking it through in the car so it will ramble a little. The headline is that the spread between the two markers is wider than last year and I do not think either of them is doing anything wrong. Both have degrees in the subject and both have moderated before, and the difference is entirely in how they treat the middle of the range, which is the hardest part to write a rubric for. What is happening is that one marker starts from the top and takes marks away, the other starts from the bottom and adds them, and on a strong script they land in the same place while on a middling script they end up two grades apart. I have seen this before and the fix is not a longer rubric, it is a shared exemplar that both of them mark in front of each other. Everyone minus the external examiner can make the Thursday slot, and honestly the external is the one person who does not need to be there for that conversation. The point I want to make in the meeting is that this is a calibration issue rather than a competence issue, because the moment it gets framed as competence one of them will stop volunteering and we will be worse off. Second thing, and this is smaller, the submission portal has been down three times this month and students have noticed, so someone should say something about it before a student does. Third, if we are minus one marker in the summer we should decide that now rather than in June when nobody is answering email.

input: Okay this is the monthly update for the community channel and I am dictating it on the bus home because if I leave it until tomorrow it will not get written at all, so it is going to be long and I will tidy it later. Start with the numbers, or rather start with the thing everyone will ask about first, which is the outage on the ninth. We were down for about forty minutes in the evening and the cause was boring, it was a certificate that nobody had put a reminder on, and the fix was boring too, and I would rather say that plainly than dress it up. What was not boring was how many people wrote in to say they had assumed it was their own connection, which tells me our status page is not doing its job, and that is on me because I am the one who keeps saying we will move it and then does not. So that is the first commitment for this month, the status page moves off the same host as the app, because a status page that goes down with the app is decoration. Second thing, the community translations. We now have the interface in nine languages and seven of those came entirely from people in this channel who were not asked and did not want anything for it, which I find genuinely difficult to write about without sounding like a press release, so I will just say thank you and leave it there, sparkles emoji. The Turkish and the Vietnamese ones in particular went through three rounds of review between people who had never met, and the review threads are worth reading if you want to see how much care went in. Third, and this is the one I have been putting off, the roadmap slipped. The offline mode is not shipping this month and probably not next month either, and the reason is that the first version worked on my machine and nowhere else, which is a sentence I have now said out loud twice, skull emoji. I am not going to give a new date because the last two dates were wrong and a third wrong date is worse than no date. What I will do is post the actual blocker list so people can see what is left rather than trusting a date. Fourth, housekeeping. The old forum is read only from the end of the month, everything is archived, nothing is being deleted, and if you had a thread you care about it will still be there. Somebody asked whether we could keep the crying laughing emoji reaction from the old forum, which made me laugh, and no, the new platform has its own set and I am not fighting that battle. Somebody else asked whether the fire emoji in the release notes was ironic and I have decided not to answer that. Last thing, and it is small, we hit the point where more questions in the channel are answered by other users than by us, which happened quietly about three weeks ago and I only noticed when I went looking for something to answer. That is the healthiest signal this project has, and it is worth more than any of the numbers I opened with.

input: Note towards the emoji section of the accessibility guidance, and I am recording it rather than typing because I want the argument in the order I actually think it, not the order that looks tidy in a document. The starting position, which I still hold, is that emoji in official communications are not decoration and cannot be treated as decoration, because a screen reader reads the name out and the name is often nothing like what the sighted reader took it to mean. The example I keep coming back to is the crying laughing emoji, which announces as face with tears of joy, and which a lot of younger readers now use to mean something closer to resignation than amusement, so the announced name and the intended meaning have drifted apart entirely. That is not an argument for banning it. It is an argument for not putting it in a sentence where the meaning depends on it. The second thing, and this is the one the comms team will push back on, is repetition. Three fire emoji in a row announce three times, and a reader who cannot skip past them has to sit through all three, which is a small thing once and a genuinely tiring thing across a whole newsletter. So the guidance should say one, at the end, never in the middle of a sentence, and never as the only carrier of meaning. I want to be careful about the tone of this because the last version of the guidance read as though it disapproved of emoji, and that got it ignored. It should read as though it disapproves of emoji doing work that words should be doing. The third point is the one I am least sure about. We had a request to allow the thumbs up emoji as an acknowledgement in internal threads, on the grounds that requiring a written reply is slower and people stop replying at all, and I think that request is reasonable. An acknowledgement carries no information beyond itself, so there is nothing for a reader to lose. But once you allow it there, someone will use it to answer a yes or no question, and then the whole thread depends on a symbol whose announced name is thumbs up sign. I do not have a clean rule for that yet and I would rather write the guidance without one than write a rule I know will be gamed. Fourth, and then I will stop, the sparkles emoji has become a house style marker in half our channels and nobody decided that. input: Right, this is the full write up of the settlement delay for the incident review, and I am dictating it because it is going to be long and I would rather get it down while the order of events is still clear in my head than write four tidy paragraphs next week that leave out the awkward parts. So, timeline first. The first alert fired at twenty past two in the morning on the batch lag monitor, and the on call was Femi, and he acked it within about four minutes, which is faster than the target and worth saying because the rest of this is not going to be flattering. What he saw was the settlement batch sitting at zero rows processed with no error anywhere, and the runbook for that state sends you to the retry, so he ran the retry, and the retry also sat at zero rows with no error. At that point he did the right thing and escalated rather than running it a third time. I picked it up at about ten to three. The thing that made this hard is that every dashboard was green. The queue was green, the database was green, the partner connection was green, and the batch itself reported healthy because the health check only asks whether the process is alive. I spent the first twenty minutes convinced it was the partner side, because it had been the partner side twice this year and both times it looked exactly like this, and I want that written down because it is the reason the diagnosis took an hour longer than it should have. It was not the partner. What it actually was is a schema migration that went out on Friday afternoon and added a not null column to the settlement table with a default, and the batch builds its insert from a column list it reads once at startup, so the running process had the old list and the new column had no value coming in, and the insert failed silently because the error handler for that path logs at debug and debug is off in production. So the batch was doing its work, failing, catching its own failure, and reporting healthy, in a loop, for four and a half hours. The way I found it was the trace, and if you want to follow the same path yourself it is saved at obs dot ledgerworks dot io slash traces slash settlement dash lag dash 3140 and the useful part is about two thirds of the way down where the same insert appears eleven times in a row with nothing between the attempts. The runbook change I have already made is at wiki dot ledgerworks dot io slash sre slash settlement dash batch and it says, in the first line rather than buried at the bottom, that a green health check on this batch means nothing and you check the debug log before you check the partner. That is the single most useful sentence in the whole document and it needs to be the first thing anybody reads at two in the morning. Now the fixes, and there are three of them and they are not equal. The first one is done, which is that the error handler on the insert path logs at error rather than debug, and the condition on the retry now checks that the processed count is greater than zero ampersand ampersand the batch reported no failures, so a silent failure cannot present as a success any more. The second one is the health check, and that is the real fix, because the health check should assert that the process did work and not merely that it exists, and I have not written that yet because it needs a conversation about what work means for a batch that legitimately has nothing to do on a bank holiday. The third one is process rather than code, and it is that a migration that adds a column to a table a long running process writes to cannot go out on a Friday afternoon, and I know everyone nods at that and then does it again in six months, so I would rather it went in the deploy checklist than in a document like this one. A few things that are not fixes but belong in the record. Femi ran the retry once and escalated, which is exactly right, and the fact that the retry made it worse is not on him, it is on the runbook that told him to run it. The customer impact was about four hundred settlements delayed by five hours, nothing lost, nothing duplicated, and the reconciliation the next morning came out clean, which is the one genuine plus in this whole story. Two people asked why we do not just alert on the debug log, and the answer is that the debug log is off, so that is circular, and I have put a star next to that question on the review page because it comes up every time and deserves a proper answer rather than my tired one. The dash in the trace name is not a typo, it is how that tool names things, and somebody will point that out otherwise. And the point I want to land in the review, more than any of the individual fixes, is that we had four hours of a system telling us it was fine while it was not, and every one of the three fixes above is really the same fix, which is that healthy has to mean did work rather than is running.

input: Note on the Ferrand tender translation before I hand it back, and I am dictating it because my hands have had enough for one day and there is a lot to say. The file came in as a scan, which nobody told me, so the first two hours went on retyping rather than translating, and I have logged that separately because it is not translation time and should not be billed as translation time. On the substance, the source text is a French tender document written by somebody who is fond of very long sentences, and the house style for the client is short ones, so almost every paragraph needed splitting, and that is where the punctuation questions come from. The heading on the second section should read Clause four colon termination for convenience, because the source has a colon there and the client's own template uses colons in headings, so both reasons point the same way. In the schedule of charges the source runs three obligations into one sentence with commas, and commas will not hold that much weight in English, so the first obligation ends at delivery semicolon the second begins at inspection, and I have kept the same structure for the third rather than inventing a fourth sentence. There is one place I have flagged rather than decided. The source has an exclamation in the safety warning, which in French reads as emphasis and in English reads as shouting, and the client's guidance says never use one in a formal document, so in the margin note I have written Do not send exclamation mark and left the decision to whoever signs it off, because that is a tone judgement and not mine to make. A few smaller things. The colon in the citation on page eleven is wrong in the source and I have left it wrong with a note, because correcting somebody else's citation inside a tender is how you end up in an argument about what else you changed. The period the document keeps referring to is the guarantee period rather than a punctuation mark, which sounds obvious written down but caused me genuine trouble for about ten minutes because the sentence around it is about drafting. And the point the client made in the brief about matching the register of the original is the one thing I have consistently prioritised over literal accuracy, so if they read it back and it feels less formal than the French, that is deliberate and I can defend it line by line. Last thing, the glossary. I have added eleven terms and removed two that were wrong, and one of the two I removed had been wrong in every document we have sent that client for three years, which nobody had noticed, so somebody should decide whether we say anything about that or quietly stop using it. My view is we say something, but it is not my call and I would rather raise it here than in front of them.
