input: This is my note for the trainees about dictating punctuation, and I am recording it because I say the same six things every September and I would rather they had it in writing. The first thing to understand is that the machine hears words, so when you say a punctuation name you are saying a word and the only thing that decides whether it becomes a mark is where it sits. That sounds abstract until it goes wrong, and it goes wrong in attendance notes more than anywhere else, because an attendance note is the one document where you are describing what somebody said as well as saying it yourself. If your client used the word colon in a sentence, and you dictate that sentence, you do not want a mark there. If you are dictating a heading and you say colon between the heading and the subject, you do. Same word, and the machine has to work out which from everything around it, which is a lot to ask and it will sometimes get it wrong, so read it back. The second thing is that a semicolon is almost never what you want in correspondence. I am not being fussy about that, it is a practical point: a semicolon in a letter to another firm invites the reader to think you are being careful about something, and if you are not being careful about anything in particular you have just added a signal you did not intend. Use two sentences. The third thing is the exclamation mark, and the rule there is simple, which is that we do not use one, ever, in anything that leaves this building. If you find yourself dictating exclamation mark you are writing an email you should not send. Fourth, the period. Half our documents are about a guarantee period or a notice period, and the word appears in both senses in the same paragraph often enough that you should assume the machine will get one of them wrong at some point. Read it back. Fifth, and this is the one nobody believes until they see it, dictating brackets around an aside works well and dictating them around a citation does not, because a citation already has punctuation of its own and the two sets fight. Put the citation in afterwards. And sixth, which is not really about punctuation at all, if you are dictating for more than about ten minutes you will start speaking in longer sentences than you would write, and everybody does it, so when you read it back the first thing to look for is a sentence that goes on for four lines. That is not a punctuation problem, it is a breathing problem, and you fix it by splitting the sentence rather than by adding a mark in the middle of it.

input: This is the setup note for whoever onboards next, and I am dictating it because the written one is nine months out of date and I keep meaning to fix it properly. Read it in order, because the order matters more than it looks. First thing, do not install the toolchain from the website, install it from the internal mirror, because the website version pulls a different compiler patch level and you will spend a day on an error that has nothing to do with your code. Second, the config lives at tilde slash dot config slash ledgerworks slash cli dot toml and not where the old note says it does, and if you have a file in the old location the tool will read it and silently prefer it, which is the single most common way a new person loses an afternoon here. Delete the old one rather than editing it. Third, and this is the part I want to be careful about because it bit two people last month, every command in our docs is written without the dry run flag and you should add backtick dash dash dry run backtick to anything that touches the ledger until you have seen the plan output at least once. It prints what it would do and exits. There is no reason not to, and the one time somebody skipped it we spent a morning reversing a migration that had gone out against the wrong environment. Fourth, permissions. You need read on the staging bucket and write on nothing at all for the first two weeks, and if that feels restrictive it is deliberate, and it is not a comment on you. Ask in the channel when you need something rather than filing a ticket, because the ticket queue is a week deep and the channel is minutes. Message at priya dash s directly if it is blocking you and she is around, she has said repeatedly that she would rather be asked. A few things that are not steps but will save you time. The star next to a build in the dashboard means somebody pinned it, not that it passed, which is a design decision I have complained about twice and lost twice. The dash in the environment names is load bearing, so staging dash two and staging two are different things and only one of them exists. The point of the two week read only period is that our staging data is real customer data with the names changed, so a mistake there is still a mistake worth avoiding. And the plus side of all this ceremony, which I do believe even on the days it annoys me, is that nobody here has taken production down in about three years, which for a team this size is unusual. Last thing, when you have finished the setup, write down every step where this note was wrong, and send me that list rather than a thank you. That list is the only thing that keeps a document like this alive, and the reason this one is nine months stale is that the last three people were too polite to send it.

input: Notes for the study group session, and I am recording this instead of typing because my laptop is with the repair shop for another week. The topic on Thursday is reading code out loud, which sounds trivial and is not, and the reason I picked it is that three of us in that group learned everything from written tutorials and none of us can talk about code on a call without stumbling. I noticed it properly in the mock interview last month. The interviewer asked me to walk through my solution and I got as far as the second line and simply stopped, because I did not know how to say what was on the screen, and the silence was much worse than a wrong answer would have been. So the session has three parts. The first part is names, and by names I mean the spoken forms, because a tilde has a name and a backtick has a name and most of us learned both as shapes rather than as words. I want everyone to be able to say them without hesitating, and the test I am going to use is reading a command line aloud from a screenshot with no preparation. The second part is the ones where two names compete. The at sign is the obvious one, because it is at in an address and it is at in a handle and it is something else again in a decorator, and in my first language we do not have a common name for it at all, so I have been quietly avoiding saying it out loud for two years. The dash is another, because dash and hyphen and minus are three words for what is usually the same key, and which one you say tells a listener something about whether you mean prose or a flag or arithmetic. The third part is the harder one and it is listening rather than speaking, because when somebody dictates a command to you over a call you have to hold the whole thing in your head while they say it, and if they say the words in an order you are not expecting you lose it. We will practise that in pairs. One more thing for the group. Somebody asked whether we should just share screens and stop talking about code at all, and I understand why, but the interviews are not going to change, and neither is the on call handover, so the skill is worth the awkward hour. Bring a screenshot of something you have written yourself rather than a textbook example, because the textbook examples are all clean and nothing we actually write is.

input: This is my methods note for the supplementary material, and I am dictating it because the deadline is Friday and I write faster this way even allowing for the tidying afterwards. Take it as a draft of the reasoning rather than final wording. The sample is the same one described in the main text, so I will not repeat the recruitment detail here, except to say that the exclusion we added late, which is participants who completed the task in under 20 seconds, removed 14 people and did not change any of the substantive results, and I have said so in the supplement because leaving it out would look like we were hiding it. On the model, we fit the same specification as the pilot with one change. The pilot treated the exposure as continuous and that was wrong, because the distribution is bimodal and the linear term was doing something meaningless in the middle, so here the exposure is binary at the threshold the pre registration specified, which is a dose less than or equal to 4 units in the first week. That threshold was chosen before we saw the outcome data and I want that stated plainly in the supplement because a reviewer will ask. The random effects are by site and by session, and the variance component for session is small enough that a reviewer may ask why we kept it, and the answer is that the pre registration said we would and I would rather keep a term that does nothing than drop a term because it did nothing. For the power calculation, which is the part I expect to be challenged on, the target was 10 to the power of 6 simulated draws and we ran that in full rather than the smaller number the pilot used, so the interval on the power estimate is narrow enough to report as a single figure. The power of the study for the primary outcome comes out at what the protocol assumed, which is honestly luckier than it is impressive, because our assumed effect size came from two studies that we now know were both underpowered themselves. Then the thing I keep going back and forth on. The secondary outcome is measured three times a week and the analysis treats those as independent measurements within a participant, and they clearly are not independent, and the correlation structure I have used is the simplest one that is defensible rather than the one I think is true. I have written that sentence into the supplement almost verbatim, because a reviewer who spots it and finds it already acknowledged will treat us differently from a reviewer who spots it and thinks we missed it. input: These are my notes for the stats refresher I have to run for the analyst intake, and I am talking them out loud first because every time I write this deck I make it too mathematical and they stop listening in the first ten minutes. The audience is people who use numbers every day and have never been taught the vocabulary, which is a very specific gap and not the same as not knowing the material. Start with what goes wrong in practice rather than with definitions. The single most common thing I see in this team is somebody quoting r squared at a stakeholder as though it were a measure of whether the model is any good, and I do not blame them for it, because every tool we use prints it at the top of the output where the most important number goes. So the first session is about what that quantity does and does not tell you, and the demonstration I use is two models with the same r squared where one is obviously useless, because nobody forgets that once they have seen it. The second session is about power, and here the vocabulary problem is worse, because power has an ordinary English meaning and a technical one and they overlap just enough to be confusing. When somebody says the study had no power they usually mean the sample was small, and that is close enough to be useful, but the calculation itself is about the probability of detecting an effect that is really there, and until you have said that sentence out loud a few times it does not stick. I will do that one with a simulation they can run themselves rather than a formula, because the formula convinces nobody in a room like that. Third session, percent versus percentage point, which sounds pedantic and costs real money. Half the reporting errors I have had to correct in two years are somebody saying a rate went up by 5 percent when it went up by 5 percentage points, and once that number leaves the building in a slide it is very hard to get back. I want them to be able to say which one they mean without thinking about it. Fourth, and this is the one I care most about, uncertainty in plain language. They will all be asked, by somebody who does not want to hear it, how confident they are, and the honest answer is usually a range and a caveat, and there is a way of saying that which sounds competent and a way of saying it which sounds evasive. The difference is mostly practice. We will do it as an exercise where I play the stakeholder and interrupt, because that is what actually happens. Last thing, and I will put it at the end of the deck rather than the start: nobody in that room needs to be able to derive anything, and if I have made them feel that they do then I have run the session badly. They need to be able to describe what they did to somebody who will make a decision from it, three times a week, without misleading anybody by accident.

input: This is the write up of the emoji reaction test for the design review, and I am dictating it because the numbers are simple and the interesting part is all commentary. We tested three reaction sets on the internal build for two weeks. The short version is that the set with the eyes emoji in it got used about twice as much as the other two, and I do not think that is because people love that particular symbol, I think it is because it is the only one in the set that means I have seen this and I am not replying, which is the most common thing anybody wants to say in a thread. The rocket emoji was the opposite. It was in every set, it tested badly in all three, and when we asked people why, the answers split cleanly by age, which was not something we had designed for and is probably the most useful thing in the whole study. Anybody under about thirty read it as sarcasm by default. Anybody over about forty read it as enthusiasm. Nobody read it as ambiguous, which is the part that worries me, because two groups who are each certain and who disagree will misread each other quietly rather than asking. My recommendation, and I know product will not like it, is that we ship the smallest set and let people add their own rather than curating one, because every argument in this document is really an argument about what a symbol means to a particular person, and no set we pick is going to survive that. The counter argument is discoverability and it is a fair one. Last thing for the review, the thumbs up emoji is the one nobody mentioned in the interviews at all, which I noticed only when I read the transcripts back, and I think that is because it has become punctuation rather than a reaction.

input: This is my handover for the login work because I am on the other team from Monday and there is one thing in here that will bite whoever takes it. The feature itself is done and behind the flag. What is not done is the session expiry path, and the reason is that I found a second bug while I was in there and I did not want to fix two things in one branch. Here is the state of it. The guard in the middle of the handler now reads if the token is missing double pipe expired, which is right, and that part is tested. What is not right is what happens after, because on expiry we clear the cookie and redirect, and the redirect goes to the login page with no return path, so the user lands on login, signs in again, and ends up on the dashboard rather than back where they were. Nobody has complained yet because the expiry window is long, but they will once we shorten it, and shortening it is on the roadmap for next quarter, so this is a fix with a deadline even though it does not look like one. The second bug is smaller and stranger. If two tabs expire at the same moment they both try to refresh and one of them wins, and the loser gets a response it does not expect and shows the generic error rather than the login page. I have not written that up as a ticket yet because I am not sure whether it is worth fixing or worth designing away. My instinct is designing away. On testing, the flag is off in staging and on for my own account only, and the pipe from the auth service to the audit log is the thing to watch when you turn it on, because it doubles in volume and last time that filled a disk. Ask Femi about that rather than me, he is the one who cleaned it up. Last thing, the point I want to make about the whole area is that the session code has three different ideas about what expiry means in it, and every bug in here for the last year has really been that, so if you have the appetite, fix that rather than the symptoms.

input: Notes on the plumbing tender for the flats before I lose the paperwork again. Three quotes in and they are not comparing like with like, which is my own fault for sending a vague spec. The first one prices the riser and the branches together, the second one prices the riser only and says branches to be agreed, which means the number will go up, and the third one is the most expensive and is the only one that mentions the boxing in, so it is probably the honest one. What I want to do is send all three of them the same list of what is included and ask them to reprice, which will annoy at least two of them, and one will drop out, and I would rather that happened now than halfway through. On the technical side the only real decision is where the new pipe runs, because there are two options and the cheap one goes through the cupboard the tenant uses, and I have learned not to make that choice on a spreadsheet. So somebody needs to knock on and ask her, and it should be me rather than a contractor. The second decision, which is smaller, is whether we do both floors at once and have everybody without water for a day, or do it in two visits and pay for the extra day. My instinct is one visit and warn everybody twice, because the two visit version always turns into three. There is a plus to doing it in one go which is that the making good gets done once as well. Last thing, and this is the bit I keep forgetting, the freeholder has to be told in writing before anything starts and there is a notice period, so if I sit on this for another fortnight the notice period pushes the work past the point where I wanted it done.

input: Site note for the Al Wakrah school extension, Thursday evening, and this is for the file and for Hassan because he is covering for me on Sunday. The block work on the north elevation is finished up to the ring beam, all of it, and the mason left the last course clean so we do not need to cut anything on Sunday morning. The ring beam steel has been on site since Tuesday, twelve millimetre and eight millimetre, and it is stacked behind the site office under the sheet because there is no place in the yard, it is all formwork. Now the pour. The pour is booked for Sunday at 6, and the truck is supposed to arrive to the site at 6 sharp, which never happens, so I told the batching plant 5:30 and I will take whatever time they give me. We need seven cubic metres for the beam and the two columns, and I ordered eight, because the last time we ordered exactly and we finished half a metre short and the second truck cost us the whole morning. Eight cubic metres, C32/40, and the slump I want is 100 millimetres and not 150, because the beam is deep and narrow and a wet mix will segregate on the way down. The pump is not needed, we can barrow it, and I have four men for the barrows and two on the vibrator. About the vibrator, the small one is finished, the bearing is gone, and the store in Al Khor said they can give me another one on Saturday afternoon but they close at 6, so somebody has to go before 6 or we are pouring with one vibrator and that is not enough for a beam this deep. Please make this the first thing on Saturday. The formwork is checked twice, once by me and once by the carpenter, and the props are at 900 centres and not a metre, which is what the drawing asks. There is one thing I am not happy with, the kicker on the middle column is out by about 15 millimetres to the east, and it is inside the tolerance on the drawing but it is the second column this week that comes out to the east, so somebody is setting out from the wrong face and I want to find out who before we start the first floor. Not on Sunday, after the pour. The inspection, the consultant is coming Sunday at 8 and he wants to see the steel before it is covered, so nothing gets poured before he signs the sheet, and if he is late we wait, because last month we poured before he came and he made us break out a metre of slab to look at the bars. We wait. Last thing, water. The tank was filled on Wednesday and it is half now, and for a pour and the curing after it we need it full, so the water truck has to come Saturday as well, same as the vibrator. Two things for Saturday, the vibrator and the water. Hassan, if you read only one line of this, read that one.

Two things for Saturday, the vibrator and the water. Hassan, if you read only one line of this, read that one.

input: Okay, the plan for the column rename, and I am dictating this because I have to send it to the data team tomorrow and I think better talking than typing. The column is customer_status in the orders table, and it has to become order_status, because it never meant the customer, it meant the order, and every quarter somebody joins it to the customers table and gets a number that is wrong and then we spend a day explaining it. Last quarter it was the finance dashboard and the number was off by about 4,000 rows. So the rename itself is one line, but the rename is not the problem, the problem is everything that reads it. I counted, and there are nineteen things that read that column. Seven of them are dbt models in our own repo, and those are easy, I change them in the same pull request and the tests catch anything I miss. Four are Looker views, and those are also fine but they are in a different repo with a different owner, so that is a second pull request and Marta has to approve it. Three are scheduled queries that somebody wrote in the console and never put in a repo, and those are the dangerous ones, because they will just start failing at 3 in the morning and the owner will find out from a Slack alert. Two are exports to the vendor, which have a contract on the column names, so those cannot change at all and they need a view with the old name on top of the new one. And the last three I cannot identify, they are service accounts in the query log and nobody answers when I ask in the channel. So the approach is the boring one, add and deprecate, not rename. Step one, I add order_status as a real column and backfill it from customer_status, and the two are kept in sync by the model, so for a while both exist and both are right. The people that own the downstream dashboards is not going to notice anything at this point, which is the whole idea. Step two, I move the nineteen readers over, one at a time, and I mark each one in the ticket as I go, and for the three I cannot identify I add a log line so the next time they query customer_status I know who they are. Step three, and this is the one that needs a date rather than a sprint, customer_status becomes a view that reads order_status, and it stays like that for one quarter with a deprecation notice in the description, so anybody who is still reading it sees the notice in the column metadata. Step four, after the quarter, the view goes and the vendor keeps its own view, because the vendor contract is not going to change this year. On the timing, I do not want to do step one in the same week as the month end close, because if anything goes wrong with the backfill the finance team is the loudest and the most correct to be loud, so I would start the week after the close, which is the week of the eleventh. The backfill itself is about forty minutes on the current table size, and it is idempotent, so if I have to run it twice nothing breaks. One thing I still owe, the naming. If order_status is the new name then the same column in the returns table is called status and it should probably be return_status, and that is a separate ticket and I am not putting it in this one.

input: Right, debrief notes on the candidate from this morning, and I want to get these down before I read anybody else's feedback because otherwise I will just agree with whoever wrote first. Overall I am a weak yes and I will explain what the weak is doing. The coding part went well and better than the transcript will make it look. He started with the brute force, he said out loud that it was the brute force and that he would come back to it, and then he actually came back to it, which is rarer than it should be. The optimisation he landed on was the right one, the hash of prefix sums, and he got there in about eighteen minutes with one hint from me, and the hint was small, I asked him what he was recomputing. He tested it himself without being asked, including the empty input and the single element case, and he found his own off by one in the window boundary, so I did not have to point at anything. That is a clear pass on the coding. The system design is where the weak comes from. The question was the notification fan-out, the standard one, and for the first twenty minutes it was good, he asked about the read pattern before he drew anything and he asked how late a notification is allowed to be, which is the question I am actually listening for. Then he put a queue in and everything after the queue got vague. When I asked what happens if a consumer dies halfway through a batch he said the queue would handle it, and when I pushed he said at least once delivery, which is the right phrase, but he could not tell me what the consumer has to do to make at least once safe. And I do not think that is a knowledge gap, I think it is that he has always worked in places where the platform team owned the queue, so he has consumed the abstraction without ever having to run it, and that is a very common shape and it is fixable in a quarter. So the weak yes is, strong on the code, honest about his own reasoning, and thin on the operational side of anything asynchronous. What I would want to know before I turn the weak yes into a yes is how he behaves when he does not know something and there is nobody to ask, and I did not create that situation in my hour, which is my fault and not his. If somebody else in the loop pushed him on the ambiguous requirement and got a good answer, I will move to a yes on that. One process note while I am here. The transcript of the coding round is going to look worse than the round was, because he talks while he thinks and most of what he says is discarded a sentence later, and whoever reads only the transcript will see a lot of wrong statements. That is not what happened. Somebody should say that in the loop rather than. Actually somebody should say it in the debrief meeting rather than letting the written record be the thing we decide on.

input: Referee report on manuscript 2026-0418, for the editor, and I will send the confidential comments separately. I recommend major revision. The paper is worth publishing and it is not publishable in this form, and I want the report to make both halves of that clear, because the authors will read the first sentence and stop. Let me take the contribution first. What the authors do that is new is the identification strategy in section 4. Only by comparing the two cohorts that were assigned by the lottery do they get a comparison that is free of the selection problem, and that comparison is the paper. Everything in sections 5 and 6 rests on it, and if it holds the result is important. So my first request is not a criticism, it is that section 4 is currently three pages and it should be six, and the two pages of descriptive statistics in section 3 can go to the appendix to pay for it. Now the problems, and there are two that matter and several that do not. The first is the attrition. Table 2 reports the balance at baseline and it is convincing, but nowhere do the authors report the balance among the cases that remain at the second follow-up, and the attrition is 19 percent, which is high enough that the baseline balance tells us little about the analytic sample. This is the one I would hold the paper for. It is also easy to fix if their data permits it, and if it does not permit it, then it must be said plainly in the limitations rather than left for a reader to notice. The second is the standard errors. They cluster at the district level and there are eleven districts, and with eleven clusters the asymptotic argument does not hold, so the confidence intervals in Table 4 are almost certainly too narrow. Rarely is this fatal, but here the headline effect has a lower bound close to zero, so the correction may change the conclusion rather than decorate it. I would ask for the wild bootstrap and I would ask for the interval it produces to appear in Table 4 next to the current one and not in a footnote. Then the smaller matters. The literature review omits the 2021 replication, which found the opposite sign in a neighbouring setting, and I do not think the omission is deliberate, but it must be discussed. The instrument is described in words in section 4 and never written as an equation, and it should be, because I read it three times and I am still not certain whether the second stage includes the cohort fixed effects. The figures are unreadable in greyscale. And the abstract claims a causal effect while the conclusion is properly hedged, which is the usual asymmetry and the abstract should come down to meet the conclusion. On tone, for the editor. This is a careful paper by people who understand their data, and the two substantive problems are both problems of reporting rather than of design, so I would encourage them rather than the reverse. Should the authors address the attrition and the clustering, I would expect to recommend acceptance without seeing it a third time.

input: Notes on the French strings review, second pass, and this is for Camille and for whoever picks up the ticket after me. The settings screen is done and I am happy with it. The two places I changed the register are the delete confirmation, which was tu and should be vous because it is a destructive action and the tone has to match the rest of the product, and the empty state on the archive, which was too formal for what is basically a joke. Everything else in that file I left alone. The export is the problem. We lose sometimes the accents in the export, and it is not every string, it is the strings that go through the CSV path, so I think it is the encoding on the file writer and not the translation file itself, because the same string in the interface is correct. I put three examples in the ticket, the ones with e acute and c cedilla, and the pattern is that the accent survives the interface and dies in the CSV. Second thing, the plurals. French needs a different form for zero than English does, English says zero items and French wants the singular, and right now we are using the English rule for both, so the counter reads zero elements with an s and it looks wrong to every French user who sees it. That is not a translation fix, it is a code fix, and I have written it as a separate ticket. Third, and this is small, the date format in the invoice PDF is still the American one, and nobody has complained, but somebody will.

input: Firewall audit notes for the quarterly review, and this is the short version, the full table is in the spreadsheet. There are 214 rules on the edge and 61 of them have not matched a packet in ninety days. Of those 61, forty-one are for hosts that no longer exist, and I have the list, and those I will delete on Thursday in one change with one rollback. The other twenty are the interesting ones. Nine are for the payment path and they have not matched because the payment path moved to the private link in March, so the rules are dead but deleting them is a conversation with the payments team and not a change I make alone. Six are inbound from the vendor ranges and the vendor says they still need them, and I do not believe the vendor, but I am not going to break a vendor integration to prove a point in an audit, so those stay with a note. Five I cannot explain. They were added in 2022 by an account that no longer exists, the ticket references in the comments point at a system we decommissioned, and the destination is 10.42.7.0/24 which is not routed any more. I want to delete those five and I want somebody to say yes with me in writing first. On the risk side, the thing that concerns me is not the dead rules, it is rule 88, which is a permit any any from the management subnet that was added during an incident in January and never removed. That one is not dead, it matches constantly, and it is doing the work of about six specific rules that nobody has written yet. Writing those six rules is real action item from this audit, and it is a week of work, not an afternoon.

input: Retro note for the jam build, and this is just for us, not for the itch page. What worked is the scope. We cut the third level on the Friday night and after that everything was possible, and if we do not cut it we are still fixing the collision on the Sunday morning instead of polishing. So the lesson is cut early, cut on the first night, and the second lesson is that the person who wants to cut is always right at 2 in the morning. What did not work is the audio. I imported the wrong sample rate on Saturday and everything sounded muddy on the laptop speakers, and we only found it when Dewi played the build on her phone, so we lost maybe two hours re-exporting. Next time the audio pipeline is set up before the jam starts, not during. The shader was fine, santai, nobody noticed it and that is the point of a shader. On the judging, we got 14th out of 190 which is better than last time, and the comments say the same two things, the movement feels good and the tutorial is confusing. The tutorial is confusing because we wrote it in the last forty minutes, which is exactly what we said we would not do. Last jam also we do this and we promised each other, never again. So for the next jam, one rule, the tutorial gets written at the halfway point, when we still know what is confusing and we still have time to change the game instead of explaining it.

input: Itinerary note for the Rocheteau group, four people, arriving the twelfth. Day one is only the transfer from the airport and the hotel in Thamel, nothing else, because they land at 4 in the afternoon and by the time the bags come out it is evening. Day two is the drive to Syabrubesi, and I have booked the jeep and not the bus, because last season the bus took eleven hours and two of the clients were sick. The jeep is seven hours if the road at Trishuli is open and nine if it is not, and there is no way to know until the morning. Day three they walk to Lama Hotel, five hours, easy, and I have told the guide to keep it slow on the first day because the group is not young. Day four is Langtang village and this is the day that matters for the altitude, so the guide has to listen the briefing at the lodge and not skip it like he did in October. Day five is Kyanjin Gompa and then they have the acclimatisation day, and the acclimatisation day is not optional even if they feel strong, and I will put that in the confirmation email so nobody argues about it on the mountain. Coming down is three days on the same route. On the money side, the permit is paid, the TIMS is paid, the jeep is paid half now and half on the day, and the lodges are not paid because they never are. One thing I still need from them is the insurance certificates, all four, and without the certificates the guide will not take them above Langtang, so please chase it this week.

input: Design doc dictation, the section on the ownership model, first pass. The two things that makes this hard are the same two things that make every permissions model hard, which is that ownership is not a single relationship and that it changes over time. Let me take them in order. Ownership is not single because a document has a creator, an account that pays for it, and a team that the account has delegated it to, and today we store one owner_id and we resolve the other two by convention, which means the convention lives in four different services and two of them are wrong. The proposal is one owner record per document with a type on it, and the type is one of creator, billing, or delegate, and a document can have all three at once. Second, ownership changes, and it changes in ways that are not a simple transfer. When somebody leaves the company their documents do not become unowned, they become owned by their manager's team, and when a team is dissolved its documents go to the parent team and not to the individual who dissolved it. Right now both of those are cron jobs that run nightly and neither of them is tested, and the second one has been failing silently since the reorg in March. What I want out of the review is a decision on one thing only, whether the owner record is authoritative or derived. If it is authoritative then we have to write a migration for eleven million documents and we have to handle the ones where the convention disagrees with itself. If it is derived then we do not migrate anything but every read pays the resolution cost, and the resolution cost is three queries. I have a preference and it is authoritative, but I would rather the review argued about it than nodded at it.

input: Spec note for the fixture on the second bracket, and this is the version that goes to the shop, not the sketch from Tuesday. Only when the jig is clamped at both ends can we measure the run-out, so the measuring step has to come after the clamping step in the sheet and not before it. The run-out limit is 0.05 millimetres over the full rotation and the gauge we have reads to 0.01, which is enough. Not once in the last forty parts have we been outside the limit, so the process is capable, and I say that only because somebody will ask whether we need the tighter gauge and we do not. What we do need is the second locating pin. With one pin the part can rotate about it by roughly two degrees, and two degrees at the far end of the bracket is 0.4 millimetres, which is eight times the run-out limit, so the single pin is why the two bad parts in March were bad. The pin is a standard 6 millimetre dowel and the hole is a reamed H7, and the drawing has to say reamed, because the last time it said drilled and we got a hole that was 6.2. Hardly ever does a print detail matter this much, but this one does. On the sequence, load the part, clamp the near end, clamp the far end, then measure, and only then mark. The old sheet had the marking before the measuring, which is how a part gets marked good and then measured bad, and then somebody has to decide, and that decision should not exist.

input: Right, this is my write up of the queue incident from Tuesday night and I am talking it out because I will not remember the order of it by tomorrow, so the first thing is that the alert fired at 23:14 and it was the consumer lag alert, not the disk one, and when I logged in the queue depth was sitting at 4,000 messages and climbing about 200 a minute, which on its own is not scary because we have run at 30,000 before Christmas and nothing fell over, but the climb rate was the thing that worried me because it does not usually climb when the consumers are healthy, and all six consumers were reporting healthy, all six of them, which is why I spent the first twenty minutes looking in completely the wrong place. So I restarted the two consumers on the older node at about 23:40 and that did nothing at all, the lag just kept going, and then Kasia noticed that the schema registry had been redeployed at 22:50, so the consumers were healthy in the sense that the process was up but every single message was failing validation and going straight back onto the queue, and once we rolled the registry back to 4.11.2 the depth drained in about nine minutes. input: These are my notes from the site meeting about the courtyard and I want them down before I get back to the office and lose half of it. The client has finally accepted that the two old planters have to go, which unlocks the whole west edge, so the paving can run continuous from the door to the wall and we do not need the step we drew in November. I said I would price both options by Friday. The paving they liked is the sawn sandstone at 62 a square metre which is over budget, and the alternative is the tumbled version at 41 which I think looks better in a small courtyard anyway, so I am not going to fight them on the cheaper one. Drainage, the channel has to be on the west edge because everything falls that way, and the contractor wants it in before the paving rather than cut in afterwards like they did at the last job, which I completely agree with. Lighting is not decided and I told them it does not need to be decided until the walls are up, so please do not chase them about it this week.

input: Okay this is the note for the risk review on Thursday and I am dictating it because writing it makes me hedge everything, so here is the honest version. The strategy has done 14% since January which everybody is happy about, and I am not going to argue with the number, but the way we are reporting the downside is misleading and I would rather say so before somebody outside the team notices. We publish a single drawdown figure of 6% and that figure is month end to month end, and month end to month end is a very kind way to measure a strategy that takes most of its pain intraday and gets it back before the close. If you measure peak to trough on daily marks the same period gives you 11%, and if you measure it on intraday marks it is closer to 15%, and none of those three numbers is wrong, they just answer different questions, and the question a new investor is asking is the intraday one whether they know it or not. So drawdown, and I mean peak to trough on daily marks here, not month end to month end, is the number I want on the tear sheet, with the other two in a footnote so nobody can say we buried anything. I have run it back to 2021 and the worst daily number is 11% in the March window, the same window everybody remembers, and 14% is still 14% after that so the story does not actually get worse, it just gets honest.

input: This is the summary of where we got to on the rate limiting, and it is longer than it needs to be because I changed my mind twice while I was writing the code. The original plan was a fixed window of 600 requests a minute per key, which is simple and which everybody understands, and the problem with it is the boundary, because a client can send 600 at 12:00:59 and another 600 at 12:01:00 and we have effectively allowed 1,200 in a second and the graph looks fine. So I moved to a sliding window with a one minute span and ten second buckets, which costs us six counters per key instead of one, and Redis is not going to notice six counters per key at our volume. Every endpoint should get the sliding window, and when I say every endpoint I mean the write endpoints only, not the read ones, because the reads are already behind the cache and rate limiting them would just make the cache less useful. Deploy wise I want it behind a flag and I want it on for the two noisiest integrations first, which is the payments webhook and the old partner sync, and both of those have retry logic that will show us immediately if we have got the numbers wrong. One thing I have not solved is what we return, because 429 with a Retry-After header is correct and half the clients in the field ignore Retry-After, so we may end up logging the ignores for a month before anybody fixes their side.

input: Okay, this is me thinking out loud about the coffee supplier before I ring Dana back, and I want the whole thing in one place because every time we talk about it I forget half of what I decided the week before. So the situation is that we have been buying from the same roaster since 2019 and I have no complaint about the coffee at all, the coffee is good, everybody says the coffee is good, the complaint is the delivery, because they moved to a Thursday route about four months ago and Thursday is the worst possible day for us. We open at 6:15 and the morning rush is done by 9:30, and on a Thursday the driver gets to us somewhere between 10:00 and noon, which means Marcus is signing for beans in the middle of the lunch prep and twice now we have run the last hour of Thursday morning on the dregs of the previous bag, which is not the end of the world but it is the kind of thing regulars notice and do not mention. The new roaster, the one Dana put me on to, delivers Tuesday and they will do a standing order, and their price is $18.50 a kilo against the $16 we pay now, which is a real difference when you are going through twenty two kilos a week. Twenty two kilos, that is what we averaged over the last three months, and it was closer to eighteen before we put the second grinder in, so the number is going up not down. So if I switch I am paying about 14% more for the beans and I have to decide whether the Tuesday delivery and the standing order are worth that, and the honest answer is I do not know yet, which is why I want the numbers written down instead of arguing with myself in the car. What I do know is that the labour side is not free either, because the Thursday delivery is costing me Marcus for about forty minutes and Marcus is the only one who can run the counter and the bar at the same time, so that forty minutes is not the same as forty minutes of anybody else's time. Yusuf can do the counter fine and Yusuf cannot do the bar under pressure yet, and that is not a criticism, he has been here six weeks. The other thing on my list is the grinder, because the second one is out of warranty in March and the burrs are due, and a set of burrs is about $180 fitted, and if I am honest the whole machine is worth about $1,200 and I would rather spend the $180 twice than replace it this year. And going back to the bean price I gave, that is wrong, it is $18.50 a pound and not a kilo, I have the quote sheet in front of me now, which changes the whole comparison and is exactly why I am not agreeing to anything on the phone this afternoon. So what I want to say to Dana is thank you for the introduction, I like the Tuesday route, and I need a week to run the real numbers against what we actually go through, and if the standing order can start at a smaller volume for the first month then I will try it, because the risk of switching is not the price, the risk is that the coffee tastes different and the regulars decide something has changed. That is the whole thing. One more note for myself, whatever happens I am not moving the bean order and the milk order onto the same day, because if one delivery goes wrong we lose the morning twice over, and we learned that the hard way in the summer.

input: This is my note after the clinic this morning, dictated in the car park before I forget the order of it, and it is mostly about the Ferreira family because there are two of them on my list today and I need to keep them straight in my own head. The father came in first, he is the one with the knee, and he has been walking on it for three weeks longer than he told me last time, which I only worked out because he mentioned the wedding and the wedding was the 2nd. The knee is not surgical yet in my opinion and I said that plainly, but I also said that if he keeps walking eight kilometres a day on it then we are having a different conversation in the autumn, and he took that reasonably well. I have put him on the same anti inflammatory as before, the one he tolerated, and I have asked for the standing X-ray rather than the lying one because the lying one told us nothing useful in April. The daughter is the second one and hers is completely separate, it is the iron, and her ferritin came back at 11 which is the lowest I have seen from her and she is tired in a way that she is describing as normal now, which is the part I do not like. Normal is doing a lot of work in that sentence. So she is on the tablets, one a day with orange juice and not with tea, and I want her back in eight weeks with bloods done a week before so I am reading the result and not chasing it. When I say the tablets I mean the ferrous fumarate rather than the sulphate, because the sulphate gave her stomach trouble in the spring and she stopped taking it without telling anybody, which is exactly how we got to 11. Both of them asked about the same thing at the end, which is whether any of this is genetic, and I gave them the same honest answer, which is that the knee is wear and the iron is diet and neither of those is a family curse. Now, the part I want to think about. There is a third Ferreira, the son, and he is not my patient, he is at the practice on the other side of town, and the father mentioned that he has been getting the same tiredness. I am not going to do anything with that because it is not mine to do anything with, but if the daughter's iron does not come up on treatment then the household is worth a thought rather than just the patient, because they eat the same food and they cook it in the same pans. Admin, the standing X-ray needs the form and the form needs the reason written properly or it comes back, so please write mechanical knee pain with weight bearing and not just knee pain. The daughter's bloods are full blood count and ferritin only, nothing else, she has had enough needles this year and I do not need the rest of it to make the decision. And if either of them rings before those appointments, the answer is yes I will speak to them, because both of these are the kind of thing where a two minute phone call in week three saves a wasted appointment in week eight.

input: This is the handover for the regression run before I go on leave, and I am dictating it because the written version always ends up shorter than what is actually in my head, so it will ramble and I would rather it rambled than left something out. Where we are is that the full suite is green on staging as of last night, 1,240 cases, and green with three skips, and the three skips are the ones we agreed to skip because they need the card reader hardware and the card reader is still in a box on the third floor. So green means green minus the hardware, and if anybody asks you whether the suite is green the honest answer is yes with three hardware skips, not just yes. The part that is not settled is the checkout flow on the mobile web build, because it passes on the emulator every single time and it fails on the real Samsung about one run in four, and one run in four is the worst possible failure rate because it is often enough to matter and rare enough that people stop believing you. I have spent two days on it and I do not have a root cause, I have a shape. The shape is that when it fails, the confirm request goes out twice, and the second one comes back with a 409, and the app shows the 409 to the user as a generic error, so from the outside it looks like the payment failed when actually the first request succeeded and the order is sitting in the system perfectly fine. That is the bit that worries me more than the flake, because a customer who sees an error and pays again is a refund and a phone call. I have logged it as QA-2214 with the video attached, and I have put the har file on the shared drive under the sprint folder, not the QA folder, because the QA folder is full and IT have not extended it since I asked in June. Next thing. The performance numbers are better than we thought. The search endpoint is at 340 milliseconds at the 95th percentile against the 500 target, and the basket endpoint is at 210, and both of those are with the cache warm which is arguably cheating, but the cold numbers are 480 and 260 so even cold we are inside the target. I would report both, warm and cold, because if you only report the warm ones somebody will run it cold in front of a customer and we will look like we were hiding something. The one number I am not happy with is the first load on a cold cache on 3G, which is 6.2 seconds, and nobody has agreed a target for that so it is not technically a fail, it just feels like one. Third thing, and this is the one I need you to actually do rather than just know. The escalation contact at the payments provider is not the person in the wiki. The wiki has the old integration manager and she left in February. The person you want is Chinh, and I will spell it because everybody gets it wrong including their own ticket system, that is C H I N H, and his direct line is in my signature on the last thread with them. If the double confirm turns out to be on their side, and I think there is a decent chance it is, then you want to be talking to him and not to the general support queue, because the general support queue closed my last ticket as no fault found in nine hours without asking me a single question. Last thing, the release checklist. I have ticked everything except the accessibility pass on the new date picker, which is genuinely not done, and I do not want that ticked on my behalf while I am away, because the last time a checklist item was ticked optimistically we shipped a component that could not be reached by keyboard at all and we found out from a user. Leave it unticked. If it blocks the release then it blocks the release, and that is the correct outcome. Everything else, the 1,240 cases, the three skips, QA-2214 and the two performance tables, is in the sprint folder with today's date on it. And one genuinely last thing, if the Samsung is needed for anything else next week then take it, because I would rather somebody else made progress on their own bug than have it sitting on my desk waiting for me to come back and look at a flake that has already been logged, and the har file plus the video are enough for anybody to pick the double confirm up without the handset in their hand at all, which is the whole reason I recorded both of them instead of just writing down what I saw.

input: Okay, renewal notes for the Halcyon account before the call tomorrow, and I am going to talk the whole thing through rather than send the number, because Priya is picking this up if I am out and she needs the history and not just the number. So we are at 42 seats on the old rate, which is $19 a seat, and the renewal quote we have out with them is $23 a seat, and that is an 18% increase which I know sounds aggressive but the old rate was a launch rate from 2023 and they know it was a launch rate because it says so on the original order form in the first line. The two people who matter here are Renata, who runs operations and who actually uses the product every day, and Bea, who is the CFO and who has never logged in once. I met them both in Austin in January and she is the one who will decide this, Bea I mean, so everything we send has to survive being read by somebody who has never seen the product and who is looking at a line item. Renata loves it, Renata has been our champion for nearly two years, and Renata cannot sign anything over $10,000, which is exactly why the champion story only gets us so far on its own. The number on the table is 42 times $23 times twelve, so about $11,600 a year, and that is the number that trips the approval, and if we came in at 40 seats instead of 42 we would be under it, and I am genuinely not sure whether shaving two seats to duck an approval is clever or whether it is the kind of thing that gets noticed in an audit and costs us the relationship. My instinct is that it gets noticed. What I want to do instead is offer the three year term at $21 a seat, which is less than the 18% and more than we are getting now, and which gives Bea a story she can tell her board about locking a price for three years while inflation is doing what it is doing. input: Notes on the hall booking before I email the committee, and I want the reasoning in here as well as the decision because somebody always asks in the meeting why we did not just keep the Saturday. Midweek the hall is free on a Wednesday afternoon and the 41 still runs its old route on weekdays, which nobody seemed to know until Gwen mentioned it. input: This is my write up of the usability sessions from this week and I want it down while the sessions are still fresh, because the video takes a day to come back and by then I will have smoothed the edges off what I actually saw. Six participants, five completed the main task, and the one who did not complete it is the interesting one rather than the failure, because she did not fail the task, she refused it, she said she would never enter her address into a form that had not told her why it needed the address. Nobody else asked that question, and I think nobody else asked because the other five had all used a delivery app before and she had not. On the main task, the median time was two minutes forty and the range was one minute fifty to four minutes ten, and the slow end is entirely the date picker. Everybody struggled with the date picker, and by everybody I mean all six including the one who abandoned the form, which is unusual because a component that fails for everyone normally fails loudly and this one fails quietly, people just take longer and do not mention it. Two of them tried to type the date instead of picking it and neither of them noticed that typing works. The confirmation screen tested well and the wording we argued about for two weeks was not noticed by a single participant, which is the most useful thing in this whole write up.

input: Right, this is the note on the reconciliation job before standup, and the short version is that it is not broken, it is doing exactly what we told it to do and what we told it to do is wrong. The job runs at 02:00 and pulls the previous day's settlements, and it matches on the provider reference, which is the right key. Where it goes wrong is the window. We ask for settlements between 00:00 and 23:59 on the previous day in UTC, and the provider stamps them in local time, which for the Nairobi merchants is UTC plus three, so every settlement that lands between 21:00 and midnight UTC is stamped on the following day at their end and falls outside our window. That is about 4% of volume and it is the same 4% every day, which is why the unmatched pile has been growing at a steady rate instead of spiking, and a steady growth is much easier to ignore than a spike. We caught it because Wanjiru asked why the unmatched count was 312 on a Monday and 318 on a Tuesday and 325 on a Wednesday, which is a suspicious kind of tidy. The fix is either to widen the window by three hours on each side and accept the duplicates, which the matcher will handle because it matches on reference and not on time, or to convert at the provider boundary and store both stamps. I want the second one, and I want it in the same change as the backfill, because a fix that leaves 4% of last quarter unmatched is not a fix, it is a smaller version of the same problem.

input: This is the note on the consultation responses before I draft the summary, and I want to be careful about one word in particular because the whole reading of the evidence turns on it. We had 412 responses, which is more than the last two consultations put together, and 61% of them were from individuals rather than organisations, which is unusual for a technical consultation and is worth saying in the summary rather than burying in an annex. On the substance, most of the individual responses are about one paragraph, paragraph 14, and almost none of them are about the parts we expected to be controversial. Support, and I mean support for the proposal as drafted here, not support for the general direction, is at 38%, which is much lower than the covering letter implied and which I am not going to soften. If you count the responses that support the direction while objecting to the drafting, it goes up to 71%, and both of those numbers are true and they answer different questions, so the summary needs both with the definition attached to each. The eleven organisational responses are more or less unanimous and they all raise the same implementation timetable point, which is that eighteen months is not enough for the smaller providers, and two of them say twenty four and one says thirty six.

input: Okay so this is my note for the project report and I am recording it because I have been staring at the document for an hour and written nothing, so let me just talk through what actually happened and clean it up later. The idea was a Nepali handwriting recogniser for the Devanagari set, and the reason I picked it is that the existing datasets are all printed text and my grandmother's letters are not printed text, and I wanted something where the failure cases were interesting to me personally. Data first. I collected 3,200 samples from 40 writers, which is 80 characters each, and the 40 writers are almost all students from my department which is the biggest weakness in the whole thing because they are all between 19 and 24 and they all write quickly. My grandmother writes nothing like them. I split it 70 20 10 by writer and not by sample, which took me two attempts to get right because my first split had the same writer in train and test and my accuracy was 96% and I was very happy for about a day. After I fixed the split it was 81%, and 81% is the real number. The model is a small convolutional network, four blocks, about 1.1 million parameters, and I tried a pretrained ResNet first and it was worse, which surprised me until I realised the pretrained features are all for photographs and my inputs are 64 by 64 binary images with nothing in them but strokes. Training took nine minutes on the lab machine and about forty on my laptop, so I did all the experiments on the lab machine and all the debugging on the laptop. The confusion matrix is the interesting part of the report. Almost all the remaining error is between four character pairs that differ by one stroke, and two of those pairs are ones my own handwriting confuses, which I only noticed because I put my own samples in the test set as a sanity check. Going back to the number of writers I gave earlier, that is wrong, it was 40 writers who agreed and 34 who actually submitted, so it is 34 and the sample count is 2,720 rather than 3,200. I checked the folder while I was talking. Everything else stands, and for the report I want to be honest that the writer diversity is the limitation rather than dressing it up as future work, because a recogniser that only reads the handwriting of fast young engineering students is not the thing I set out to build. One more thing for the report, and it is the part I am least sure how to write, which is that the whole project only became interesting once the accuracy stopped going up, because up to that point I was tuning and after that point I was actually looking at which characters failed and why, and the why is a hand thing rather than a model thing, and I do not know how to say that in a methodology section without it sounding like an excuse for an 81% result on a task that other people have solved much better with much more data than I could collect on my own in a term.

input: This is the design note for the retry work and I am going to talk it out because the written version keeps turning into a decision record when it is not a decision yet, it is a set of things I now believe. First belief, the retries are not the problem, the retries are the symptom, and every time we have tried to fix retry behaviour by tuning the retry policy we have made the graph look better and the system worse. We did that in March and we did it again in July. The July one is worth remembering because we reduced the retry count from five to three and the error rate went down and the number of duplicate charges went up, and it took us six weeks to connect those two facts. Second belief, the real problem is that the write path is not idempotent, and it is not idempotent in a very specific way, which is that the request carries an idempotency key but the key is generated by the client on each attempt rather than once per logical operation. So a client that retries generates a new key, and a new key is a new operation as far as we are concerned, and we are correct to treat it as a new operation. The bug is upstream of us and it is in a library that four of our five biggest integrations use. Third belief, we cannot fix it by asking them to upgrade. I have asked. The maintainer agrees the behaviour is wrong and the last release was fourteen months ago. So what I actually want to do is accept a client supplied key when it is stable and fall back to a server derived fingerprint when it is not, and the fingerprint is the account, the amount, the destination and a two minute bucket. That is not a perfect key and I am not pretending it is. It collapses two genuinely separate identical payments inside the same two minutes, which for a subscription platform is rare and for a marketplace would be unacceptable, and we are a subscription platform. Fourth belief, and this is the one I expect an argument about, we should log every collapse and review the log weekly rather than alerting on it, because an alert on a rare correct behaviour trains people to ignore alerts, and we already have three of those. What I do not want is another March, where we shipped a policy change, the dashboards improved, everybody moved on, and the actual defect sat there for four months getting more expensive. So the order I want to do this in is the fingerprint first behind a flag with the collapse log on from day one, then a week of watching the log with nothing acting on it, then turn it on for the one integration whose traffic I understand best, which is the partner sync and not the payments webhook, and only after that the rest, and if at any point in that sequence the collapse log shows a pattern I did not predict then we stop and I write this note again with whatever I learned in it.

input: Okay so this is the migration note for the billing service and I want to get it down before the review on Thursday because I keep losing the thread on it. The short version is that we are moving the invoice writer off the shared Postgres box and onto its own instance, and the reason is not load, which is what everyone assumes, the reason is that the shared box is on Postgres 13 and the writer needs the generated columns we get in 15. Load is fine. Load has been fine for a year. I want to say that clearly because the last time I brought this up in standup two people started talking about connection pooling and we lost twenty minutes. So the plan is three phases and the first phase is the one I actually care about. Phase one is a read only replica of the billing schema on the new instance, running 15, and we point the reporting jobs at it, which are the ones that do not care about being a second behind. The reporting jobs are Metabase and the nightly revenue export, which is the thing Priya wrote, and there is also that old cron that emails the finance team a CSV every Monday, which nobody owns and which I would honestly like to delete but that is a different conversation. Phase two is the writer itself and that is where the risk lives, because the writer holds an advisory lock while it numbers invoices and if two writers ever run at once we get duplicate invoice numbers, and duplicate invoice numbers are the kind of thing that ends up in a support ticket six weeks later when somebody in accounts payable notices. So phase two is a hard cutover with the writer stopped, not a rolling one. We stop the writer, we wait for the replica to catch up, we check the sequence, we promote, we start the writer against the new instance. Maybe four minutes of no invoicing, and invoicing is asynchronous anyway so nobody outside the team sees it. Phase three is decommissioning the old schema and I am not going to plan phase three in detail yet because we always discover something in phase two that changes it. Now the bit I need feedback on, and this is really why I am writing it down, is the sequence. The invoice number sequence is not a Postgres sequence, it is a row in a table called billing_counters with a single column called next_invoice_no, and it is updated inside the same transaction as the insert, which is why the advisory lock exists. Whoever built it that way did it because the invoice numbers have to be gapless for the auditors, and a Postgres sequence is not gapless, it burns a value on rollback. So the design is correct, it is just fragile, and the migration has to preserve it exactly. My worry is the replica. On the replica that counter row is whatever it was at the moment the last WAL segment was applied, so if we promote while the writer is still running we will start again from a number we have already used. Hence the hard stop. I have written the runbook at docs slash runbooks slash billing dash pg15 dot md and the checks are in there as a list you tick off, and the important one is the third check, which is comparing next_invoice_no on both boxes and refusing to promote unless they match. Refusing, not warning. I have seen a warning get clicked through. On timing, I would like to do phase one next week, because the reporting load is what is actually annoying people day to day even though it is not the reason for the migration, and phase two in the window after month end close, so the eighth or the ninth, and I will confirm with Dana which of those two the finance team prefers because they are the ones who feel it. The instance itself is already provisioned, it is a db dot r6g dot xlarge in the same subnet group, and I sized it the same as the shared box on purpose so that if this turns out to be a mistake we can move back without arguing about instance types. Cost is about 240 dollars a month more, which I have already run past Marcus and he was fine with it. The one thing I have not solved is the test story. There is no staging billing data worth anything, the staging invoices are all from a seed script and they all have sequential numbers with no gaps, so staging cannot tell me whether the gapless check works. I think the honest answer is that we rehearse phase two against a restored snapshot of production in a throwaway instance, and we do it twice, once cleanly and once where I kill the writer halfway through on purpose to see what the check does. That is a day of work and I think it is worth a day. If anyone reading this thinks it is not worth a day I would genuinely like to hear why, because I have been wrong about that kind of thing before and it is cheaper to be told now than on the eighth.

input: Right, this is the fortnightly update for the platform group and I will send it as is because I do not have time to pretty it up. Three things happened. The first is that the API gateway migration is done, all of it, including the two internal services we thought we would have to leave behind, and the reason we got those over the line is that Aditya found they were only using the gateway for TLS termination and nothing else, so they could point straight at the load balancer and we did not have to port their auth middleware at all. That saved us most of a sprint. Second thing is the on call rotation. We have been running a five person rotation since March and it has been too thin, people are getting paged on their second week back from leave, so we are going to eight. That means bringing the two people from the data platform side who have been shadowing since June into the rotation properly. Hold on, going back to that rotation number, it is six, not eight, because Dana's team pulled their two people back for the warehouse migration and I only found out on Friday. That is still better than five but it is not what I promised in the last update and I would rather say so plainly than quietly change the number. Third thing, and this is the one I want people to actually read, is the incident on the fourteenth. The short version is that a config push took the search index offline for fifty one minutes in the middle of the European morning, and the reason it took fifty one minutes and not five is that the rollback path assumed the old config was still in the bucket and it was not, because the same push had overwritten it. So there was no rollback, there was only a rebuild, and a rebuild is forty minutes. We have three follow ups from that and they are all owned. Priya is versioning the config objects so an overwrite cannot happen, Tomas is adding a rebuild time check to the runbook so nobody spends ten minutes discovering it, and I am rewriting the incident template because ours does not have a field for what the rollback assumed, which turns out to be the question that mattered. On the things I am worried about, the honest list is short. Hiring is slower than I said it would be, we are two offers out and neither is signed. The dependency on the warehouse migration is real now that Dana's people are on it, so if that slips our rotation stays where it is for longer than I want. And I still have not written the design note for the read path work, which is now three weeks late, and I am going to block Thursday morning for it rather than promise it again. Everything else is on track and I will do this again on the twenty eighth.

input: So this is my note for the report on the pothole detection project and I am recording it now because tomorrow I have the lab and then I forget everything. The dataset is the one we collected ourselves on the ring road between Kalanki and Balaju, three passes, one in the morning around seven when the light is flat, one at midday, and one at about half past five when everything is orange and the shadows are long, and the reason for three passes is that the first model we trained on morning data only was useless in the evening, it was calling every shadow a pothole. Total is about eleven thousand frames after we dropped the ones where the phone was pointing at the sky, and out of those we have annotated four thousand two hundred, and Sujata is doing another thousand this week. The annotation is bounding boxes only, no masks, because masks would take us until next year and the professor said boxes are enough for the report. Model is YOLOv8 nano, and we picked nano and not small because the whole point is that it should run on a phone, and on my phone, which is a Redmi Note 11, nano gives me about eighteen frames per second and small gives me seven, and seven is not usable when you are moving. The metrics right now are mAP at fifty of zero point six one and mAP at fifty to ninety five of zero point three four, which sounds bad but the fifty to ninety five number is always bad for this kind of object because a pothole does not have a clean edge, two annotators will draw the box differently by twenty percent, so the ceiling on that metric is our own agreement and not the model. I want to write that in the report properly with the inter annotator number in it, which we have not measured yet, and measuring it is one afternoon of two people boxing the same two hundred frames. The failure cases are the interesting part and there are three kinds. Manhole covers, which are round and dark and the model loves them, patched repairs where the tar is a different colour from the road but the surface is flat, and wet patches after rain which look like holes to me also so I cannot really blame it. For the report the section order should be. Actually for the report the section order should be dataset, then annotation protocol, then model choice, then metrics, then failure cases, then the deployment note at the end, and the deployment note is short because we have not deployed anything, we only have the phone demo. One more thing I must not forget, the professor asked for the split to be by pass and not random, so the evening pass is the test set and it never appears in training, because if we split randomly then frames from the same three seconds of road end up on both sides and the numbers become meaningless.

input: Right, this is the note for Sunday, the christening lunch, seventy covers, and I want to write the braise down properly because last time I did it from memory and we ran short on the sauce. Start the day before. The shin, I have ordered twelve kilos of shin from Bruno and it comes in on Friday afternoon, and I want it cut in pieces the size of your fist, not smaller, because small pieces fall apart in the pan and then it is not a braise it is a ragu. Season it heavy and leave it on trays in the walk in overnight uncovered so the surface dries, that is the whole trick, a dry surface browns and a wet surface steams. Saturday morning we brown it in the big rondeau in batches, six or seven batches, and do not rush it, if the pan is crowded nothing happens. Onions, carrots, celery, and I am not going to weigh those, it is two big trays of the mirepoix we cut on Friday. Wine is 3, that is 3 litres, the Sangiovese from the box not the good stuff, and reduce it until the pan smells sweet and not sharp. Then the stock to cover, tomato paste, two tins of tomatoes crushed by hand, and the herb bundle. Lid on, oven at 150, four hours, and check at three. Sunday it only needs reheating and the sauce reduced, and Marta will do the polenta because she does it better than me. One more thing, the polenta. Marta uses the coarse one from the sack and it takes forty minutes with someone standing there, so she needs a second pair of hands from twelve, and I will ask Dario because he does not mind stirring. And the bread. We are short on bread, I only have six loaves and seventy people will eat nine or ten, so somebody has to go to Fiorella on Saturday evening and buy four more, and if she has the big round ones take those because they cut better for a table like this. Write that on the board so I do not forget it, that is the kind of thing I forget.
