input: This is the outline for the docs restructure and I want it in front of Yuki before the planning meeting on Wednesday. The problem we are solving is not that the docs are wrong, they are mostly right, the problem is that a new user cannot find the one page they need in the first five minutes, and we know that from the support tickets, forty percent of the setup tickets last quarter were answered by linking a page that already existed. So this is an information architecture problem, not a writing problem, and I want to say that clearly at the top because the last time we did this it turned into a copy editing project and we spent six weeks changing headings. The structure I want is four top level sections. Getting started, which is one path and not a menu of paths, and that is the change that matters most, because right now there are three ways in and a new user has to choose between them before they know anything. Then guides, which are task shaped, how do I do the thing. Then reference, which is generated and which nobody reads front to back. Then a troubleshooting section, which we do not have at all today and which is where those forty percent of tickets should have been answered. On sequencing, I would do troubleshooting first, because it is new, it does not break any existing links, and it is the one we can measure. Getting started is the risky one because every blog post and every tutorial links to those pages, so that needs redirects and a proper audit before anything moves, and the reference, meaning the generated API reference and not the hand written SDK notes, is going to move regardless because the tooling changed in the last release.

input: Site note for Tuesday, block C. The rebar for the columns, it arrived on Sunday night but the delivery is short, twelve bars of the sixteen millimetre and none of the twenty, so we cannot start the columns on the east side and I have moved that crew to the slab instead. I called the supplier twice this morning. First time nobody answers, second time I get the same man who promised me Sunday, and he tells me the twenty millimetre is on a truck from Zarqa and will be here Thursday. I do not believe Thursday. What I have done is this. The slab pour on the west side is ready anyway, formwork checked yesterday by me and by Khaled, so we pour Wednesday morning early before the heat, and that keeps the crew busy and keeps the programme honest. The consultant wants to see the reinforcement before the pour, which is normal, and he comes at seven, so the pour starts at eight and not at six as I said to the men yesterday. Somebody must tell the concrete plant. Two other things. The water tanker did not come again and the curing on the block B columns is now three days behind what the spec asks, and this I have written in the log formally because it is not the first time. And the site fence at the corner near the mosque is down again, second time this month, and until it is fixed I am not leaving the compressor there overnight.

input: This is the memo about the seminar for next term and I would like Ellen to have it before the curriculum committee meets, because if it goes past that meeting we lose another term. The seminar is the one on evidence and inference that I have wanted to run for four years, and the shape of it has finally settled, so let me put it down while it is clear. It is a fourteen week seminar, two hours once a week, capped at twelve students, and the cap is the whole point rather than an administrative convenience. Below about fifteen people everyone speaks, above it three people speak and the rest take notes, and I have taught both and there is no comparison. The reading is heavy but narrow. Four books over the term, not fourteen articles, because I want them to live inside a long argument rather than sample opinions, and the books are the Hacking, the Cartwright, the Freedman collection, and one more that I have not decided between two candidates. Assessment is where the committee will push back. There is no final examination. There are three short papers of about two thousand words each, spaced so that each one comes after a book rather than at the end of the term, and every paper is rewritten once after comments, and the rewritten version is the one that is graded. That doubles my marking and I have accepted that. The reason is that the skill I am trying to teach is revision under criticism, and you cannot examine that in three hours in a hall. Participation is a quarter of the grade, which I know is contested, and I will defend it on the ground that a seminar with no stake in attendance becomes a lecture with poor attendance. Logistics. It should be Tuesday or Thursday afternoon, not morning, because the graduate students teach in the mornings. The room needs a table that people sit around, which rules out the two rooms in the new building, and I would rather be in the old seminar room with the bad radiator than in a lecture theatre with tiered seats. I will need a teaching assistant for the marking, one section only, and Ellen thinks that is fundable from the departmental line. On prerequisites, and this is the part I want the committee to read carefully, the seminar is open to all graduate students, well, to all graduate students in the philosophy and statistics programmes, and anyone else needs to speak to me first, because the second book assumes a probability course and without it the middle of the term is misery. I would rather have that conversation in advance than have three people drop out in week six. If the committee wants a compromise I can be flexible about the cap and about the day, but not about the rewriting, and not about the examination. Those two are the seminar.

input: Okay so this is my summary of the week for the meeting with Rafi bhai on Sunday and also for myself because I keep forgetting what I already tried. The task is still the same, we are trying to see whether a small model can do the citation intent classification without the graph features, and the reason I care about this is that the graph features are the expensive part, you need the whole citation network in memory to compute them and nobody deploying this has that. So the question is how much we lose without them. Baseline is the SciBERT numbers from the original paper, macro F1 of zero point eight two on the ACL ARC set, and they use the graph. My first run without graph features gave zero point seven one, which is a big drop, and I spent two days thinking my code was wrong before I accepted that it is just a hard task without structure. Second thing I tried is adding the surrounding sentences, one before and one after the citation sentence, and that took it to zero point seven six, so context recovers about half of what the graph was giving. This is interesting result and I think it goes in the writeup. Third thing, and this did not work, is a contrastive objective on the section headings, the idea being that a citation in related work behaves differently from one in method and the model should learn that separation for free. It did not learn it. Zero point seven six five, which is noise. I am not going to pursue that unless somebody tells me why it should have worked. On data, the ACL ARC set is small, about two thousand seven hundred labelled citations, and the label distribution is terrible, background is over half of it and future work is under two percent, so the macro F1 swings a lot between seeds. I am now running every configuration with five seeds and reporting the spread, which I should have done from the start, and it changes how I read my own earlier numbers, because the difference between zero point seven one and zero point seven six is real but the difference between seven six and seven six five is inside one standard deviation. For next week I want to try two things. Freezing the lower layers, because the model is small and the data is small and I think we are overfitting the encoder, and the checkpoint from the domain adaptive pretraining that Fatima has on the shared drive, which is trained on the same corpus and might just be better. Both are cheap. One more note for myself, I must write down the exact seeds and the commit hash in the experiment log every time, because I lost a good result last month and could not reproduce it, and losing a result twice would be embarrassing.

input: This is the summary from the retro and I will put it in Confluence tomorrow but here is the substance while it is fresh. Fourteen people in the room, which is too many for a retro and is something we should fix before the next one. Two themes came out. The first is the review queue, and this is the same theme as last time and the time before, pull requests sit for two days and nobody feels able to say whose job it is to pick them up, so we agreed to try a rotating reviewer of the day for two sprints and see whether the queue drains. The second is the staging environment, which last sprint break twice in the middle of demo preparation, and the cause both times was somebody deploying a branch by hand, so we are turning off manual deploys to staging and if that hurts we will hear about it quickly. There was a third thing that is not actionable and I want to say it anyway, which is that people feel the roadmap changes without them being told, and that is not something the team can fix inside a retro, so I am taking it to the product meeting on Thursday and I will come back with an answer even if the answer is no. input: Right, these are my notes from the trustees meeting on the ninth so that Gwen can write the proper minutes from them, and I am going to go through it in the order we took it rather than the order on the agenda, because we did not follow the agenda. Present were six of us and two apologies, and we were quorate, which I mention because last time we were not and we had to take everything again by email. First was the boiler. The boiler is the thing that will decide what kind of year we have. The quote from the firm in Newport is eleven thousand four hundred including the flue work, and the quote from the local man is nine thousand two hundred but he cannot start until March, and March means another winter of the hall being cold on Tuesday evenings, which is when the toddler group meets and they are the group that keeps the lights on. So it is not really a decision about money, it is a decision about the toddler group, and I said that in the meeting and I want it in the minutes in something like those words. We did not decide. We agreed to ask the local man whether he can do the flue in November and the rest in March, which nobody thought of until Bryn said it in the last five minutes, and that is typical of Bryn and I mean that as a compliment. Second was the lettings income, which is up, and I want to be careful here because up is doing a lot of work in that sentence. The hall took four thousand one hundred in the year to March against three thousand six hundred the year before, so up by five hundred, but half of that is one wedding reception that we will not get every year, so the underlying number is up by about two hundred and fifty and I would rather report it that way than take credit we have not earned. Gwen will put both figures in. Third was the safeguarding policy, which is out of date, and this one is genuinely straightforward and only needs somebody to do it. The template is on the county council website, it is a form filling exercise of about two hours, and Rhian has offered, so Rhian is doing it before the next meeting and I will chase her the week before because everybody offers and then December happens. Fourth, and this took the longest and produced the least, was whether we apply to the lottery fund for the kitchen. My view, and I said it, is that we are not ready to apply, because the application asks for two years of accounts signed off and ours are not signed off, and there is no point spending six weeks on a bid that fails on a box we cannot tick. Two people disagreed and thought we should apply anyway to learn the process. We did not resolve it and it comes back next time. Under any other business, the fence, again, and the fence is now four meetings old and I am starting to think we should just pay somebody rather than wait for a volunteer with a van. Next meeting is the fourteenth of next month, in the hall if the heating is on and in Gwen's front room if it is not, and I mean that literally, we have done it before.

input: This is the timeline for the incident last night, and I am writing it while I still remember the order, because the order is the part everybody argues about afterwards. Times are UTC. At 22:14 the first alert fires, which is p99 latency on the checkout service crossing four hundred milliseconds, and that alert is noisy so nobody looks at it immediately, which I do not think is wrong, it fires maybe twice a week and it is usually a batch job. At 22:19 the second alert fires, which is the error rate on the payments API, and that one is not noisy, it has fired four times in a year. Karolina picks it up at 22:21. At that point the symptom is that about one request in six to the payments API is returning a 502, and the pattern is not random, it is one of the six pods, so it looks like a single bad pod and the obvious move is to delete it and let the deployment replace it. She does that at 22:26. The new pod comes up and starts failing the same way within about ninety seconds, and that is the moment the incident actually starts, because now we know it is not the pod. From 22:30 to 23:05 we are looking in the wrong place. We are looking at the payments service and the problem is in the connection pool configuration of the sidecar, which had been changed six hours earlier in a completely unrelated pull request that was described as a logging change. Nobody was hiding anything, the change genuinely was mostly logging, and the pool setting was one line in a config template that nobody reviewing it would have connected to payments. I want that written plainly because the temptation in a postmortem is to find somebody who should have noticed, and in this case the review was reasonable and the outcome was still bad. At 23:05 Marek finds it by diffing the running config against the previous release rather than by reading code, and that is the lesson I actually want people to take from this, when the code looks innocent, diff the state. Rollback of the sidecar config goes out at 23:12 and the error rate is back to normal by 23:15. Total customer impact is fifty six minutes, of which the first twelve are the noisy alert nobody trusted. Three follow ups. Making the sidecar config part of the release diff we already look at, which is small work and is mine. Splitting the latency alert into a fast one and a slow one so that the noisy version stops training people to ignore it, which is Karolina's. And a wider question about whether config templates should be reviewed by the service owner even when the pull request is not about their service, which is not a follow up I can close, so I am raising it as a discussion and I will show this timeline on the postmortem meeting tomorrow.

input: Okay so this is my working note for the Halden case study before I start writing it, and the reason I am doing a note first is that I interviewed three people and they told me three different stories and I need to decide whose story the piece follows before I write a word. The client is Halden, they make scheduling software for dental practices, which sounds dull and is actually the most interesting bit, because dental practices are small businesses run by people who did not want to run a business, so every product decision is really a decision about somebody's Tuesday afternoon. That is the angle. Person one was the CEO and he gave me the version that is on their website, we saw a gap in the market, we built a better product, growth followed. I am not using it. It is not untrue, it is just the shape every case study has and nobody reads. Person two was a customer, a practice manager in Stockport who has used three of these systems, and she gave me the thing I actually want, which is that the reason she stayed is that when the system went down on a Monday morning somebody phoned her back within four minutes and it was a person who knew what a recall list was. That is the story. The piece is about that four minutes. Person three, and this is the one I need to check the spelling on, is their head of ops, Yolanthe, that is Y O L A N D E, and she is the one who built the support rota that makes the four minutes possible, which is not a technology story at all, it is a staffing story, and she was very clear that they overstaff support on Monday mornings and understaff it on Friday afternoons on purpose because that is where the calls actually are. So the structure I want is the practice manager first, in her words, then the four minutes, then how the rota works, then what it costs them, and the CEO gets two lines near the end and no more. Length about twelve hundred words. I need two more things before I can write it. The exact downtime figure, because I have four minutes for the callback but I do not have how long the system was actually down, and those are different numbers that everybody will confuse. And permission to name the practice, which I have verbally from the practice manager but not in writing, and if I cannot get it in writing then she becomes a practice manager in Greater Manchester, which is weaker but still works. One thing I want to avoid is the word seamless. They said it four times between them and it means nothing, and if it appears in my draft it means I have run out of ideas.

input: This is the handover note for the date picker work because I am on leave from Thursday and Minji is picking it up. Current state, the new picker is on the branch feature slash date picker rewrite and it works, but it is not ready to merge and I want to be honest about why rather than let her find out. What works. Keyboard navigation is complete and it follows the ARIA pattern properly, arrow keys move by day, page up and page down move by month, home and end go to the start and end of the week, and the whole grid is one tab stop, which is the part everybody gets wrong. Screen reader announcements are done and tested with NVDA and with VoiceOver, and the announcement on month change says the month and the year, not just the month, because without the year you get lost in December. Range selection works for the simple case. What does not work is the range selection when the two dates are in different months and the user is navigating with the keyboard, because the focus management and the selection state are fighting each other, and the reason they are fighting is that I have two sources of truth in there, the focused date and the selection anchor, and the tests that cover this path is passing for the wrong reason. That is the sentence I most want Minji to read. The tests pass because they assert on the rendered class names and the class names are correct while the announced state is wrong, so the test suite is green and the component is broken for exactly the users this rewrite was for. I did not have time to fix the tests and I did not want to delete them, so they are still there and they are still lying. Second thing that does not work is the locale handling for the first day of the week. It reads from the browser locale, which is right, but it caches the value at module load, which means changing the app language does not change the picker until a reload, and one of our biggest customers switches language in the app. That is a small fix and I have left a comment with the line number. Third, the styles are not final. Ravi has a design and I have implemented about eighty percent of it, and the twenty percent I skipped is the transition when the month changes, which is deliberately unimplemented rather than half implemented, because a broken transition is worse than none. Two things I would ask Minji not to do. Do not merge it behind a feature flag to unblock the sprint, because the old picker and the new one both listen for the same escape key and having both mounted causes a real bug we have already seen once. And do not fix the failing case by making the tests stricter first, fix the two sources of truth, because the tests will tell you nothing useful until that is one thing instead of two.

That is the sentence I most want Minji to read. The tests pass because they assert on the rendered class names and the class names are correct while the announced state is wrong, so the test suite is green and the component is broken for exactly the users this rewrite was for. Third, the styles are not final. Ravi has a design and I have implemented about eighty percent of it, and the twenty percent I skipped is the transition when the month changes, which is deliberately unimplemented rather than half implemented, because a broken transition is worse than none. Two things I would ask Minji not to do. Do not merge it behind a feature flag to unblock the sprint, because the old picker and the new one both listen for the same escape key and having both mounted causes a real bug we have already seen once. And do not fix the failing case by making the tests stricter first, fix the two sources of truth, because the tests will tell you nothing useful until that is one thing instead of two.

input: This is my note on the consultation response before I write it properly, and I am dictating it on the bus so it will be rough. The council's own figures say ninety two percent of stops in the city are accessible, and that number is true and it is also useless, because a stop counts as accessible if it has a raised kerb, and a raised kerb with a parked van in front of it is not accessible on the day you need it. I want to make that point with an example rather than an argument. The ask is that the accessibility criterion is written into the scoring, not the appendix. That is the whole thing and if I write more than a thousand words I have failed.

input: Referee comments on the Larsen manuscript, second round. The revision addresses my main objection about the sampling frame and I am satisfied with the new appendix, so my recommendation is minor revisions rather than another full round. Three points remain. The first is that section 4 still reports the pooled estimate without the by site breakdown, and since the authors now concede in their response that the effect is concentrated in two of the seven sites, the pooled figure on its own is misleading and the breakdown belongs in the main text rather than in supplementary material where nobody will go looking for it. The second is smaller but it recurs. Table 3 gives standard errors to three decimal places while the point estimates are given to two, and the caption asserts that that the two columns are on the same scale, which cannot be right and reads as though the errors were more precisely known than the quantities they attach to. The third is a wording matter I raised last time and which has not moved. They describe the design as quasi experimental in the abstract and as observational in the methods, and those are not interchangeable in this literature, so they should pick one and use it throughout. I would also gently suggest the discussion could lose a page, since the final two paragraphs restate the limitations already set out on page 11, but that is a preference and not a condition and I would not hold the paper up over it.

input: Notes on the Kwon paper before I forget what the argument actually was. Their claim is that that particular benchmark is saturated, not that benchmarks in general are, and I think the distinction matters more than the reviewers gave it credit for, because the saturation they demonstrate is entirely in the two easiest of the six splits and the hard split has barely moved in three years. So when they say the task is solved they mean solved in the sense that the headline number is above 95, and that number is an average over splits of wildly different difficulty, which is the same problem we ran into with our own evaluation last year and never properly wrote up. What I want to check is whether the per split numbers are in the appendix or only in the repository, because if they are only in the repository then the paper as printed does not support the strong reading, and a reader who stops at the abstract will take away the wrong thing entirely. Worth citing alongside arXiv 2109.07276 in the related work, since both are really about a single reported number hiding the case you actually care about. output: Notes on the Kwon paper before I forget what the argument actually was. Their claim is that that particular benchmark is saturated, not that benchmarks in general are, and I think the distinction matters more than the reviewers gave it credit for, because the saturation they demonstrate is entirely in the two easiest of the six splits and the hard split has barely moved in three years. So when they say the task is solved they mean solved in the sense that the headline number is above 95, and that number is an average over splits of wildly different difficulty, which is the same problem we ran into with our own evaluation last year and never properly wrote up. What I want to check is whether the per split numbers are in the appendix or only in the repository, because if they are only in the repository then the paper as printed does not support the strong reading, and a reader who stops at the abstract will take away the wrong thing entirely. Worth citing alongside arXiv 2109.07276 in the related work, since both are really about a single reported number hiding the case you actually care about. The PDF is in the shared folder under Kwon 2026 and the underlining on the second page is mine rather than the authors, so ignore it.

input: I am thinking out loud here so treat this as a draft rather than a decision. The problem with the current importer is that it does everything inside one transaction, so a single bad row rolls back a file that took 40 minutes to read, and the customers who hit that are always the ones with the biggest files, because a bigger file has a better chance of containing one bad row. What I want to do is split it into a read phase and a write phase, with the read phase writing a staging table and nothing else. The read phase must not touch the live tables at all. The read phase must not touch the live tables at all. Then the write phase can run in batches of a thousand and record which batches succeeded, so a failure halfway through leaves the customer with half their data loaded rather than none of it, and they can retry from where it stopped instead of starting again. The bit I have not worked out is what to do with rows that are valid on their own but conflict with something already in the live table, because those cannot be caught in the read phase by definition. Maybe they just come out as a report at the end and a human looks at them, which is not elegant but is better than what we have now. If you have half an hour this week I would rather talk it through than write it up, because I keep changing my mind about the staging table.

input: Minutes for the tenants association meeting, Tuesday evening, nine present and two apologies. We started on the bin store, which has come up at every meeting since January. The council will not empty the store while the gate is padlocked, and the gate is padlocked because the store was being used by people who do not live in the block. Nobody in the room could see a way round that which does not involve somebody taking responsibility for unlocking it on a Wednesday morning, and nobody volunteered, so the position is unchanged and I said I would write to the housing officer again. Then the entry phone, which now works on three of the eight flats. The contractor has been out twice and both times he has told us the fault is in the wiring rather than in the handsets. The fault, he says, is in the wiring and not in the handsets, and he was quite firm about it, so the association will ask him to put that in writing before it approves any further visits. On the money, there is 1,240 in the account and the insurance falls due in September, which leaves less room than people think. Nothing at all was decided about the planters. We closed at half eight and the next meeting is the second Tuesday in October in the same room, and I will send this round once somebody has checked my numbers.

input: You know the place on the corner that used to be the launderette? input: This is the summary for the trustees on where the planning application has got to, and I will send the full papers separately because there are 40 pages of them and nobody is going to read 40 pages before Thursday. The short version is that we are further on than we were in June but the timetable has slipped again, and the reason it has slipped is not the objections, it is the drainage report, which we were told would take three weeks and has taken nine. The consultants have finally sent it through and the finding we needed is in there, the site drains to the north east and not into the culvert that runs under the lane, which is what the objectors have been saying all along and what the 2019 survey also said, so that is now on the record twice. The problem is that the same report recommends a soakaway on the corner where we had drawn the bin store, and moving the bin store means moving the access, and moving the access means the whole layout drawing has to be redone, which is another 2,400 and about a fortnight of somebody's time. I have asked whether the soakaway can go under the parking instead and I am waiting to hear. Meanwhile the count county council have written to say the consultation period is being extended by 21 days, because two of the statutory consultees were not notified when they should have been, which is not our error and does not cost us anything except time, but it does mean the committee date moves from the 14th of next month to some point in the month after, and they will not say when until the extension closes. That has a knock on effect on the funding, because the grant we were awarded in March is conditional on the work starting before the end of the financial year, and if the committee does not sit until then we cannot start, and the funder has already refused one extension to a different project this year so I would not assume they will give us one. What I would like from the trustees on Thursday is a decision on two things. The first is whether we go back to the funder now and tell them the timetable has moved, which is honest and probably safer, or whether we wait until we have a committee date and go to them with something definite, which is what the chair would prefer. The second is whether we authorise the 2,400 for the redrawn layout out of reserves, because if we wait for the trustees to meet again in October we lose another six weeks and the drawing has to be in before the committee papers are printed. My own view is that we tell the funder now and we authorise the drawing now, because both of the alternatives amount to hoping that something turns up, and we have been doing that since the spring. I will put both of those in the papers as recommendations with the numbers behind them, and I will bring the drainage report itself in case anybody would rather see the map than my description of it.

input: These are my notes from the partnership meeting for the annual report, and the numbers in here are provisional until the county publishes, so please do not quote any of them outside the group yet. The count county wide came in at 61, which is up from 54 last year and up from 49 the year before, and the temptation is to read that as a straight rise and say things are getting worse, but the methodology changed this year and I want that said plainly in the report rather than buried in a footnote at the back. Two districts counted on a different night from everybody else, and one of them counted on two nights and took the higher of the two figures, which is not what the guidance says to do. So the honest sentence is that this year's count is not comparable with last year's, and that the trend over five years is upward but the size of this year's jump cannot be attributed to anything with confidence. What I do think is comparable is the age profile, because that is collected the same way in every district and has been for six years, and it has moved a long way: the share of people counted who are under 25 has gone from about a fifth to just over a third, and it has held at roughly a third in each of the last three years, so it is not a single year artefact. The service response has not moved with it at all. We still have exactly two beds in the whole county commissioned specifically for under 25s, and both of them are in the north, which is where the fewest young people were counted. I have asked the commissioners for the occupancy figures on those two beds and they have sent me an annual average, which is useless for this argument, so I am going to ask again and ask for it by month. On funding, the grant that pays for the outreach worker ends in March and there is no successor scheme announced, and I have written to the two MPs whose constituencies cover most of the county and had a reply from one of them, which was polite and said nothing at all. The other has not replied in six weeks and I will chase both of them after the recess. For the report itself I want the age profile to be the headline rather than the total, because the total is the number the press will pick up and it is the number I am least able to defend, whereas the age profile is the finding that actually tells the commissioners something they could act on if they wanted to. Can you draft the methodology box, three or four sentences, and be specific about which districts differed rather than writing some districts, because vagueness there will read as though we are hiding something when the entire point of the box is that we are not.

input: Update on the house for anybody who has asked, and I am dictating this once and sending it to all of you rather than saying the same thing four times on the phone. The building control officer came on Wednesday and passed the foundations, which was the thing I was most worried about because of the tree, and he said the root barrier we put in was more than he would have asked for, so that is one thing that has gone right this month. The steel arrived on Thursday and it is the wrong length, 4.2 instead of 4.8, and the fabricator says the drawing he was sent said 4.2, and the drawing I have in front of me says 4.8, so somebody has sent him an old revision and it will take ten working days to make the right one. Ten days is not the end of the world on its own but it holds up the first floor, which holds up the roof, which holds up everything after that, and the roofer is booked for the middle of next month and has already told me he will not hold the slot open. So the honest position is that we are three weeks behind rather than the one week I told you last time, and I would rather say that now in one go than keep revising it downwards every fortnight. On the money, we are still inside the contingency but only just, because the drainage connection cost 1,900 more than the estimate after they found the old clay pipe under the path, and the skip hire has gone up twice since we started in April. I have stopped saying yes to small extras on the spot, so if anybody suggests something to you while I am at work, the answer is that I will price it in the evening, not yes. The bit I actually need help thinking about is the kitchen, because the units have a fourteen week lead time and if I order them now I am guessing at a wall that does not exist yet, and if I wait until the wall exists we have no kitchen until the spring and we are washing up in the bath for four months. My instinct is to order the carcasses now and leave the worktop until later, since the worktop has to be templated on site anyway and cannot be ordered off a drawing. The scaffolding is going up. Up on the Tuesday morning, so the parking will be gone for about a month, and I have told the neighbours on both sides and put a note through the door of the one who is away until the 9th. If anybody wants to see it before it is plastered then this weekend is the time, because after that it is all boards and you cannot see what was there before. I will send photographs either way, and I will send the revised programme once the fabricator has confirmed his date rather than before, because the last programme I sent was out of date by the time any of you read it.

input: Notes for the newsletter piece about the residential trip, and I am going to ramble a bit so take what is useful and leave the rest. The main thing parents want to know is why the cost has gone up. Up at the gate the figure people are quoting each other is 40 more than last year, and that is roughly right, it is 38, but nobody has told them what the 38 is for and in the absence of an explanation people assume the worst. So the piece should say plainly that the coach hire is 22 of it and the centre put its per night charge up by 8 in January, and the remaining 8 is the insurance, which we have had to change providers on because the old policy no longer covers the water activities. If we say that, most people will accept it, and the ones who cannot afford it need to know before the deposit deadline rather than after, so the sentence about the hardship fund has to be in the first paragraph and not at the bottom where it was last year. Second thing is the kit list, which is too long and frightens people. Half of it is things nobody has ever needed, and every year at least one family goes out and buys waterproof trousers for 30 that get worn once, when we have a box of them in the store cupboard that anybody can borrow. So can the list say clearly which items can be borrowed and which have to be their own, because at the moment it reads as though all of it has to be bought new. Third, and this is the one I keep forgetting to raise, we need a better answer on phones. Last year we said they would be collected in and then in practice they were not, and two children rang home on the first night, which upset several other children who had handed theirs in properly. Whatever we decide this year, it has to be the same for everybody and it has to be written down in the letter, because the problem last time was not the policy, it was that different staff applied it differently and the children noticed within an hour. The other thing worth a line is the medical form, because three of them came back last year with the emergency number left blank and we did not find that out until we were already on the coach, so the form needs to say that a blank number means the child cannot travel, which sounds harsh written down but is easier than ringing round a village hall at ten at night. I would also like a line in there thanking the two parents who came as helpers, by name if they are happy with that, because we ask for volunteers every year and we never say anything about the ones who actually come. Can you draft it and send it back to me before it goes to the office, and keep the whole thing to one side of A4, because the four page version we sent in the spring did not get read by anybody I spoke to.

input: Right, this is going to be long and I am not going to tidy it as I go, so bear with me. I want to get down everything that happened with the bank this week while it is still fresh, because I am going to have to put it in a complaint and if I leave it a fortnight I will have lost half of it. It started on Monday when the app updated itself overnight. I did not ask it to update, it just did, and when I opened it the whole navigation had changed. The buttons that used to be along the bottom are now behind a menu, and the menu is a button that my screen reader announces as button, just the word button, with no label on it at all, so there is no way for me to know what it does except by pressing it and finding out. I pressed it. It opened a list of eleven items and the first one was announced as heading, and the second one was announced as heading, and both of them were actually links, which means the list is not a list as far as I am concerned, it is eleven things I have to go through one at a time in the hope that one of them is Payments. Payments turned out to be the seventh. It used to be the first thing on the screen. So I rang the number on the back of the card and I was in the queue for 40 minutes, and I want to be fair here, the woman I eventually spoke to was very good, she was called Marianne and she stayed on the line with me for another 25 minutes while we worked out between us what had changed. Marianne could not see my screen and I could not see hers, so what we did was she read me the layout from her side and I told her what my screen reader was saying on mine, and it turns out the app has a separate accessibility setting now which is off by default and which nobody told anybody about. Off by default. That is the thing I want in the complaint, because turning it on fixed about half of what I had been fighting with for three days, and if Marianne had not spent those 25 minutes on it with me I would still be pressing button to find out what button does. The other half is not fixed. The card freeze control is a switch that announces its state before you change it rather than after, so it tells you it is off, you turn it on, and it still says off until you leave the screen and come back, which means I have twice now frozen a card I meant to unfreeze and once unfrozen a card I meant to freeze. That is not a preference, that is money. I am not doing that again, I am not doing it again, I will ring instead, which rather defeats the point of having the app at all. Then on Wednesday I got an email saying they had noticed unusual activity and I should log in to confirm it, and the link in that email went to a page my screen reader read out as a table with no headers, and I am not putting card details into something whose structure I cannot read. So I rang again and there was no unusual activity at all, it was the app being reinstalled on my phone that had triggered it, which is their own update doing it to itself. 40 minutes in the queue the first time, 40 minutes again on Wednesday. I have written both of those down because when they reply they will tell me the average wait is four minutes. What I want out of the complaint is three specific things rather than an apology, and I am going to say that in the first paragraph so it does not get filed as feedback. The accessibility setting should be on by default, or there should at least be a prompt about it on the first launch after an update. The switch should announce its state after the change and not before, and I will quote the guideline number for that because I have looked it up and it is not ambiguous. And they should stop describing the release in the notes as improved navigation when the navigation they improved was the only part of the app I could actually use. I will dictate the letter itself tomorrow when I am less annoyed, because at the moment every version I write in my head ends with a sentence I would not want in writing. Can you find me the reference for the switch thing though, I have got it somewhere in the folder from the training in March, and it is either in the slides or in the handout and I cannot remember which.

input: Okay, this is me thinking out loud about the reindex, so it is not a proposal yet and I will probably contradict myself somewhere in the middle. The situation is that the search index is rebuilt nightly from scratch, which takes four and a half hours and used to take 40 minutes, and the reason it has grown is not the document count, it is the number of fields we analyse per document, which has gone from nine to 31 over about two years because every team that wanted something searchable added a field and nobody has ever removed one. The nightly rebuild is the only path we have to a correct index. The nightly rebuild is the only path we have to a correct index. So when it fails, and it failed twice last month, the index is a day stale and there is nothing to do except run it again and wait, which means a failure at two in the morning is a bad afternoon for everybody. What I want is incremental updates plus a weekly full rebuild, with the weekly rebuild existing as a safety net rather than as the mechanism, so that if it slips a day nobody notices. The hard part is not the incremental path, it is knowing when the incremental path has diverged from the truth, because a silently wrong index is worse than a stale one, and stale we can at least detect by looking at a timestamp. So I think we need a checker that samples, say, a thousand documents an hour and compares the indexed version against the source of record, and alerts on any mismatch rather than on a mismatch rate, because a rate threshold is how you end up ignoring the first real bug. A thousand an hour is nothing in load terms, we do more than that in a minute of ordinary traffic. And whatever we build has to be restartable, because the thing that actually hurt us last month was not the failure itself, it was that a failed run left the temporary index behind and the next run refused to start until somebody deleted it by hand, which cost three hours of somebody's morning to work out because the error message says permission denied rather than saying there is a directory in the way. The second thing I keep going round on is what to do about the 31 fields. My instinct is to cut them back before we build anything, on the grounds that we are about to make the pipeline more complicated and it is cheaper to delete a field now than to migrate it twice. But the last time somebody tried to remove a field they could not find out who was querying it, because the query logs do not record which fields a query touched, only the raw query string, and half the queries are generated by a client library that expands into something nobody wrote by hand. So the honest sequence is probably to add field level query logging first, watch it for a month, then cut the fields nobody actually queries, and only after that change the indexing path. That is three months before we touch the thing we are actually trying to fix, which nobody is going to like when the complaint on the board says search is slow overnight. Maybe there is a middle route where we ship the incremental path for the nine original fields, which we know are used because the product is built on them, and leave the other 22 on the nightly rebuild until the logging tells us which of them matter. Two pipelines is ugly and I would normally argue against it, but two pipelines with a clear rule about which fields go where is less ugly than one pipeline that takes four and a half hours and falls over. The thing I have not thought about at all is the read side, because an incremental index changes when a query sees a write, and at the moment everybody reasons about it as whatever you wrote today is visible tomorrow, which is simple and wrong in the other direction. If writes become visible in seconds then some of the code that reads immediately after writing will start getting the new value where it used to get the old one, and I have no idea how much of that code exists. Probably some of it depends on the delay without anybody having decided that it should. Can you look at the reindex timings in the dashboard before we talk, specifically whether the four and a half hours is spread evenly or whether it is one stage, because if it is one stage then this whole conversation might be a profiling job rather than an architecture job, and I would much rather find that out before I write anything up. Also do not repeat any of this to Dana yet, she has heard three versions of the plan from me already this quarter and I would like the next one she hears to be the one I actually mean.

input: This is the running note for the Henderson group, seven people, arriving on the 12th and out on the 27th, and I will keep adding to it as things are confirmed so read the bottom first if you are looking for the latest. Flights are booked and the inbound is the evening one, landing at 19:40, which means we lose the first evening to the drive and I have told them that twice now because the itinerary they were sent originally said day one Bhaktapur and that was never realistic. So day one is the hotel in Kathmandu and nothing else, day two is Bhaktapur and Patan together which is a long day but it works, and the trek does not start until day four. The permits are the thing holding everything up. I have the TIMS cards for six of the seven and the seventh is stuck because I need her pass passport number for the form and the copy she sent through is cut off at the bottom of the page, and the number is exactly the part that is missing, so I have emailed her twice and I will ring tomorrow if there is nothing back. Everybody else is done and the cards are with the office in Thamel. On the trek itself, the teahouse at the second stop has changed hands since I was last up and the new owner wants the whole group's payment in advance, which is not how we have ever done it, and I would rather find an alternative than send money to somebody I have not met. There is another place about 40 minutes further on which I know is fine, and 40 minutes at the end of that day is not the end of the world, but it does mean the third day starts shorter, so I want to look at the whole schedule again rather than patch it. Two of the group are vegetarian and one of those does not eat egg, which is worth telling every lodge in advance rather than at the table, because the dal bhat is fine but the breakfast is where it goes wrong. Also the older gentleman, Mr Reid, has asked about altitude and whether the second night is too high, and I have said we can add a night at the lower lodge and I meant it, so if he asks again the answer is still yes and the cost difference is small. Can you chase those two directly rather than through the group email, because the group email goes to the son who booked it and he has been forwarding things a week late. I will send the final version once the permits are all in hand, and I would rather send it late and correct than early and wrong, given what happened with the Marsden group in the spring.

input: Notes on the trip for the file, and please keep the wording as I say it because the last version somebody tidied for me ended up sounding like a press release and I had to rewrite the whole thing. The short point is that the transfer at Frankfurt does not work and we should stop booking it. On paper it is 70 minutes, which sounds like plenty, but you cannot pass passport control with that connection unless the first flight lands early, because the queue at the transfer desk was 35 minutes on its own and there is a bus between the two piers that only runs every ten. I made it and my colleague did not, and she spent the night in a hotel the airline paid for and arrived in the middle of the first session, having missed the part she was actually there to hear. So the recommendation is a minimum of two hours for that airport specifically, and I would rather we wrote that down as a rule than left it to whoever is booking to notice. On the conference itself, the sessions were better than last year and the rooms were worse: two of the four rooms had no working microphone on the second day and the organisers dealt with it by asking speakers to project, which does not work in a room of 200 people and effectively excluded anybody hard of hearing from those sessions. I said so on the feedback form in those words. There was no induction loop in the main hall either, which the printed programme claimed there was, and I only checked because somebody in our group asked me to, so that was not optimism on their part, it was in writing and it was wrong, and I have kept the page. The useful part was the corridor rather than the programme, as it always is. I had three conversations that are worth following up and I will send the details separately, but the one that matters is with the group in Lyon who have the same problem we have with the annotation pipeline and have solved about half of it, and they are willing to share the tooling if we contribute the guidelines back. That seems to me a good trade and I would like to say yes before somebody in procurement invents a reason it is complicated. On expenses, I have the receipts for everything except the taxi on the last night, where the driver had no printer and I paid cash, and it was 28 including the tip. If that is a problem then it is a problem, but I am not inventing a receipt for it. Last thing, and this is a request rather than a report: if I am going again next year I would like to know before the abstracts deadline rather than after, because the whole point of going is to present something and I have now twice gone as an attendee because the decision came too late to submit anything.

input: We can, can roll the change back but I want to be honest about what that actually buys us, because the rollback only puts the old image back on the two web nodes and it does not touch the schema, and the schema is where the problem is. The migration added a not null column with a default, and the default was computed per row rather than as a constant, so the write path is now doing work it never used to do on every insert. Rolling back the image means the old code writes to a table that has a column it does not know about, which is fine for inserts because of the default, and not fine for the nightly export, which selects star and then positionally maps the columns. So my order would be to leave the image where it is, drop the default and backfill in batches of five thousand overnight, and only then decide about the rollback. If we do have to roll back before that, somebody has to pin the export to an explicit column list first, and that is a ten minute change that nobody has reviewed. I have written all of this in the incident channel as well but the channel is moving quickly and I would rather it was somewhere it can be read properly. The one thing I am not sure about is whether the read replicas have caught up, and until I know that I would not promise anybody a time.

input: Timeline for the Friday incident, and I will write it up properly later but I want the times down while I still remember them. 21:14 the first alert fires on checkout latency, and nobody acknowledges it because the rota had not been updated after Marek swapped his on-call week with Agnieszka. 21:31 a customer email arrives saying the basket empties itself, which is the first sign that this is not only slow but actually losing state. 21:40 I get paged by the secondary path and I am online at 21:44. The first thing I look at is the session store, because the basket lives there, and the session store is fine, it is the token service in front of it that is returning 503 on about one request in six. 22:02 we take the token service out of the load balancer in the Frankfurt zone and the error rate drops but does not go to zero. 22:19 Agnieszka finds that the deploy at 20:50 had shipped a config change that halved the connection pool. We put the old value back and the errors stop within a minute. We put the old value back and the errors stop within a minute. 22:35 we call it, and the last affected request is at 22:21 by the logs. Two things I want to come back to: the rota, because a swap that lives only in a private message is not a swap, and the pool size, because that number should not be in a config file that anybody can edit without a review.

input: I have been going round in circles on the pricing page all morning so I am going to say the whole thought out loud and then decide. The problem is not the number, the problem is that we are asking people to choose before they know what they are choosing between. Right now the free tier and the paid tier are described in the same eleven words each, and the only difference a visitor can actually see is the price, so of course they take the free one and of course they never come back. What I think we should do is stop describing tiers and start describing the moment somebody hits the wall. You hit the wall when you have more than one project. That is the moment. That is the moment, and everything on that page should be arranged around it. So the free tier keeps one project and says so in the heading rather than in a footnote, and the paid tier is not called Pro because Pro means nothing, it is called whatever the second project is worth to somebody. I am not sure about the annual toggle. Everybody has one, which is not a reason, and ours is doing the twenty percent thing where the monthly price is quietly the anchor. Leave it for now. The bit I want somebody to argue with me about is the heading, because if the heading is wrong then none of the rest of it matters and I have watched three people read that page and none of them read past it.

input: Status on the importer, and this is longer than usual because there are three separate things going on and only one of them is the thing I was asked to do. The importer itself is done and merged, it reads the vendor CSV in chunks of two thousand rows, validates against the schema before it touches the database, and writes a rejects file next to the input rather than failing the whole run, which is what the support team asked for. The part that is not done is the retry, because the vendor endpoint returns a 200 with an empty body when it is rate limiting us, which is not something you can retry on without also retrying genuinely empty days, and I do not want to guess. I think I think we should ask them, and if they will not change it then we key off the response time instead, because the rate limited response comes back in under fifty milliseconds and a real empty day takes about two seconds. The third thing is that Priyanka found the importer is being run twice on Tuesdays by two different cron entries, one of which nobody remembers adding, and it has been harmless because the writes are idempotent, but it doubles the vendor calls and that is probably why we are being rate limited at all. I have not deleted the second cron entry because I want somebody to say out loud that it is not theirs first. Review is open, the diff is large but most of it is the fixture files.

input: Notes for the post about writing schedules, and I want to keep the honest version rather than the version that makes me sound organised. The claim everybody makes is that you should write at the same time every day and the reason given is habit, and I do not think habit is the real reason. I think I think better in the morning, and that is a different claim, because it is about the quality of what comes out rather than about whether anything comes out at all. When I write in the evening I produce roughly the same number of words and about a third of them survive the next morning, which is not a scheduling problem, it is that in the evening I cannot tell the difference between a sentence that is finished and a sentence that is merely typed. So the advice I would actually give is to find the part of the day where your judgement is best and put the editing there, not the drafting, because drafting badly is recoverable and editing badly is not. The other thing I want to say, and this is the bit people will argue with, is that the two hundred words a day rule is fine for a book and useless for a post, because a post has to be one shape and you cannot get to a shape in two hundred word increments. Either write the whole thing badly in one sitting or do not start. I will soften that before it goes out but I do not want to lose it entirely.

input: Figures for the board pack and I want to flag the two places where our number and finance's number will not agree, because last quarter we found that out in the room. Revenue for the quarter is 1.42 million against a plan of 1.5, so we are 5.3% under, and the gap is almost entirely the two enterprise renewals that slipped from March into April rather than anything in the base. Gross margin is 71.4%, uh-huh, which is up 90 basis points on the quarter and the improvement is hosting, not pricing, so I would not describe it as pricing power in the commentary. Net retention is the number that will be argued about. We have it at 104% on the cohort definition we have always used, which counts a downgrade in the same month as an upgrade as net zero, and finance have it at 99% because they net it monthly. Both are defensible and they are not the same metric, and my suggestion is that we show ours with the definition written underneath it in one sentence rather than switching definitions this quarter and having to explain a break in the series. Cash is fine, 8.1 months of runway on the current burn, and the only thing that changes that materially is the hiring plan, which assumes six people in Q3 and we have hired one. I would rather present six and explain the delay than quietly restate it to two.

input: Referee notes on the submission, and my overall position is a major revision rather than a reject, because the experiment is sound and the framing is not. The authors claim a new result about transfer, but what they have measured is that a model which had had exposure to the target vocabulary during pretraining performs better than one which had not, and that is a finding about the pretraining corpus rather than about their method. Section 4 is where this becomes visible. Table 3 reports two conditions and the caption describes them as matched, but the second condition uses the 2024 crawl and the first uses the 2023 crawl, and the 2024 crawl contains the evaluation domain. I do not think this is deliberate, I think it is the sort of thing that happens when two students prepare two halves of a table, but it has to be fixed before the claim in the abstract can stand. The parts I would keep entirely are the ablation in 5.2 and the honest reporting of the failure at long context, which is the most useful paragraph in the paper and which a lot of authors would have left out. My concrete requests are three: rerun the matched condition on a single crawl, restate the abstract claim as being about vocabulary coverage, and report variance across seeds, because five seeds are mentioned in the text and only a mean appears in the table. If those are done I would accept it without a further round, and I am happy to be the reviewer who sees it again.

input: I want to get all of this down while it is in my head because I have to send it to the housing officer tomorrow and if I leave it until the morning I will write three lines and none of them will be the important ones. So the position is that the lift has been out since the 6th, which is sixteen days now, and I have reported it four times, twice by phone and twice through the online form, and each time I get a reference number and each time the reference number is different. The one from Tuesday is HR-2291. The one before that I do not have because the confirmation email went to the old address, which is a separate problem I have also reported. What I want to say to her is not that the lift is broken, because she knows that, it is that the process for reporting it is producing four separate tickets for one fault and nobody is joining them up. The practical effect on me is that I live on the fourth floor and I use a cane and I have not been out of the building since Thursday except for the two times a neighbour came up with me. I have not been out of the building since Thursday except for the two times a neighbour came up with me. I am not going to say that in a way that sounds like I want sympathy, because what I actually want is a date, but she needs to know that this is not an inconvenience about shopping bags. The other thing I want to raise is the notice. There was a paper notice put up in the entrance on the 9th and I did not know it was there for four days because nobody told me and I obviously cannot read it, and when my neighbour read it out it turned out to say that the repair was scheduled for the 12th, which came and went. So the request is a phone call rather than a letter, and if there has to be a letter then an email as well, and the email has to go to the address I gave them in March and not the one they have on the old tenancy record, because that is the account I cannot get into any more since the password reset went to a phone number I no longer use. I will say all of that in about six sentences tomorrow. Tonight I just want it written down so that when she asks me for the dates I am not counting backwards from memory while she waits, because that is what happened last time and I ended up agreeing that it had been about a week when it had been eleven days, and then that number is the one that goes in the file. One more thing and then I will stop. The neighbour who came up with me is the lady in flat two and she has a bad hip herself, and I am not going to keep asking her, so if the answer tomorrow is another two weeks then I want to know what they do in that situation, whether there is somebody who brings shopping or whether that is a different department I have to ring separately and start again with. And if it is a different department then I want the name of it spelled out, because the last time somebody gave me a department name over the phone I wrote down what it sounded like and it was not a real department, and then the person I rang next could not find it and told me I must have misunderstood. I did not misunderstand. Somebody said a word quickly and I wrote down the word I heard, and there is no way for me to check a word like that on my own, which is the part that people who can see a screen do not think about. So: the date, the department, and how it gets to me. Those three.

input: I am driving so this is going to ramble but the gist is that I do not think we should take the Fairfield job, and I want to explain why before I say it to them, because when I say it to them I want one sentence and not this. The money is fine. The money is actually better than fine, it is about a fifth more per day than the Whitmore contract, and if it were only the money I would have signed it last week. The problem is the access. They have two loading bays and both of them are shared with the tenant next door, and the tenant next door is a bakery that starts at four in the morning, so our window is either before four or after two in the afternoon, and after two in the afternoon the school run turns that road into a car park. I have sat in it. I have sat in it twice now, once for forty minutes with a full van, and forty minutes with a full van is not a scheduling problem, it is a cost, and nobody has put that cost in the quote because the quote was built off the Whitmore numbers where we drive straight in. The second thing, and this is the one that actually worries me, is that the site contact is the same man who ran the Peterlee job, and on Peterlee we were told the floor would be clear and it was not clear, and when we raised it he agreed it was not clear and then billed us for standing time anyway, which we did not chase because it was two hundred pounds and I had had enough of him by then. So it is not that I think he is dishonest exactly, it is that everything with him is a conversation and none of it is in writing, and we are not big enough to absorb another one of those. If we do take it then my conditions are that the access window goes in the contract in hours and not as reasonable access, that standing time is ours to bill and not his, and that we price the first week as a trial. And if he will not put the access window in writing then that is the answer, and honestly I think that is the answer, because I asked him for it in April and I asked him again in June and both times he said it would not be a problem, and it would not be a problem is not a term. Right, I am at the depot. Send me whatever the updated numbers are and I will look at them tonight, but do not tell them anything yet. Actually one more thing while I am sitting here. Whatever we decide, do not put the Fairfield quote and the Whitmore quote in the same email to me, because last time you did that I read the wrong total on the phone at a set of lights and told a client a number that was not his number, and that took two weeks to unpick. Separate emails, subject line with the site name first, and the total in the first line rather than at the bottom under the breakdown. I know that is a fussy request. It is a fussy request because I am reading these things in a van and not at a desk, and the breakdown is for the office and the total is for me. Same with the Peterlee invoices if he ever sends them, which he will not.

input: Notes on Mrs Okonjo, second visit, and I want the detail down because the referral letter said frozen shoulder and I do not think that is what this is. Range on the right is better than the letter suggests, she gets to about a hundred and ten degrees of passive abduction and about ninety active, and the end feel is not capsular, it is guarded, which is a different thing. Where she is genuinely restricted is external rotation at the side, maybe twenty degrees, and that is the one that fits a capsular pattern, so I am not dismissing the referral, I am saying the picture is mixed. Pain is worst at night and she describes it as being in the upper arm rather than the joint, and she has been sleeping in a chair for three weeks, which is its own problem because she is seventy one and the chair is doing nothing for her back. Strength testing was limited by pain rather than by weakness as far as I could tell, but I could not isolate the rotator cuff properly today and I have written that down rather than guessing. Plan is three times a week of the pendulum and the wall walk, twelve repetitions each and not to the point of pain, and I have written it on the sheet in large print because she said she could not read the last one. I have moved the app appointment to the Thursday because the Tuesday clashes with her dialysis, and she was quite worried about telling me that, which tells me something about how the last place made her feel. Two things for the letter back. First, ask whether the imaging was of the shoulder or of the cervical spine, because if the arm pain is referred then everything I have just written is the wrong treatment and I would rather find that out now than in six weeks. Second, the diabetes is not mentioned anywhere in the referral and she volunteered it today, and frozen shoulder with diabetes is a different prognosis conversation and she has not had that conversation with anybody. I have not started her on anything loaded. If the Thursday works then I will reassess external rotation at three visits and if it has not moved at all by then I will send her back rather than keep her. Two more things for the file. She is on her own during the day and her son does the shopping at the weekend, so anything I give her to do has to be doable with one arm and no help, which rules out the doorframe stretch I would normally start with because it needs her to hold a position she cannot get into unassisted. I have given her the pendulum leaning on the kitchen counter instead and I have written the counter into the sheet so she does not try it on the back of the chair, which is what she did last time and the chair moved. And she should not be sleeping in that chair for another three weeks. I have said that to her twice now and I do not think she believes it is important, so I would like it in the letter as well, in a sentence of its own, because a thing in a letter from a doctor lands differently than the same thing from me in her kitchen, and I would rather use that than keep repeating myself and become the person who nags her about furniture.

input: Two things about the clinic system before I forget them, and neither is clinical, so pass them to whoever is dealing with the software people. The app appointment reminders are going out at four in the morning. I do not know why and I do not think anybody chose it, but three patients have now told me they were woken by their phone, and one of them is the gentleman with the sleep problem who I have spent two visits telling to keep his phone out of the bedroom. So either the reminder goes out at a reasonable hour or we turn it off for the over seventies, and I would rather fix the time than turn anything off, because since the reminders started the non attendance rate has gone from about one in six to about one in twelve and that is the single most useful thing that has happened here in a year. The second thing is the notes field. It is one box with no structure and it holds about two hundred characters before it silently stops accepting them, which I found out last month when half a plan disappeared between the visit and the letter. I have been writing the real notes elsewhere ever since, which is not a solution, it is me working around a bug. What I need is either a longer field or a warning when it is full, and if the answer is that a longer field is a big change then the warning is fine and I will keep writing the long version somewhere else. The other thing I would ask for, and this is a want rather than a need, is that the reminder text should say the room number, because we moved the physiotherapy rooms in February and people are still going to the first floor and then walking back down, and for a patient with a shoulder that is thirty seconds of nothing but for a patient with a knee it is the most painful part of their day. None of this is urgent except the four in the morning one, and that one I would like fixed this week if somebody can simply change a number in a settings page. And a third thing which I forgot, which is the cancellation flow. If a patient cancels through the application it does not free the slot, it marks it as cancelled and leaves it grey, and grey slots are not offered to anybody, so we have been running with two or three dead slots a week that look full on my screen and are not. Whoever built that presumably meant it as a safety feature so a slot is not given away twice, and I understand that, but the effect is that a cancellation with four days notice is worth nothing to us when it should be worth a whole appointment. If the fix is that a cancelled slot becomes bookable again after somebody confirms it, that is fine, I will confirm them, it takes a second. What I cannot do is spot them, because they look the same as a booked slot unless I click on each one.

input: Right, minutes of the residents meeting, seven of us there and I am writing this from my own notes so if I have somebody's number wrong then correct me rather than arguing about it in the group. First item was the bins. The collection has moved to Wednesday, it moved in March and the notice went to the letting agent rather than to us, which is why nobody knew, and the upshot is that the bins have been going out on Tuesday night and coming back in on Thursday and standing full in between. Agreed that whoever is first up puts them out on Tuesday night anyway because that is the only night anybody is reliably in, and that Dan will put a laminated sheet on the inside of the door with the day on it in large type. Second item, the front door closer. It has been slamming since the summer and two people have raised it separately, and the quote we have is four hundred and twenty pounds which nobody thinks is reasonable for a closer. Agreed to get two more quotes and that Nadia will ask the company who did number fourteen because theirs was done for about half that. Third item was the parking and this is the one that took an hour. The two marked spaces belong to flats one and two and everybody knows that, but the unmarked space at the end has been used by whoever gets there first for about six years, and the new tenant in flat five has started leaving a cone there, which is what actually caused the meeting. What was said, and I am trying to write this fairly, is that there is no legal claim on the unmarked space by anybody, and that we we should not go to the freeholder about it because once the freeholder is involved the likely answer is that the space gets marked for nobody and we all lose it. Agreed that the cone goes, that nobody parks there for longer than a weekend, and that we revisit it in six months if it is still causing trouble. Fourth item, the intercom, deferred because the person who knows about it was not there. Fifth, and this was not on the agenda, the damp in the stairwell has come back in the same corner as two winters ago and it is above the flashing that was repaired then, so it is the same fault and not a new one. Agreed to write to the freeholder about that one, because that is structural and it is his, and to send the photographs from the last time alongside the new ones so it is obvious it is a recurrence. Next meeting is the second Tuesday in November at Nadia's. Two things that were raised at the end and are not really items. Somebody asked whether the meeting could be earlier in the evening because seven is difficult with children, and nobody objected to half past six in principle but nobody wanted to be the person who decides it, so I am putting it in these minutes as a question and whoever replies first effectively decides. And the other one is the group itself. Three people have said separately that they find it stressful because it is used for both the bins and for arguments, and the suggestion was a second group for anything urgent, which I think is how you end up with two groups nobody reads. My own view, which is not a minute, is that we keep one group and the meeting minutes go in it as a message rather than as a photograph of a piece of paper, because the photograph is what stopped Nadia reading the last set and she is the one who chases the quotes.
