input: Note on chapter four before I send it back to Gwen, and I am dictating it because I have the draft open in front of me and I lose my place every time I switch windows. The chapter is nearly there and what is wrong with it is structural rather than anything to do with the evidence, so please do not read this as me reopening the argument. The problem is that three of the recommendations are buried inside paragraphs and a fourth one is in a footnote, and a reader who skims, which is every reader we actually have, will finish the chapter thinking it recommends nothing. That is the whole point of the note. Two specific changes and then the reasoning. The section heading on page 28 should read Transport slash Access rather than Transport and Access, because the two are treated as one thing throughout the chapter and the and in the heading promises a section about each. And the Bridgend quote on page 31 runs to about ninety words, of which the useful part is the first clause and the last one, so I want the middle cut and the cut marked with dot dot dot rather than paraphrased, because paraphrasing somebody's account of losing her bus route is precisely the thing we said in the methods section that we would not do. Now the reasoning. The evidence is fine. The two interviews I was worried about in September both hold up against the council figures, and the figures themselves came back from the statistics team unchanged, which is more than we got last year. So I do not want to touch the argument. What I want is for the argument to be findable by somebody who has eleven minutes and four other chapters to get through, and at the moment it is not. One thing I would like Gwen's view on rather than deciding myself, which is whether the recommendations should be repeated in the executive summary or whether having them in both places makes the chapter look thinner than it is. I can see it either way and she has read more of these than I have.

input: Notes on the Djibouti corridor before the Monday call, and I am recording this in the yard because the office is full of people arguing about something else. Three things and none of them are new, but all three are getting worse and I would rather they were said out loud than raised one at a time over six weeks. The first is Yonas. He is our star driver on that run, he has done it more times than anybody else here, and he is leaving in March to drive for the cement company, and we have known that since August and done nothing about it. Nobody else on the roster has run the corridor in the rainy season and that is not a thing you learn from a briefing. The second is the customs point at Galafi. The queue there has gone from a half day to a day and a half since they changed the paperwork, and the drivers are absorbing it by sleeping in the cab, which is not a plan, it is a thing that has not gone wrong yet. input: Right, this is the long version of the carry screen argument for the risk committee pack, and I am dictating it because it is going to take a while and I would rather get the reasoning down while it is still in the order I think it rather than the order that survives a slide deck. Start with what the screen is for, because half the disagreement in the room last week was people arguing about different things. The screen exists to stop us putting size on in names where the carry looks attractive and the only reason it looks attractive is that the volatility is about to go up. It is not a signal. Nobody on the desk has ever claimed it is a signal. It is a filter, and a filter that removes twenty names and keeps eighty is doing its job even if none of the eighty makes money, because the eighty are the ones we then have an actual view on. That distinction has been lost somewhere between the desk and the committee and I want it back in writing. Now the mechanics, and this is the part I need somebody to check rather than agree with. The screen runs nightly. It takes the trailing three month realised volatility for every name in the universe, and it drops anything where vol greater than or equal to 25 because at that level the carry number is noise dressed up as an edge. Then for what survives it ranks on carry divided by vol, which is the whole of the cleverness and it is not very clever, and it keeps the top quartile. There is one override, which is that anything the credit team has flagged in the last five days comes out regardless of where it ranks, and that override has fired four times this year and been right three of those times, which is better than I expected when we put it in. The output is a list, not a portfolio, and it goes to the desk at seven in the morning. So far so ordinary. Here is the part the committee actually objected to, and I think they were half right. The volatility cut is a hard cut. A name at 24.8 stays and a name at 25.1 goes, and there is nothing principled about where that line sits, it came out of a backtest that ended in a period where 25 happened to separate the two regimes cleanly, and I would not defend the number itself for a second. What I would defend is having a cut at all, because the alternative that keeps getting proposed is a smooth weighting, and a smooth weighting means every name is in the portfolio a little bit, which is how you end up with two hundred positions and no view on any of them. So my proposal is that we keep the hard cut, move the number to whatever the current regime says rather than what the backtest said, and review it quarterly rather than never. Two things I want to be honest about before anybody signs this off. The first is that the desk is genuinely divided on it and I am putting forward the majority view rather than a consensus, and Wen thinks the whole screen should be retired, and her argument is better than mine on the theory even if mine is better on the operations. The second is that a good half of the committee's objection last week was that somebody in the deck had confused percent with percentage points in two places, and once that came out nobody trusted the rest of the numbers, which is fair. That has been fixed and it was my mistake rather than the analyst's. One last plus and then I will stop. Since the screen went in, the number of names we size up and then unwind inside a fortnight has fallen by about two thirds, and whatever else is arguable about the methodology, that part is not.

input: This is my note on the Kadikoy drawings before the coordination meeting, and I am recording it rather than writing it because there is a lot to say and I say it faster than I type, so take it as thinking out loud rather than a formal comment sheet. The short version is that the structural set and the services set have drifted apart again and the reason is not carelessness on anybody's part, it is that we changed the floor to ceiling height in September and only half the consequences of that were followed through. Let me go through it floor by floor because that is the only way it makes sense. On the ground floor everything is fine. The double height space works, the columns land where they landed before, and the only comment I have is a small one about the reveal at the entrance, which is drawn as a sharp edge and will not survive being built by anybody working at the pace this contractor works at. On the first floor is where it starts. The services drawing still shows the old ceiling void, which means the ducts are drawn in a space that no longer exists, and nobody has flagged it because the plan looks identical, it is only in section that you see it. That is the sort of thing that gets found on site and then gets solved on site, badly, by somebody with a grinder. On the second floor the same problem exists and it is worse, because the second floor is where the meeting rooms are and the acoustic ceiling was the whole point of the ceiling height conversation in the first place. If the ducts stay where they are drawn we lose the acoustic ceiling, and if we lose the acoustic ceiling then the meeting rooms are just rooms, and the client will notice that within a week of moving in even if he cannot say why. The third floor is fine, and the fourth floor is fine, and I want to say that clearly because a note like this reads as though everything is broken and it is two floors out of five. Now the thing I want to argue about in the meeting, which is not really about the drawings. Every time we change a dimension there is a conversation about who tells the services engineer, and every time the answer is that whoever remembers tells him, and every time that works until it does not. I would rather we had a dull mechanism than a reliable person, because the reliable person goes on holiday. My suggestion is that any change to a level, a height or a grid goes on one list, and the list goes out on a Friday whether or not there is anything on it, and if there is nothing on it that takes ten seconds to read and everybody gets the reassurance. That is a plus for me even in the weeks when nothing changes. On the drawings themselves I have marked the sections in red and there are eleven marks, and only three of them are the ceiling problem, the rest are small things: a door swing that fouls a radiator, a stair nosing detail that is drawn twice and differently, and a run of glazing where the mullion spacing does not divide into the bay and somebody has drawn a slightly narrower panel at the end and hoped nobody would look. I have looked. It is a hundred and forty millimetres narrower and you will see it from the street. The last thing, and it is the one I feel worst about, is that the client asked in July whether the ceiling change would affect the services and somebody told him no, and I do not know who and I do not want to find out, but he is going to remember that he asked. I would rather we opened the meeting with that than had it arrive halfway through.

input: Okay this is the setup note for the demo build so that whoever runs it at the expo on Saturday is not learning any of this on the day, and I am talking it through because the written version I made last time was three lines long and useless. Read the whole thing once before you touch anything, because the order is the part that matters and none of the individual steps are hard. Some background first, because it explains why the setup is odd. The demo is the same build as the internal one except that saving is turned off and the intro is skipped, and both of those are flags rather than a separate branch, which was a deliberate decision after the disaster in March when we shipped a demo branch that had drifted three weeks behind the main one and nobody noticed until a journalist found a bug we had already fixed. So there is one build. The demo is that build with two flags. If somebody tells you on Saturday that there is a demo branch, there is not, and please do not create one. The machine is the small black one, not the tower, and it has the graphics card we borrowed rather than the one in the spec sheet, which matters because the frame pacing is different and the fix for that is in the config rather than in the game. Now the hardware, which is where the actual trouble is. The controllers pair over Bluetooth and they will pair to the wrong machine if the tower is switched on, so switch the tower off at the wall and not just at the button, because at the button it still advertises. There are four controllers and only three are charged, and the fourth one takes about two hours from flat, so put it on when you arrive rather than when you need it. The screen is the venue's and we have not seen it, so budget half an hour for that going wrong, and take the long HDMI cable rather than trusting theirs. If the screen refuses to do anything sensible at 4K then drop to 1080 and nobody at a three metre viewing distance will ever know, and I would rather that than you spending forty minutes on a resolution nobody asked about. Somebody will ask you about the release date. The answer is that we are not saying yet, and that is not me being coy with you, it is genuinely not decided, so please do not improvise a quarter. Okay, the actual startup sequence, and this is the bit to get right. Power the machine, wait for it to settle, then start the server before the game, because if the game goes first it caches an empty manifest and the only fix is a restart. The server is a one liner and it wants to be pointed at the venue config rather than the default one, so run it with the config in tilde slash dot config slash expo slash venue dot json, and then confirm it is actually up by opening localhost colon 8080 in the browser on that machine before you launch anything. Once you have seen that page you are safe. If it misbehaves during the day, the log is worth keeping rather than losing, so append it with the log path and greater than greater than run dot log so we still have the earlier part of the session, and then message me the file rather than describing what you saw, because what you saw and what happened are usually different things. Last thing, and it is a plus rather than an instruction: the star rating on the itch page went up three times this month and most of that was after the trailer, so the point of Saturday is the trailer as much as the build.

input: Handover note on the training scripts before I go back to uni, and I am talking it through because the README is already wrong in two places and I would rather say why than fix it badly. Everything runs from the repository root rather than from inside the scripts folder, so it is dot slash scripts slash train dot py and not the other way round, and the reason is that the config loader resolves paths relative to where you invoked it and not relative to itself. That is a design decision I inherited and I do not like it, but changing it would break the two notebooks Farhan uses. The other thing is naming. The checkpoint files use camel case and everything else in the repo uses snake case, which is my fault, and it means the loader has a small mapping table in the middle of it that looks like a bug and is not. If anybody has a spare afternoon that mapping table is the thing to delete, and deleting it properly means renaming the checkpoints, which means telling Farhan first.

input: Incident notes for last night while it is still fresh in my head. The alert fired at 01:12 our time and the first thing I did was look at the checkout service, because that is where the errors were showing and the error rate there was about 8%, which is high but not the worst we have seen, so I did not page anybody else straight away. What I missed for the first twenty minutes is that checkout was fine and the thing behind it was not, and the read readiness probe on the payments pod had been failing since about 00:40 without ever taking the pod out of rotation, because it is configured with a failure threshold of 30 and a period of ten seconds, so it needs five whole minutes of continuous failure before it does anything and it kept recovering just inside that window. So traffic kept going to a pod that could not talk to the database and roughly one request in twelve landed on it, which matches the error rate almost exactly. I rolled the pod at 01:48 and the errors went to zero inside a minute, and then I sat and watched it for half an hour because I did not believe it. Actions are, drop the failure threshold to 6, alert on probe failures rather than on error rate, and work out why that pod lost its connection pool in the first place, which I have not done.

input: Handover for whoever picks up the pager next week, and I am dictating this on the way home so it will ramble a bit. Read readiness probe output before you restart anything, because we have had two incidents this quarter where somebody rolled a pod that was perfectly healthy and the actual fault was upstream of it, and the probe output is the quickest way to tell those two apart. The payments pod is the one to watch. It is on chart version 4.2.1, the values file lives at deploy/payments/values-prod.yaml, and the connection pool size in there is 20 which is almost certainly too low for the traffic we now get on Fridays, but changing it needs a database side change as well so do not touch it on your own. If the pool is exhausted you will see it in the pod logs as a wait timeout rather than as an error, so grep for wait timeout and not for error. The other thing is the nightly export at 02:30. It has failed twice, both times because the bucket credentials had rotated and nobody updated the secret, and both times it failed silently and wrote a zero byte file, so if anybody asks whether the export ran the answer is that a file existing does not mean it ran. Ring me if the payments pod goes again, I would rather be woken than read about it.

input: This is for the Thursday review, and I would rather send you a long note than try to say it in the meeting. The pilot ran for six weeks on the two Manchester sites and the headline is that the drop out rate came down from 31% to 19%, which is a bigger move than we expected and is the number I want to talk about. The caveat is that the two sites are not comparable, because the Oldham site had a full time coordinator from the first week and the Salford site did not get one until week four, and the Salford numbers only start improving in week five, so a fair reading is that the coordinator is doing the work rather than the app. The other thing worth saying is that the people who stayed in the programme used the reminder feature about four times a week, and the people who left used it once or not at all, but I cannot tell you which way that causation runs and I would not put it in the summary as though I could. On the funding question, we have have not heard anything from the Trust since the acknowledgement in March, and I have chased twice, so I am assuming nothing and building the September plan as though the answer is no. If it comes back positive we can widen it to Salford and Oldham both, which is what I would want anyway.

input: Notes on the reviewer comments before I forget them, and I will tidy this into a proper reply tomorrow. Reviewer two is right about the baseline and I am not going to argue with it, because we compared against the 2023 configuration and by the time we submitted there had been a release that changed the default tokeniser, so our baseline was weaker than the one a reader would reproduce today. That is a rerun rather than a rebuttal. Reviewer one is a harder problem, because the objection is that the effect could come from the ordering of the training data rather than from the method, and we had had the same worry ourselves in February and never resolved it properly, we just fixed the seed and moved on. So the honest answer is that we cannot rule it out with the runs we have, and the cheap version of the experiment is three seeds on the small split, which is about nine hours on the shared machine and can be done before the deadline on the 14th. Reviewer three asks for a limitations paragraph and that costs nothing, so I will write it and it will say the two things above plus the fact that everything here is English only. I would rather concede all three points and rerun the baseline than write a clever reply that a fourth reviewer takes apart.

input: Weekly update, and it is longer than usual because the run finished last night and I want to write it down while I still remember what I changed. The short version is that the 0.6B with the new data mix is better than the last one on everything except the thing I care about most, and I do not fully understand why yet. The training itself was uneventful, 3 epochs, batch size 16 with gradient accumulation of 4, learning rate 1e-4 on a cosine schedule with 200 warmup steps, which is the same as run 11 except that run 11 had 2 epochs, and the loss curve here looks almost identical to run 11 until about step 1800 and then this one keeps going down for another 400 steps before it flattens out. Eval is where it gets interesting. On the held out set it goes from 91.2 to 93.8 exact match, and on the no-op slice, which is the one I actually care about, it goes from 97 down to 94.6, so it has got better at editing and worse at leaving things alone, which is exactly the trade I was told to avoid. I went through 60 of the no-op failures by hand this morning and about 40 of them are the same failure, the model turns a perfectly ordinary sentence into a list when the speaker happened to say three things in a row, and the reason is almost certainly that I doubled the layout examples in this mix without doubling the counterexamples that go with them. So the fix is not a hyperparameter, the fix is data, and I would rather write 200 more counterexamples than tune the learning rate again. The other thing worth writing down is that the check checkpoint at step 2000 is better on the no-op slice than the final one at step 2400, only slightly, 95.4 against 94.6, but it is consistent across all three seeds, which makes me think the last few hundred steps are where it learns to be too eager. I have kept both and they are in the bucket under runs/2026-08-19/ with the config sitting next to them. Two smaller things. First, the tokenizer warning that we have been ignoring for weeks does actually matter, because it was quietly dropping the leading space on the target, and that is worth about half a point of exact match on its own, and I only found it because a diff looked strange to me and not because anything failed. Second, evaluation takes 40 minutes now and most of that is loading the model 6 times in a row, so I will cache it between slices and that should get us to about 10 minutes, which matters because I am running it four or five times a day. What I need from you before Thursday is a decision on whether we care more about the edit metric or the no-op metric, because I can move either one and I cannot move both at the same time, and I would much rather you tell me which it is than have me guess now and defend the guess in the review. If I do not hear from you I am going to assume the no-op slice wins, because that is what the spec says and because a model that edits text nobody asked it to edit is the one people uninstall.

input: This is the handover for the ingest pipeline and I am recording it rather than writing it because I leave on Friday and there is more here than I will type. Check checkpoint sizes before you copy anything between environments, because the staging bucket has a 5 GB object limit that production does not have, and the last two people who moved a checkpoint across found out about that limit halfway through a copy that then left a truncated file behind with a perfectly normal looking name. If you see a checkpoint that is exactly 5 GB it is truncated, it is not a coincidence. The pipeline itself is three stages and only the middle one is interesting. Stage one reads the vendor drop from sftp at 03:15, and it is dumb on purpose, it does not validate anything, it just lands the file in raw/ with the date in the name and writes a row to the manifest table. Stage two is the parser and that is where everything goes wrong when it goes wrong, because the vendor changes their column order about twice a year without telling anybody and we match on header name rather than position for exactly that reason, so if you ever see a change that makes the parser match on position, that change is wrong no matter how much faster it is. Stage three writes to the warehouse and takes about 20 minutes, and if it fails it is safe to rerun because the write is idempotent on the natural key, which is the vendor reference plus the drop date and not the row id, and the row id changes on every parse so do not use it for anything. The alerting is deliberately quiet. There is one alert, it fires when the manifest table has no row for today by 05:00, and that is the only condition that has ever mattered in two years. Everything else is a dashboard and nobody looks at the dashboard, and I would leave it that way rather than add alerts that get muted in a month. Two things I never finished. The retention job still deletes from raw/ after 90 days but it does not delete the parsed copies, so we are holding about 4 TB we do not need, and there is a ticket for it that has been open since March. And the vendor sends us a second file on the last working day of the month that nothing consumes, it just sits there, and I have asked twice what it is for and never got an answer, so either it matters to somebody who has never mentioned it or it can be turned off. If something breaks and you cannot work out which stage, look at the manifest table first, because the row tells you which stage last touched the drop and that has saved me an hour more times than I can count. Ring me if it is really bad, I would rather be asked than read about it later.

input: Notes from the retro before I lose the shape of it, and this is for me rather than for the team channel, so it is going to be blunt in places. The outage was 47 minutes and the customer facing part of it was about 20 of those, and the thing I keep coming back to is that we had three separate signals in the hour before it and not one of them reached a human being. The disk alert fired at 14:02 into a channel that was archived back in June. The latency graph was visibly wrong from about 14:10, and Priya says she did look at it and assumed somebody else had it, which is a completely reasonable thing to assume and is also how this happens. And the support queue had two tickets by 14:15 that said the same thing in different words, and both of them were tagged as a billing question because that is what the customer thought it was. So the failure is not the disk. The disk is boring, the disk filled up because the log rotation job has been silently failing since the base image changed, and that is a two line fix that Marek has already done. The failure is that we have three routes for a signal and all three of them end somewhere nobody is standing. On the human side, and this is the part I do not want to write in the channel, the reason nobody escalated for 25 minutes is that the two people who were confident enough to escalate were both off, and the two who were on shift are both new, and I have been saying since February that we would find out about that gap the hard way. So it is on me, not on them, and I will say that in the retro itself as well. Dave brought me a double double and we went through the timeline on paper, and doing it on paper rather than in the doc is what made the three signals obvious, because on paper you draw them and then you draw where they went and the page is just empty on the right hand side. I am going to keep doing that. What I want out of this, and I would rather have three things that happen than ten that do not, is that every alert route gets checked against a channel that exists, the support queue gets a rule that pages when two tickets in ten minutes mention the same product area, and the escalation path stops depending on who happens to be brave. And we should should have caught it in the readiness review in May, because it is on the checklist and the checklist was signed, and I would like to know whether the review is a real review or whether it is a form we fill in, because if it is a form then I would rather delete it than pretend. I will write the customer note tonight, and I am going to say the number, 47 minutes, rather than say brief interruption, because they can read a graph as well as we can.

input: This is my read on the external review and I want it on record before the call on Thursday, because I suspect the call is going to be about tone rather than about findings. There are eleven findings and nine of them are fair. The two I would push back on are the session fixation one, which is a real class of bug but is not reachable in our flow because the session is minted after the redirect and not before it, and the dependency one, where they have flagged a transitive package as vulnerable and the vulnerable code path is a command line entry point we never invoke. I would rather say plainly that those two are accepted risks with a reason than argue about severity, because arguing about severity is how a report turns into a negotiation and then nobody trusts the numbers. Of the nine, three are worth doing this week. The first is the admin endpoint that is still reachable from the office network, and the concern is that that endpoint predates the gateway and so it never got the same authentication path as everything else, which means the only thing protecting it is an IP allowlist that also covers the guest wifi. That is the one I would fix first even though they scored it medium, because the fix is small and the blast radius is not. The second is token lifetime. We issue refresh tokens with a 90 day expiry and rotate nothing, and the review is right that this is indefensible, and the reason it is indefensible is that we chose 90 days in 2023 for a mobile client that no longer exists. Fourteen days plus rotation is where I would land, and yes that will generate support tickets in the first week, and I would take the tickets. The third is logging. We log the full authorization header on a 401, which is exactly the thing you do not do, and it has been that way for about eighteen months, and every one of those logs is in the same index that half the company can read. That needs the log line changed and it also needs the index purged, and the purge is the part somebody will forget, so put it in the same ticket rather than a follow up. The remaining six are hygiene, and they are real, and they will sit in the backlog like every hygiene finding I have ever seen unless we attach them to something. My suggestion is that we take them as a single piece of work in the next quarter with one owner rather than six tickets with none. On the report itself, I want us to publish it internally with the two pushbacks written underneath rather than summarise it, because a summary of a security review is how you get a second review that finds the same things. And whoever is on the call should say out loud that the admin endpoint predates the gateway, because it explains nine years of decisions in one sentence and it is true.

input: Okay I am in the car so this is going to ramble a bit, this is my read on the Fairhaven renewal after the call this morning. They are going to renew, I am ninety percent sure they are going to renew, but they are going to make us work for it and the working is all going to be about the seat count. So the question everybody keeps asking me is whether we should have discounted last year. Should we have discounted last year? No. We should not, and the reason is that the whole problem this year is that they think 40 seats is expensive, and if we had gone to 32 dollars a seat last year they would think 40 seats is expensive and we would be making less money while they thought it. The price is not the issue. The issue is that they bought 40 seats for a team that was 40 people and the team is now 28 people, so they are looking at a bill for 12 seats that nobody logs into, and honestly if I were them I would be annoyed about that too. So what I want to do is go in and offer to move them to 30 seats at the same rate, not a discount, a smaller number of seats at the same rate, because that is a number they can defend internally and it does not set fire to the rate card for everybody else. And if they push past that and ask for 30 seats at a lower rate then we talk, but I want to see them push first, because the last two times I have opened with the discount and the last two times they have taken the discount and then asked for the seat reduction as well.

input: Okay, this is for Sunil and it is going to be long, because I have been stuck on the same thing for three days and I would rather explain the whole thing once than send it to you in five messages across a week. So the setup is the same one I described to you before, I am training a LoRA adapter on top of the 0.6B model with rank 16 and alpha 32, and the loss is masked to the completion only, which I am fairly confident is right because when I trained without the mask the model learned to repeat the prompt back at me before it answered, and that stopped the moment I masked it. The data is 1,200 rows of my own dictation cleaned up by hand, and about 40 percent of those rows are no-ops where the output is the same as the input, and that 40 percent is deliberate because the first adapter I trained edited absolutely everything, including sentences that were already correct. So here is where I am stuck. On short inputs it is good. On short inputs it is honestly better than I expected, it fixes the retraction cases, it leaves the questions alone, it does not answer anything, and the no-op rate on held out short rows is around where I want it. On long inputs it falls apart, and it falls apart in a specific way, which is that it does not truncate and it does not refuse, it rewrites. I give it four hundred words of me talking and I get back two hundred words of much tidier prose that says roughly the same thing in a voice that is not mine. Nothing is missing exactly, it is just been through a summariser. And the first thing I want to ask you is whether that is a data problem or a training problem, because I can argue it both ways and I have been arguing it with myself for three days. The data argument is that almost all my rows are short, my median input is something like eleven words, so the model has never seen a long example and it is doing the only thing it knows how to do, which is edit heavily, because on short rows heavy editing is correct. The training argument is that the sequence length is 1,024 and the long inputs are getting truncated during training in a way I have not noticed, and the model is learning to stop early. I did try to test that second one and this is where I want you to check my reasoning, because I do not trust it. I took one 600 word input and I ran it through the base model with no adapter, and the base model also shortened it, which I read as evidence that the adapter is not the cause. But the base model shortens everything, that is its whole personality, so I am not sure that test proves anything at all. Does that test actually distinguish the two hypotheses, or have I just shown that both models are bad at long text for possibly different reasons? The other thing is the packing. I am packing multiple examples into one sequence to make the batches efficient, and the padding is masked, but I have not verified that the attention is actually blocked across the boundary between two packed examples, and if it is not blocked then a long example is being trained with a completely unrelated short example sitting in its context. Is that worth checking before I change anything else, or is it a thing every implementation already handles and I am inventing a problem? I ask because I have now spent three days on this and two of those days went on things that turned out to already be handled. What I think I should do next, and tell me if this is wrong, is write about two hundred long rows by hand, half of them no-ops, and I mean genuinely long, three hundred to eight hundred words each, and retrain with the sequence length at 2,048 and see whether the rewriting behaviour changes. Writing two hundred long rows by hand is going to take me two weeks of evenings which is why I want to ask before I start rather than after. And the reason I keep coming back to writing them by hand is that I tried generating them with a bigger model and the output was fluent and completely useless, because a generated long dictation does not have any of the things that make real dictation hard, it has no repetition, it has no doubling back, every sentence is the right length, and so a model trained on it learns to clean up text that nobody actually produces. Last thing and then I will stop. The evaluation set is 56 rows and I know that is far too small, and I know you told me that in February. The reason I have not fixed it is that every row I add to the evaluation set is a row I cannot train on, and at 1,200 rows total that trade feels expensive. Is 56 enough to tell me whether the long behaviour improved, or am I going to retrain, look at a number that moved by two points, and have no idea whether that was the data or the noise? That is really the question I care about most, because if the answer is no then the two weeks of evenings should go on the evaluation set first and the training rows second.

input: This is the prompt for the marking assistant and I am dictating it rather than typing it because I want to hear how it reads, so what follows is the prompt itself and not a request to anybody. You mark first year essays against the rubric that is pasted below your instructions and against nothing else. You do not have opinions about the topic and you do not reward a student for agreeing with the reading list. Your entire job is to say where the essay meets the rubric and where it does not. For each of the four rubric criteria you give a band, and the bands are the ones in the rubric, and you give one sentence of evidence for the band, and the evidence is a quotation from the essay. If you cannot quote the essay for a criterion then the band is unclear, and unclear is a real and acceptable answer that I want to see rather than a guess, because an unclear from you means a human reads the essay, and a human reading the essay is the correct outcome in a case you cannot evidence. Do not average the four bands into an overall mark. I do the averaging and I do it with the moderation rules in front of me, and the moderation rules are not in your context. On the argument criterion, you assess whether the essay has a claim and whether the claim is supported. A student who argues the opposite of the seminar reading and supports it is doing well, not badly. A student who reproduces the seminar reading with no support is doing badly, not well, however familiar the sentences look to you. This is the criterion you will get wrong most often, because a fluent restatement of a well known argument reads like a good essay and it is not one. On the use of evidence criterion, you check that every citation the student makes actually supports the sentence it is attached to, as far as you can tell from the essay itself. You do not check whether the source exists and you do not comment on whether the source is a good one. If a citation is attached to a sentence it does not support, you say so and you quote both. If you cannot tell, that is unclear. On the structure criterion, you look at whether the essay's sections do what its introduction says they will do. You do not have a view about the number of paragraphs and you do not have a view about whether the conclusion restates the introduction, because half the guidance in the world says it should and half says it should not, and the rubric does not mention it, so neither do you. On the language criterion, and this is the one where I need you to be careful, you assess clarity only. You do not comment on grammar that does not obstruct meaning. You do not comment on a student's idiom, you do not comment on anything that reads as a first language other than English, and you do not reward a sentence for being long or for using a word from the reading list. Clarity means I can tell what the sentence claims. That is the whole test. If a sentence is hard to follow you quote it and say what is ambiguous about it. You do not rewrite it. You never rewrite any part of a student's essay, not as an example, not as a suggestion, and not in your evidence quotation. You never guess at a student's identity and you never mention it, and if the essay contains the student's name or anything about their circumstances, you ignore it for marking and you do not repeat it in your output. If the essay declares a disability or an adjustment, you ignore it entirely for the purposes of the band and you flag it separately in one line at the end so the adjustment gets applied by a person. If you think the essay is plagiarised, you do not say so and you do not hint at it. You say the argument criterion is unclear and you write, in the flag line at the end, that the essay needs a human read, and you say nothing about why. An accusation from you is worse than useless because it cannot be evidenced and it goes into a record that follows the student around for three years. Your output is four criteria, each with a band and a one sentence evidence quotation, then the flag line if there is one. No preamble, no summary, no encouragement, and no marking out of a hundred anywhere in your answer. If the essay is empty or is not an essay, you say not markable and you stop. That is the whole prompt. I will read it back once more before I paste it, because the last version of this had a sentence telling it to be fair, which meant nothing to it and gave me three paragraphs about fairness on every essay.

input: Minutes for the trustees meeting, or my version of them anyway, and I am dictating this on the way home while I still remember who said what. Six of us were there, Gwen chaired, and Alun sent apologies again which is the third meeting in a row and somebody is going to have to have a conversation with him about that, and it will be me, because it always is. The first item was the lease on the hall and the lease is the whole meeting really, everything else was ten minutes. The landlord wants 1,400 a month from January, and we are paying 950 now, and the increase was announced in a letter that arrived in July and that nobody opened until September, which is a separate problem I am not going to write into the minutes but which I want recorded somewhere. So can we afford 1,400? No, not as we are. We can afford about 1,100 without touching the reserves and we can afford 1,400 for maybe five months if we do touch them, and touching the reserves for rent is the thing every trustee training course tells you not to do, so that is not a plan, that is a way of arriving at the same meeting in May with less money. Gwen's position, and she made it well, is that we go back to the landlord and offer 1,150 with a three year term, because a three year term is worth something to him and the empty hall down the road has been empty for eight months, so he knows what the alternative to us looks like. Bethan thinks we should go to 1,250 straight away because she thinks 1,150 gets refused and we lose two weeks, and she may well be right, but I would rather lose two weeks than start above the number we can actually pay. The second item was the toddler group and the toddler group is fine, it is full, there is a waiting list of nine, and Rhian has asked whether she can run a second session on Thursday mornings, and the honest answer is that we cannot say yes until the lease is settled, and I hated saying that because a waiting list of nine is the best problem this charity has had in four years. Who tells a full toddler group to wait? We do, apparently, until January. input: I am putting the whole question in one message because I have asked three people and had three different answers and I want to ask it properly. The situation is that my mother transferred the house to my brother and me in 2019, both names on the deed, equal shares, and she carried on living in it and she still lives in it, and she pays the council tax and the utilities and we have never paid her anything and she has never paid us anything. She is 81 now. So the first question is whether that transfer counts as a gift with reservation of benefit, because she is still living there, and if it does count as that, does the seven years even matter, because I keep being told the seven years is the thing that protects you and I also keep being told that the seven years does nothing if she never actually gave up the benefit of living in the house. Which of those is right, and does it change anything that we never charged her rent? Somebody told me we should have been charging her a market rent and that not charging it is the whole problem, and somebody else told me charging rent would have created an income tax problem for us instead, so I would like to know whether both of those can be true at once. Second question, and this is the one that actually worries me. My brother got divorced in 2022, and his half of the house was in his name during the divorce, and it was not raised in the settlement as far as I know, and I do not know whether that is because his solicitor decided it did not need to be or because nobody mentioned it. Is that a problem now, three years later, and is it my problem or only his? He says it is settled and finished and I do not want to keep asking him about it, but the house is half mine and if there is an argument coming I would like to know about it before it arrives. Third question, which is smaller. If she needs care, and at 81 she probably will at some point, does the local authority look at the 2019 transfer when they assess her, and is there a time limit on that or not? I have been told there is no time limit at all for deprivation of assets, which sounds like it cannot be right, and I have also been told it is six months, which sounds too good to be true, and those two answers are so far apart that one of them is just wrong. And the last thing is not really a question, it is more that I want to know whether I need a solicitor for this or whether it is straightforward enough that I am wasting money, because the reason I have three answers already is that I asked a friend, my accountant, and my brother's ex-wife's brother, and none of them do this for a living. My mother, for what it is worth, would rather nobody looked into any of it, which I understand, and which is also why nobody has looked into any of it for six years.

input: This is the prompt for the notes assistant that reads my clinic notes at the end of the day, and I am saying it out loud because I write badly when I type and I want to hear whether it makes sense. You are a summariser that reads a day's clinical notes and produces a handover list for the doctor on tomorrow. You are not a diagnostic tool, you do not suggest diagnoses, you do not suggest investigations, and you do not comment on management. If a note contains a diagnosis you carry it across as written. If a note contains a differential you carry that across as written too, and you do not rank it or add to it. For each patient you produce three lines. The first line is the identifier I used in the note and nothing more, no name, and if I wrote a name you replace it with the identifier and you do not include the name anywhere in your output. The second line is what was found and what was done, in my words wherever possible, and if you cannot say it in my words in one line then you say it in two and you do not compress it into something shorter and less accurate. The third line is the outstanding action and who holds it, and if the note does not say who holds it then you write the action and then unassigned, and unassigned is a useful answer because it is the thing that gets missed. Every drug name, every dose, every route, and every frequency is copied exactly as I dictated it, including the units, and if a dose looks wrong to you, you copy it exactly and you add a single line at the end of that patient saying check dose, and you do not say what you think the dose should be. I mean that specifically. A suggested dose from you in a handover list is the most dangerous thing this whole system could produce, because the next person reads a number in a clinical document and has no way of knowing that a model wrote it rather than a doctor. If a note is incomplete, and some of them will be because I dictate them between patients and I get interrupted, you carry across what is there and you write incomplete note at the end of the patient. You do not finish my sentence for me and you do not infer what I was about to say. An incomplete note that is visibly incomplete is safe. An incomplete note that somebody smoothed into a complete sentence is not, because it reads as though I said something I did not say. You never add a patient who is not in the notes, you never merge two patients who sound similar, and if two identifiers are close enough that you are not sure whether they are the same person, you output both and you write possible duplicate, and again you do not resolve it yourself. Your output is the patient list in the order I dictated it, not sorted by urgency, because I dictate them in the order I saw them and the doctor on tomorrow knows my clinic order. No summary at the top, no count of patients, no note about how many actions are outstanding, and nothing at the end telling me that this is not medical advice, because I know what it is and I wrote you. That is it. Read that back to me before I paste it in, because the version I wrote last week had a line asking for a priority order and I took it out for a reason and I want to be sure it is actually gone.

input: Right, this is the brief for the piece and I am talking it through because I write these better after I have said them. Take the interview transcript, the one with the Ferrand woman from the co-op, and pull out the section where she talks about the first winter, and build the whole piece around that section rather than around the funding story, because the funding story is what every other write-up of this has led with and it is the least interesting thing about it. Open on her describing the greenhouse in February with no heating in it. Do not open with the grant. Then give me the background in about two hundred words, and by background I mean how the co-op started and how many members it has, which is 34 now and was 6 at the start, and that is the only place in the piece where I want the membership numbers, because if I put them in twice it starts to read like a report. Keep the 34 and the 6 in the same sentence. Then the middle section is the disagreement, and this is the part I need you to be careful with. Two of the founding members left in 2023 and they left over the decision to sell through the supermarket, and one of them spoke to me and one of them did not, and the one who did not has not refused, she just has not replied, which is not the same thing. So write it as one member's account with the other side noted as unavailable, and do not characterise her silence as a refusal to comment, because that phrasing implies something and I do not know that the something is true. Then the section on what they actually grow, which can be short, and use her words for the varieties rather than the Latin, because she named four tomatoes in the interview and the way she named them is better than anything I would write. input: This is the note about how the release bot should behave, and I am dictating it because the version in the ticket is three lines long and everybody has interpreted it differently. So the bot posts the release notes, and it posts them once, when the tag is pushed, and it does not post again when somebody edits the tag message afterwards, because we had four notifications for one release last month and two of them were somebody fixing a typo. The format is that it lists the merged pull requests grouped by label, and the groups are the three labels we actually use, and if a pull request has no label it goes in a group at the bottom called unlabelled, and the unlabelled group is deliberately ugly because the point is to make people label their work. It does not guess the label from the branch name. We tried that and it guessed wrong about a fifth of the time, and a wrong group is worse than no group because nobody checks a confident answer. Inside each group it uses the pull request title exactly as written, and it does not rewrite the title, it does not capitalise it, it does not strip a prefix, and it does not shorten a long one. If somebody writes a bad title then the release notes have a bad title in them and that is the correct outcome, because the fix belongs in the title and not in the bot. The only thing it adds is the number and the author handle. Then it does not include anything at all about what the change means for users. No summary line, no impact assessment, and specifically no plain English restatement of a technical title, because the two times we shipped that behaviour it produced a sentence that was wrong in a way that took a support engineer forty minutes to unpick with a customer. If somebody wants a user facing note they write one in the description and mark it, and then the bot copies it across verbatim, and verbatim means verbatim, including the typo. On the ordering, newest merge last, not first, because the notes get read top to bottom by somebody trying to work out what changed since the last release they looked at, and the chronological order is the useful one even though the reverse order looks better. On the failure case, which is the part the ticket does not cover at all. If the bot cannot reach the API it retries twice and then it posts nothing and it opens an issue, and it does not post a partial list, because a partial release note is indistinguishable from a complete one and somebody will act on it. Nothing is worse than a list that looks finished and is not. And the last thing, it never tags a team and it never tags an individual, it posts into the channel and that is all, because the previous version tagged the release manager and the release manager is on a different continent and the release goes out at two in the morning her time.

input: I am writing this up as a question for the mailing list because I have been round it twice and I want somebody to tell me I am wrong. We have a service on 10.42.7.19 that talks to an internal API over mutual TLS, and the client certificate was rotated on the 3rd, and since the 3rd about one request in forty fails with a handshake failure and the rest are fine. One in forty. Not all of them, which is what I would expect from a bad certificate, and not none of them, which is what I would expect from a good one. The error on the client side is a bare handshake failure with no alert description, and on the server side there is nothing at all in the log for the failing requests, which I read as the connection dying before the server got far enough to log anything, but I am not confident about that reading. So why would a certificate rotation produce an intermittent failure rather than a total one? The obvious answer is that there are two instances behind the load balancer and only one of them picked up the new certificate, and I checked that, and there are two instances and both of them have the new certificate, and I checked the fingerprints by hand rather than trusting the deployment. The second answer is session resumption, that something is holding a session ticket from before the rotation, and one in forty is roughly what I would get if a small pool of long lived connections were doing that, and that is the answer I believe, but I do not know how to prove it without turning on a level of logging that I cannot turn on in that environment. Is there a way to confirm resumption is the cause from the client side only? And is one in forty actually consistent with that, or am I fitting a story to a number?

input: Notes from the pricing review, and I am going to be honest that half of this is me thinking out loud so treat the confident bits as confident and the rest as not. The headline is that the self serve tier is converting at 2.1 percent and it was 2.4 percent in the quarter before, and everybody in the room wanted to talk about the 0.3 and I do not think the 0.3 is real. It is 0.3 on a base that includes the December spike, and the December spike was the campaign, and the campaign is not running now, so comparing the two quarters straight across is comparing a quarter with a campaign in it to a quarter without one. The thing I actually want to know, and nobody in the room could tell me, is whether the customers who came in during the campaign are retaining at the same rate as the ones who came in normally, because if they are not then the 2.4 was never real either and the whole comparison is noise. Can somebody pull retention split by acquisition month for October through February? That is the one number I need before the next meeting. Then the second half of the review was the enterprise pipeline, which is fine, it is 14 opportunities and it was 11, and Rahul walked through the three that are late stage and all three are waiting on procurement rather than on us, which is the good kind of late. And then the thing that came up at the end which I want to write down before I forget it, which is that two different people described the middle tier as the one nobody chooses, and I have heard that from three people now, and three people saying the same sentence independently is usually worth more than a dashboard.

input: Design doc thoughts before I write the actual document, and this is the third time I have tried to write this section so bear with the tone. The question the reviewers are going to ask is why we are not just using the queue we already have, and I need to answer that in the first page rather than on page four where I put it last time. So why not use the existing queue? Because the existing queue is at least once and this path cannot tolerate at least once, and that is the whole answer, and everything else in the document is downstream of that one sentence. input: Hive notes for the two colonies at the allotment, Saturday the ninth, and I am saying this out loud because by the time I have washed the smoker out I will have forgotten which hive was which. Hive one first. Nine frames of brood, nine, which is more than I expected for the ninth of May, and the queen is laying in a tight pattern with almost no gaps, so she is fine and I did not need to find her. I did see her anyway, on the third frame from the left, marked white from last year. Varroa drop on the board was eleven mites over five days, which works out just under three a day, and that is under the threshold I use, so nothing goes on until after the flow. I put the second super on and an eke under the crown board because the fondant block from March is still sitting there half eaten and I cannot be bothered to scrape it off yet. Hive two is the problem. Hive two has been the problem since the swarm in April. There are two frames of brood, no eggs that I could see, and four charged queen cells on the face of the fourth frame, which either means they have superseded or they are about to go again and I genuinely cannot tell which. What do you do with four cells when the colony is already this weak? I have left all four for now, because knocking three down and picking the wrong one is worse than letting them sort it out themselves. Feeding one to one syrup from Tuesday, two litres a week, and I will look again on the twentieth.

input: Repair log for the A500, and I am dictating it because my hands are covered in flux and I want the order of things down before I forget it. The board is a Rev 6A, serial ends 4471, and it came in dead with no video at all, just the power light. First thing was the battery on the trapdoor RAM card, which had leaked exactly the way everybody says it does, and the corrosion had run about ten millimetres along the tracks under U11. I lifted the battery, neutralised with vinegar, washed the area down with isopropyl and put it under the lamp for an hour. Two tracks were open, one from U11 pin 12 across to the resistor pack and one going off to the CIA at U7, and I bridged both with kynar. After that it gave me a green screen, which means the CPU is alive and it is failing the Kickstart checksum, and the ROM sitting in there is a 1.3 and not what the label on the case claims. Kickstart 1.3, not 2.05. I swapped in a known good 1.3 off the parts board and it came up to the insert disk hand, so either the original ROM is the fault or the socket is, and I have not worked out which yet. Recapping is next. It wants the full set, and the two I care about are the 47 uF 16 V radials near the audio filter, because both of those measured high ESR on the meter, 4.2 ohms and 3.8 ohms against a spec of well under one. Write this up as a proper forum post later, with photos of the U11 area.

input: Observing log, night of the third into the fourth, back garden, and I am recording it now because I never write it up in the morning. Set up at half nine with the twelve inch Dob, collimated before I started and it was only a whisker out. Seeing was three out of five and it did not improve, transparency four, no moon until after two. First target was M57 at 120 times and it took the O-III filter well, the central hole obvious, no sign of the central star which at this aperture on a three I would not expect. Then NGC 6543 at 200 times, which is the best I have ever seen it from this garden, definitely the best, because the blue is unmistakable and there is real structure in it if you look slightly to one side rather than straight at it. Averted vision is the whole trick there. I went for the Veil after that and got nothing at all, which I think is the streetlight the council put in on the corner in April rather than anything to do with the sky. Two doubles to finish, Albireo split easily at 60 times and the colour contrast is as good as everybody says it is, and then Epsilon Lyrae which needed 200 times and a lot of patience. The focuser is slipping under the weight of the two inch diagonal and I will have to deal with that before winter. Three hours ten minutes in total, packed up at twenty to one because the dew was beating the heater.

input:
## INC-4408, checkout 5xx spike

**Impact:** 11 minutes, 2,140 failed checkouts, 03:41 to 03:52 UTC.

**Cause:** the connection pool in payments-api was sized 20 per pod and the pod count dropped to two during a node drain, so the pool could not cover the retry storm from the mobile client.

**What we are changing**

- Pool size moves to 60 and is read from config rather than baked in.
- The node drain gets a PodDisruptionBudget so it cannot take us below four.

The retry backoff on the mobile side is a separate ticket and is not part of this.
output:
## INC-4408, checkout 5xx spike

**Impact:** 11 minutes, 2,140 failed checkouts, 03:41 to 03:52 UTC.

**Cause:** the connection pool in payments-api was sized 20 per pod and the pod count dropped to two during a node drain, so the pool could not cover the retry storm from the mobile client.

**What we are changing**

- Pool size moves to 60 and is read from config rather than baked in.
- The node drain gets a PodDisruptionBudget so it cannot take us below four.

The retry backoff on the mobile side is a separate ticket and is not part of this.

input:
### Rotating a worker token

Run this on the worker and not the control plane:

```
sfctl token rotate --worker w-4412 --ttl 720h
```

The old token keeps working for 15 minutes after rotation, which is deliberate so that in-flight jobs finish. If you see `token not found` then the worker id is wrong, because a revoked token gives you `token revoked` instead.

Do not rotate more than one worker at a time. The scheduler treats a rotating worker as unhealthy, and two at once trips the minimum healthy count.

input: So this is for whoever picks up the backtest job after me new line the short version is it is not the model it is the data loader new line I spent most of Tuesday convinced the covariance step was the problem because that is where the profile pointed, 60 percent of wall time, but the profile is lying because the loader holds the GIL while it decompresses and the covariance thread just sits there waiting and gets billed for the wait new line what actually fixed it in the prototype was reading the parquet files once into a shared arrow buffer and letting every worker map it, which took the 40 minute run down to about 9 minutes on the same box with no change to any number that comes out the other end, and I checked the outputs match to the last decimal on the 2024 sample new paragraph the thing I did not finish is the memory ceiling, because mapping the whole buffer means we hold the full universe in memory and on the big runs that is somewhere near 40 gigabytes, which is fine on the analytics box and not fine on the shared one, so somebody needs to decide whether we cap the universe or ask for more memory before this goes anywhere near production.
output:
So this is for whoever picks up the backtest job after me.
The short version is it is not the model it is the data loader.
I spent most of Tuesday convinced the covariance step was the problem because that is where the profile pointed, 60 percent of wall time, but the profile is lying because the loader holds the GIL while it decompresses and the covariance thread just sits there waiting and gets billed for the wait.
What actually fixed it in the prototype was reading the parquet files once into a shared arrow buffer and letting every worker map it, which took the 40 minute run down to about 9 minutes on the same box with no change to any number that comes out the other end, and I checked the outputs match to the last decimal on the 2024 sample.

The thing I did not finish is the memory ceiling, because mapping the whole buffer means we hold the full universe in memory and on the big runs that is somewhere near 40 gigabytes, which is fine on the analytics box and not fine on the shared one, so somebody needs to decide whether we cap the universe or ask for more memory before this goes anywhere near production.

So the sequence is trigger first, then backfill oldest to newest in batches of about 50000, then the reconcile query, and only after the reconcile comes back with zero differences do you flip the read path.

The bit that always goes wrong is the reconcile query itself, it compares counts and sums per day and it will report a difference on the current day forever because rows keep arriving while it runs, so you have to exclude today or you will chase a phantom for an afternoon like I did.
